activities.name: [14] PRE-SOLO: Endorsement/Document Check
activities.what: What: The review process for checking that the student pilot's logbook and records are complete prior to solo flight.
activities.why: Why: To help ensure the pilot is prepared to legally act as pilot in command while soloing.
activities.groundPrep: NOTE: This is just a reminder to administer the pre-solo written test. Be sure to review and correct it to a 100 percent before authorizing solo flight.

checklistItems.name:
- Student Pilot Certificate

- Government Issued Photo ID

- Medical Certificate (if required) 14 CFR 61.23
checklistItems.teachingTips: Be sure to get started on helping the pilot through the process of getting their student pilot certifcate and medical early. You can help them with the Student Pilot certifcate in IACRA during one of your first training sessions. That way there won't be delays in getting it when they are ready for solo. Be sure to give helpful guidance on where to get a medical and on the process for any medical issues they may have. Be sure to check on any possible medical issues using the AOPA website, AOPA Pilot Information Center (1-800-USA-AOPA), or by doing a "practice" exam with an AME so they don't unintentionally get denied a medical certificate.

checklistItems.name: - Logged ground and flight training on applicable areas of 14 CFR 61.87
checklistItems.teachingTips: During the initial stages of training it can be easy to have the pilot's flying skills ready for solo before you provide and log all of the areas of required pre-solo ground training. Make sure to space it out and assign the pilot homework so you can be well prepared and not have to delay their solo. Use the aeronautical knowledge list and progress bar in the program to help you ensure the student will be ready on time.

checklistItems.name:
- Pre-solo aeronautical knowledge 14 CFR 61.87(b)

- Pre-solo flight training 14 CFR 61.87(c)(1) and (2)

- Solo flight (first 90 calendar-day period 14 CFR 61.87(n)
checklistItems.teachingTips: These three endorsements are the bare minimum requirements for certifying a student for their first solo. Be sure to check for any additional endorsements to cover any special operational requirements in your area. Take the time to explain the range of student pilot endorsements to the pilot so they can help you verify that everything is complete and remains current during their training.

checklistItems.name: - Solo flight (each additional 90 calendar-day period 14 CFR 61.87(p)
checklistItems.teachingTips: This likely the most common endorsement that gets missed unintentionally. Set up a system of reminders in your calender, scheduling software, etc. to help ensure that a student pilot doesn't overfly a 90 day solo endorsement. Explain the process to them so they can help you ensure currency.

checklistItems.name: - Endorsement of U.S. Citizenship recommended by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA): 49 CFR 1552.3(h)
checklistItems.teachingTips: While not required if the school is keeping copies of the pilot's records, it still is a good idea to add this one to the pilot's logbook to provide an extra layer of recordkeeping in the event that TSA inspects the pilot's logbook. Check out AOPA's Guide to TSA's Alien Flight Training/Citizenship Validation Rule in the Prep section.

checklistItems.name:
- Pre-solo flight training at night 14 CFR 61.87(o)

- Solo takeoffs and landings at another airport within 25 nm 14 CFR 61.93(b)(1)

- Solo flight in Class B airspace 14 CFR 61.95(a)

- Solo flight to, from, or at an airport located in Class B airspace 14 CFR 61.95(b) and 91.131(b)(1)
checklistItems.teachingTips: These endorsements are particular to the local training environment. Just take care to consider and provide any applicable endorsements to the pilot. Show the pilot the list of possible endorsements and make sure they understand their importance and limitations.

commonErrors.details:
New pilots are often not aware that there are required endorsements. 
Take the time to explain the purpose of each one and especially the time limits on the 90 day solo fight ensorsements so they can actively help prevent accidently overflying a solo endorsement.

New pilots are often not aware that there are required endorsements. 
Take the time to explain the purpose of each one and make sure they understand the limitations of their solo privileges.

Unintentionally overflying a 90 day solo endorsement.
This will usually stem from two causes. Not knowing about the endorsement time limit or just losing track of the time. Teach the pilot about the endorsement and it's time limit. Then set up a system of checks/reminders in calendars and/or scheduling software to help prevent them from flying on an expired endorsement.

Confusion about how to get a medical.
It's likely that the process of getting a medical and student pilot certificate will be completely new. Clearly explain their purpose and give clear guidance on how to go about acquiring them. Consider developing a handout with the documents and process to apply for the Student pilot certificate in IACRA, how to find your local AME, and how to apply for a medical (FAA's MedXPress).

Not realizing that they must carry their certificates, ID, and logbook during solo flight.
Explain the requirements to the pilot as they get close to solo and spot check them to be sure they have a made a habit of bringing them on every flight.

activities.name: [27] X/C: Private Pilot Qualifications
activities.what: The regulations that govern aircraft operations by a private pilot
activities.why: To ensure that a private pilot operates within the legal boundaries of their certificate and privileges
activities.groundPrep: NOTE: This list is similar to the Student Pilot Qualifications plan, but is intended to teach the pilot about the legal requirements and regulations for operations after they receive their private pilot certificate

checklistItems.name: Requirements for certification, recent flight experience, and recordkeeping
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Start with rote memorization by quizzing the pilot about all the certificate and aircraft recordkeeping necessary for him or her to remain current and the aircraft airwrothy. Then move to scenarios that involve real-life decisions, such as determing what can be defered, the difference between calendar months and days, and so on.
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: Privileges and limitations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Spend time in the regulations discussing private pilot limitations, a common area of misunderstanding. Move past rote learning with scenarios, such as charity flying, splitting of costs, common carriage, and weather and equipment limitations.

checklistItems.name: Medical certificates: class, expiration, privileges, temporary disqualifications
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Cover the concept of how higher class medicals can be used to meet lower class medical privileges, how to utilize BasicMed if desired, and the basics of special issuance.

checklistItems.name: Documents required to exercise private pilot privileges
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Discuss which documents must be on the pilot's person (certificate, identification, medical) and those that should be at home (logbook).

checklistItems.name: Part 68 BasicMed privileges and limitations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: BasicMed is a program that enables pilots to fly most general aviation aircraft without seeing an aviation medical examiner. Instead, the pilot can see his or her own physician every four years, and take an online medical course every two years. Pilots must get an FAA medical one time, after which they can let it expire and transition to BasicMed. Learn more at https://www.aopa.org/advocacy/pilots/medical/fit-to-fly-pilots

commonErrors.name: Misunderstanding BasicMed
commonErrors.details: Caution the pilot that BasicMed is not a no-medical solution. It is an alternative form of certification that keeps the relationship between a pilot and his or her doctor. The pilot must remain healthy to fly, and self-certify every flight.

commonErrors.name: Caution when talking to an AME
commonErrors.details: Caution the pilot about trusting an AME in an exam as a confidential source. Advise the pilot to be sure he or she is going to pass the medical exam before applying. You may want to recommend that they reference the AOPA Medical website or to consult the medical team at 1-800-USA-AOPA before visiting the AME. They can also schedule a "practice exam" with the AME if they are concenred about any medical issues.

commonErrors.name: Misunderstanding pilot privileges in terms of compensation
commonErrors.details: Many pilots don't understand the concept of incidential to the business, the requirements for charity flying, and even some basic weather limitations. Work with the pilot so that he or she knows where to find the answers to these questions, starting with the regulations, moving to letters of intrepreatation, and non-FAA resources, such as AOPA and others.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting key dates for currency
commonErrors.details: Pilots often forget basic inspection and recent experience dates. Work with the pilot on a system that verifies these limits, such as setting up an electronic logbook, calendar reminders, or a currency flow chart.

activities.name: [26] X/C: NTSB 830
activities.what: The Federal rules and regulations governing aircraft accident and incident reporting for operations within the U.S.
activities.why: To permit us to operate legally as pilots

checklistItems.name: National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) accident/incident reporting
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot mark Section 830 in his/her FAR/AIM so that it is easy to find, if need be. Stress that this is one section of the FARAIM that they may NEVER use, but just as lifeguards need to learn CPR and hope they never NEED to use it, all pilots need to know about the National Transportation Safety Board and its duties when there has been an incident or accident.
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: NTSB 830.2 Definitions
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
After reviewing these definitions, create scenarios that test the pilot's understanding of how to apply them. You might consider looking at news reports of aircraft incident and having the pilot determine if the NTSB should be called based on the details of the event.

- An accident is an occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft which takes place between the time any persons boards the aircraft WITH THE INTENTION OF FLIGHT and when all such passengers have disembarked.

- An accident is an occurrence in which any person suffers death or serious injury.

- Serious injury is defined as injuries requiring hospitalization for more than 48 hours within seven days of accident. 

- Serious injuries includes bone fractures, other than simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose, severe hemorrhaging, nerve muscle or tendon damage, any injury involving any internal organ, and 2nd or 3rd degree burns.

- An accident is one in which the aircraft receives substantial damage.

- Define substantial damage by defining what it is NOT: 
According to NTSB 830, Engine failure or damage limited to an engine if one engine falls or is damaged is NOT substantial damage.

- Bent fairings or cowling are NOT substantial damage.

- Dented aircraft skin or small puncture holes in the skin or fabric is NOT substantial damage.

- Ground damage to the rotor if we are flying a helicopter or propeller blades is NOT substantial damage.

- Damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories brakes or wingtips is NOT substantial damage.

- Substantial damage IS anything that could influence the strength, performance, or flight characteristics of an aircraft.

checklistItems.name: NTSB 830.5 Immediate notification
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Note that IMMEDIATE NOTIFICATION of the NTSB has to happen when there has been an aircraft accident.

- Stress that we need to immediately notify the NTSB when a required crew member is unable to perform normal flight duties because of an inflight injury or illness.

- We need to immediately notify the NTSB when there is an inflight Fire Flight Control system malfunction or failure -- stress that this goes back to the SAFETY part of NTSB. If enough reports are generated, the FAA gets involved and perhaps an AD will be issued to address the control system issue.

- We notify the NTSB immediately when an airplane is overdue and believed to have been in an accident. Use this notification to stress the need to use a FLIGHT PLAN and FLIGHT FOLLOWING and perhaps to text their CFI when the depart for the final leg of their XC flight. You need to know if they are overdue.

- We notify the NTSB immediately when there is an airplane collision in flight. Point out to the pilot that midair collisions are almost always catastrophic which is why we emphasize vigilance on looking for traffic and collision avoidance.

checklistItems.name: NTSB 830.6 Information to be given in notification
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Advise the pilot that the NTSB often sends a form to a pilot's involved in an accident AFTER the event. If you have the information below at your fingertips filling out the form will go much quicker.

Perhaps making a reference card listing the information to be given in notification to the NTSB. This information is also readily found on the NTSB website. The information must include:

(a) Type, nationality, and registration marks of the aircraft;
(b) Name of owner, and operator of the aircraft.
(c) Name of the pilot-in-command.
(d) Date and time of the accident.
(e) Last point of departure and point of intended landing of the aircraft;
(f) Position of the aircraft with reference to some easily defined geographical point;
(g) Number of persons aboard, number killed, and number seriously injured -- seriously injured is defined by the NTSB.
(h) Nature of the accident, the weather, and the extent of damage to the aircraft, so far as is known; and
(i) A description of any explosives, radioactive materials, or other dangerous articles carried. If you are flying a Cirrus Aircraft or another with a ballistic parachute, realize that the aircraft parachute is propelled by a rocket, which, if it has not fired is an deployed explosive device. Warn any rescuers or law enforcement who respond to the accident about the rocket.

checklistItems.name: NTSB 830.10 Preservation of aircraft wreckage, mail, cargo, and records
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Explain that the NTSB treats aircraft accidents like a crime scene. You do not move wreckage unless it is being done to rescue people or to preserve the wreckage from further damage (like moving a wrecked aircraft off the beach so it is not dragged out with the tide). Often the owners of the aircraft will send out a go-team to collect cargo. If there is mail onboard, the United States Post Office sends out a representative to pick up the mail. Understand that the removal of the aircaft from the accident site should be best handled by professionals to avoid further damage. ALWAYS document the accident/incident with video or photography and be prepared to turn those images over to the authorities IF asked. If able, take photos/video of the wreckage.

checklistItems.name: NTSB 830.15 Reports and statements to be filed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Remind the pilot that one of the responsibilities of the PIC is the safe operation of the aircraft. That means, should the aircraft be involved in an accident or incident, the operator of the aircraft should be ready to file a report with the NTSB.

If it is an incident for which immediate notification is required per 830.5(a) a report will be file ONLY AS REQUESTED. Note there is a 10 day window to file a report after an accident. A report should be filed within 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing.

The forms can be obtained online, Google NTSB accident form, from NTSB field offices, NTSB headquarters in Washington DC, and from the local Federal Aviation Flight Standards District Office. Advise the pilot that the crewmember statements should be obtained as soon as possible. Stress that the report should contain the facts of the accident or incident as it appeared to the crewmember. Find the address of the nearest NTSB field office, and supply it to the pilot.

commonErrors.name: Thinking that you do not need to file an accident/incident report because you are the owner of the aircraft or were along at the time of the accident/incident.
commonErrors.details: It does not matter who owns the airplane, and even if there aren't any witnesses, you must follow the notification protocol.

commonErrors.name: Assuming the FAA determines what constitutes an accident/incident, and therefore everything needs to be reported to the FAA in addition to the NTSB.
commonErrors.details: Explain that the FAA gets involved for the following reasons: an accident, if someone calls them to get salvage rights to recover the aircraft, or to put out a NOTAM to restrict airspace over the scene, such as closing a runway temporarily when an airplane has gone over on its back.

commonErrors.name: Assuming that every time an aircraft runs off the runway, does an unscheduled off-airport landing, collides with a pole, fence or other ground object qualifies as an accident.
commonErrors.details: Have the pilot LIST the criteria for accidents, THEN list the criteria for INCIDENTS.

commonErrors.name: Assuming the NTSB will punish the pilot after an accident or incident.
commonErrors.details: Clarify that it is the role of the NTSB to determine what caused the accident -- stress here that it is usually NEVER a single thing, but rather a chain of events that lead to accidents/incidents. It is the FAA that determines if sanctions should be taken against the pilot.

commonErrors.name: Thinking the NTSB will determine the cause of the accident in a few days.
commonErrors.details: Explain that it usually takes 18 months for the NTSB to issue a PROBABLE CAUSE in an accident.

commonErrors.name: Thinking a wing strike or ground collision is automatically an accident.
commonErrors.details: Unless you do more than $25,000 in damage to the other object, a ground collision is an incident. However, if you taxi off the taxiway because you are texting on your phone and not paying attention and collide with a $70,000 airplane and chop it to pieces with your propeller, it is an accident.

commonErrors.name: Failure to understand that the an accident, as defined by the NTSB, is treated like a crime scene where there may be witnesses.
commonErrors.details: Do not embellish or speculate on the cause of the accident, simply answer the questions.

commonErrors.name: Thinking the NTSB will send out someone to investigate the accident/incident right away.
commonErrors.details: Explain that the NTSB does not have a lot of people to deploy. They will send out a go-team for high profile accidents such as airliners, the crash of a warbird entity (The Collings Foundation B17), or a celebrity accident. Often the NTSB simply sends an information form to the pilot involved and it is up to the pilot to return the completed form. It is good practice to document the scene with video or photographs.

commonErrors.name: Being in a hurry to remove wreckage, and doing so in a manner that creates more damage.
commonErrors.details:
It seems every non-towered airport has a story about an accident where well intentioned neighbors used their pickup trucks to drag the aircraft off the runway by throwing a rope around the tail of the aircraft and pulling it, resulting in greater damage. 

Only move the wreckage unless it is to rescue persons, turn off the airplane, reduce the risk of fire damage, etc. Do not relocate the aircraft unless you have been given permission known as "release" by the NTSB. This may come in the form of a telephone call from the NTSB after you have reported the incident accident.

commonErrors.name: Assuming that every time an aircraft runs off the runway, does an unscheduled off-airport landing, collides with a pole, fence or other ground object qualifies as an accident and that the NTSB has to be called.
commonErrors.details: Have the pilot list the times the NTSB MUST be called. Stress that there are many situations when the NSTB must be called, but it is not just in the event of a crash.

commonErrors.name: Thinking you MUST immediately file a report with the NTSB.
commonErrors.details: Note that the 10 day protocol will allow the pilot to gather information, such as the names and contact information of the crewmembers, passengers, and/or witnesses.

commonErrors.name: Thinking that if you file a report with the NTSB your flying career is over.
commonErrors.details: It isn't, necessarily. It is the FAA that would order a re-examination flight or impose any sanctions or limitations. Often the best course of action is to find a qualified instructor to obtain remedial training. It can do wonders to restore your confidence and if you are sanctioned by the FAA, that fact that you immediate took action to address any skill or proficiency issues goes a long way to showing the FAA you take flying seriously and may lessen any punitive measures.

commonErrors.name: Assuming that law enforcement or rescue personnel will notify the NTSB.
commonErrors.details: It is the PIC's responsibility to notify the NTSB.

activities.name: [13] PRE-SOLO: Written Test
activities.what: The review process for assessing the a student pilot's aeronautical knowledge of the critical areas prior to solo flight.
activities.why: To help ensure the pilot is prepared to safely act as pilot in command while soloing.
activities.groundPrep: NOTE: This is just a reminder to administer the pre-solo written test. Be sure to review and correct it to a 100 percent before authorizing solo flight.

checklistItems.name: Create a pre-solo written test.
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
From 14 CFR 61.87

(b) Aeronautical knowledge. A student pilot must demonstrate satisfactory aeronautical knowledge on a knowledge test that meets the requirements of this paragraph:

(1) The test must address the student pilot's knowledge of—

(i) Applicable sections of parts 61 and 91 of this chapter;

(ii) Airspace rules and procedures for the airport where the solo flight will be performed; and

(iii) Flight characteristics and operational limitations for the make and model of aircraft to be flown.

(2) The student's authorized instructor must—

(i) Administer the test; and

(ii) At the conclusion of the test, review all incorrect answers with the student before authorizing that student to conduct a solo flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Give the student ample time to complete it - maybe even a week or two. That way they can be thorough with their answers and will have time to research anything they may not recall. Remember that this a learning experience and an opportunity to review aeronautical knowledge that can help them operate safely and legally during their upcoming solo flight.

checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use the Air Safety Institute Instructor's Guide to the Pre-Solo Written Test to help you build your test.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be sure to build a pre-solo written test that meets the required areas of 61.87 (b)(1), but more importantly make one that will assess the important knowledge areas the pilot will need to know for safe solo flight in your local area. Consider things like local airspace, systems or procedures specific to the training aircraft, emergency procedures, and any regulation areas where student pilots commonly have difficulty. Prepared premade solo tests are a good option to either use or to customize to your local area.

Be sure to review the pre-solo written test with the pilot. It's a great opporunity to idenitfy any misunderstandings and correct them.

commonErrors.details: New pilots may think it's a stressful situation that they have to complete totally from memory. Assure them that it is one where they can look up material as needed and that it is really a learning experience to be sure they understand the critical knowledge areas before flying solo.

activities.name: [25] X/C: Emergency Equipment and Survival Gear (IX.D)
activities.what: A procedure to familiarize and prepare for dealing with a forced landing or emergency in the conditions appropriate to operations
activities.why: To be prepared for the appropriate conditions that may be faced during emergency aircraft operations. For example: water for over wilderness areas, flotation device over water, clothing for cold weather or terrain, etc.

checklistItems.name: Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) operations, limitations, and testing requirements
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Use the need for an ELT as a chance to review the AVIATE inspection acronym and the location of the ELT and the activation mode. Some aircraft have a manual activation, others are activated from impact, but they don't always go off on impact and sometimes rough handling, like pushing an airplane on a ramp, can set off an ELT. Remember you cannot hear the ELT going off UNLESS you have the radio tuned to 121.5. The ELT can be test at the top of the hour and often ATC will ask us to monitor that frequency if there is a report of an ELT going off in the area .
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Fire extinguisher 
  - operations and limitations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The location of the fire extinguisher should be part of the safety briefing. However, some passengers will become anxious when you mention the word fire just as they become anxious when you talk about rapid egress from the aircraft after an unscheduled off airport landing (sounds so much better than crash). Instead, during the passenger safety briefing point to the fire extinguisher and tell the passenger "If we have to get out of the airplane in a hurry, like if there is a spider on board, wait for the airplane to come to a complete stop, take your headset off, take your seatbelt off, and get out of the airplane, heading back toward the tail. See that fire extinguisher there? I plan to use that against the hostile spider."  If flying with another pilot, tell the copilot he or she is responsible for the use of the fire extinguisher -- pull the pin, take a big breath then aim at the base of the flames.
If the aircraft does not have a fire extinguisher, remember a leather jacket can be used to beat out flames.

checklistItems.name:
Emergency equipment and survival gear needed for:
   - Climate extremes (hot/cold) 
   - Mountainous terrain
   - Overwater operations
   - Identify appropriate equipment and personal 
     gear
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Stress the need to file a flight plan and if able obtain flight following so that someone will always know where you are. 

Consider giving them a basic review of survival skills including the following ideas. 

Encourage the pilots to adopt the motto "dress to survive, not arrive" meaning always dress as though the aircraft could to an unscheduled off airport landing someplace. Assign homework of making or obtaining a small survival kit that can be carried in the pilot's gear bag. This small kit would be supplemental to any kit that is carried aboard the aircraft for example, when flying over the mountains. The personal survival kit should include a signal mirror or whistle, fire starting materials (can't go wrong with a zippo lighter) 10 feet of parachute cord, a first aid kit, a flashlight with extra batteries, a multipurpose tool, gallon sized ziploc bags, a mylar emergency blanket, a pencil and small notebook. Include a few energy bars in the personal kit. When overflying mountains add extra clothing to the kit, especially a cap to prevent the loss of body heat throiugh the head. Make sure wool clothing is onboard - "cotton kills" because it leaches body heat when wet, Wool still keeps you warm when wet. Over water make sure everyone onboard the aircraft has a life vest easily accessible and they are worn but NOT inflated in the aircraft. An inflatable life raft  should also be onboard. In extreme cold climates extra warm clothing and a wool blanket should be available. Extra food should be carried for the extreme climate flights (energy bars are easy to pack). Water should also be carried. Teach the pilot how to make a solar still. 

Stress that the pilot should stay with the airplane if able, since the ELT, if activated will help search crews find you. Remember that the crews are looking for the wreckage. If the airplane has gone down in the forest, however, the tree canopy may spring back over the crash site hiding it. If the survivors can find an open spot, stamp an arrow pointing to wreckage into the grass or build an arrow out of logs or rocks or even carve into the dirt. Encourage the pilot to ALWAYS carry a paper sectional because a paper sectional is much more useful than a tablet when the aircraft has experienced an unscheduled off airport landing. Parts of the aircraft can be salvaged for shelter -- oil from the engine can help make fire, the carpet seats and headliners can be used for warmth.

commonErrors.name: Confusing ELT inspection with battery replacement.
commonErrors.details: Do not confuse "when does the ELT have to be inspected" with "when do the batteries of the ELT need to be replaced?  Make sure the pilot can find the FAR 91.207 (e) and (f) and tab it in their FARAIM for the checkride .

commonErrors.name: Confusion type of fire extinguisher allowed.
commonErrors.details: Most fire extinguishers are secured in aircraft by external means, such as a bracket. Make sure the copilot knows how to release the extinguisher from the bracket. Identify the type of extinguisher is correct for the aircraft --- you don't just grab one off the shelf at Walmart and hope for the best.

commonErrors.name: Failing to be prepared for an off airport landing.
commonErrors.details:
So many pilots do not plan for unscheduled off-airport landings because of invulneralbilty, or they think they will simply "call for help" on their cellphone. Encourage the pilot to carry at least one paper sectional at all times, because the paper sectional can be turned into shade, a hat to protect from sun, a shelter, as toilet paper, and even made into little oragami boats with notes written on them and sent down stream where they are found by campers, letting the authorities know where you are. (The writer found mushroom hunters lost on Mt Rainier when they spotted a Safeway bag floating down stream. They flew up stream and found them on a rock waving.)
Stress that the best defense to getting found is a flight plan, using flight following, and staying with the aircraft. The Civil Air Patrol and other search and rescue units will be looking for the airplane since individual people are much harder to see.

Include after the landing triage: 
1. determine extent of injuries, treat them. When you are PIC it is imperative that you treat your own injuries first so that you can care for others . 

2. Determine resources: taking everything out of your pockets and gear bag and the airplane to determine what you have, and how it can be put to use.

3. Care for injuries, shelter, water and food in that order for physical needs.

4. Be prepared to be uncomfortable for while. Survival is 90% mental .

activities.name: [01] PRE-SOLO: Introduction to the Flight Training Process
activities.what: An overview of the process of learning to be a pilot
activities.why: To better navigate the steps and take advantage of the varied opportunities in aviation

checklistItems.name:
Opportunities and Adventure in Aviation
- Types of Aircraft and Flying
- Types of Pilot Certificates (Overview - Not regulatory specifics)
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Be sure to start the process by finding out the pilot's goals and why they want to learn to fly. Share with them a combination of your own good experiences and ideas on how flying will help them realize their goals. Let them know that as they enter a new community with it's own language that it is okay to ask questions. Assure them that they will someday be the one sharing their knowledge with a new pilot in training.

Give them a brief overview of the various types of aircraft and certificates/ratings, but focus specifically on the rating and individual goals that they have described to you. Remember to avoid getting too technical - their knowledge will grow as they progress in their training.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Process of Becoming a Pilot
- Flight and Ground Training
- Airman Certification Standards (ACS)
- Typical Milestones (Solo, Cross-Country, Checkride) - at each stage there will be written documentation (endorsements, pre-solo written, stage checks, etc.) to make sure you're well prepared
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Help the pilot understand the overall structure of the training process and its stages, but avoid getting too detailed to help prevent overloading or overwhelming the pilot with breadth of flight training. Be sure to explain the Airman Certification Standards (ACS) or Practical Test Standards (PTS) as the literal defining document for their eventual checkride. Assure them that you will guide them through the process and will make sure they are prepared for the checkride. Make sure that you refer the pilot back to the ACS/PTS throughout their training so they can become familiar with the checkride requirements.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Knowledge and Skill Tests
- FAA Knowledge Exam ("Written Test")
- FAA Practical Test ("Checkride")
checklistItems.notesToPilot: It can be useful to relate this part of the process to a typical driver's license test - a multiple choice test and the actual driving test with an examiner. Assure the pilot that their training will have them well prepared for the test. Be sure to recommend test prep materials/resources that fit their learning preferences.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Documents
- FAA Student Pilot Certificate
- FAA Medical Certificate (if required)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Consider having the pilot provide their identification materials so you complete the required TSA citizenship check and to request their student pilot certificate from IACRA. If required, explain the process for getting a medical certificate. Consider providing the name(s), address(es), and contact information for the local aviation medical examiner(s) (AME). Be sure to provide guidance on which level of medical certificate they might require and how to access MedXpress. You can also direct them to AOPA's website or medical team (1-800-USA-AOPA) for any questions they may have.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be sure to clarify which class of medical certificate that they will need to exercise their desired level of pilot certificate (e.g., someone who is planning to fly only recreationally does not need a first class medical). 

Another common misconception is that if a pilot switches to BasicMed following their initial medical certificate they they will not be able to get a standard medical certificate again. If they desired to get a standard medical certificate again, all they would need to do is complete a standard medical exam just like they would have if their medical had expired.

checklistItems.name:
Materials
- FAA Handbooks
- FAR/AIM
- FAA Advisory Circulars (AC)
- AOPA Resources
- Other
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Introduce the pilot to the learning materials that they will use throughout their flight training including the various resources provided by the FAA and AOPA. Be sure they understand the process of training and how home study will be assigned. Explain the use of the syllabus/training system so they will be know how to most effectively prepare at home.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Selecting a Flight School and a Flight Instructor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: You may want to recommend that they read AOPA's article on how to select a good flight school in the resource section. A good practice is to have the pilot fly with a few instructors to ensure they find the best for their learning style. Also assure them that it is okay to switch instructors if they find that the current instructor is not a good fit at some point in the future. Remember that they are the customer and are making a big commitment in funding and completing their flight training.

Sit down early in the process to cover the syllabus, which should satisfy the requirements for Part 61 or 141.

checklistItems.name: Medical certificates: class, expiration, privileges, temporary disqualifications
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Explain the different medical standards, expiration dates, and the ability to revert a high class to a lower class. Discuss BasicMed and how the pilot may use it in the future. 

Be sure to explain to any new pilots that are going for their medical that they should consult a reliable resource before going to the AME for the official exam. Unfortunately it is quite common for people to go the AME without realizing that they have a medical condition that may cause trouble in the certification process. Recommend that they check into it first before going to the AME for their official exam. Consider recommending that they consult AOPA's medical portion of the website, give the medical team a call at 1-800-USA-AOPA, or request a "practice exam" from the AME to find out whether they have any disqualifying or difficult issues. This way they can go to the actual exam with the appropriate medical paperwork prepared or will at least have the option of taking a different route towards flying (e.g., sport pilot using their driver's license as a medical).

checklistItems.name: Documents required to exercise student pilot privileges
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Spell out the need for the student to carry his/her certificate, driver's license, and necessary endorsements.

commonErrors.name: Confusion when applying regulations to complex scenarios
commonErrors.details: While the basics are easy to remember, more complex scenarios, such as using one rating to keep all privileges current, is challenging. Once the student understands the basics use scenarios to discuss more complex issues.

commonErrors.name: Underemphasis or misunderstanding document expiration dates
commonErrors.details: The most common privileges and limitations new pilots have challenges have with is expiration dates of solo authorizations, weather limitations, and so on. Go over the physical documents with the pilot and point out expiration dates. Have the pilot note the expiration date in his or her date book, and explain the consequences for breaking these limitations. Although rare, some solo students have also been known to take passengers, and even pets, on solo flights. Explain the reasons this isn't allowed.

activities.name: [07] PRE-SOLO: Operations of Systems: Flight Controls and Powerplant (I.G: K1a-c, K2)
activities.what: The subject matter concerning the mechanical operation of the aircraft's flight controls, engine, and propeller
activities.why: To enhance understanding and therefore safety in operating the aircraft

checklistItems.name:
Primary Flight Controls
-Major control systems, including potential aerodynamic impacts of using each control
-Elevator, rudder, ailerons
-Adverse yaw, pitch stability
-Unusual configurations
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The confusion around flight control function must be nipped early in training, and is most effectively done at the airplane. After a briefing with a model of the various flight control functions take the pilot to the parked airplane and demonstrate control functions from inside and outside the aircraft, showing how each moves in relation to the yoke/stick and rudder pedals. 

New pilots often confuse aileron movement. With a basic aerodynamic understanding you should be able to demonstrate at the parked airplane how increasing the camber on one wing increases lift while reducing it on the other decreases lift. To coordinate aileron movement with the proper yoke movement, demonstrate how when grabbing the yoke a thumb pointed up points to the up aileron. 

Explain that the rudder is only used for coordination, not for starting a turn. Point out the difference between the rudder and the vertical stabilizer. 

Show the relationship between the elevator and lift in a downward vector, and how the elevator works in concert with the center of gravity. Cover the differences in control handling between a T-tail and conventional tail, especially in light aircraft. Describe how control is less effective at low takeoff and landing speeds from the lack of propeller airflow. A basic aerodynamic discussion should make the pilot easily aware that because a stabilator moves the entire horizontal tail surface, less control pressure if required to make a pitch change. That's why it's used for high-speed aircraft. For smaller and slower GA aircraft it's a way to better harmonize controls.

With confusing concepts, such as adverse yaw, use a model. By understanding that more lift brings more drag, it is easy to see how the nose is pulled back in a turn.

checklistItems.name:
Secondary Flight Controls, their function and abnormalities
-Lift augmentation, such as flaps and leading edge devices
-Trim, including in-flight and ground adjustable, and inoperative trim
-Lift canceling devices, such as spoilers
-Autopilot usage
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Not every aircraft has secondary flight controls. But for those that do, it should be clear to the pilot the difference between primary and secondary, and the practical implications of that. This helps to keep someone from controlling with trim, relying on flaps, and so on. 

It's important in a discussion of flaps to describe that flaps both increase lift and drag. By doing exercises at incremental flap settings a pilot can better see that some settings add more lift than drag, while others add more drag than lift. Discussing their use on takeoff and landing, and why the handbook recommends certain settings, can help deepen the understanding. 

Pilots don't have to know all leading-edge devices, but using them in a quiz will help evaluate their aerodynamic knowledge. Discuss why some aircraft have spoilers and others don't. Explain the alternatives to spoilers, and what to do if they fail. 

Discussing on the ground the way in which trim tabs move helps pilots gain a deeper understanding of aerodynamics. In addition to spending time at the airplane covering how and why airplanes have trim tabs, spend time discussing the role of trim in hands-off flight, and its use solely as a secondary control. That can lead to flight demonstrations of trimming for an airspeed, leveling off by using trim only after setting pitch and power, and the use of trim in the pattern. Simply point these out, discuss their basic function, and discuss what must happen if they are missing, or seem overly deflected. 

Autopilot use is an advanced skill and should only be introduced after the pilot can fly without automation. Teach autopilot in the context of levels of automation. So in addition to what various modes do and what drives the autopilot, discuss the philosophy of when to use autopilot--or not--and why.

checklistItems.name:
Powerplant operation and abnormalities, including
-Reciprocating engines, induction systems, carburetor systems, and mixture control
-Carburetor icing, carburetor air temperature gauge
-Combustion, detonation, preignition
-Ignition, starting, and exhaust system operation and failures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Find an airplane undergoing an annual, or spend some time with the cowling off the airplane describing the various powerplant systems. Nothing works better than hands-on exposure, especially if a mechanic is present to answer questions and give the pilot tips. 

Don't forget to teach proper leaning, which often happens in the cross-country phase. Discuss lean of peak and when it's ok to run in that condition. 

With modern fuel-injected engines it can be easy to forget to introduce carburetor icing. If your school has an airplane with a carburetor, take the pilot to the airplane and discuss it's operation. Show the pilot the carburetor icing chart to help explain how carb ice can happen in a broad range of temperatures. Just because it's summer doesn't mean the pilot shouldn't use carb heat. Describe various failure points of fuel injection, including the difficulty of hot starts. Practice hot starts when possible.

checklistItems.name:
Indications of and procedures for managing system abnormalities or failures
-Complete or partial power failure
-Engine roughness or overheating
-Loss oil pressure
-Smoke or fire
-Fuel starvation/exhaustion
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Spend time in the aircraft specific manual detailing how to respond to various failures. Give scenarios that will help the pilot think through unusual or abnormal problems. Many instructors give the manual only minor attention in training, or assign it as a study item. Go over various emergencies and systems issues, and make sure the pilot has committed to memory those items that are required in quick-thinking situations. Then drill those emergencies in the simulator. Also give the pilot a chance to think creatively to unusual problems, and discuss these issues afterward to help him or her learn from the decisions. Prepare a range of scenarios in your lesson plans and tweak them to the particular student. 

Many avoidable problems, such as fuel exhaustion, happen because pilots don't have a personal system in place to prevent it. Work with the pilot to develop a system, such as never taking off with less than an hour of reserve, or diverting when there's 90 minutes of fuel left, or switching tanks every 30 minutes. This applies to most systems, including items such as regular panel scans to quickly identify problems.

checklistItems.name: Propeller operation and failures for fixed-pitch and adjustable systems
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If possible, spend time in the shop with a technician and the pilot discussing propeller care and repair. Most pilots know to check for nicks in the propeller, but don't know what is a safe and allowable limitation. Every propeller has a standard, so work to find it with the pilot. Also discuss propeller safety and hand propping safety.

Once new pilots understand the basics of how a constant-speed propeller works, use the aircraft handbook as a guide for how best to operate it. Although there is lots of discussion about pulling throttle before rpm, and thus avoiding over-square, much of that advice has been updated. Each aircraft handbook should have some guidance on when and how to change power, and engine manufacturers will supplement that as well. Also explain that power changes are the most common times for power failures, so careful consideration should be made to emergency landing options.

commonErrors.details:
Confusion about aileron operation.
It's easy to be confused over aileron movement when turning the yoke. Demonstrate how when holding the yoke a thumbs up points to the up aileron on a full deflection. 

Misunderstanding basic turns.
Many pilots don't understand the basics of turns. Ask the pilot to explain how an aircraft turns, and pay careful attention to his or her understanding of the relationship between ailerons, elevator, and rudder. Remind the pilot that rudder is used only for coordination.

Failure to establish fuel minimums.
Fuel exhaustion continues to be a major accident cause in general aviation, and it's one of the most avoidable. Work with the pilot to develop personal fuel limitations.

Unfamiliar with flap operating limitations.
All aircraft have flap limiting speeds. Pilots sometimes forget these numbers or how to identify them. For models with flaps setting limitations or cautions, such as some Cessna 172s while slipping, discuss why the limitations or recommendations exist, rather than simply pointing them out. 

Misunderstanding the use of trim.
Most pilots want to use trim too early as a primary control. Reinforce its use as a secondary control by showing on the ground that it is secondary to the elevator, ailerons, and rudder. 

Improper use of autopilot.
Pilots often misunderstand the proper use of autopilot and its modes. Use scenarios to discuss proper use of modes, and how and when to select the proper level of automation.

Failure to recognize trim malfunction and how to correct it.
There have been many accidents involving a failure to recognize trim malfunction and improper response upon recognition. Quiz the pilot on how to handle trim malfunctions. During a flight, at a safe altitude, try to get the airplane well out of trim to simulate a runaway trim scenario.

activities.name: [19] X/C: Weather Theory (I.C: K3)
activities.what: The subject matter of how and why weather conditions occur and develop
activities.why: To increase the safety of flight by being able to make informed decisions regarding flight in various weather conditions

checklistItems.name: Atmosphere
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: Composition of the Atmosphere
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Make pilots aware that our atmosphere is made up of 78% Nitrogen and 21% Oxygen. All the remaining gases (argon, hydrogen, helium, ozone, nitrous oxide, water vapor, etc) make up the remaining 1%.

Instructors can create their own “atmosphere” by using three clear plastic or glass jars. Fill one around 78% full, and add a small amount of cyan printer ink to give it color. Fill a second around 21% full and add magenta printer ink. Combine these two elements in the third jar to creates a model of earth’s atmosphere, which will turn blue—just for fun. A drop of black ink can make up the trace gasses. (This exercise may be more appropriate for guest-speaker duty at local schools than in day-to-day flight instruction.)

checklistItems.name: Atmospheric Circulation
checklistItems.teachingTips: A high pressure system can be visualized as a volcano. It is the meteorological equivalent of a hill or mountain-like shape with wind bubbling out the top and sliding down the sides. A low pressure system acts like a bathroom drain, drawing air in from an adjacent high pressure system. Wind rolls down the sides of highs and rushes down into lows.

checklistItems.name: Atmospheric Pressure
checklistItems.teachingTips: The fact air has weight is counter-intuitive, even though we’ve all been taught this in every science class we’ve ever taken. Still seeing is believing so: Take two identically-sized balloons, tie them to a wood dowel, and hang the dowel from a wire so it balances with the dowel perpendicular to the horizon. Now, blow one balloon up. The balance bar will tilt downward on the side where the balloon is filled with air. This is because: (1) the inflated balloon has a greater density than the uninflated balloon, as you’ve forced air into it; which proves the point (2) air has weight!

checklistItems.name: Measurement of Atmosphere Pressure
checklistItems.teachingTips: Once pilots can better visualize air having weight, the PHAK’s (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge) illustration of levitating scales (Figure 12-4) makes more sense.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
In the United States we refer to atmospheric pressure as being so many inches of mercury. When written it reads, "X in Hg," where "X" is a measurement. Standard Pressure is 29.92 in Hg. The abbreviation "Hg" is the scientific symbol for the element used to measure atmospheric pressure in a barometer, mercury. 

You can use an aneroid cell from a non-serviceable altimeter to show how air pressure is measured and indicated in the airplane (along with pointing out that having glass columns of mercury in our planes would be problematic, at best).

checklistItems.name: Altitude and Atmospheric Pressure
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Once pilots accept that air has weight, it is fairly easy to recognize that the lower air pressure found at altitude means the air molecules are less densely packed than they are at sea level. 

The atmosphere at 27,000 feet MSL still contains 21% oxygen, but that oxygen is at such a low pressure, with molecules so widely spaced, the supply is insufficient to support human consciousness for long periods of time. 

That less dense air found at altitude also affects the operation of the engine, propeller, and airfoils - all of which depend on air density and pressure to perform properly.

checklistItems.name: Altitude and Flight
checklistItems.teachingTips: Design a scenario that involves landing your aircraft on a warm day with three passengers, ¾ fuel, and 50 lbs of baggage at a somewhat short, high altitude airport. As an example you can use the mythical 2,500-foot long KWHO, located in Whoville, near the mountain home of the Grinch (elevation 7000' MSL). Using performance tables from your aircraft's POH, the effect of altitude and density altitude on aircraft performance can be brought to life.

checklistItems.name: Altitude and the Human Body
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Instructors can adapt portions of aeromedical lesson plans to include regulatory oxygen requirements as well as weather and altitude issues. These discussions can reinforce the importance both of topics simultaneously.

Explain that the atmosphere at all levels contains approximately 21% oxygen. But at altitude that oxygen can be at such a low pressure, with molecules so widely spaced, the supply is insufficient to support clear decision-making, desirable pilot performance, or even human consciousness for long periods of time.

checklistItems.name: Wind and Currents
checklistItems.teachingTips: The atmosphere can be considered a fluid, albeit a low density one, The atmosphere moves from high pressure systems to low pressure systems. This phenomenon is what we call, "wind." That being the case, the movement of the atmosphere obeys the laws of fluid dynamics. An instructor can demonstrate the motion of the atmosphere by relating the wind to the motions of other, more readily visualized fluids, such as streams, rivers, oceans, and even water captured in a bottle.

checklistItems.name: Coriolis Force
checklistItems.teachingTips: See links in resources.

checklistItems.name: Wind Patterns
checklistItems.teachingTips: There are a number of apps that show current wind patterns in live motion. These can help pilots get the big picture of how wind moves over large geographical areas, and help them to visualize, in real time, the patterns of wind around highs and lows and the flow between them. One example is windy.com

checklistItems.name: Convective Currents
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Using a hot plate, gas grill, or other heating surface, the vertical movement of small columns of heated air can be demonstrated by holding a long strip of tissue paper over the heat source and showing how it rises.

Steam or smoke from industrial sites can demonstrate this concept well, too. As the heated gas rises, it moves with the wind, widening as it rises higher and cools to the point that it dissipates from view entirely.

checklistItems.name: Effect of Obstructions on Wind
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Wind can be visualized as running water. It “pours” over landforms, “runs” around buildings and barriers, and “splashes” up when it hits blunt objects. 

Rivers and streams can be used as prime examples of this concept. The water cannot penetrate rocks, sandbars, docks, or other obstacles in its path, so it must change course to flow around or over them. The wind does the same thing as it encounters buildings, mountains, and dense trees. The wind flows as the water might, around and over obstructions in its path.

checklistItems.name: Low-Level Wind Shear
checklistItems.teachingTips: Using a large fan turned on high, gently “pilot” a paper airplane into the air flow with a gentle toss (note: the wider-winged glider-style is better for this demonstration than the prototypical dart-style. The Nakamura Lock is a good model: https://www.origamiway.com/plane-nakamura-lock.shtml). As the airplane flies into the rapid change in airflow, you will see it's flight become disturbed quickly.

checklistItems.name: Wind and Pressure Representation on Surface Weather Maps
checklistItems.teachingTips: These types of maps can be compared to topographic maps (or sectional charts). High pressure areas are higher “terrain,” like hills and mountains. And in fact, in the invisible atmosphere, highs are, well, truly higher. Meanwhile, lows are the valleys and low lands. Just like with maps, tightly spaced lines show “steep terrain,” while widely spaced lines show mild changes. If the map were made 3-D and water were poured on it, the flow of the water would duplicate the flow of wind between the highs and lows. On steeper terrain, the water will flow faster, and in the same way, wind is stronger in areas depicted with more tightly space lines. The little wind icons on maps are arrows, with the round point being the arrow head, and the wind barbs being feathers. These arrows fly through the air with the wind.

checklistItems.name: Atmospheric Stability
checklistItems.teachingTips: A stable atmosphere can be compared to calm water in a pond, while unstable air can be compared to the surf on the beach.

checklistItems.name: Inversion
checklistItems.teachingTips: Why do you stir your drink after adding ice? To spread the cold throughout the drink, as the cold fluid tends to hug the ice cubes. In the same way, in a temperature inversion, cold ground can super-cool the air near it, resulting in warm air higher in the atmosphere, and colder air near the surface.

checklistItems.name: Moisture and Temperature
checklistItems.teachingTips: The evening weatherman often stays it will be "dry-and-cold" or "hot-and-muggy" in his forecast. Bearing in mind that "muggy" is another way of saying humid, these are actually accurate memory aids for the moisture-carrying capacity of air. Cold air can't hold as much moisture, while warmer air can hold increasingly more.

checklistItems.name: Relative Humidity
checklistItems.teachingTips: Relative Humidity is sometimes assumed to be a constant by pilots, despite the name relative. Instructors should ensure pilots understand that relative humidity is a percentage of the maximum moisture that the air could hold at a given temp. So, 65% relative humidly at 85-degrees F is a heck of a lot wetter than 65% at 65-degrees F!

checklistItems.name: Temperature/Dew Point Relationship
checklistItems.teachingTips: This can be imagined to be similar to a balloon popping: Just like when air pressure exceeds the strength of the wall, and the balloon pops; the atmosphere cannot hold water beyond a certain combination of humidity and temperature and the water vapor “pops” into clouds (or fog, or dew, or frost, or rain, or snow).

checklistItems.name: Methods by Which Air Reaches the Saturation Point
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Dew and Frost
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots might assume that a light layer of frost is too thin to affect aerodynamics and too light to affect weight, but they do not realize that the danger of frost is increased drag. Instructors can ask pilots if they’d want to fly a plane with sandpaper for wing covering; or to envision frost as a wing-long speed brake.

checklistItems.name: Fog
checklistItems.teachingTips: There are a lot types of fog in the Aviation Weather book from the FAA. One way to help new pilots differentiate between them is to make sure they understand the conditions that causes each type of fog to form. What is causing the cooling that brings the moisture out of the air? If possible, use some silly analogies to help them remember (e.g., coastal advection fog is the kind you often see in Scooby Doo cartoons often accompanied by a fog horn. So maybe calling it Scooby Doo fog and saying "advection" like the sound of fog horn could help them remember this one.)

checklistItems.name: Clouds, Ceiling, Visibility
checklistItems.teachingTips: Clouds are like snowballs: Water vapor forms around a “nuclei” and build up layers, much like rolling a snowball across the ground to make it larger to build a snowman.

checklistItems.name: Precipitation
checklistItems.teachingTips: When teaching about any form of precipitation instructors can tell pilots that anything that is heavy falls from the sky, and the same is true of H2O in all its various guises. When water vapor tranforms into liquid water, hail, or snow--once the mass is great enough to overcome updrafts in the clouds, it will fall to earth.

checklistItems.name: Air Masses
checklistItems.teachingTips: Air masses can be compared to countries on a map: Masses originate from the same “countries” and have “cultures” to match. For instance, a polar air mass forms over a polar region and, as you might expect, has a cold, dry "culture." The tropics evoke warm damp beaches, and likewise thier air masses match.

checklistItems.name: Fronts
checklistItems.teachingTips: For better visualization, look for “3-D” renderings of fronts online. See the resource section for some videos that can help pilots better visualize fronts.

checklistItems.name: Warm Front
checklistItems.teachingTips: Warm fronts are like a hat with a bill. The hat may be on your head, but the bill extends far in front of your face. In the same way, the high altitude leading edge of a warm front extends far forward of its surface position or location on a weather map. Likewise, the curved symbol for a warm front, resembles a ball cap’s bill. Another memory aid is to make the connection between a warm front what looks like beads of sweat on the front symbology.

checklistItems.name: Flight Toward an Approaching Warm Front
checklistItems.teachingTips: After educating pilots on the weather associated with the movement of a warm front, instructors can ask pilots to describe the weather they’d expect to encounter flying towards a warm front.

checklistItems.name: Cold Front
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can help pilots remember the symbol for cold fronts by pointing out that the triangle-like symbol resembles an ice cycle. Or a knife, as cold fronts bring more violent weather.

checklistItems.name: Fast-Moving Cold Front
checklistItems.teachingTips: Fast-moving cold fronts are like automobile wrecks: The sky crumples up when they hit other air mases (squall line).

checklistItems.name: Flight Toward an Approaching Cold Front
checklistItems.teachingTips: After educating pilots on the weather associated with the movement of a cold front, instructors can ask pilots to describe the weather they’d expect to encounter flying towards a cold front.

checklistItems.name: Comparison of Cold and Warm Fronts
checklistItems.teachingTips: The divergent speeds of fronts can be remembered with the memory cue that when it’s cold you move quickly to get back in doors, and when it’s warm you can take your time.

checklistItems.name: Wind Shifts
checklistItems.teachingTips: Wind patterns around storm fonts can be directly visualized in real time with weather apps such as “Windy.” (www.windy.com)

checklistItems.name: Stationary Front
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can tell pilots that a stationary front on the map means they could be stuck at the station waiting for a bus or a train; as this type of front can park over an area for days along with it's associated weather.

checklistItems.name: Occluded Front
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can compare an occluded front to a tail-gating traffic accident. The faster moving cold front overtakes a warm front and smashes into it, sending the warm front flying into the air. As the pieces of both vehicles (fronts) rain down on the accident scene, the parts mix. Likewise, with an occluded front, pilots can expect weather phenomena associated with both warm and cold fronts.

checklistItems.name: Thunderstorms
checklistItems.teachingTips: T-storms are like an explosion of weather energy, fascinating to watch, but filled with an array of hazards.

checklistItems.name: Hazards
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can ask pilots to make a list of T-storm hazards. In most cases, as there are such a diverse range of hazards—and so many of them. The list of hazards will help demonstrate to the pilot just how many things can “go wrong” in the vicinity of T-storms.

checklistItems.name: Squall Line
checklistItems.teachingTips: Give pilots the visual that a squall line is like a ten-foot tall electric fence: No realistic way over or under, and you'll get zapped if you try to go through.

checklistItems.name: Tornadoes
checklistItems.teachingTips: Be sure the pilot can identify the weather (both in forecasts and in real time) associated with tornado generation to help them remain well clear of the hazard.

checklistItems.name: Turbulence
checklistItems.teachingTips: To helps pilots visualize what happens with turbulence, consider comparing it to 4-wheeling over rough terrain or watching a pot of water boil before pasta is added. Lots of instabilty causing the air to roil and bubble.

checklistItems.name: Microbursts
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can use a flat-bottomed sink to create a model of a microburst. Turning the faucet at high volume abruptly will cause the stream of water to splash out in all directions as it strikes the surface of the sink, mimicking the basic structure of a microburst.

checklistItems.name: Icing
checklistItems.teachingTips: The effect of rime ice can be demonstrated with a smart phone wind tunnel app (such as Wind Tunnel Free), which dramatically shows the change of airflow around a “roughed up” airfoil. To demonstrate the effect of clear ice on an airplane create a large, thin ice sheet on a cookie sheet and demonstrate the weight of the ice on a kitchen scale. Ask the pilot to do some quick math to extrapolate the size of the cookie sheet to the size of the training plane’s wings, and thus estimate the weight increase from a layer of clear ice.

checklistItems.name: Hail
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can tell pilots that flying through hail is like taking a hammer to their airplanes. Well, dozens of hammers. Pilots should be reminded about clear-air hail is possible a number of miles away from the storm as T-storms can launch hail out for a considerable distance—like lava from an erupting volcano.

checklistItems.name: Ceiling and Visibility
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can compare cloud ceilings to the ceiling of a room—the bottom layer of clouds above you is just like the ceiling above your head in the classroom. Visibility can be broken into its root word, “to be visible.” Visibility is how far away we can see things.

checklistItems.name: Lightning
checklistItems.teachingTips: An unexpected risk from lightning is temporary blindness from the bright flash. While there’s no work around for this—other than staying the heck away from storms that producing lightning, instructors should ensure pilots are aware of the risk. One possible way to help mitigate the effect is to turn up the cockpit instrument lights to help avoid not being able to see them while their eyes are adjusting.

checklistItems.name: Engine Water Ingestion
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can ask pilots: What do you think would happen to a turbine engine in a water landing? How long would it work before being flooded? Then they can follow up with telling pilots that the updrafts in a thunderstorm can exceed the terminal velocity of falling rain drops, creating “pools” of water in the air inside of storms that can exceed the maximum designed water ingestion of the engines.

checklistItems.name: Effect on Altimeters
checklistItems.teachingTips: T-Storms have a ping-pong ball effect on altimeters: Their readings "bounce" up and down when navigating a T-Storm. Readings rapidly fall with the approach of the storm; rise again with gust front; then return to baseline as the front passes. Oh, and just like a ping-pong match, the whole process doesn’t take long: The entire down, up, return cycle can take place in 15 minutes--with 100 foot errors in un-adjusted altimeters.
