activities.name: [02] Pre-SOLO: Aerodynamics, Stalls, and Spin Awareness (VII.A-D)
activities.what: The science of the forces and limitations on an airplane in flight.
activities.why: To help the pilot keep the airplane within a safe operating envelope while in flight.
activities.groundPrep: See Prep Tab

checklistItems.name: Aerodynamics of Flight
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Have a model aircraft similar to the training aircraft in use to help the pilot visualize how their aircraft works in terms of aerodynamics.
Have a whiteboard to draw cross sections of the wing to demonstrate lift; use a contrasting color of ink to draw airflow over the wing
Use pictures and videos to help illustrate the topic. See the AOPA Air Safety Institute online course on Essential Aerodynamics for some useful interactive graphics and videos.

checklistItems.name: Four Forces of Flight (overview)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Draw airplane on whiteboard or have a image of an aircraft in flight and label LIFT, WEIGHT, THRUST and DRAG.
Explain that the construction of the airplane determines its weight and therefore the amount of thrust/lift required to get it in the air. Make sure the pilot understands lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, and that the pilot is responsbile for making sure the aircraft is not overweight, and that the engine and propeller create thrust.

checklistItems.name: Properties of Air (Density, Viscosity, Friction, Pressure)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Density: Draw air on a whiteboard by using blue dots to represent air molecules. On cold days the dots are close together. On warm days the molecules spread out as heated air expands. Insert red dots to demonstrate water molecules to show density altitude caused by humidity.
Viscosity: Compair thicker air -- caused by colder temperatures -- to handholds used on a climbing wall. When the cold air molecules are plentiful, like the handholds on the wall, climbing up is easy. Cold air over the wing generates a lot of lift.
Friction: Tell the story of Howard Hughes with the H-1 racer and the countersunk rivets. The skin of the airplane was like glass and it moved through the air faster than anything ever created because of decreased skin friction.
Pressure: Illustrate diminished air pressure by stacking books on a desk -- the book on the bottom is feeling the most pressure, the book on top is at a higher altitude therefore has less pressure. The air in the atmosphere works the same way.

checklistItems.name:
Lift
- Theories in the Production of Lift
- Newton
- Bernoulli
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
While explaining lift can create some heated debates among pilots, the pilot will likely be best served by focusing on practical simplicity. Using the analogy and experience that most people have of "flying" their hand outside of a car window provides a relatively intuitive way to understand lift (and drag). Depending on their personality and background, either a simple explanation based on pressure differences (Bernoulli) or on action/reaction (Newton) will be effective with most new pilots. In both theories, relay that both the upper and lower surfaces of the wing are working simultansouly to create lift. While in reality both theories are acting in conjunction, you can focus the pilot on the process of air being deflected downward and therefore pushing the airplane upward (Newton) or on how the high pressure below and low pressure above the wing create a pressure differential that creates a lifting force (Bernoulli). The main point is to help the pilot develop an understanding that will equip them to intuitively understand how to keep the wing flying and avoid unintentional stalls as they operate the aircraft.

The actual principles of lift generation are incredibly complex and a detailed understanding is not really necessary for a pilot to safely and practically operate an aircraft. However, if the pilot is really curious you can then discuss it in more depth or refer them to a more detailed source like NASA's index of Aerodynamic Slides. The key to accurately explain lift theories is to help the pilot understand that both the Bernoulli and Newtononian theories are intertwined and working at the same time. Also take care to avoid passing along the widespread incorrect theories of lift that are addressed on NASA's index of Aerodynamic Slides.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: For explaining Newtonian principles: Ilustrate "for every action equal and opposite reaction by tossing a tennis ball against the wall and catching it on the rebound.

checklistItems.name:
Airfoil Design
- Parts of the wing (leading edge, trailing edge, chord line, camber)
- Relative wind and angle of attack (AoA)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Using a good illustrations can help keep the pilot from feeling like this is vocabulary lesson. Be sure to show how relative wind and angle of attack are not the same as pitch or related to the horizon. Using a model airplane and a pointer (representing the relative wind) can be used to demonstrate how the relative wind and angle of attack have nothing to with the horizon.

checklistItems.name: Stalls
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Use an illustration or draw a cross section of three wings: one in level flight, one approaching stall, one stalled. Note the lack of airflow which will result in reduction of airspeed and lift. Discuss all the warnings that a stall is about to happen (e.g., quieter airflow, stall horn, sloppy control pressure, buffet).

There are also some videos that show a stall occuring that can help illustrate what happens when a stall occurs. See the Resource section for an example video from NASA entitled "Smoke Lifts."

checklistItems.name: Spins/Spin Awareness
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Explain that spins happens the wing is stalled and the airplane is yawing. During a stall the wing is still creating some lift, just not enough to keep the airplane aloft. Explain how during a spin, one wing is more deeply stalled than the other and that difference in lift causes the spiral rotation characteristic of a spin.

Emphasize the goal of stall and spin recogntion and avoidance. If the pilot prevents yaw during a stall, no spin will happen. One good technique to help pilots when performing stalls is to have them look outside and monitor the airplane's nose against a visible reference like a cloud or on a forward angle towards the ground. If they use the rudder to prevent the nose from moving during stall practice, the airplane will not yaw.

To recover from a spin, use PARE (or manufacturer's recommended procedure):
Power - to idle to prevent acceleration during recovery. Ailerons - neutral to prevent further aggravating the stall. Rudder - opposite of rotation to stop. Elevator - forward to break the stall.

checklistItems.name:
Drag
- Induced
- Parasite
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Stress that pilots control drag by presenting more aircraft into the relative wind with a slip, and flaps are used to generate drag for landing.

Stress that Induced drag ALWAYS comes from the production of lift. A good way to help a new pilot understand induced drag is to refer back to their experience of "flying" a hand outside of a car window. If they pay attention they'll notice that angling their hand against the wind both pushes it up and backwards. Draw a diagram showing the hand's force vector. It angles up and back. Then breakdown the vector's components. The part of the force that pushes up is lift and the part that pulls back is induced drag. The higher the angle of attack or amount of lift, the more induced drag is created.

Stress that Parasite drag ALWAYS comes from the production of lift. The faster you fly the more parasite drag incurred. A potential example here is to imagine swimming in a pool in a swimsuit versus fully clothed. It is much harder with drag created by clothes that resist your forward movement through the water.

checklistItems.name: Thrust
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: The concept of thrust is relatively intuitive for most new pilots, but how to control power and adjusting for turning tendencies will likely be new concepts. Emphasize how a balance between thrust and drag are required for constant airspeed flight.

checklistItems.name: Basic Propeller Principles
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot that the propeller is a rotating airfoil, kind of like a wing on a rotisserie. dDraw the pilot's attention to the shape of the prop, the camber and flat side just like a wing.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Note that in all American airplanes the prop rotates to the right as seen from the cockpit.

checklistItems.name: Turning Tendencies
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
PAST is the acronym:
P- P-factor, use a toy gyroscope to demonstrate how changes in pitch affect the spinning propeller blade due to gyroscopic precession especially at slower speeds. Note that precession causes left-turning tendencies for a tailwheel aircraft when the tais raised, but is actually a right-turning tendency when rotating a tricycle gear aircraft.
A- Asymentrical thrust - use model prop to show size of the blade leading edge on the up movement.
S- Spiraling slip stream: dmeonstrate with a ribbon from the nose of the aircraft then striking the tail on the left side causing the nose to turn left.
T- Torque: hold prop of toy airplane and rotate the aircraft body to the left to illustrate the principle of action/reaction (i.e., right turning propeller causes a left rotating airplane).
Stress that the right rudder is the control to use to correct left turning tendency and that the left turning tendencies are more pronounced at high power and high angle of attack.

checklistItems.name: Weight
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Like thrust, weight is an intuitive concept for new pilots. The new concept will be the aircraft's weight and balance limitations. But here, just emphasize how lift and weight must be in balance for steady-state flight as they will learn specifics of calculating weight and balance in a later session.

checklistItems.name: 4 forces in Climbs/Descents
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Draw an airplane in profile and label the forces as lift, weight, thrust, and drag. Note that when in unaccelerated flight, all forces are in balance (e.g., lift vs. weight and thrust vs. drag). The forces become unbalanced when a change in pitch or airspeed is occuring. But once back in a steady state climb or descent, the forces are back in balance. One of the most common misunderstandings is that an airplane climbs due to excess lift or descends by a decrease in lift. It is excess thrust along the upward flight path that causes an airplane to climb and gravity (or weight) along the descending flight path that causes the airplane to descend.

checklistItems.name: Turning Flight
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: One way to help new pilots understand the forces in turns is to introduce the concept of a "lift" checking account. Part of your "lift dollars" are used to keep the airplane in straight and level flight, and it is the horizontal component of lift that pulls it around the turn, so when you bank the aircraft you must increase lift by more throttle or increased pitch or both because the "straight and level" account is being depleted.

checklistItems.name: Load Factors
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Relate the idea of load factor to the feeling of getting pushed sideways in a car when going around a sharp turn. It's the force of your inertia and the constantly changing direction of the car that causes you to feel the apparent sideways pulling force.

Explain that since the airplane uses the horizontal component of lift to turn, more lift overall must be created to maintain altitude in a turn. Like the car analogy, the lift pulling the airplane around the turn causes the apparent force the we feel as G-force or load factor. Too much load factor on the airplane can cause damage to the airplane's structure (just like too much load factor on the pilot can cause unconsciousness). There are limits that must respected to fly safely.

checklistItems.name: Aircraft Design
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Stress that aircraft design reflects the intended use of the aircraft. Exceeding the limits, like doing aerobatics in a light trainer (e.g. C172 or Archer) would be akin to taking the family sedan off roading. Damage and hazards are likely.

checklistItems.name: Steep Turns and Stalling Speed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Emphasize that the stalls during a turn happen at a higher airspeed than it does in straight and level. Be sure the pilot understands the relationship between angle of attack and stall. By then connecting the concepts of increased lift (and hence a higher AoA) being created in a turn with reaching the critical AoA, you can make the relationship between bank angle and higher stalling speed clear to the pilot.

checklistItems.name: Flight Manuevers
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Steep turns and spirals generate the most G forces during flight. Help the pilot learn how maneuvering can lead to increased load factors and unintentional stalls. Focus them on the concept of critical angle of attack and how bank angles, and pulling on the yoke during a recovery can lead to increased load factor or accelerated stalls.

Emphasize the need to obey the placards in the aircraft that warn against certain maneuvers and practices.

checklistItems.name: Vg Diagram
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Help the pilot understand what the limits of the Vg represent including the areas that illustrate the airspeed indicator markings and key V speeds. This might be a good time to explain maneuvering speed in more detail. Get across the main concept that Va is an angle of attack rather than a specific airspeed. Using the AoA concept helps to explain why Va changes with weight and also how it works: at a high enough 1G AoA, the wing will reach critical AoA before creating enough lift (force) to damage the plane. Starting from too low of an AoA means the wing has the potential to create more lift (force) than the airframe can handle. See the article "A New Look at Maneuvering Speed" in the Resource section.

Stress the importance of obeying and staying within the aircraft envelope.

checklistItems.name: Rate and Radius of Turns
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
One useful analogy is to relate it to turning a bicycle or in a car. Going fast requires a wider turn arc than going slow. So more speed results in a wider turning arc while flying.

When explaining the rate of turn, remind the pilot of how an airplane uses lift in a horizontal direction to turn the airplane. Then explain that as the bank angle steepens, the quicker the rate of turn. Relate this by explaining that using more horizontal lift to turn the plane also results in a faster rate of turn.

checklistItems.name: Wingtip Vortices
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Obtain youtube video of wingtip vortices -- impress that all aircraft create these: the bigger the wing, the bigger the vortices. The are physical manifestations of wake and should be respected. Flying through a larger airplane's wake tubulence can result in an uncontrollable rolling motion. Teach the pilot to avoid and, if needed, recover from an unintentional wake tubulence encounter. Refer to the AOPA article "Proficiency: In the Vortex" for more details and an illustrative video.

checklistItems.name: Ground Effect
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The key here is to help the pilot understand when ground effect occurs and how it affects the airplane (i.e., floating during landing or flying before the airplane is capable of leaving ground effect). Explain how ground effects changes the airflow around the wing (upwash, downwash, and wingtip vortices) resulting in a decrease of induced drag. This means that climbing out of ground effect results in an increase in drag which could be a dangerous situation if the airplane is too heavy or does not have enought power or airspeed to continue the climb. And not taking it into account on landing could result in overrunning the runway.

One of the most challeging things about teaching ground effect is helping the pilot understand how changing the wingtip vortices can affect how much induced drag is created. One to explain this is to review the explanation of induced drag and then explain that when the airflow around the wing is altered by the ground, it changes the average relative wind and causes the Total Lift vector to move forward. When the lift vector shifts forward, the rearward vector of lift (induced drag) is reduced.

checklistItems.name: Axis of an Aircraft
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Obtain a model aircraft and insert wooden dowls on the three axis of movement. Print PITCH, YAW and ROLL on the dowels that correspond to those axis. Roll, yaw and pitch the model during lecture. Stress that the axes all converge in the aircraft's CG .

checklistItems.name: Stability
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA

checklistItems.name: Types: Static, Dynamic, Longitudinal, Lateral, Vertical
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips: Use a marble and an inverted bowl on a flat surface to demonstrate negative static stability, ergo the marble rolls off the inverted bowl and keeps going. When the marble is dropped in the bowl it rolls up the other side until the oscillations stop demonstrating static and dynamic stability. Additionally, using an airplane model to demonstrate the motions associated with the different types of stabilty can help the pilot visualize what is happening.

checklistItems.name:
Weight and Balance Effects
- Performance
- Aircraft Structure
- Stability and Control
- Load Distribution
checklistItems.notesToPilot: NA
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be sure the pilot understands the detrimental effects of overloading or loading the aircraft out of balance. An overloaded aircraft will climb poorly (if at all) and could potentially damage the landing gear on contact with the runway. Additionally overloading can lead to airframe damage or failure since the airframe is designed and deisgnated with limits.

Attempting to operate an aircraft out of its balance limits could result in the inability to control it. Be sure the pilots understands how forward and aft of limit loading could lead to hazards like wheelbarrowing or a stall due to over-rotation. Consider using NTSB reports about overloaded aircraft or aircraft with unsecured loads to illustrate the effects.

An aircraft said to be inherently stable will be easier to control while an unstable aircraft will be harder to control. In the air, demonstrate how the aircraft can "fly itself" when properly trimmed out. A good way to help pilots understant the concept is to explain how some aircraft like military fighters are designed to be unstable and hard to control because they need to be so manueverable versus a training aircraft that is designed to be inherently stable to make control a bit easier for new pilots.

Consider using a traditional paper airplane to help demonstrate roll stability. Giving the airplane wings a nice "V" shape will help it maintain a wings level bank. Folding the wings into a inverted "V" shows a pretty dramatic tendency to roll uncontrollably. You can use this oppotunity to explain dihedral.

Note there is no such thing as "calling shotgun" in a small airplane -- the weight must be loaded to make it so the nose can be raised and lowered easily. Demonstrate weight shift calculations with real world examples.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
At a safe altitude, the CFI should slide his/her seat back an inch or forward and inch so the change in CG can be experienced. Encourage pilot to carry 10 feet of parachute chord (compact and easy to get at Walmart) to tie down loads. Note tie down rings like those in the C172 baggage compartment.

Do some training with someone in the backseat so the pilot can get used to the sensation of weight in the backseat. Have the person in the backseat shift around during the flight within limits -- so the pilot can experience this.

You can do a stability demonstration in the aircraft. Once it's trimmed for level flight, push the yoke forward and then let go. Most stable training aircraft will go through a series of gradually dampening pitch oscillations. After a few cycles the airplane will return to its original altitude and airspeed. (NOTE: you may need to provide some gentle rudder pressure to prevent inadvertant bank changes depending on the airplane.)

commonErrors.name: Confusion about excess lift causing a climb and vice versa.
commonErrors.details: In steady state flight (e.g., climbs, descents, straight and level, etc), the forces are in balance. Clarify the point that it is when pitch or airspeed is changing that signals an imbalance in the forces. For example, adding throttle causes a temporary imbalance in thrust vs. drag. As the airplane speeds up, drag increases until they are again in balance at a higher airspeed. For climbs or descents, lift vs weight is only out of balance during pitch changes and return to balance when a new steady pitch attitude is established. The challenge here is showing the balance among the force vectors that are angled and must be broken down into vertical and horizontal components to show the balanced relationship.

commonErrors.name: Not considering wake turbulence warnings.
commonErrors.details: Advise the pilot to accept the wake turbulence waiting time when offered by the tower. At non-towered airports train them to notice when an aircraft takes off and lands because that's where the major hazard begins and ends.

commonErrors.name: Failure to respect the potential danger of moving a "hot" prop.
commonErrors.details: Teach them to respect the prop -- no pictures with your hand on it!

commonErrors.name: Thinking all drag is bad.
commonErrors.details: Drag can be a useful tool. For example, drag from flaps allows a steeper angle of descent without increasing airspeed.

commonErrors.name: Becoming confused by of the incorrect theories of lift including: equal transit theory, half venturi theory, and skipping stone or barn door theory of lift.
commonErrors.details: Refer to the NASA Index of Aerodynamic Slides that discusses these theories (https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/airplane/short.html) and help the pilot understand the practical application of lift needed to safely operate an aircraft.

commonErrors.name: Failure to understand that the four forces work opposite one another and that they are controlled by the pilot.
commonErrors.details: Emphasize the concept of balancing opposing forces (e.g., thrust vs. drag, and lift vs. weight). Help the pilot understand that when the forces are not in balance, something is changing (e.g., thrust > drag = acceleration and vice versa). One particular concept to clarify is that when lift is out of balance with weight, a change in pitch is occuring rather than thinking about altitude. Illustrate this by explaining that once established in a steady climb or descent, pitch is stable because lift and weight are in balance again. The more complex balance of the forces in climbs and descents are covered later in the lesson.

commonErrors.name: Confusing an aerodynamic stall with the engine quitting.
commonErrors.details:
Explain that a stall is a temporary reduction of lift and does not necessarily involve a loss of engine power.

MISUNDERSTANDING: Explain that pulling the nose of the aircraft up does not automatically result in a increase in lift and a corresponding gain in altitude. The airflow over the wing must be increased.

commonErrors.name: Confusing lateral, longitudinal and vertical axes.
commonErrors.details: Consider using colors Red for Lateral, Green for longitudinal, and Blue for Vertical on balsa wood airplane model. Then you can note which axis of the aircraft they represent.

commonErrors.name: Thinking a stall automatically results in a spin.
commonErrors.details: Emphasize that a spin cannot happen unless the aircraft is stalled and REMAINS stalled. Also, most private candidates are NOT required to do spin training -- if them wish to try spins, use a simulator or an approved aircraft and a CFI.

commonErrors.name: Failure to recognize the need to balance the load in the aircraft and or to make sure the load is secure.
commonErrors.details: Stress the need to secure all loose objects such as baggage -- recommend the pilots carry 20 feet of parachute chord in their gear bags for load securing. FYI: a case of aviation oil still in the cardboard box weighs approximately 25 lbs.

commonErrors.name: Overestimation of what the aircraft can do structurally.
commonErrors.details: Pilots who play video games or who have seen lots of TV movies will have an inflated sense of what the aircraft can safely do structurally. Attempts to issue a zero G can often result in broken rear windscreens or worse structural damage/failure. Warn the pilot against this and help develop a healthy respect for its limits.

commonErrors.name: Attempting to steer on the ground with the ailerons.
commonErrors.details: Stress rudder to correct left tendency. Take the aircraft up to altitude and achieve level flight. Put feet flat on floor. Put aircraft into cruise flight, then add more power watch the nose yaw to the left to illustrate the left turning tendencies.

commonErrors.name: Failure to use enough rudder in a turn which can lead to a skid or spin.
commonErrors.details: Failure to add power in a steep turn to compensate for the loss of the vertical component of lift. If the pilot pulls the yoke/stick back and the pilot has poor rudder control this is where spins come from -- demonstrate this manuever at high altitude in case a spin happens. Help the pilot understand the correct amount of rudder required when executing a steep turn due to the inherent overbanking tendency during the turn.

commonErrors.name: Overcontrolling by new pilots who may be used to simulators and are surprised by the feeling of load factor the first time they do a steep turn.
commonErrors.details: Introduce them to the maneuver gently; standard rate, 20, 30 then 45 degrees of bank until they recognize the sensation .

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to use the rudders to maintain coordination.
commonErrors.details: Help pilots understand the theory of adverse yaw and how to apply it practically when flying. Many pilots will think that rudder needs to be applied throughout a steady state turn rather than while rolling into and out of turns. Help them understand that rudder is mainly needed while rolling and that the pressures can usually be relaxed or or at least adjusted while established in the turn depending on the amount of bank.

commonErrors.name: Pilots who play a lot of flight sim may have unrealistic expectations of the aircraft's power and control responsiveness.
commonErrors.details: Be on guard for "rocketship" takeoffs and 40° banked turns on takeoff.

commonErrors.name: Confusing an aerodynamic stall with engine stopping.
commonErrors.details: Emphasize to the pilot that a stall is a temporary reduction in lift caused by exceeding the critical angle of attack. A stall does not often result in a crash unless it occurs close to the ground. Stalls are preventable and you see/hear/and feel them coming. The purpose of learning stalls is to recognize the onset and take prompt and correct action to prevent or recover from it.

activities.name: [20] X/C: Weather Information (I.C. K1, K2, K4)
activities.what: The process of getting, reading, and interpreting weather information in preparation for flight
activities.why: To increase the safety of flight by being able to make informed decisions regarding flight in various weather conditions

checklistItems.name: Weather Briefings
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can tell pilots that briefings are the various ways that weather experts tell us what they see, and what they expect will happen in the future. One thing to consider is helping them develop the skills to take advantage of the self-service option when getting a weather briefing. It can be a useful skill - especially on good weather days. Be sure they know how to effectively sort through the weather and NOTAM information so they don't miss any critical information. Of course, assure them that they can always supplement a self-briefing with a call to Flight Service to ask questions or just double check on their assessment.
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: Outlook Briefing, Standard Briefing, Abbreviated Briefing
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can teach pilots about the three types of briefings by having them think of them in terms of phases of flight. The outlook briefing is used in the first phases of flight planning, the standard brief is used right before launch, and the abbreviated is an update for a delayed flight.

checklistItems.name: Flight Service Station (FSS)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can have pilots think of flight service as their 24-hour weather store!

checklistItems.name: Observations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can tell pilots that aviation weather observations are simply what you can observe (or see)—in other words, real-time data. Observations include data collected by people or automated systems on the ground, data from weather balloons, and data collected from aircraft—either by automated systems or fellow pilots.

checklistItems.name: Surface Aviation Weather Observations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teaching trivia: May be made by people or automated stations.

checklistItems.name: Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Purists will disagree, but learning to read the obtuse language of METARS (and TAFs) may not be necessary for all pilots. Many flight apps will translate METARs into plain English, and internet based translator abound. In fact, Flight Service’s METAR text service has a “PT” option for Plain Text, or as we like to call it, "Plane" Text. :-)

Note, however, that some weather products do not have a plain text option, such as the new Graphical Area Forecast. Therefore, there may be some value in continuing to teach pilots how to decode weather products.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Hard on the budget, but awesome for the soul and mind are METARmaps Real-Time Weather Wall Art pieces which would look great on your training center wall!

For instructors who prefer to teach “METAReze” to pilots, consider gamifying the terms using flash cards for group instruction with small prizes for winners.

checklistItems.name: Upper Air Observations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teaching trivia: 75 K weather balloons are launched per year, and more than 220,000 observations are made from airplanes per year.

checklistItems.name: Pilot Weather Reports (PIREPs)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
New (and experienced) pilots will often find interepreting PIREPs due the number of abbreviations that aren't included in other weather reports. Emphasize the value of getting (and giving) weather reports from pilots to help provide the motivation for learning to interpret PIREPs.

Using a tablet computer with an aviation app (like an electronic flight bag) instructors can call up real time PIREPs. While many of these will come from airliners, it serves to demonstrate how different weather can be higher in the atmosphere. Sometimes a fine-looking day on the airport can be a wild ride at the flight levels!

checklistItems.name: Radar Observations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors should ensure that pilots understand the differences in the four common types of radar used in aviation reporting (NEXRAD, terminal Doppler, “tower” radar, and airborne radar—which is not commonly seen in GA aircraft.)

checklistItems.name: Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: If possible a tour of the nearest ARTCC is an ideal way for pilots to learn the limitations of air traffic radar when it comes to detailed weather avoidance. Phone numbers are listed in the Chart Supplement.

checklistItems.name: Satellite
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Some GA aircraft receive weather data from satellite subscription services, if so equipped, instructors should ensure that pilots are comfortable with the interface and the product options.

checklistItems.name: Weather Charts
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Instructors should inform pilots that weather charts may either show current weather or forecast weather.

Make sure that pilots are familiar with how to interpret the charts. A great training tool is to practice using the charts on www.aviationweather.gov as they often have the chart legend right on the charts or just a click away.

checklistItems.name: Surface Analysis Chart
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: For positive transfer of knowledge, Instructors can compare surface analysis charts to broadcast TV “weather man” charts of the country, with highs, lows, fronts, etc.

checklistItems.name: Weather Depiction Chart
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can have pilots think of the weather depiction chart as a “METAR Map,” with flight rules additionally shown.

checklistItems.name: Aviation Forecasts
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can tell pilots that aviation weather forecasts are events that weather experts expect will happen in the future. This approach can be useful to reinforce that pilots should not take forecasts as a guarantee of inflight weather conditions, but rather a probability. It's important to continually monitor the weather conditions both visually and through inflight sources to ensure a safe and successful flight.

checklistItems.name: Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: As the TAF is the linguistic cousin of the METAR, they can easily be co-taught to pilots; with instructors emphasizing that the METAR is “now” and the TAF is “future.” It's useful to teach TAFs and METARs together since they use a lot of the same text coding.

checklistItems.name: Graphical replacement for Area Forecasts (FA)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Instructors will no doubt be delighted to be rid of the long text with no vowels that made up the old Area Forecast product. That said, the interactive replacement  on www.aviationweather.gov has many complex features with a medium-to-steep learning curve. Best practice is a hands-on tutoring session, being sure to introduce the “slider” on the top that allows pilots to view current weather and preview future weather from the same screen. A major training advantage is that each type of chart is accompanied by legend which promotes learning the symbology. You can find it at https://www.aviationweather.gov/gfa/help

The graphical area forecasts found in typical weather briefings tends to be a series of static charts that can differ slightly from the aviationweather.gov product. Be sure to review how to interpret each with the pilot.

checklistItems.name: Inflight Weather Advisories: AIRMET, SIGMET, Convective Significant Meteorological Information (WST)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
To help teach pilots how to recognize the common inflight advisories, there are a few word games that can be deployed. For a Sierra AIRMET, think the Sierra Nevada or High Sierra as a way to remember that a Sierra AIRMET involves mountains (IFR and mountain obscuration). Likewise, Tango is for turbulence, or "T" for turbulence (plus strong surface winds, low level wind shear, and associated nastiness). Zulu, as in the classic movie Ice Station Zulu, deals with icing and freezing levels. You might also remember Z for "zero" or really cold - icing and freezing.

Be sure to show the pilot the graphical representation of the boundaries that make determining where the advisory applies much easier than trying to use the textual description. Aviationweather.gov and most briefing sources will have that option.

Instructors should ensure that pilots know that unlike some other weather advisories, Convective SIGMETS are issued even with rosy weather, to ensure none are missed; and rather than using the phonetic alphabet, they are simply numbered.

checklistItems.name: Winds and Temperature Aloft Forecast (FB)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can help demystifying these forecasts by pointing out that the data is presented in a six-digit number, which should be envisioned as having a break in the middle. The first three digits are the direction the wind is coming from, and the second three digits are its speed. This is just like an AWOS or ATIS which will report direction before velocity (positive transfer of knowledge!). Of course, at higher altitudes, a + or – after the six-digit string is the temp. Instructors can tell pilots that the lack of a temperature reading means the forecast is for winds nearer the surface.

checklistItems.name: Significant Weather Prognostic Charts
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors should encourage pilots to view these “kindergarten art” weather charts as a way to quickly take in large scale ceiling and visibility conditions, without in-depth study or interpretation. Like a stop light, red is bad for VFR flight, yellow cautions a bumpy ride—although puffy blue clouds are not as fair weather as you might think!

checklistItems.name: ATC Radar Weather Displays
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Weather Avoidance Assistance
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Showing a picture or video of what ATC's weather display looks like as compared to a normal weather radar display might help the pilot better understand the limitations. Also be sure to mention that controllers can change how much weather is diplayed to help them better see the air traffic, so they may not realize the extent of the weather the pilot is flying through.

checklistItems.name: Electronic Flight Displays (EFD) /Multi-Function Display (MFD) Weather
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Weather Products Age and Expiration
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots often assume they have the iPad equivalent of cockpit radar. Instructors should be sure their pilots understand the length of delay inherent in the system (as much as 15-20 minutes). Challenge pilots to think about how much unstable weather can change in 20 minutes.

checklistItems.name: What Can Pilots Do?
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors should encourage pilots to think about EFD and MFD weather as a strategic tool, not a tactical one. A good example of this is NOT to use EFD and MFD weather to “thread the needle” between thunderstorms, but rather to use them to plan, hundreds of miles away, the best routes for severe weather avoidance. From a distance, even a mild course change can steer pilots clear of foul weather.

checklistItems.name: NEXRAD Abnormalities, NEXRAD Limitations
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots may not realize that rain and hail are undistinguishable from each other on NEXRAD. While there is no specific solution for this, instructors can use this fact as an example of why pilots should rely on multiple sources of information when investigating weather for a flight.

checklistItems.name: AIRMET/SIGMET Display
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: If so equipped, instructors should show pilots how AIR- and SIGMETs can be displayed graphically on a MFD, showing the geographical range of the warning area, which can be compared to country lines or state borders are shown on a map.

checklistItems.name: Graphical METARs
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Not all aviation weather products use the same color-coding system to report flight categories from METARS. Flight Service online maps, NOAA’s Aviation Weather Center, and ForeFlight use the following system:  VFR as Green MVFR as Blue IFR as Red LIFR as Hot Pink (Officially called Magenta, but it doesn’t look like any magenta we’ve ever seen before)  However, Garmin Pilot displays use a different color system: VFR as Blue MVFR as Green IFR as Yellow LIFR as Red  Note: Adding to the confusion, ForeFlight also uses Green, Blue, Orange, and Red color dots to indicate the age of weather reports.   Instructors should ensure pilots are aware of the color coding system that their chosen products use, how to edit them, and be alert to confusion when using multiple sources to access weather.

checklistItems.name: Data Link Weather,  Data Link Weather Products, Flight Information Service-Broadcast (FIS-B)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors should ensure that pilots understand that while virtually every weather product in the universe flows though FIS-B / ADS-B, the data if for informational purposes only, and is not an “official” weather product.

checklistItems.name: Pilot Responsibility
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: When it comes to weather, we are at risk of drowning in a sea of plenty. Gone are the days of venturing beyond the horizon into the unknown. Now it’s possible to spend so much time studying weather that there’s no time left to fly! Instructors should encourage pilots to widely sample weather products, then choose a limited number that makes sense to them, and provide a variety of information. Of course, this should ALWAYS include an official briefing.

commonErrors.name: Overestimating the detail of ATC weather displays
commonErrors.details: A common error among new pilots is to assume that ATC radar, in addition to showing aircraft, also shows weather phenomena with the same level of detail that other weather radar products do. Instructors should be sure to instruct their pilots on the limitations of ATC radar, when it comes to weather.

commonErrors.name: Not understanding the limitations of in-cockpit weather
commonErrors.details: A common error for some pilots is to think of ADS-B In “radar” as cockpit radar. Instructors should ensure that pilots understand the delay built into the product, and the danger of using ADS-B radar images for making tactical decisions inflight.

commonErrors.name: Confusing the source of wind direction
commonErrors.details: A common error for new pilots is to be confused about the fact that wind is forecast and reported in the direction it is coming FROM, not the direction it is blowing TO. To help pilots remember this, instructors can ask pilots to picture an old-fashioned wind vane, which points into the wind--the direction it is coming from.

commonErrors.name: Failing to use METARs to get an idea of the big weather picture
commonErrors.details: Because they are small in coverage radius, a common error among pilots is to question the value of METARs for “big picture” analysis, and become fixated only on departure and destination METARs. Instructors can demonstrate that, by viewing METARs on tablet maps or online maps, pilots can help form a visual picture of the pattern and trend of weather over large areas, as seen through the lens of flight rules

activities.name: [18] X/C: Performance and Limitations: Weight and Balance
activities.what: The process of determining an aircraft’s Center of Gravity (CG) for flight operations
activities.why: To determine/provide the safest and most efficient operation of the aircraft

checklistItems.name:
Weight and Balance Basics
- Effects of weight on aircraft performance
- Overstressing the airframe
- Decreased performance (e.g., takeoff, climb, landing, etc)
- Center of gravity
- Explain the concept (e.g., like a seesaw, etc.)
- Effects on flight stability (in and out of limits)
- Limits to aircraft controls (e.g., landing, stall recovery, etc.)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
It can often be more benefical to explain the "why" behind weight and balance before the "how." If a new pilot understands the risks surrounding flying out of balance and overweight, he or she will be less likely to do it. Because airplanes will often fly slightly overweight, pilots often think it is perfectly safe. Use accident records to show the consequences of flying even a bit out of the envelope. These accidents happen routinely, especially at higher elevations. The biggest risk of flying out of CG are control limits and stability, so a discussion on those points is important to help the pilot understand the importance of calculating CG.

Explaining center of gravity is more complicated, and is best done with a diagram, or even an airplane model balancing on a pencil. Using an analogy of a seesaw or teeter totter is one of the most intuitive ways to teach arm, moment, and CG balance. Focus in on leverage using the length (arm) of where a person is sitting. A small child will need to sit on the end of the seesaw to maximize their leverage against an adult who will have to "scoot" towards the middle (fulcrum) to balance out the seesaw. Decreasing the distance (arm) of the heavier load decreases the overall moment.

It is also useful to apply this analogy to the airplane as a large seesaw with it hanging on the center of lift (fulcrum) and the balance between the CG which rests forward of the center of lift and is opposed by the tail down force created by the horizontal stabilizer. Point out that on most GA aircraft, the CG is located a short distance (arm) forward of the center of lift and the taildown is futher back a long arm. This analogy can be further utilized when explaining pitch stability by analyzing the effects of airspeed on taildown force during pitch changes.
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Terms and Definitions (Suggested order for teaching)
- Center of gravity (CG)
- Arm
- Moment
- Basic empty weight
- Standard empty weight
- Datum (reference line)
- Station
- CG arm
- CG limits
- CG range
- Useable fuel
- Unsuable fuel
- Payload
- Useful load
- Maximum landing weight
- Maximum ramp weight
- Maximum takeoff weight
- Maximum zero fuel weight
checklistItems.teachingTips: When discussing the terms it can be helpful to relate them directly to the aircraft. For example, rather than simply saying that the datum is the theoritical reference point, show where it is on the airplane. Show what an arm is, and how its lenth impacts CG.

checklistItems.name:
Calculating Weight and Balance
- Using basic math (e.g., weight x arm = moment, arms of loading stations, filling out a weight and balance form)
- Loading graph
- Center of Gravity Moment Envelope
checklistItems.teachingTips: Start by explaining basic calculations, and move on to various loading scenarios and discussions on how to remain within weight and balance. Trying weight and balance calculations on different models can help pilots better grasp the concepts and move beyond using specific aircraft tools as a crutch. Finally, in order to support the student calculating a weight and balance for every flight, help him or her create a spreadsheet or other tool that makes calcuating it quick and easy.

commonErrors.name: Trying to load an aircraft like you load a car which can potentially lead to overloading.
commonErrors.details: Review the concepts in this lesson so that pilots gain a clear understanding of weight and balance limitations and potential hazards created by exceeding them.

activities.name: [17] X/C: Performance and Limitations: Performance Charts and Theory (I.F.)
activities.what: The process of determining the airplane’s ability to accomplish maneuvers which serve a specific purpose
activities.why: To operate the airplane safely in varying conditions and to increase awareness of potentially dangerous situations

checklistItems.name:
Importance of Performance Data
- How and why aircraft performance decreases with increases in:
- Altitude (height)
- Temperature (heat)
- Moisture (humidity)
- Aircraft limits (service ceiling)
Effect of pilot technique/skill
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Performance charts are often taught as a strictly mechanical exercise, asking the new pilot to determine parameters for different segments of the flight. Although things can start there, the discussion should progress beyond it. Work with the pilot to have a broader discussion about the judgement and decision making of aircraft capabilities. Performance charts help only to inform decisions, and shouldn't be used as a way to justify poor judgement. This is best explained using scenarios. If a pilot looks at the situation broadly, and critically, the performance charts can be one tool in that decision chain. For example, set a scenario with the pilot where he or she is flying a long cross-country that goes from lower elevations and continues through higher elevations. What are the risk considerations of such a trip? What must the pilot consider? This will help the pilot think critically about the impacts of fuel planning, proper cruise altitude selection, airport requirements, and more. It takes the discussion away from the mechanics of using a specific chart to a more real-life decision making scenario. 

It's a trite expression, but performance charts are determined through a combination of test pilot skills on a specific day under specific conditions, and theoretically by extrapolating that data. It's important that pilots understand they will most likely not be able to achieve those numbers.

checklistItems.name:
Calculation skills
- How and why to use interpolation
Performance Speeds
- True Airspeed
- Indicated Airspeed
- Calibrated Airspeed
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Give the pilot a series of written questions to evaluate his or her ability to understand the charts. To increase complexity and add reality to the exercise, include questions that require interpolation. They must know the rote skills before continuing on.

Spend time in handbooks from a few different models so the pilot understands how different manufacturers present different charts, and remember not to skip the important assumptions about which airspeed is being used and how that may differ from what they see in the cockpit.

checklistItems.name:
Calculating Density Altitude
- Standard atmosphere (temp 15C and pressure 29.92)
- Pressure altitude
- Using a density altitude chart and/or calculation
checklistItems.teachingTips: To be effective, instruction on density altitude must go beyond rote learning to include scenarios. During the lesson bring up current weather reports and airport information of a few places at higher elevations. It can help to pick airports that make decisions obvious, such as Leadville, Colorado, and those that make things more difficult, such as those in the middle elevations of New Mexico, Arizona, and Idaho. Showing how easy it is to exceed aircraft capabilities in places the pilot wouldn't assume can have a strong impact on learning.

checklistItems.name:
Takeoff and Landing Performance Calculations
- Definitions (e.g., ground roll, 50' obstacle, rotation, etc.)
- Performance speeds
- Best rate of climb (Vy)
- Best angle of climb (Vx)
- Effect of airport/runway environment
- Runway surface and gradient
- Water on the runway
- Wind (headwind, tailwind, crosswind)
- Crosswind and Headwind Component Chart
- Airplane configuration
checklistItems.teachingTips:
As with other performance charts, you must go beyond rote knowledge with the pilot. He or she should be able to fully describe when and why to use various climb speeds, what runway surfaces can do to performance, and how to best evaluate a runway for takeoff or landing. Help reinforce these topics by creating scenarios that challenge their assumptions, and get them to consider when and how to implement performance charts. 

The AOPA Air Safety Institute recommends adding 50 percent to runway performance charts. You can show why this is important by asking the pilot to estimate when you will leave the ground, stop your landing roll, and so on. Making it a game can reinforce the lesson that performance charts are only the start of a decision-making process.

checklistItems.name:
Stall Speed Performance Charts
- Effect of load factor on stall speed
checklistItems.teachingTips: One of the most important things a pilot can understand about stall speed is that it changes. Focusing too much on the level, unaccelerated power on and power off stall speeds in the manual can give the impression that the airplane always stalls at that speed. There are graphs that show the relationship between load factor and stall speed, and the discussion should start there. Better yet, have the student perform stalls at an increased load factor to see it first-hand.

checklistItems.name:
Climb Calculations
- Time, fuel, and distance to climb charts
- Fuel burn for startup, taxi, runup
- Effects of temperature and wind
- Leaning for maximum performance

Cruise Performance Calculations
- How to use Cruise Chart
- Selecting power settings
- Effect of temperature
- Leaning the mixture
checklistItems.teachingTips: Once the pilot understands how to use climb and cruise charts, apply the charts on a flight and work together to see how accurate the charts are for the aircraft. Most are quite close, and confirming their accuracy (or inaccuracy) can help the pilot understand their use. The cruise performance charts are also a great place to explore altitude impacts on aircraft performance. Once the pilot has calculated for a certain altitude ask him or her to pick one with a lower fuel burn, or with a higher cruise speed, and discuss the tradeoffs of selecting for each. Run through some scenarios about long-distance flight, or the fuel implications of operating at higher power settings.

checklistItems.name:
Fuel Management 
- How to use Range and Endurance Charts 
- Effect of wind on range performance
checklistItems.teachingTips: Fuel exhaustion continues to be the prevalent and easily preventable accident in aviation. It's up to instructors to instill strong habits early to avoid this problem. Start by carefully going over the performance and endurance charts, including how mixture settings and altitude can impact fuel consumption. Create scenarios that push the available fuel limits to gain an understand of the pilot's thought process in this area, and provide guidance on the safety outcomes. It can be very helpful to compare the book to real-world results. Like takeoff and landing charts, ask the student to calculate fuel consumption on a cross-country flight and fuel when you return to verify the accuracy of the calculations. Finally, press upon the student not to trust the gauges, and instead get a good average fuel burn and use time as the only reliable indicator of consumption.

commonErrors.name: Not knowing when to use a performance chart.
commonErrors.details: Many density altitude accidents occur because the pilot never thought to check the performance of the aircraft. Most pilots know how to use a performance chart. Getting them to understand when to use them is the most effective thing the instructor can do. Try scenario-based training, looking at accident reports, or actually flying to an airport with a higher elevation.

commonErrors.name: Not realizing the effect of aircraft configuration on performance.
commonErrors.details: Airplane configuration can have a big impact on runway performance. Try various configurations and see if the pilot can predict what will happen as a result of the changes, and then discuss the results.

commonErrors.name: Not knowing how to evaluate and cruise altitude selection.
commonErrors.details: New pilots often select altitudes only because their instructor asked them to. Especially after the first cross-country, let the student take the lead on the best altitude to fly, and then challenge him or her to explain why a certain altitude was chosen. Discuss the impacts of changing the altitude in the face of weather, terrain, or airspace.

commonErrors.name: Failing to apply knowledge of how stall speeds can change.
commonErrors.details: Because the discussion of changing stall speeds is often theoretical, pilots tend to forget the importance of the discussion. Through accident reports, applied learning, and demonstrations, it's easy to see how and why the stall speed changes.

activities.name: [05] PRE-SOLO: Traffic Patterns including Collision, Wake Turbulence, and Windshear Avoidance (III.B.K1-4; R1-3)
activities.what: a flight maneuver used by aircraft to flow into and out of an airport in an orderly manner in a rectangular pattern
activities.why: to provide a safe and orderly entry/exit to the airport environment

checklistItems.name: Airport Traffic Patterns and Operations
checklistItems.teachingTips: Perhaps no other topic in aviation is more hotly debated than traffic patterns. That's partly because there are few rules, but many guidelines. Teaching new pilots the difference between what is required and where they have latitude can be tricky. The best thing you can do is stick to the recommended procedures during the first course of training, and then discuss and practice variations later on.

checklistItems.name: Standard Airport Traffic Patterns
checklistItems.teachingTips: The standard traffic pattern is a rectangular course around the runway, generally 800 to 1,000 feet above the ground, with left hand turns, a mid-field downwind entry, and a straight-out or 45-degree departure. Yet the only part that is mentioned in the regulations is that turns should be to the left unless otherwise noted. The rest of it is up to the pilot. Flying a traffic pattern is complex because it layers on increasingly difficult skills of slow flying with moderate banks, navigation, and rapid communication. It's best to shed some of these responsibilities for new pilots, and only add on layers when he or she is ready. To teach the theory, start with drawings, move to physical movements around a room or hangar, and then transition to a simulator.

checklistItems.name: Non-Towered Airports
checklistItems.teachingTips: Stress to the pilot the need to operate in a predictable manner, and to always be on the lookout for other traffic. Many pilots rely only on the radio. Discuss the need to rely on visual scanning, and explain common dangerous spots in the pattern.

checklistItems.name: Safety Considerations
checklistItems.teachingTips: Airspeed control, mid-air collisions, and task oversaturation are the most significant risks of flying a traffic pattern. Spend time on the ground covering these issues, and only when the pilot can correctly explain the procedures by memory, and in detail, should they be allowed to solo.

checklistItems.name: Runway Status Lighting Systems.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Runway Status Lighting Systems are in use at only the biggest Class B airports. Discussing the system and how it works is a great introduction to runway incursion avoidance and the various tools that are available to the pilot. Here, stress the need to be absolutely sure of taxi instructions, to verify before continuing if there is any concern, and to learn to recognize airport signs, markings, and lighting as an aid in this. Sometimes it helps to play ATC recordings of professional pilots asking ATC for clarification, which shows that even pros need help and are tripped up sometimes.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: This is a great opportunity to bring in personal experiences. Maybe as a pilot you've misunderstood signs or markings, and had to ask for clarification. Or you could discuss a time in which you made a mistake. These personal stories are a great way to convey information, and they help the student understand that all pilots make mistakes or have misunderstandings, and really good pilots seek clarification with ATC.

checklistItems.name: Runway selection for the current conditions
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the new pilot the various ways to determine wind direction and how an active runway is determined. This can be a difficult mental exercise for some pilots, so it can be helpful to read weather reports and ask the pilot to determine the active runway.

checklistItems.name: Right-of-way rules
checklistItems.teachingTips: Right-of-way rules are best taught on the ground with scenarios. Once the pilot learns the regulations, quiz them on various scenarios, especially those they are likely to encounter. Airplane and helicopter, airplane and glider, and airplane and balloon are probably the most common.

checklistItems.name: Use of automated weather and airport information
checklistItems.teachingTips: The biggest challenge to obtaining weather at an airport with an automated station is incorporating it into your workflow. Work with the pilot to find the best place to do this in pre-flight planning, and when approaching the airport. The bigger challenge is finding weather sources at airports without weather reporting. Teach the pilot to use all resources, including nearby airports, unicom, wind socks, other pilots, and so on.

checklistItems.name: Landing clearances (including full stop, touch and go, the option, low approach)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Abiding by landing clearances is the most important element of collision and runway incursion avoidance. Thankfully, the pattern is easy to understand. A clearance for "the option" enables the pilot to perform a full stop, low approach, touch and go, or stop and go. Sometimes if the option isn't requested the tower will issue only a touch and go clearance, or a landing clearance. Work with the student to incorporate a method that ensures the right landing clearance. This could be a part of a short final memory checklist, or a call and response with the pilot and instructor early in training. 

Landing clearance is a perfect opportunity to teach PIC authority. Like takeoff clearances, you can explain to the student that the tower isn't giving a command to land, so much as it is granting a request. If the pilot doesn't want what's being granted he or she can and must ask for something else.

checklistItems.name: Takeoff clearances (including immediate, line up and wait)
checklistItems.teachingTips: Takeoff clearances are similar to teaching landing clearances. Work with the pilot to make sure they understand the various clearances, and read it back to air traffic control.

checklistItems.name: Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)
checklistItems.teachingTips: LAHSO is an operation that works only if everyone is on the same page. The AIM has a good amount of information on this that the pilot should study. There, it explains weather and certificate minimums and procedures. If possible, run through a LAHSO scenario on the ground and then visit an airport with LAHSO in effect. You may have to consult with ATC in advance to arrange a LAHSO clearance.

checklistItems.name: Wake Turbulence
checklistItems.teachingTips: The theory on avoiding wake turbulence is fairly straightforward. Plan to take the pilot to an airport where these theories are put into practice, or if that's not possible, discuss scenarios the pilot may encounter and how to avoid them.

checklistItems.name: Windshear Avoidance
checklistItems.teachingTips: Windshear avoidance is best understood by studying the conditions in which it is most likely to exist, as well as the techniques to recognize and recover from it. Teach the pilot that if they see airspeed changes of 10 knots on final approach to go around and either try again or head to a different airport. Airlines have strict windshear limits, and it works well when GA pilots do as well.

commonErrors.details:
Not listening properly to ATC instructions, and complying with instructions the pilot doesn't want.

Some new pilots are so focused on flying and watching for traffic that they miss the proper landing clearance. For example, many pilots have performed touch and goes when only being cleared to land. Work with the pilot on a prompt that ensures everyone is on the same page. For example, you could ask the pilot to call out his or her given landing clearance on short final to confirm it's correct (I'm cleared to land, I'm cleared for the option, etc). Similarly, pilots will sometimes accept a clearance, even if it isn't what they want. Maybe they've been cleared to land, but they want the option. Discuss the need to ask for exactly what they want, and how to seek common understanding with ATC in these cases.

Many pilots, but especially those who are new to flying, are sometime reticent to use their PIC authority.
- Runway selection is a great example of this. Relate to them the importance of accepting only those runway assignments they agree with, and how and when to request a new runway when they aren't comfortable.

Confusion on accepting a LAHSO clearance.
- Pilots sometimes gets confused that just because the ATIS mentions LAHSO that the pilot must abide by it. Instead, that is an advisory, and LAHSO is only in place when an aircraft is issued and accepts a specific clearance.

Getting too close or crossing to the hold short lines without a clearance.
- New pilots can sometimes see the hold short lines as a guide rather than a hard stop. One technique is to say that there exists above the lines an imaginary gate that only lowers when the tower clears the pilot for takeoff or to line up and wait, and the pilot acknowledges that takeoff clearance. 

Feeling pressure to accept a takeoff clearance.
- Takeoff clearances are another great opportunity to discuss PIC authority. It can be helpful with reluctant pilots to explain that in granting a takeoff clearance ATC isn't giving a command so much as granting a request. If the pilot isn't ready to accept something, such as an immediate takeoff, he or she can easily say no.

Oversaturation is common in the beginning of training.
- The instructor can help by ensuring the pilot has an intimate understanding of procedures, radio communication, potential risks, and so on. Much of this can and should be reinforced on the ground, where role playing and scenarios will help ensure it is committed to memory before having to face the real thing. Also be sure to take the building block approach to the required skills. For example, 1. being able to identify the legs of the traffic pattern, 2. then knowing the power settings, target airspeeds, and aircraft configuration at the key points in the pattern, 3. determining pattern entries for various scenarios, 4. handling radio communications, and 5. handling non-standard procedures or unexpected situations.
