activities.name: [15] X/C: National Airspace System (I.E)
activities.what: The subject matter of the classification of airspace in the U.S.
activities.why: To provide a safe flight environment

checklistItems.name: Types of airspace/airspace classes and associated requirements and limitations.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Discuss how airspace makes a safer flight environment. Refer to the airliner crash over the Grand Canyon in 1956 as one event that triggered both the creation of the FAA and the airspace rules we have today including "positive control" by ATC of all airliners in all airspace.

checklistItems.name: Charting symbology.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Point out how thicker bold lines indicate more restrictive airspace (Bravo and Charlie are more restrictive than Delta and Echo). 

In general, blue indicates more restrictive airspace than magenta (Bravo vs Charlie, Delta vs Echo to the Surface, Restricted and Prohibited Airspace vs MOAs)

Show examples of vertical and horizontal airspace boundaries, where to find operating hours, controlling agencies, etc.

checklistItems.name: Overview of Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips: Provide an overall view of the different types of airspace ... e.g. Controlled vs Uncontrolled vs Special Use Airspace. Using a diagram like the AOPA "Airspace at a Glance" reference card can be helpful when introducing the topic.

checklistItems.name: Operating in the Various Types of Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips: All airspace exists for a reason and has vertical and horizontal boundaries, operating times, and rules for operating inside that airspace. For each type of airspace cover these items. This helps pilots get used to thinking about and planning for operating in our National Airspace System.

checklistItems.name: Basic VFR Weather Minimums
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Discuss how VFR weather minimums exist to support pilot "see and avoid" responsibilities. Minimums go up in airspace with faster aircraft or when ATC is not controlling all aircraft in that airspace. Ask the pilots how much time do they want to see and avoid a plane going the other direction, descending or climbing out of a cloud, etc. relate that to two aircraft traveling at 100 kts each (200 kt closure rate) vs one at 100kts and one at 200kts (300 kt closure rate!)

Easiest to teach what the most common weather minimums are: 3SM vis with 1000 ft above, 500 ft below and 2000 horizontal clearance from clouds (aka 3-152s) used in Charlie, Delta and Echo airspace at all times and then teach the exceptions for Class B, G, and E above 10,000 feet. 3-152s is easy for pilots to remember because it relates to Cessna 152s. Even if the pilot doesn't fly a C152, they know what one is.

Rod Machado's Airspace Memory Aid from his Private Pilot Handbook is another useful way to help pilot's memorize VFR weather minimum requirements. See the video in Resources section.

checklistItems.name: Operating Rules and Pilot/Equipment Requirements
checklistItems.teachingTips: Does the airspace require a clearance to enter, radio contact or no radio at all? Is a transponder/ADS-B required? Unique transponder code? Does ATC control the movement of the aircraft or just provide traffic advisories? What are the minimum pilot certificate / training requirements ?

checklistItems.name: Controlled Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
When teaching airspace it helps to use memory aids that link the airspace class "letter" with the types of planes that operate in that airspace, it's location or a requirement related to operating in the airspace. 

Note: When airspaces overlap the most restrictive airspace rules will take precedence. Airspace associated with specific airports, e.g. Class C, D and E may revert to lower class airspace with less restrictive rules when the airport tower is closed. Ensure the pilot knows where to find tower operating hours and if the airspace reverts or not.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
A exercise to evaluate if the pilot is able to apply his/her knowledge of airspace rules is take a sectional chart and draw a line from one airport to another airport that is some distance, and many different classes of airspace away. As the pilot to describe the airspace, VFR Wx Minimums, Equipment, Communications Requirements and Certificate Requirements for each airspace encountered at one altitude on that route. 

Another variation to check the pilot's understading of the vertical limits is to pick a spot on the chart and have the pilot identify all of the types of airspace starting from the surface and ascending straight up until reaching Class A airspace.

checklistItems.name: Class A Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Sample Memory Aid: "Above". All aircraft operating in this airspace are operating IFR, the vast majority are jets flying hundreds of nautical miles an hour with potentially hundreds of passengers per plane. 

No VFR weather minimums here. No VFR allowed.

checklistItems.name: Class B Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Sample Memory Aid: "Busiest", "Busy" or "Biggest". This is around and above the busiest airports in the country with the most commercial traffic. Jets operating up to 250 knots. ATC controls ALL aircraft in B airspace, including VFR aircraft. 

Using a Terminal Area Chart (TAC) point out the blue boxes with the name of the controlling ATC facility and frequency to use when approaching Class B airspace to request a clearance for entry into or through that airspace. The appropriate frequency depends on the direction the aircraft is coming from. 

Because of the positive control - VFR Weather Minimums are merely 3SM visibility and clear of clouds. Keep relating the VFR weather minimums and other airspace rules back to the types of operations that occur in that airspace.

checklistItems.name: Class C Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Sample Memory Aid: "Commercial" or "Congested". These airports are the commercial hubs of aviation nationwide. Jets operating up to 200 knots under positive ATC control are operating with VFR pilots that are communicating with ATC, but not necessarily being directed by ATC.

Using a chart point out the magenta boxes with the name of the controlling ATC facility and frequency to use when approaching to land at a Class C airport. The appropriate frequency depends on the direction the aircraft is coming from. 

Discuss how to determine what happens when the tower closes at the primary airport. Many Class C airports revert to Class E when the tower is closed.

checklistItems.name: Class D Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Sample Memory Aid: "Discuss" or "Dime-sized." These are often very busy airports mostly patronized by light GA aircraft. GA pilots have to communicate (discuss) with ATC before entry. 

Discuss how to determine what happens when the tower closes at the Class D airport. The airspace will revert to Class E or Class G.

checklistItems.name: Class E Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
When teaching airspace, skip Class E and do it after covering Glass G. After Class G is taught, Class E stands for "Everywhere Else". It is only charted where it goes below 1200 feet AGL or it abuts Class G airspace that goes above 1200 feet AGL. Be sure to explain that the faded blue line that depicts Class E airspace starting at 1200' AGL is rare to find now in the continental US. It is helpful to teach that unless otherwise noted, assume that Class E begins at 1200 AGL.

Point out how the cut outs of Class E going to 700 feet or the surface surround airports that have instrument approaches. These cut outs help ATC provide safe separation of IFR aircraft from VFR aircraft when approaching and departing the airports. 

Remember to discuss the additional equipment requirements when operating in Class E above 10,000 MSL - faster aircraft equals increased VFR Wx Minimums and transponder required to help ATC provide separation between fast aircraft.

checklistItems.name: Uncontrolled Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips: A useful exercise for evaluating the pilot's ability to apply knowledge of Class G operating rules, Minimum Safe Altitudes and VFR Sectional Symbology is to select two Class G airports at least 100 NM apart and ask the pilot to describe how they will navigate and what altitudes they would fly if they had to fly from airport A to airport B with 2SM visibility in the day time.

checklistItems.name: Class G Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Sample Memory Aid: "Ground". Think of Class G airspace as a thin layer of paint covering a topographical map of the US. The layer is 1,200 feet thick. When the layer is thicker (up to 14,500 ft), thinner (only 700 ft) or absent (e.g. Class E to the surface) it will be charted. Otherwise the airspace is not charted.

Glass G goes up towards 14,500 in some areas of the Rocky Mountains, Sierra Nevadas and Alaska.

Unlike all other airspace this airspace has different VFR Wx Minimums depending on time of day, the aircraft's proximity to the Class G airport, height above the ground (AGL) and height above sea level (MSL).

checklistItems.name: Special Use Airspace
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Many special use and other airspace areas are not very common, make sure to show the pilot examples of what each airspace looks like. If there is not one in the local area, refer to the following examples in order to show the pilot what they look like on a VFR Sectional or Terminal Area Chart. Websites with VFR charts and/or tablet applications make it easy to look up these areas without having to purchase the charts for examples. 

For all of these airspace types, discuss what activities occur there, how a pilot can find out hours of operation, dimensions and how to enter.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Use cross country flight planning scenarios traveling through areas with special use airspace to evaluate the pilots ability to apply their knowledge of special use airspace to flying in the US.

checklistItems.name: Prohibited Areas
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Example: Camp David

Don't even try to go here - it's prohibited. If there is a prohibited area nearby, show the pilot how to determine the top of that area.

Note Prohibited and Restricted areas have the same markings - a blue hashed boundary. Blue indicates more restrictive rules.

checklistItems.name: Restricted Areas
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Examples: Numerous restricted areas in the Western US, California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona

Make sure the pilot knows how to determine the floor and top of the airspace, active times and who the controlling agency is. Restricted airspaces are often "cold" on weekends, national holidays, and make great shortcuts when cold. 

Speaking with a Briefer, VFR Flight Following and querying ATC are methods to determine if the restricted area is active, or if the pilot may be allowed through the area when active.

Note Prohibited and Restricted airspace have the same markings - a blue hashed boundary. Blue indicates more restrictive rules.

checklistItems.name: Warning Areas
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Examples: Found off the coast in the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans and Gulf of Mexico

Planes straying into an active warning area may be shot down. Do not enter without coordination with ATC.

checklistItems.name: Military Operation Areas (MOAs)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Examples: Numerous military operations areas in the Western US, California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona. "Demo 1, 2 & 3" MOAs near Washington, DC.

Military training operations and exercises occur here. Jets are allowed to fly over 250 kts below 10,000 MSL when the MOA is active. Flying in an active MOA risks disrupting training operations. Recommend either avoiding when active or getting VFR flight following when flying in this airspace so ATC can direct the aircraft around the training operations as needed.

Ensure the pilot knows how to find the operating hours, dimensions, and controlling agency contact information on the VFR Sectional.

Note: MOAs and Alert Areas have the same markings - a magenta hashed boundary. These are less restrictive than Prohibited and Restricted areas.

checklistItems.name: Alert Areas
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Example: Travis Air Force Base (KSUU) 

Alert areas for military use are similar to MOAs except a waiver is required for aerobatic activities or airspeeds over 250 kts, etc. Treat Alert areas like MOAs when flight planning and flying VFR.

Ensure the pilot knows how to find the operating hours, dimensions, and controlling agency contact information on the VFR Sectional.

Note: MOAs and Alert areas have the same markings - a magenta hashed boundary. These are less restrictive than Prohibited and Restricted areas.

checklistItems.name: Miscellaneous Activity Areas
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Inclues operations like: Aerobatic Practice Area, Glider Operations, Hang Glider Activity, Ultralight Activity, Unmanned Aircraft Activity, Parachute Jumping Area with Frequency, Space Launch Activity Area

These areas may be charted, in the Chart Supplement and/or described in NOTAMS. A careful review of all three resources is needed to ensure safe flight in any location. Careful review of right of way rules is required when operating near gliders and ultralight aircraft. Parachute jumping areas need to be avoided when active if not coordinating with the jump pilot, and unmanned aircraft are not necessarily restricted to lower altitudes. High altitude (>400ft agl) UAS operations will be NOTAMed.

checklistItems.name: Controlled Firing Areas (CFAs)
checklistItems.teachingTips: These are not charted. The military uses spotter planes to shut down firing when non participating aircraft enter.

checklistItems.name: Special Flight Rules Areas (SFRA)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Example: Washington DC Special Flight Rules Area, Grand Canyon, Niagara Falls, Los Angeles Area, New York's Hudson River Corridor, Pearson Field near Vancouver, WA, etc.

Instructors can familiarize themselves with these areas nationwide in FAR Part 93. SFRAs are also indicated on the VFR Sectional with a blue SPECIAL NOTICE box describing where to get the special air traffic rules for the area. 

If training in an area with an SFRA make sure to include the specific rules in training. Otherwise the pilot needs to know they exist, how to find them, and that special rules apply to aircraft flying in those areas.

checklistItems.name: Special Air Traffic Rules (SATR)
checklistItems.teachingTips: These are the rules that govern operations in the SFRAs. The rules are defined in FAR Part 93 and found on VFR sectionals / in chart supplements that apply to an area that has an SFRA.

checklistItems.name: Local Airport Advisory (LAA)
checklistItems.teachingTips: These are found in Alaska only. They provide services similar to class D airports but operate when the tower is closed.

checklistItems.name: Military Training Routes (MTRs)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Military aircraft operate on these training routes at very high speeds. They may announce their activities on Guard (121.5) otherwise there is no communications requirement for these aircraft. 

Recall the altitudes the route uses by noticing the "backwards" numbering system. Routes with a 4 digit number have all segments below 1500 feet, routes with a 3 digit number have all segments above 1500 feet. 

Use Caution! There have been near midair collisions between military and non-military aircraft on these routes!

checklistItems.name: Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFR)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure the pilot understands the different reasons for TFRs and how to determine the TFR active time, dimensions, base and top, and procedures for operations in the TFR, if applicable.

Pilots can expect TFRs near any active fire fighting areas, even if there is not a TFR stay clear in order to avoid disrupting aerial firefighting activities. 

Stadium TFRs are not shown on the FAA's TFR Map webpage, but are shown in the TFR list. Stadiums are now depicted on aeronautical charts with a magenta diamond to help identify where potential stadiam TFRs may be. Most tablet applications will show active and planned stadium TFRs. Stadium TFRs do not extend more than 3,000 AGL. 

TFRs can pop up at any time. The best defense from violating a TFR is getting a recorded briefing from an FAA approved source, use VFR flight following, check for TFRs immediately before departure and, if possible, while en route.

checklistItems.name: Published VFR Routes
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Make sure pilots understand the difference between a VFR Transition Route, VFR Corridor and VFR Flyway. Pilots need to understand the rules for the VFR Transition Routes/Corridors prior to using them. 

Example: VFR Transition Routes and Corridors around New York City and Los Angeles - shown on the primary airport's Terminal Area Chart (TAC)

checklistItems.name: Terminal Radar Service Areas (TRSAs)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Example: TSRA around Palm Springs (KPSP), CA.

These are not common in the US anymore. It is similar to Class C airspace, except aircraft are not required to talk with ATC or receive traffic advisories unless entering the Class D airspace of the primary airport.

checklistItems.name: National Security Areas (NSAs)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Example: small NSA east of Livermore Airport (KLVK), CA

These may be charted or issued by NOTAM. Areas that pilots are asked to avoid flying in / through for reasons of national security.

checklistItems.name: Intercept Procedures
checklistItems.teachingTips: If a pilot does wander into a VIP TFR, Restricted or Prohibited Area or the Washington SFRA, etc. they can expect to be intercepted. Make sure the pilots know the intercept procedures and what to do if finding themselves escorted by one or more fighter jets. See the AOPA Intercept Procedures Card in the resource section.

checklistItems.name: Parachute Jumps (not permitted in Class A, B, C, or D without ATC authorization)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Show examples of the parachute symbol on local charts. 
Show where to look up drop zone locations and active times.
Encourage the use of flight following and/or monitoring the CTAF frequencies of airports with parachute activities nearby to avoid collisions with skydivers.

commonErrors.details: TFR's do not necessarily prohibit all aircraft from flight within their boundaries. Careful review of the published TFR will describe how aircraft are allowed to transit through, depart from or arrive at airports within the TFR area, if allowed. If unsure, remain clear!

VFR Flyways are often confused with VFR Transition Routes and Corridors. VFR Flyways are published examples of routes that aircraft can use to transition around Class B airspace without requiring ATC clearances. 

It is always recommended to get VFR flight following when operating near Class B and C airspace.

Pilots will commonly assume the lack of a charted symbol for specific operations means they are not occuring in that area. NOTAMS and the Chart Supplement are essential to identify all areas with unusual activity that may impact the safety of flight.

Many pilots believe they cannot fly through a MOA at all, or they can fly through with no repercussions. Neither is entirely accurate. Private pilots can enter and fly through MOAs without permission or contact with the controlling agency. However, it is prudent to get VFR flight following to help with separation from very fast moving military aircraft and to minimize disruption to training activities.
Be sure the pilot understands when they might be allowed to enter into the charted boundaries of a Restricted area (e.g., when it's not active, with permission, etc).

FAA knowledge testing on airspace will refer to "controlled" vs "uncontrolled" airspace. Any time the written test refers to uncontrolled airspace it is referring to Class G airspace. In those situations pay special attention to the aircraft's altitude above ground level and time of day.
"Uncontrolled" doesn't mean no rules for operation.

Absence of a parachute symbol on the chart does not mean there will be no parachute activity in an area. Charts are updated every 6 months. Drop zones can be added between updates. Not all drop zones are at airports. 
Briefers will often offer information about drop zones that are active but not charted.

Pilots are often unaware that transponders/ADS-B out are required when flying anywhere ABOVE class C airspace.

FAA knowledge testing often refers to the Class C "outer area". This is a 20 NM radius area around the primary airport of that Class C airspace. ATC will happily provide radar service (VFR flight following) to aircraft in this area. Pilots are not required to request those services however. 

Pilots who do not fly into Class C airports think they can simply contact the tower of the primary Class C airport to enter Class C airport, similar to Class D airspace. Emphasize contact needs to be made with the local approach facility first. Approach will provide a unique squawk and transition the pilot to the tower when appropriate.

A radar vector from ATC into Class B airspace is NOT a clearance into that airspace. Make sure pilots understand they MUST be "CLEARED INTO" or "CLEARED THROUGH" Class B before entering. If ATC mistakenly provides a vector into Class B airspace (or doesn't respond to radio calls) the pilot needs to remain clear.
Class A airspace does have a "top" which is FL600, above that is Class E.

Common misconception is controlled airspace means planes have to be under positive ATC "control" at all times. It does not. It does mean ATC exercises control of aircraft operating under instrument flight rules in that airspace.
The ADS-B requirement will go into effect on January 1, 2020. Any location a mode C transponder is required today will require ADS-B Out on and after that date.

Airspace violations are one of the most common VFR pilot deviations each year. They are also the easiest for the FAA to prove using ATC radar. Do not rely on tablet display to remain clear of airspace, ATC radar is less precise and may show the plane in airspace when the tablet display shows clear. When remaining clear of airspace remain at least 5 miles clear and several hundred feet above or below whenever possible. Be aware of transponder/ADS-B requirements when operating in/near class B and C airspace.
Make sure pilots understand that TRSA are not like other airspace where there is a requirement to enter, but rather it is a service that will help with traffic avoidance.

Pilots often think if ATC tells them to do something that is "two way radio communications" it is not. The ATC facility must state the aircraft's full tail number in order for two way radio communication to be established. "Aircraft calling standby" or even "Aircraft calling make 4 mile right base for runway 31" is not two way communication.

Pilots expect all pilots at non-towered Class E or G airports will use standard self announce procedures. This is not the case, it is extremely important that all pilots operating at these airports be looking for aircraft that are not speaking on the radios while operating near and at these airports.

Pilots are often unaware of the change in VFR Wx Minimums and Transponder/ADS-B requirements when operating over 10,000 MSL in Class E airspace.

activities.name: [06] PRE-SOLO: Radio Communications (III.A.K1-7: I.G: K1g)
activities.what: The procedure of communicating with ATC both with and without radio
activities.why: To efficiently communicate with ATC and enhance safety through clear exchange of information and clearances

checklistItems.name: Proper radio communication procedures and ATC phraseology
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots are often more afraid of radio communications than they are of flying. Assure them ATC is not the police and they will not lose their certificate if they flub a radio call. Some of the following techniques can help a pilot become more comfortable with radio work. 

If you operate at a towered airport, call the tower and request the opportunity to bring one or more of your students up on a tour. Getting to see the controllers face to face helps pilots become much more comfortable on the radios.

Provide an overview of the ATC system ... walk through an imaginary flight from the home airport to a towered airport destination of the pilot's choice. Talk through the hand offs and areas of responsibility of clearance delivery > ground > tower > TRACON > ARTCC > TRACON > tower > ground. 

Provide a simple formula for initial contact with ATC. Example: The 5 Ws. Who you're talking to. Who you are. Where you are. What you want to do or ask for. With ATIS code. Simulate the process with the pilot having them talk through what they would say and you pretend to be the ground controller, tower controller, etc, etc. Practice this in the classroom with a map of the airport and areas like the ramp, taxiways, run up areas and runways are drawn, then move a drawn plane about the map as the different radio calls are practiced. If the pilot is a more physical learner, practice outside with a chalk diagram of the airport on the ground they can walk around. 

It is helpful for a pilot to write out flash cards or a script of what they plan on saying and what ATC will reply back with. They can review the script prior to pushing the transmit button, which will reduce delays on frequency and potential errors. Practice the script for the day on the ground before getting into the airplane. Emphasize knowing what to say BEFORE hitting the transmit button. 

Encourage the pilot to borrow a handheld radio and spend a morning or afternoon at the home airport (or nearby towered airport) where the can watch the planes and hear the radio calls being made on ground and tower frequency. Being able to see the planes at the same time as hearing the radio calls is extremely helpful. While the pilot is at home they can listen to services like LiveATC.net to get used to what pilots say and what ATC says. In this case best to be listening to VFR tower and ground frequencies rather than TRACON or Center frequencies since those will be mostly IFR traffic. 

Simple instructions for how to respond to ATC: always use full tail number until ATC abbreviates first, read back all clearances, acknowledge information and say NOTHING when ATC tells the pilot to stand by. Emphasize the importance of reading back assigned runway numbers, taxiway letters, hold short instructions, and the aircraft tail number whenever provided an instruction including those items. Teach the power of the magic words "SAY AGAIN", "SAY AGAIN SLOWLY" and "UNABLE". When all else fails it is totally OK to speak plain English, tell the controller you are a student pilot and need an explanation or help.

Make sure the pilot is familiar with the AIM Chapter 4 Section 2 - Radio Communications Phraseology and Techniques, Pilot / Controller Glossary and the Non-Towered Airport Operations Advisory Circular 90-66B to learn proper radio communications procedures. 

Don't introduce radio work on the first lesson but do transition them to doing more and more radio calls as they train. A pilot needs to be fully competent on the radio before soloing at towered and non-towered airports.

checklistItems.name: Radio Equipment (Operation of Avionics)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Make sure the pilot knows how to operate all avionics in their aircraft including: how to select a radio to talk and/or monitor, how to program a frequency - especially how to select a X.X25 and X.X75 frequency - like 123.375, how to adjust squelch and side tone for their radio, how to monitor and speak on a frequency, how to know if they are monitoring or transmitting on a frequency, how to verify the radio is transmitting, how to test for reception and volume prior to contacting ATC, how to adjust the volume on their own headset together with the volume on the radios. 

Test and verify receive functions on both radios (if equipped) prior to contacting ATC. Then contacting ATC will help verify the transmit function. On some radios a small "TX" will appear on the radio or a light will flash when the pilot is transmitting.

checklistItems.name: How to obtain proper radio frequencies
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Frequencies are available in the Chart Supplement, in the airport description and on the airport diagram (if available) and on VFR Sectionals and Terminal Area Charts. The ATIS will include the tower frequency to use when approaching an airport. 

Discuss how frequencies may change between VFR chart publications and Chart Supplement publications. Check NOTAMs for the airport before flying. Check the Aeronautical Chart Bulletins in the Chart Supplement for changed and new frequencies for the departure, destination and alternate airports. Once published in the Aeronautical Chart Bulletin the frequency changes will no longer be NOTAMed.

Flight service frequencies are often included in the Chart Supplement for airports. Show the pilots how to determine flight service frequencies enroute using VORs and remote communications outlets. It is very valuable to demonstrate how to get updated weather information via Flight Services on at least one cross country flight. 

Many EFB apps do update and provide all relevant frequencies for each airport. Make sure to double check those frequencies before using.

checklistItems.name: Radar assistance
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Make sure to introduce the pilot to the benefits of using radar services from ATC early in their training. This gets the pilot used to talking with ATC, reduces "mic fright" and gets them used to working with ATC which can be an emergency resource for the pilot. 

Have the pilot review the AIM Chapter 4 Section 1 - Services Available to Pilots to learn more about the various services VFR pilots may take advantage of in the United States.  Benefits of radar services include: assistance with collision avoidance, radar vectors and directions, the ability to ask, real time, about the status of Restricted Areas, MOAs, and TFRs, improved situational awareness based on communications with other planes and easy access to emergency assistance because the pilot is already speaking with ATC who knows the pilot's aircraft type, destination, etc. 

Teach both methods of making initial contact with ATC to request VFR Flight Following. Unfortunately, some ATC facilities prefer all information in the initial contact, other facilities want as little information as possible. Let the pilot know which is prefered by the local facility. 

One method uses the PATER memory aid. P = position, A = altitude, T = type, E = equipment, R = request. Example: "Midtown Approach, Cessna 12345, over the ABC VOR at 3500 feet, 172/G requesting VFR Flight Following to Midtown airport. 

Second method is very short: "Midtown Approach, Cessna 12345, VFR Request" and then ATC will assign a squawk code and ask the pilot for the rest of the information when they are ready to listen. 

Ensure the pilot knows their aircraft type and equipment codes. Currently, ATC seems to prefer the old Domestic Flight Plan equipment codes like "/G" for GPS equipped rather than the more complex codes in the ICAO Flight Plan format.

checklistItems.name: Appropriate use of transponders
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Mode C transponders, if equipped, should be on and on ALT reporting when the aircraft is being operated, including on the ground. This is a change from earlier guidance which used to request transponders be on STDBY when on the ground. 

When entering a squawk code make sure to read back the assigned code and then enter it carefully. Check the transponder on every engine start up and verify the transponder is set to 1200 unless a unique squawk has been assigned. 

Unique transponder codes are required for operations in Class B airspace and whenever receiving VFR Flight Following/Radar Services.

checklistItems.name: Equipment issues that could cause loss of communication
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Discuss common causes of false radio failures including: incorrect frequency, volume too far down, headset not securely plugged in, transmitting or listening on the wrong radio, and being too far away from transmitter or receiver (in the case of being too far turning off the squelch may make it possible to receive successfully). Be sure to teach the pilot how to use the handheld mic and cabin speaker that installed in most airplanes. This can be used as a backup if the headset were to fail. Have them practice using this at least once during flight training so it won't be an unknown if they need it at some point in the future.

The radio will be one of the first things that fails when a plane's electrical system is failing or depleted due to alternator failure. Make sure to check the alternator and cycle the alternator if recommended by the POH when previously functional radios appear to be failing. 

Broken antennas or connections from radio to antenna can cause communications issues. During preflight verify all antennas are intact and without interference from debris. If a radio's functions are intermittent make sure an avionics technician checks the radio and connections between radio, antennas, and headset connectors.

checklistItems.name: Lost communication procedures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize troubleshooting and checking for common causes of false radio failures listed above as a first step when communications are lost. 

If receiving VFR flight following and the pilot is able to receive but not transmit ATC will usually have the pilot use the IDENT function on the transponder to acknowledge instructions from ATC. Continue the flight as instructed. 

If the pilot is not able to maintain two way communication (e.g. able to transmit but not receive or complete radio failure), squawk 7600. Consider landing at a nearby non-towered airport as soon as possible, then calling ATC to let them know the plane is on the ground safely. Alternately continue to the destination airport (towered or non towered), carefully enter the airspace and observe light gun signals for a landing clearance. 

Most modern headsets offer bluetooth functionality that will connect with the pilot's mobile phone. The pilot can use their phone in the air, if low enough. The clearance delivery phone numbers now published in the Chart Supplement for airports can be used to contact ATC the nearest TRACON or Center in case of lost communication in the air or on the ground.  It is also helpful to have the phone number of the local tower stored in the cell phone in case of lost communications. The pilot can talk to the tower and obtain their landing clearance by phone. 

Hand held radios are also helpful however, the majority have a weak transmission signal so the pilot may need to get quite close to the airport in order for the tower to hear the pilot's transmissions. Some hand held radios have connections for an external antenna which may provide more range.

checklistItems.name: ATC light signal recognition
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Teach the pilot to do their runup facing the tower if at all possible, this will allow the pilot to see light gun signals if they lose communications with the tower. 

Most commercially available kneeboards have the ATC light gun signals etched on them. If it is not, the pilot can make a card they can keep in their wallet or kneeboard for each access if needed or create a document they can access on their tablet in flight. 

Ensure the pilot knows how to acknowledge light gun signals at night and during the day. 

Most towered airports are happy to show pilots on the ground or in the air what light gun signals look like when requested. Make sure to do that at least once in the pilot's training so they know what to expect if they have a two way radio communications failure in flight.

checklistItems.name: FCC Radio License (for international flight)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
This is the 2nd "R" in the ARROW memory aid. This is only required for International Flight (e.g. flights into Canada, Mexico, etc.) 

To obtain a Restricted Radio Telephone license go to the FCC License Manager Link below. Register for a "FRN" and then request a ""Restricted Operator"" (RR) License. The license costs approximately $70 and requires no testing. Once the fee is paid and processed the pilot's license will be emailed to the email address used to obtain the FRN.

commonErrors.name: ATC light signal recognition
commonErrors.details: Pilots don't know what to do when they see (or are asked about) the red/green "exercise extreme caution" signal. This signal is similar to ATC telling the pilot about low level windshear, to watch for a flock of birds on final, or watch for a dog running on the taxiway. The pilot can proceed per the prior light gun signal.

commonErrors.name: Lost communication procedures
commonErrors.details: Communications are lost most often due to error rather than actual radio failure, emphasis of troubleshooting will help the pilot quickly resolve the situation the majority of the time.

commonErrors.name: Radar assistance
commonErrors.details:
When receiving radar services, if a pilot receives an instruction from ATC, they must proceed per that instruction unless the safety of flight is threatened or they obtain an amended clearance. This is sometimes inconvenient, but must be done. The pilot cannot simply cancel flight following to avoid following an instruction they don't want to do.

It is very common for pilots to get a new frequency, read it back quickly and incorrectly, then switch to the incorrect frequency before ATC has a chance to correct the frequency readback. When getting new frequencies from ATC, take time to write the new frequency down, read it back, and pause for a second before switching frequencies. This lets ATC correct if needed, and the pilot will then have a record of good frequencies on the flight in case of a mistaken frequency input.

commonErrors.name: Appropriate use of transponders
commonErrors.details: Pilots often forget to reset their transponder to 1200 at the completion of a flight. Ensure the pilot verifies the correct transponder code on start up.

commonErrors.name: Equipment issues that could cause loss of communication
How to obtain proper radio frequencies
commonErrors.details:
Pilots often do not double check and verify the frequency printed on the chart is actually current. 

Inexperienced pilots will often contact a Class C tower directly prior to entry into Class C airspace, this is incorrect. Ensure they know how to determine the correct frequency to contact prior to entry into Class C airspace using the VFR chart and/or Chart Supplement.

commonErrors.name: FCC Radio License (for international flight)
commonErrors.details: On occasion a pilot, if asked, will recite the ARROW memory aid without understanding what the FCC license is for or when they need it. It's important they know when various portions of acronyms apply.

commonErrors.name: Proper radio communication procedures and ATC phraseology
commonErrors.details:
Radio communications require careful listening and situational awareness to verify instructions received are intended for the aircraft. If ATC issues an instruction that doesn't make sense, ask for clarification! Do not just blindly do as asked as ATC can make mistakes as well. In the end the pilot is the final authority and responsibility for the safe conclusion of the flight, not ATC. Remember: ""If a pilot makes a mistake, a pilot gets hurt. If a controller makes a mistake, a pilot gets hurt."" 

Pilots not using the correct location on initial contact with ATC. For example, contacting Ground Control and mistakenly stating they are in front of the terminal building out of habit, because that's what they normally do, when they are actually at an FBO. ATC cannot see your tail number from a long distance, and, if they see a plane of the same type sitting at the terminal building they will issue a taxi clearance based on the location provided. In addition, numerous near mid-air collisions have happened due to pilots not stating their actual position - out of habit or lack of understanding, responding to clearances intended for other planes, etc. 

Pilots do not know what is required for "two way radio communications" to be established and the difference between two way radio communications and a clearance. ATC must state the aircraft's full tail number for two way radio communication to be established. 

Pilots speak immediately after switching frequencies. This is potentially dangerous, a pilot may block an important communication for another plane. Teach pilots to switch frequencies and then pause for a breath or two before speaking.  Also, it is not required to respond as fast as possible. Take time to understand what was said and formulate a response, then key the mic and talk.

Pilots using slang or radio communications procedures for other disciplines, e.g. police radio phonetic alphabet, slang like "10-4",  "got him on the fish finder", "rolling", etc. are unacceptable.  Make sure the pilot is aware of and reviews the aviation phonetic alphabet and the Pilots/Controllers Glossary.

Pilots think they have to wait for the pilots they hear on the same frequency several airports away to finish talking before they can talk. When several airports are on the same frequency a pilot's transmission will be heard at the local airport primarily and distant communications will not interfere. 

Beware of expectation bias. This is the fact that people tend to hear what the expect to hear. If flying at a familiar airport and hearing the same clearance 99 times it is very easy to hear that same clearance the 100th time just to find out what the pilot read back was wrong. This is another reason pilots are required to do complete readbacks of runway numbers, taxiways and hold short instructions, not just say "Roger" or "Wilco".

commonErrors.name: Radio Equipment (Operation of Avionics)
commonErrors.details:
Pilots who do not know how to adjust squelch or headset volume knob will often turn up the volume on the radios to ear deafening levels. 

Verify the volume high enough that will hear ATC's response when received. One way to do this is turn down the volume, turn off squelch, and slowly turn up the volume to a comfortable but clear level. Then turn off squelch. Using the radio to check for ATIS or automated weather is another method to ensure the volume is up high enough.

activities.name: [08] PRE-SOLO: Operation of Systems: Electrical Systems (I.G: K1f, K2)
activities.what: The subject matter concerning the operation of the aircraft's electrical controls, components, and power sources
activities.why: To enhance understanding and therefore safety in operating the aircraft

checklistItems.name: Overview
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Create a “kindergarten” drawing of a typical airplane electrical system, rather than use a diagram from the POH or PHAK, which can be overwhelming to pilots who’ve never been exposed to electrical diagrams.

In today’s world, we need more electrical power than ever before. But historically, many pre-World War II airplanes didn’t have electrical systems at all. That’s hard to imagine given the profusion of electrical gadgets we now have, but it’s worth pointing out to pilots as a way of dramatically illustrating the essential message that the electrical system isn’t needed for flight.

It's realatively simple to build a model of the electical system using things like LED lights, alligator clip test wires, a battery pack, a small electric motor, etc. You can then design a series of simple circuits that show the various parts of the electricl system. (see picture in prep section)

checklistItems.name: Aircraft equipment that uses electrical power
checklistItems.teachingTips: In flight, have the pilot shut down master switch to observe which avionics still function. (Allows discernment of pitot/static and battery-backup systems, vs. systems totally dependent on a direct feed from the electrical system.)

checklistItems.name: Bus bar
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots can think of the bus bar like a power strip (a positive transfer of knowledge!).

checklistItems.name: Sources of power (alternator/generator)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
You can build a mini generator (good for teaching the magneto as well). Coil wire around a stick like object (e.g. dowel, large bolt, etc.). Then hook a small multimeter up to each end of the wire. You can hold the coil of wire and have the pilot run a relatively strong magnet back and forth along the coil. The multimeter will show a slight flow of electricty. Point how varying the speed of the magnet creates more or less electrical flow. It's a good way to make the idea of generating electricity into a concrete concept. Follow up by expanding into how an alternator uses an electromagnet to create a consistent amount of electricity at a wide rage of rpm settings. (See picture in prep section)

Remember those little spinning exercise wheels for hamsers and gerbils? The little critters run and run, and the wheel spins. Pilots can think of generators and alternators as the opposite tech. Instead of energy wasted spinning the wheel, the spinning wheel generates eletricity, and, of course, the hamsters or gerbils have turned into magnets!

checklistItems.name: Master Switch (Battery and Alternator side)
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots can think of the master like the "on-off" switch on the power strip.

checklistItems.name: Voltage regulator/ Alternator Control Unit (ACU)
checklistItems.teachingTips: Works like a noodle strainer for electricity, it lets water (proper power levels) through while holding back the macaroni (spikes).

checklistItems.name: Ammeters and Loadmeters
checklistItems.teachingTips: Tip to help pilots tell the two apart: A Load meters are like bathroom scales, they only measure what is loaded onto them.

checklistItems.name: Fuses and circuit breakers
checklistItems.teachingTips: The system works just like the “fuse box” in the pilot’s house.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: On ramp after engine start, have pilot experiment with pulling various circuit breakers to visualize the shut downs.

checklistItems.name: Overcharge/Voltage Regulator Failure
checklistItems.teachingTips: The main idea to emphasize it that an overcharge could lead to a fire. It's putting too much pressure into a water hose or pipe - let it build and something will break. It's also a good time to emphasize why's important to know the voltage output of the alternator and the battery. Then the pilot can monitor if the alternaor is providing its typical level of power. If the charge is way over - you know have an overcharge. If the level of charge is at or below the battery output level, you know you're running on battery power.

checklistItems.name: Low voltage light or annunciator
checklistItems.teachingTips: Provides instructors with an excellent ADM scenario. Suggestion: You are on a crosscountry flight in marginal VFR conditions, approixmently 45 minutes out from your destination, when the low volt light comes on. What cross checks are available to you to help you better understand the failure? What systems are at risk? Can/should you continue to your destination, or should you divert?

checklistItems.name:
Alternator failure
Electrical malfunction
checklistItems.teachingTips:
A good topic for scenario-based training!

Pilots can compare a failure of the alternator to having a low cell phone battery. With a low cell phone, un-needed apps are closed to preserve the remaining charge. In a plane we shutdown all but the most needed sytems for the same reason.

In more advanced flight training, the instructor can surreptitiously pull a circuit breaker in flight. For instance, if so equipped, electric flaps can be disabled. Will the pilot recognize the problem, or just operate the switch?
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Tips for teaching load sheading when attempting to maximize battery life: Heat=hungry. Circuits that convert electricity to heat (pitot heat, lights) devour a lot more power than systems that don’t. Hungry circuits are also fat, so larger “numbered” circuit breakers or larger fuses control subsystems that eat more power than lower rated ones.

checklistItems.name: Electrical fire
checklistItems.teachingTips: Take pilot though process of troubleshooting the location of an electrical fire by bringing one system at a time online following a total shutdown of the system. Teach them to only consider restarting systems that are critical for the flight. It's a good scenario opportunity to discuss what is critical for varioius types of flights or situations.

checklistItems.name: Ground Power Unit (GPU) receptacle and use
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots can picture these systems as extension cords for airplanes.

commonErrors.details:
Assuming the engine will quit when the Master Switch is turned off.
- A brand-new pilot may assume the engine will quit if the electrical system will fail, so shutting down the master in flight provides a dramatic reassurance.
Possible confusion on reading the “minus to plus” on ammeter vs. the load meter’s “zero and up” indication. (See the teaching tip for a suggestion.)

Not being aware that generators on older airplanes don’t produce enough juice at low RPM to keep up with the plane’s needs.
-Instructors, if teaching in airplanes with generators, need to bief students on power management during taxi. In newer planes, instructors should make pilots aware of the older systems, as pilots may encounter them in the future.

Thinking the GPU can be used to charge a dead battery.
- Clarify for the pilot that the GPU is only for helping start the engine on a cold day or for extended ground operation (e.g., practicing avioincs usage). A dead battery requires removal as charging it in the airplane could lead to a fire.

Resistance or anxiety about learning a "complex" system.
- Some pilots are resistant to learning the nuts of bolts of systems, so instructors should make it clear the purpose of understanding the stucture of the system is to provide the knowledge required to properly troubleshoot failures.

Confusion on procedures when transitioning aircraft.
- Checklists vary between airplane models, instructors can keep copies of checklists from planes with different work flows to demonstrate this.

Not realizing the some avionics, such as attitude indictors, come in both electric and “air-driven” versions. 
- Instructors, when briefing the pilot on the system in the training plane should take the oppertunity to inform pilots of differing tech in other airplanes.

activities.name: [21] X/C: Navigation Systems and Radar Services (VI.B)
activities.what: The subject matter of using ATC radar facilities or radio/satellite navigation aids to follow a course from one desired point to another
activities.why: To enable the pilot to efficiently and successfully guide the airplane from departure to destination with the aid of ATC or radio navigation

checklistItems.name:
VOR Overview
- Very High Frequency (VHF) Omnidirectional Range (VOR)
- What it is and what it does
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Use a VOR on a TAC chart during the explanation as it is easier to understand the concept of radials when you can see them.

When the VOR is in operation, one "beam" sweeps 360° while another goes on/off like a beaco. Simular to the way a lighthouse works, the beams sweep in a circle while the light on top goes on/off. The time between where the sweep beam is and the on/off results in "phase variance" which is a fancy way of saying where the beam is on its sweep. This is how we determine what radial the aircraft is on.

Stress the need to IDENTIFY the VOR when you intend to use it, and that you do not need to know Morse code to use a VOR. If you can tell a meow from a bark, you can tell a dot from a dash.

The VOR is a circa 1940s navigational aide that is still in use today. Note that VORs connect airline and IFR routes. This is important because it means the airspace in the vicinity of the VORs can be very busy as aircraft converge on the stations.

Show the client the symbology for the VORTAC (shaped like a Roman shield, usually they were established by the military), a regular VOR (hex bolt), and a VOR DME (hex bolt in the box). 

Use a Chart Supplement Directory to show the pilot where to find VOR test facilities. While testing is not required for VFR flights, explain that under IFR the VOR must be checked/tested every 30 days. It is wise to check VOR accuracy periodically for VFR flying even though it isn't mandated. Explain the record needs the date, place, bearing error and signature of the person doing the VOR check which can be a courtesy to help out IFR pilots using the plakne. Teaching tip: teach the VOR check lesson in a simulator THEN do it again while in the airplane.
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Determining your location
- Centering the Course Deviation Indicator (CDI) and interpreting a FROM indication
- Using a FROM indication to determine radial and direction from the VOR
- Using 2 VORs to triangulate location
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If available, demonstrate the use of a VOR in a flight simulator or a VOR teaching tool (e.g., FlyGo's "IFR Flight" app). Having the ability to pause and show the airplane's position on a map will make learning to use them much easier.

Use the FROM indication to determine the aircraft position in relation to the VOR. The way most people process directional information is with a "from", example "Where is the city of Cupertino, California? It is approximately 45 miles from San Francisco."

Using a simulator, have the client perform "TIMS": Tune, Identify, Monitor, then Set the VOR with a from indication, then pause the sim to note where the "aircraft" is in relation to the VOR. Note VOR radials that pass over obvious checkpoints like airports.

Still in the sim, use two VORs to triangulate the "aircraft position." Do this two or three times, then repeat this lesson in the real aircraft, noting the terrain the aircraft is over and cross referencing the position with the VFR sectional and/or TAC.

Using a computer or app based VOR simulator is a powerful and effective way to teach VOR concepts. Check your app store or a do an internet search to find what is available for your device.

checklistItems.name:
Navigating with a VOR
- Tracking a course outbound (FROM) and inbound (TO)
- Intercepting and tracking a desired course
- Correcting for wind drift (bracketing)
- Station passage indications and techniques
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Stress that TO is short for TOWARD and FR is short for FROM, or the apex of the triangle on the TO/FROM indicator should be pointed at the nose of the aircraft when flyings TOWARD a VOR and to the tail of the airplane when tracking away FROM the VOR.

Stress that since the VOR is "line of sight" we need sufficient altitude to clear any obstacles, such as mountains. Note that some radials of the VOR may be "unusable" because they are obstructed by mountains and the radials become unreliable.

Determine your position with the FROM and center up the CDI needle. Note aircraft's current position, then determine the desired course and intercept angle. 

Draw VOR as seen from above on a whiteboard showing the radials and their reciprocals (e.g., 360 FR/180 TO). Explain that interception angles will never be more than 90 degrees. Suggested rule of thumb: do not use an intercept angle greater than about 30-45 degrees to help prevent overshooting the course. 

Use a paper funnel to illustrate the "cone of confusion" noting that when flying over the station, directional indications will be lost and the pilot should maintain heading until the signal is re-established on the new side. Also note that the closer the aircraft gets to the station the closer the radials are to each other, therefore any course corrections should be minimal. Stress the need to be patient when watching for needle movement. However if the needle does not move after a period of time, check to make sure the VOR is set up correctly and consider increasing the intercept angle. When determining an intercept angle, it is typically best to avoid angles of more than 30 to 45 degrees at most.

Attempt wind correction angle at first of 10 degrees -- use the phrase "put the nose into the wind." Relate the process to the concept of a swimmer being swept downstream with the airplane as the "swimmer." If the swimmer swims at an angle, like the putting the airplane's nose into the wind, the swimmer can make a straight path across the river. 

In the sim have pilot fly directly over a VOR and watch the TO/FROM indicator flip while noting station passage. Do this a second time but allow the pilot to be slightly off course by perhaps 5 degrees. Have the pilot hold heading when passing over the station and then for an additional two minutes or so until the aircraft is approximately 5 miles from the VOR to resume tracking. This method will help the pilot avoid overcorrecting while tracking close to the VOR station.

Teach the pilot about the hazard of reverse sensing. Stress that the magnetic compass and heading indicator need to be in correcty aligned. Set the OBS for the desired course and orientation - make sure that the TO/FROM indication is correct. Then use the OBS to determine the desired heading and intercept angle. Warn the pilot that if the VOR indication is set 180 degrees or thereabouts opposite the the aircraft's heading or desired course, reverse sensing is likely. Demonstrate the silly pilot trick of trying to chase the needle during reverse sensing - then correct the VOR OBS.

Teaching tip: Picture your airplane at the bottom of the VOR indicator, then check the mag compass against the Heading Indicator, then against the OBS. Note: HSIs do not get reverse sensing because the OBS/CDI rotates with the heading indicator.

checklistItems.name:
Planning and using a VOR course
- Where to find them on a navigation chart
- Tuning and identing a VOR
- Victor airways
- Traffic hazards over and near VORs and intersections
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Use a sectional and the corresponding TAC chart, if available, to show the Victor Airways. Explain that they are "highways in the sky," and therefore can be very busy. Note the "V" designation on the radial that names the Victor Airway and the number in the box along the route that denotes the distance between stations. 

Show the pilot how to find the frequencies of the VORs and their identifiers. Stress that not all VORs are located at airports as some are stand alone out in the middle of nowhere VORs.
Explain that Victor Airways are 8 NM wide and that is hard to see on the sectional.

Stress the need to note the terrain along the VOR route. Your aircraft may not have the climb capability for a straight on approach, you may have to circle or zig-zag to gain altitude.

Note how to estimate changeover points as well as intersecting radials on the chart/sectional. 

Describe VORs like a hub. All aircraft on Victor Airways that terminate or begin at the hub have to pass over the hub consequently causing potential aircraft congestion. Encoruage the pilot to keep their head on a swivel scanning for traffic.

checklistItems.name:
Additional navigation displays/equipment
- Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI)
- Radio Magnetic Indicator (RMI)
- Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If available, demonstrate the operation of each of these displays in a flight simulator or a VOR teaching tool (e.g., FlyGo's "IFR Flight" app). Having the ability to pause and show the airplane's position on a map will make learning to use these instruments much easier.

The Horizontal Situation Indicator is a cross between a VOR and a Heading Indicator EXCEPT for the fact the HSI uses a magnetometer to automatically keep it aligned with the earth's magnetic field. It also does not suffer from reverse sensing like the typical heading/OBS comination.

The Radio Magnetic Indicator (RMI) is a combination of the HSI and the Automatic Direction Finder (ADF) and/or VOR. The arrow on the ADF, when properly tuned to a Non Directional Beacon on the ground, will point to the station. (The ADF has been removed from the Airmen Certification Standards for Private Pilots, but if there is one in the airplane or the airplane has an RMI, you better know how to use it.) When the RMI is functioning, the ADF arrow points to the NDB or VOR on the ground. To determine the BEARING to the station, take the aircraft heading, then measure from the nose of the aircraft to the heading the ADF is pointing to. This is called the RELATIVE BEARING. The MH + the RB = the Magnetic Bearing to the station. Stress that the RMI combines a Heading Indicator, a relative bearing indicator and a magnetomer.

Have the client identify the RMI needle and the ADF needle. Stress that once you figure out where the ADF is pointing to you have a frame of reference from which to orient yourself.

If the aircraft has Distance Measuring Equipment, find the correct annunciator panel before you need it. Since it is easy for the pilot to become dependent on DME to determine distances, use it sparingly at first. A good lesson is on hazy days where things look farther away than they are. Use the DME to identify distances from blatant checkpoints such as airports, noting "The DME says we are 10 miles from airport (insert name here) that's what ten miles of visibility looks like. Either in the sim or in the air use the DME to identify a location such as a VOR or an airport. While you fly, have the pilot 'count down' the DME -- noting that it will NEVER read zero because of slant range.

checklistItems.name:
Global Positioning System (GPS)
- Overview of how it works
   - CDI button
- Functions
   - Direct To
   - Nearest Airport/VOR, etc
- Flight plan
   - VFR waypoints (reference Terminal Area Charts)
   - Programming
- Limitations
   - "Head down" time while programming (e.g., traffic/obstacle avoidance)
   - Selective Availability
   - RAIM Capability
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If able, you may want to delay the introduction of GPS until the later stages of training because there is a tendency to hit DIRECT TO and forget everything else.

CLR: the oops button, go back when you make a mistake.

ENT: Enter or YES button. 

FPL: Flight plan.

Big part of knob is CHAPTER, small part of knob is PAGES.

Demonstrate scrolling through and editing a flight plan, including reversing the flight plan for a round robin flight.

Explain the concept of satellites and the "constellation of satellites" and the importance of checking RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) before you need it. Think of RAIM like bars on a cellphone -- if the guidance gets "dropped" it could prove deadly. Always check RAIM prior to flight.

Define each button and its functions: Direct To plots a path DIRECTLY TO a place, like an airport .
Course Deviation Indicator: or CDI is a needle like on the VOR -- if the needle is to the right the airplane needs to fly to the right to get on course, if the needle to the left turn the airplane to the left to get on course. 

Flight plans can be programmed "on the fly" but better yet, before taxi and takeoff. Use VFR waypoints on TAC charts to build flight plans. Program as much as you can BEFORE the aircraft taxis.

Remind the pilot that the magenta line will NOT keep you out of airspace or terrain or from hitting obstacles - you have to look outside.

If available, this is a lesson to do in the sim at first as it is easier to learn GPS buttonology on the ground than in the air.

checklistItems.name: Radar assistance to VFR aircraft (e.g., operations, equipment, available services, traffic advisories)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If able, use Flight Following in the practice area. Not only does it give you another layer of protection, it also gets the client used to having another voice in the cockpit and using a squawk code other than 1200. Stress that just because we are in "radar contact" this does not mean we do not have to keep our eyes outside during the flight. When we are squawking VFR, even with ADS-B, ATC may/will give us a heads up about other traffic on a workload permitting basis.

If you are flying an aircraft that does not have an engine driven electrical system, the concept of a transponder/ADS-B may be alien to the pilot. Walk the pilot through the FAA's procedures of calling ahead to towered airports under Mode C veil, and the FAA's ADS-B ADAPT program.** ADS-B implementation is relatively new and there is still a 'learning curve' for both pilots and FAA. Encourage the pilot to check on a monthly basis for updates/changes to policy and procedures.

checklistItems.name:
Transponder (Mode(s) A, C, and S)
- What it does and overview of how it works
- Regulatory and airspace requirements (e.g., Class B, above 10,000 MSL, etc.)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Explain that a Transponder is basically a radio that when interrogated with a signal from ATC lights up on their scope so the controller can see your aircraft. When we are asked to IDENT, it is like raising your hand in a crowded classroom. Aircraft that have engine driven electrical systems are required to have transponders. Other aircraft, like J-3 Cubs for example which have NO electrical systems, are not required to have them. As such must stay clear of airspace that requires a transponder such as Class B and airspace above 10,000 feet MSL. Stress the reason for non-transponder aircraft limitation in certain airspace is because it is very busy with typically fast moving aircraft.

Since the FAA directed that transponders should be on during taxi operations, it is a little more unsual for pilots to turn them off. However, be sure the pilot understands how the transponder can be set to OFF, STBY (standby, allowing it to warm up or cool down), ALT for Altitude, and OFF.
There are transponder codes that should be committed to memory:
1200 VFR flight
7500 Hijacking "75, I've been taken alive"
7600 radio failure  "76, get that radio fixed!"
7700 Emergency (anything from low fuel to medical issue to lost, etc.) "77 I'm prayin' to Heaven! I've got an emergency on board!"

commonErrors.name: Confusing the needles on the RMI
commonErrors.details: Fortunately they are often different colors and outlines -- one color for the ADF needle and another for the VOR. Stress the importance of determining which needle is which before you need to use them for navigation.

commonErrors.name: Fixating on DME to determine when over the checkpoint
commonErrors.details: This does not work very well as DME is slant range and will never read zero when over the checkpoint. Stress the need to look out the window and visually identify checkpoint.

commonErrors.name: Pushing random buttons without knowing their function.
commonErrors.details: Teach buttonology on the ground, or in a simulator, if available.

commonErrors.name: Negative transference occurs when the client knows a little about one system and it is incorrect procedure for the GPS to be used.
commonErrors.details: Stress the proper programming techniques. Do not attempt to use the GPS in a high workload flight until you know how to use that particular model.

commonErrors.name: Failure to ensure the GPS is connected to the navigational round dial, as in it is on GPS rather than VLOC
commonErrors.details: Always double check that, to make sure you are reading the correct system and that the correct annunciator light is illuminated

commonErrors.name: Failure to cross reference terrain beneath the aircraft with what is shown on the sectional/TAC to verify the position
commonErrors.details: It's easy get lost in the cockpit and forget to look outside. Train the pilot to constantly look outside by asking them to identify landmarks, potential landing sites, airports, etc

commonErrors.name: Failure to check RAIM before flight.
commonErrors.details: Insist upon it as part of the preflight check

commonErrors.name: Programming while taxing
commonErrors.details: Equate programming and taxiing to texting and driving and stress that it is NOT done

commonErrors.name: Over-reliance on ATC to keep us safe
commonErrors.details: While ATC participation can help, it is still up to the pilot to keep eyes outside and SEE and AVOID other traffic

commonErrors.name: Not recognizing that the controller sees the aircraft's ground track, not heading and as such the traffic calls are in response to the aircraft's track over the ground.
commonErrors.details: When looking for traffic when flying crabbed into the wind it would be wise to search the airspace in a 90 degree arc in reference to the position of the traffic.

commonErrors.name: Confusing the HSI with a common VOR.
commonErrors.details: If the client is training in an aircraft with an HSI or there is one in the fleet or in the simulator, make sure the client sees it and uses it, even if it is not the normal aircraft used for training.

commonErrors.name: Loss of situational awareness when becoming too dependent on the magenta line.
commonErrors.details: Stress that the GPS is a "nice to have" in the aircraft but it does not relieve the pilot from learning how to use the VORs, "Mark 1 Eyeball" (looking out the window), and the magnetic compass for navigation

commonErrors.name: Trying to make a course correction while within the cone of confusion before station passage.
commonErrors.details: Patience, Grasshopper! Patience! Because the radials are so close together over the station like the spokes on the hub of a wagon wheel, any attempt to correct will likely be an over correction. Better to establish a heading and stay on it until out of the cone of confusion, such as positive station passage plus a minute or so, then make the correction.

commonErrors.name: Flying low to avoid 'tripping' the airspace when the transponder is required
commonErrors.details: Teach the client that they can call the controlling agency if need be to get permission to enter their airspace without a transponder.

commonErrors.name: Failure to compensate for winds aloft when attempting to track a radial.
commonErrors.details: Be sure to stress the need to determine what the winds aloft are when using a VOR. Remember the phrase "nose into the wind" meaning put the aircraft's nose into the wind to compensate for wind drift

commonErrors.name: Impatience for the interception angle to work resulting over-correction.
commonErrors.details: Try using a timer to allow 1 min or 2 minutes to allow the correction angle to work

commonErrors.name: Using too large of a correction angle to intercept or track a radial, resulting in "S-turns across a radial.
commonErrors.details: This will take practice -- it is called bracketing and should be taught. If 20 degrees is too much, reduce it to 10 degrees, etc.

commonErrors.name: Losing situational awareness when attempting to capture a radial of a VOR.
commonErrors.details: Mitigate this by determining what radial the aircraft is ON, the determine what correction angle, if any, needs to be made to intercept.

commonErrors.name: Failure to indentify the VOR before selecting the radial to use.
commonErrors.details: Use the TIMS acronym: Tune, Identify, Monitor, Set before use

commonErrors.name: Failure to keep the aircraft on course while twisting the OBS of the second VOR to triangulate the aircraft's position
commonErrors.details: Teach the client to trim the aircraft for hands-off flight, THEN twist the second OBS for cross radial.

commonErrors.name: Failure to set the transponder to altitude prior to taxi or takeoff.
commonErrors.details: Make transponder check part of the pretakeoff flow. One good memory aid is "Lights, Camera, Action!" before taking the runway. Lights = options like strobes, landing light, etc. Camera = Transponder. Action = Mixture full rich (as appropriate) and throttle up.

commonErrors.name: Twisting the OBS until the needle centers up without noting if the ambiguity indicator is showing a TOWARD or FROM indication
commonErrors.details: Verify heading FROM the VOR or heading TOWARD the VOR. Allow the client to experience reverse sensing at least once so that they can see how it sneaks up on the pilot.

commonErrors.name: Not understanding that the VOR is LINE OF SIGHT and therefore not a reliable means of navigation below certain altitudes.
commonErrors.details: Obtain a copy of the Chart Supplement and go to the VOT page. Find the local VOR checkpoints in your area and note the altitude restrictions, then cross reference the checkpoint with a VFR sectional. Also refer the pilot to section 1-1-8 of the AIM to show them the range and altitudes limits of VORs

commonErrors.name: Reluctance to learn to use the VOR because of the ease of use of the GPS.
commonErrors.details: The magenta line and the Direct To button can make pilots lazy. Explain that the VOR is still part of a Pilot's navigational "tool kit" and knowing how to use a VOR is very much like knowing how to drive a stickshift -- you never know when you will need that skill.

commonErrors.name: Inability to find the Morse Code identifier or the frequency on the Sectional/TAC chart.
commonErrors.details: Find it before you leave the ground, and perhaps make a list on your kneeboard for quick reference.

commonErrors.name: Failure to quickly identify the VORs on the VFR sectional/TAC
commonErrors.details: Spend some time on the ground finding these things BEFORE you need them. Recommend using a TAC chart as the VOR compass rose tends to get buried in the cluttered symbology of the sectional chart.

commonErrors.name: Chasing the needle during reverse sensing, not figuring out that you are going the wrong way until the needle has given you a 90 degree deflection.
commonErrors.details: Allow reverse sensing to happen at least once -- make it a teachable moment, doing it on purpose so the pilot can see the indication of reverse sensing. The VOR shows you trying to track the 180 radial but you are heading north and every "correction" you make only puts you more off course. Use the magnetic compass and heading indicator to regain situational awareness.
