activities.name: [22] X/C: Cross-Country Flight Planning (I.D and VI.A)
activities.what: The process of preparing for and piloting an aircraft from a departure to a desired destination
activities.why: To navigate safely and efficiently

checklistItems.name:
Aeronautical Charts:
   - Sectional Charts
   - VFR Terminal Area Charts
  - Airport diagrams
Basic map and geography knowledge
  - Latitude and Longitude (Meridians and Parallels)
  - Time Zones
  - Variation
  - Magnetic Variation
  - Magnetic Deviation
  - Deviation
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
There is so much to learn when beginning cross-country practice that it can be helpful to start the pilot with the big picture, and move into details slowly. Start with a broad overview of how the Earth (the place they fly) and the charts (the tools they fly with) are different. Work down into specific charts and explain the concept of lat/long division and scale. Given the huge range of information presented on aeronautical charts, it can be helpful to consider each one as a series of layers. Ask the pilot to pick out physical layers, informational layers, and airspace layers. 

When first explaining difficult concepts such as variation and deviation, it can be helpful to start on the why and hold the how for the second step. 

Because most new pilots will use tablets during training it is essential to cover these concepts for both electronic and traditional charts. Many electronic charts, for example, don't include margin information, such as the active times of special use airspace and the legend.
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Route planning 
  - Classes and special use airspace (SUA) 
  - Selection of appropriate and available navigation/communication systems and facilities.
  - Altitude selection accounting for terrain and obstacles, glide distance of the airplane, VFR cruising altitudes, and the effect of wind.
  - Use of Chart Supplement U.S. (formerly Airport/Facility Directory)
  - Airplane Flight Manual or Pilot’s Operating Handbook (AFM/POH)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Again, start big and then go down to details. Begin by laying out the entire route, and  take a big picture over the type of airspace and terrain the route will cover. Consider things not immediately apparent on charts, such as vast rural areas, where an off-airport landing would require more time before a rescue. Although it can make sense to go direct many times, introduce the concept of shorter legs within a flight. This has many benefits. It introduces the concept of risk early in the planning, and it gives the new pilot a mindset of flexibility and problem solving. A trip from Maryland to Tennessee, for example, will travel the spine of the Adirondack mountains. While the risk may not be as great for CFIT as it is out west, the mountains produce poor weather and leave few good off-airport landing sites. Ask the pilot for creative ways to reduce risk, such as going direct across the mountains before turning off course. The same is true of special use airspace, Class B areas, water, and many other things.

Altitude selection is as important as route selection. Begin with maximum elevation figures and work up from there, taking into account weather, aircraft performance, and route length. Don't simply settle for 3,000 AGL each time. Teach the pilot to make the altitude selection a deliberate choice based on all available information.

checklistItems.name:
Basic Calculations
  - Time T = D/GS
  - Distance D = GS X T
  - GS GS = D/T
  - Converting Minutes to Equivalent Hours
  - Converting Knots to Miles Per Hour
  - Fuel Consumption
  - Fuel requirements, to include reserve
  - Flight Computers
  - Time, climb and descent rates, course, distance, heading, true airspeed, and groundspeed
  - Estimated time of arrival to include conversion to universal coordinated time (UTC)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Make sure the pilot knows how to make E6B calculations in addition to any electronic aids they may use. Also important with electronic calculations is to verify them. After inputting a route, it's a good idea to view the trip completely and verify that the time, fuel, and distance make sense.

checklistItems.name:
Charting the Course
  - Steps in Charting the Course
  - Plotter
  - Pilotage
  - Dead Reckoning
  - Wind Triangle or Vector Analysis
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Teach the pilot the differences between pilotage, dead reckoning, and using electronic aids. Then discuss scenarios where each may be appropriate to use. Pilotage may be the best option for short flights, whereas a combination of all three may be appropriate for longer trips. Right from the beginning of the training the pilot should be exercising judgement and you should be giving them the room to be able to do so. Although most flight planning is formulaic, it's important to verify the pilot's decision making through this process. As with the route calculations, make sure the pilot understands the uses and limitations of electronic aids as well as physical tools. 

Plus, spend time teaching the student how to select good checkpoints, and on subsequent flights let him or choose their own. That will give them a real-world evaluation of their skills.

commonErrors.name: Failing to consider environmental factors (e.g. airspace, weather, and terrain) during route selection.
commonErrors.details: Many pilots automatically start with a straight line between the departure and destination. That may be appropriate for some flights, but not all. Discuss early in cross-country training the virtues of flying shorter legs with deviations around airspace, weather, terrain, and more.

activities.name: [09] PRE-SOLO: Operation of Systems: Airframe Systems (I.G: K1d-e, g, l, j, l, K2)
activities.what: The subject matter concerning the mechanical operation of the aircraft's airframe systems
activities.why: To enhance understanding and therefore safety in operating the aircraft

checklistItems.name:
Fuel Systems
- Gravity-Feed System / Fuel-Pump System
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Instructors can intoduce the two primary types of GA fuel systems to new pilots by taking a walk around the ramp. Stopping at a high wing aircraft, the instructor can tell the pilot that the fuel tanks are in the wing, and fuel flows down to the engine by gravity. Next, stop at a low wing aircaft and ask the pilot, "How do you suppose the engine in this plane gets it's fuel?" This approach leads easily into a discussion of fuel pumps and thier role in both high and low wing airplanes.

Systems graphcs are often helpful in teaching. See the article on high wing fuel systems in the resource section as an example. The aircraft AFM/POH also usually contains a diagram.

checklistItems.name: Fuel Contamination / Fuel Tanks / Fuel Strainers, Sumps, and Drains
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can pour water and AvGas into a fuel strainer so pilots can witness contamination. Water will radily sink to the bottom, crerating a clear "bubble" below the fuel.

checklistItems.name: Fuel Gauges / Fuel Selectors
checklistItems.teachingTips: Gather half a dozen accident reports where pilots crashed with one tank run dry and the other tank with plenty of fuel as a way of graphically illustarting how a simple omission can result in an emergnecy, and help instill a high awarness of the issue.

checklistItems.name: Refueling Procedures / Fuel Grades
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Obtain two electric cigarette lighters, fuel one and keep the other empty and use the pair to help pilots visualize the magic interaction of spark and fuel. Obvoiusly the empty on won't catch - you can use this to illustrate the need for spark, fuel, and air to create combustion.

Keep samples of MoGas, AvGas, and Jet A in small bottles for color and smell analysis. You may consider a mix of 50/50 Jet A and 100LL - it doesn't really look any different from regular 100LL and drives home to the need to take care when refueling. The only way to differentiate them is to look for the oily residue when dripping a bit on paper or by the kerosine smell of Jet A

checklistItems.name: Fuel System Icing Prevention Procedures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be sure to review the hazards of ice in the fuel system that could occur if there is water in the system.

Let them know that using anti-icing fuel additives is like the story of Goldilocks and the Three Bears: It has to be juuuuuust right. Too little or too much results in a “marked deterioration of effectiveness".

checklistItems.name:
Oil System
- Oil leak, pressure loss
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can tell pilots an oil leak is like accidently cutting your hand with a kitchen knife. If you get medical attention quickly, it's no issue, but wating too long can lead be fatal! Teach them to evaulate the potential engine indications (e.g., low or no oil pressure and rising engine temps = imminent engine failure). Making sure the pilot knows how their aircraft's oil system works so they can effectively troubleshoot and make decisions about the flight. Any sign of oil trouble is a good reason to terminate the flight quickly. Use a simulator, if available, to practice oil system related emergencies and how to handle them. It's also a great opportunity to work the pilot on ADM.

checklistItems.name: Oil pressure or temperature gauge failure
checklistItems.teachingTips: Scenario: Oil pressure gauge suddenly drops to zero. If the oil system has suffered a catastrophic failure, what other engine monitoring indications would you expect? Review the possibilities and indications including faulty gauges versus actual oil pressure loss. It might be a good idea to review which gauges are electrical versus mechanical. You can then make a connection to what would happen to them if electrical power was lost instead.

checklistItems.name:
Hydraulic System
- Hydraulic leak
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can use an inexpensive artist’s palette from a hobby store to show pilots samples of various airplane fluids.

checklistItems.name: Heating System / Exhaust Heating Systems / Combustion Heater Systems / Fuel Fired Heaters
checklistItems.teachingTips: Open the cowl and show the pilot the routing of the cabin environmental system ducts. If your training aircraft does not make opening the cowl easy, consider go to the local maintenace shop or getting pictures of decowled airplane to show the pilot.

checklistItems.name: Carbon monoxide/exhaust leak into the cabin
checklistItems.teachingTips: See CO case studies below in the resource section to help illustrate the symptoms the pilot would experience and to drive home how serious a problem it is.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Consider tying this into a lesson aeromedical factors.

checklistItems.name:
Landing gear
- Tricycle Landing Gear
- Tailwheel Landing Gear
checklistItems.teachingTips: Walk around the ramp to show the pilot examples of various landing gear configurations.

checklistItems.name:
Brakes
Brake failure
Tire pressure loss
checklistItems.teachingTips: Doing a training session in the simulator on failures can be very effective for teaching the pilot procedures. Many sims will allow you to fail systems like the brakes on the unsuspecting pilot.

checklistItems.name:
Deicing and anti-icing
- Airfoil Anti-Ice and Deice
- Windscreen Anti-Ice
- Other Anti-Ice and Deice Systems
checklistItems.teachingTips: Use the AFM/POH to review the icing equipment installed on the training aircraft. Be sure to show pictures, videos, or a ramp walk to let the pilot become familiar with other types of icing equipment since the will likely move on to flying other airplanes after earning their certificate. See the Safety Advisor in the Resource section.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Use an app like WTunnelFree to create a simple airfoil, then change its shape to simulate icing and let pilot see the change in airflow and separation.

checklistItems.name:
Oxygen system
- Oxygen Masks
- Pulse Oximeters
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If possible, obtain samples of each major kind for “show and tell.” Letting the pilot see and, as appropriate, try each one can help make the topic a little more real for them.

Be sure to review when and why oxygen use is required when flying.

commonErrors.details:
Overconfidence in de-ice or anti-icing systems. 
Some pilots may think that having an airplane certified for icing conditions makes them invulnerable, when in reality many are only designed to escape icing conditions. VFR pilots should be avoiding icing conditions at all costs, and warning them of the real dangers of ice that can occur even in VFR conditions should help them develop a respect for the real danger that it presents.

Confusion about the need for changing fuel tanks during flight.

Cars don’t have fuel selectors, so new Pilots won’t be used to the design of airplane systems, and a surprising number of planes undertake dead-engine forced landings with one wing tank empty and the other with plenty of fuel. Instructors should ensure that new pilots understand how the systems work, and be sure to emphisize checking the fuel selector early in engine out drills as a memory item: Establish best glide, change fuel selectior, reach for checklist.

activities.name: [16] X/C: Operation of Systems: Flight Instruments (I.G: K1h, K2) Possibly taught with VIII
activities.what: The subject matter concerning the mechanical operation of the aircraft's flight instruments
activities.why: To enhance understanding and therefore safety in operating the aircraft while using flight instruments

checklistItems.name:
Pitot-Static Flight Instruments
- Impact (ram air) pressure, pitot tube, and lines
- Static pressure, static port, and lines
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Draw system on whiteboard using three different colors for airspeed, VSI and altimeter. Draw a cross section of the pitot tube to show brass tube, heating element, ceramic and metal sheath. Note the drain hole. Stress that the airspeed indicator is the only instrument directly attached to the pitot tube. Go out to airplane and point out the pitot tube static ports.

Turn on master and pitot heat, have pilot walk around the airplane at a brisk pace then come back and notice how hot the pitot tube is. Warn pilot not to rub finger over static hole during preflight because oil from hands attracts dirt which can block system. In cockpit, demonstrate alternate static, if available.

checklistItems.name:
Airspeed Indicator (ASI)
- How to read it
- How it works
- Airspeed indicator markings
- Other airspeed limitations
- Types of airspeeds (v-speeds)
- Instrument check
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Assuming analog gauge, start by explaining color coding. Stress that the color coding is universal (for example, "green is good, red is bad"). Consider using the concept of a balloon or plastic bag being filled up by holding it out the window of a car. At a stop, no inflation, but as the car speeds up the more inflated it becomes. The expandale capsule works in a similar way in the Airspeed Indicator.

During the takeoff roll "airspeed alive" call should be made -- if there is no airspeed indicated, stop the takeoff. 

Airspeed Indicator limitation: only works when there is airflow into the pitot tube. Extremely high angles (like in a slip or a stall) or not enough airspeed will cause error in the reading. "ICE T" is acronym to remember the different airspeeds: Indicate, Calibrated, Equivalent, True airspeed.

checklistItems.name:
Altimeter
- How to read it
- How it works
- Types of altitude
- Effect of nonstandard pressure and temperature
- Setting the altimeter
- Instrument check
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Assuming steam gauge instruments: 
Introduce the concept that there are three pointers on the face of the instrument: long skinny pointer is 100s feet, short one is 1000s of feet, the diamond or triangle 10,000 feet, AND the hash box goes away above 10,000 feet. Draw three aneroid wafers on a whiteboard parallel with the floor. Explain how they expand and contract in charges to atmospheric pressure and through a series of shafts and linkages, like an old mechanical clock, rotate the pointers on the dial. It may be benefical to describe the wafers like a squeeze box, an European version of the accordian (Geppetto plays one in the 1941 version of Pinnochio to celebrate the puppet coming to life). Another useful analogy is to describe it like a bag of chips or a bottle of water when flying. As you ascend the lowered atmospheric pressure causes the bottle/bag to expand (and vice versa when descending) just like the aneroid wafers.

Teach the pilot to develop the habit of checking the altimeter setting against field elevation even at ATIS equipped airports. You might considering allowing the pilot to "fail" to set the altimeter before returning to the field and land with the altitmeter not set correctly. Call attention to how the aircraft seems to be higher or lower in pattern that what is indicated on the altimeter. 

Types of altitude: Indicated, read off the face of the instrument, True above sea level "true blue sea" is a good memory aide, absolute (AGL or above ground level), and DENSITY ALTITUDE. Teach Density Altitude with "DA" for "Dang Airplane!" Higher Density Altitude reduces performance so the aircraft requires more runway to takeoff and land. Recall it with "Dang Airplane won't get off the ground and won't stop!" 

Use the analogy of a balloon filled with air (i.e., when heated up it expands) to illustrate raised pressure levels on warm days. Draw "air molecules" by using blue marker on white board -- then stretch out "the air." Point out that it will take MORE volume of air over the wing to generate lift. Exceedingly high pressure will also impact lift since the air is more compact. Teach altimeter set to AWOS or ATIS and in the absence of that, field elevation always double check setting against field elevation.

checklistItems.name:
Vertical Speed Indicator (VSI)
- How to read it
- How it works
- Instrument check
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Helping the pilot understand the VSI is to explain how it is measuring the difference between changes in outside static pressure and the more restricted pressure change from the calibrated leak. Help clarify the proces with a little bit of exageration: the outside static pressure is able to change immediately with any change in altitude while the calibrated leak (that feeds the VSI's expadable capsule) lags behind at a fixed rate. The rate of climb or descent is determined by comparing the ratio of pressure difference between the unrestructed static pressure and the calibrated leak pressure.

Find a good diagram to help the pilot visualize how the VSI and pressure differences work.

checklistItems.name:
Pitot-Static and associated flight instrument malfunctions
- Indications of and procedures for managing system abnormalities or failures
Blockage of the Pitot-Static System
- Blocked Pitot System
- Blocked Static System
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Stress that leaving the pitot tube cover on is the number one cause of pitot blockage. The airplane will still fly you just won't have indicated airspeed. This is why we learn to fly by power settings and pitch attitudes just in case. 
Brief engine/airspeed abort procedure before every takeoff to mitigate risk in the instance the pitot tube is blocked or airspeed indicator is malfinctioning. Insist on the "airspeed alive" call as you head down the runway.

Note that if the static line is blocked the VSI and ALT will not move. If the pitot tube is blocked, but the drainhole in the back is open, the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter (i.e., showing an increase in airspeed during a climb). If the VSI, Airspeed needle and Altimeter needles start waving all over the place it usually means there is WATER in the static line. Find the drain inside the cabin BEFORE you need it.

If the airplane has an alternate static source, be sure to test it during the engine runup. It's also good procedure to check pitot heat before flight, but be sure to turn it off to avoid wear and tear on the heating element.

checklistItems.name:
Gyroscopic Flight Instruments
- Gyroscopic Principles
- Rigidity in Space
- Precession
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize the 1, 2, 3 memory aid for gyro instruments. One airplane, uses two power sources, to operate three gyros. The AI (Attitude Indicator) and HI (Heading Indicator) are powered by an engine driven vacuum pump. The TC (Turn Coordinator) is powered by the aircraft's electrical system. The benefit of this arrangement is that it is very unlikely the pilot will lose both power sources and all three gyros simultaneously. 

Rigidity in space: Once spun up to speed and stabilized, gyroscopes benefit from rigidity in space. They maintain their alignment regardless of the aircraft's movement around them. This is why aircraft use gyroscopes as references to indicate the aircraft's attitude and the result of any control inputs. Friction and precession are the variables that cause errors in gyroscopes and prevent them from being completely rigid in space. 

Friction: Gyros are mounted in a gimble inside the instrument. The mounts introduce a small but unavoidable amount of friction that tries to slow the gyro, causing it to wander slightly during use. 

Precession: the wandering of the gyro in the direction of rotation -- if you can obtain a toy top and get it spinning you can demonstrate how it wanders in the direction it is spinning. You might even poke it with a pencil and watch it right itself demonstrating rigidity in space. 

Gyroscopic Demonstration: While in the classroom or on the ramp, hold a bicycle wheel upright, gripping the axle, and have the pilot spin the tire assertively. The wheel will now act as a gyroscope. You can let go of one side of the axle, still the wheel will not fall. It will however begin moving in the direction of rotation. This is a simple but very visual way to demonstrate rigidity in space, friction, and precession at at the same time.

checklistItems.name:
Attitude Indicator
- How to read it
- How it works
- Limitations (bank and pitch)
- Instrument check
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Note the color coding on the AI (Attitude Indicator). Typically the upper half is blue to indicate the sky while the lower half is brown to indicate dirt. 

Explain the horizontal hash marks and their use to a pilot. These include the marks on the vertical axis that indicate pitch upward and downward in 5°increments, as well as the hash marks or dots that indicate bank angle which are generally noted in 10° increments. 

Remind pilots that the AI does not come to life until the engine is running, the vacuum pump becomes active, and the system has a few minutes to spin up and stabilize the gyroscope inside until it achieves rigidity in space. While taxiing demonstrate this truism by noting the precession of the gyro and its inaccuracies as the aircraft moves. 

Prior to flight, explain that the AI will tumble if the aircraft pitches up or down more than 30° or banks more than 70°. 

While in flight demonstrate a standard rate turn noting the indication on the AI as well as your view of the horizon. Explain the correlation of the instrument to the reality the pilot can see through the windshield as an example of how the instrument can provide valuable information, while the view out the windshield provides an even more direct example of the same information. 

Emphasize that both the AI and the HI are vacuum instruments. If the vacuum pump system fails both instruments will become unusable. Assure the pilot that although neither instrument is required for VFR flight, their failure can present the pilot with a significant distraction. 

Try this trick for determining the correct bank angle for standard rate turns: take indicated airspeed, divide by 10, add 5, and you have bank angle. 
Example: 110 knots indicated = 110/10 = 11. 11 + 5 = 15. The correct bank angle for a standard rate turn at 110 knots is 15° which is found halfway between the first and second has marks on the top of the AI.

checklistItems.name:
Turn Coordinator
- How to read it (rate of turn and yaw)
- How it works
- Inclinometer
- Instrument Check
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The TC (Turn Coordinator) is usually powered by electricity. The TC is represented by a stylized airplane with hash marks near the wingtips that indicate level flight as well as marks to indicate a standard rate turn. Point out the "NO PITCH INFORMATION" warning on the instrument as well as the "2 min" notation. Explain that a standard rate turn takes two minutes at a rate of 3° per second to complete a full 360° turn. The pilot can accomplish this with confidence by putting the wing of the TC airplane on the lower hash mark and holding it there throughout the turn. You can demonstrate this by using the TC, the magnetic compass, and a timer. 

You may consider teaching standard rate turns initially by allowing the pilot to use only rudder, with no aileron inputs. 

The ball located below the TC is known as the Inclinometer. It indicates whether the aircraft is coordinated in a turn, slipping to the inside of the turn, or skidding to the outside. To maintain coordinated flight the memory aid is, "step on the ball."

checklistItems.name:
Heading Indicator
- How to read it
- How it works
- Limitations (precession)
- Instrument check
- Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI) (if appropriate)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Stress the need to double check the HI before takeoff. It should reflect the assigned runway heading as well as the indication read off the compass.

The HI is powered by an engine driven vacuum pump. If the engine driven vacuum pump fails the HI will not immediately indicate a failure. Instead it will begin to drift, becoming increasingly inaccurate. Pilots can check and adjust the HI when in straight and level unaccelerated flight. Be sure to make this check part of the pre-maneuver flow check.

checklistItems.name:
Gyroscopic and associated flight instrument malfunctions
- Indications of and procedures for managing system abnormalities or failures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Vacuum powered gyro failure can be the result of multiple causes, including a failure of the vacuum pump itself, a blockage in the line, or engine failure that deprives the vacuum pump of its power source. 

Make pilots aware of the importance of periodically verifying the gyro instruments accuracy by double checking the heading and attitude indicators against the magnetic compass and the horizon. Emphasize the value of monitoring suction gauge readings while in flight. 

If the vacuum system fails, it may be beneficial to cover up both the heading and attitude indicators so the pilot does not see them and react to their false indications.

checklistItems.name:
Magnetic Compass
- How to read it
- How it works
- Errors (e.g., dip, deviation, variation)
- Lags or Leads
- The vertical card magnetic compass
- Instrument check
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Explain to the pilot that the aircraft rotates around the compass, causing heading changes to appear to require backward control inputs. Explain that this is because we are veiwing the back of the compass card. You can illustrate this by drawing the cardinal directions on a plastic cup and show how it's necessary for each direction to read correctly as we turn onto a heading. Demo this effect on the ground by pointing the aircraft to any cardinal heading. If pointed North, point out that 030 degrees is to the left on the compass, but to the right in real life. As the airplane turns to the right it rotates around the compass ball until the lubber line indicates 030 degrees. 

Errors: Use the memory aid, "the North Lags and the South Leads." When turning from an East or West heading, the compass reading will change more slowly when turning to the North. Rolling out prior to reaching North on the compass will put the pilot on a North heading. The compass will catch up in a matter of seconds. When turning to the South the compass readout will move faster, requiring the pilot to roll out after reaching South on the compass. Continuing the turn and rolling out past South will put the aircraft on a South heading. The compass will appear to rotate backward to correct for its error of overshooting the actual heading. The pilot can compensate for the under/overshoot for by rolling out before or after the target heading by 1/2 the bank angle used in turn. 

Compass deviation cards are required and should be in place before any flight.
Stress the need to keep any metal objects or devices that generate an electrical field away from the magnetic compass because they can induce significant errors into the compass. 

Fun fact: The barrel type wet compass is filled with a fluid. The compass ball floats in this fluid while balanced on a gimbal. The vertical card compas is a dry installation. It contains no fluid.

checklistItems.name:
Electronic Flight Display (EFD)
- How to read it
- How it works
- Attitude and Heading Reference System (AHRS)
- Airspeed Tape
- Attitude Indicator
- Altimeter
- Vertical Speed Indicator (VSI)
- Heading Indicator
- Turn Indicator
- Tachometer
- Slip/Skid Indicator
- Turn Rate Indicator
- Air Data Computer (ADC)
- Trend Vectors
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The transition from round dials to a glass cockpit EFD can be very simple. For new pilots there is no transition to make. For pilots with a background using analog gauges, walk them through the operation and interpretation of the unit's information as you would a brand new pilot who has never flown an aircraft with a glass panel. 

With any pilot unfamiliar with the unit, power up the EFD (Electronic Flight Display) and point out the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and arrangement of the information found there. Specifically point out the Airspeed tape, the Attitude indicator, Altimeter, Heading Indicator, Vertical Speed Indicator, the trend arrows, and tick marks atop the Heading Indicator that indicate a standard rate turn. Then move to the MFD (Multi Function Display) and point out the engine gauges, tachometer, and navigation tools. If the EFD is a Garmin G1000 call attention to the fact that both boxes are identical with exactly the same button configuration and display capabilities. 

Explain that during constant rate maneuvering, the magenta lines on the Airspeed, Heading indicator, and Turn Coordinator tick marks will indicate approximately what the instrumentation will read in 6 seconds.

Explain that the Glass equipped aircraft, such as Cessna 172s with G1000 are usually heavier than their non G1000 equipped counterparts by approximately 100 pounds due to the weight of the computers required to process and feed information to the G1000 displays.

The AHRS (Attitude and Heading Reference System) is fed information from tiny sensors that can detect acceleration on the pitch, roll, and yaw axis. The sensors are coupled to fast computer chips which feed the displays.

In a typical installation the PFD (Primary Flight Display) is mounted on the left. The PDF displays information that would be taken from a traditional 6-pack installation of instruments in an analog instrument panel. The MFD (Multi-Function Display) is most often used to display navigation information and is typically mounted on the right. The ADC (Air Data Computer) information feeds information that is displayed on the left screen, the PDF. 

Be sure to demonstrate reversionary mode, also sometimes referred to as back-up mode. The G1000 system can automatically switch to reversionary mode in the event of a display failure, showing the information from the failed display on the remaining display in the same format as the pilot would see when in normal operating mode. 

Unlike vacuum pump driven instruments, computer driven electronic gyro instruments come to life in 30 seconds. There is no physical vacuum pump that needs to spool up and stabilize.

checklistItems.name:
Electronic flight deck display malfunction
- Indications of and procedures for managing system abnormalities or failures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
On EFDs (Electronic Flight Display), the color red indicates a critical warning. Red indicates there is an issue that must be resolved quickly. Yellow indicates a warning of lesser severity, but an issue the pilot should identify and correct in a timely manner. Green indicates all is good. A red X across a section of the EFD's screen indicates a malfunction.

if the aircraft enters an unusual attitude a set of red chevrons appear pointing the way back to level flight. The EFD will also automatically declutter, diplaying only the most pertinent information if the aircraft enters an unusual attitude.

checklistItems.name:
Additional cockpit instruments
- Angle of Attack Indicators
- Outside Air Temperature (OAT) Gauge
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Enforce the idea that angle of attack indicators provide important information that can be correlated to the view out the pilot's windshield. Referencing the AOA and the horizon gives the pilot more information than would be available by referencing only one of the two visual indiciations available. 

The OAT should be located prior to the flight to make sure the probe is not compromised.
Verifying the OAT should be part of the preflight inspection. The pilot can verify the OAT by checking the reading against the temperature provided by ATIS or AWOS.

commonErrors.name: Failure to identify the TC as a gyscopic instrument or thinking the TC is powered by an engine-driven vacuum pump .
commonErrors.details:
Trying to use the TC for pitch information and bank angle is also a mistake. It does not directly indicate either pitch or bank angle. Rather, it indicates rate of turn, or how many degrees per minute the aircraft is turning. 2 minutes = 360° when in a standard rate turn. 

Pilots often believe the gyroscopic instruments are active and useful seconds after start-up. They are not. It can take several minutes for the gyros to spin up and become stable.

Caution: Some older aircraft may power the AI and HI with a vacuum source created by venturi tubes mounted to the exterior of the aircraft's fuselage. The venturis provide a sufficient vacuum to reliably power these instruments, but the gyros will not be stable or reliable until the aircraft has been in the air at cruise speed for several minutes.

commonErrors.name: Not knowing how to use a compass in the event of vacuum failure.
commonErrors.details:
While the procedure for managing a vacuum pump failure generally isn't taught until pilots train for their instrument rating, it behooves any pilot to learn how to navigate by looking out the window and using a compass in the event the heading indicator fails. It is also well worth learning to do standard rate turns by the sight picture at a predictable airspeed. 

Different aircraft will cruise at different speeds which will result in a different bank angle when performing standard rate turns. Be sure to teach the appropriate values for the aircraft in use.

commonErrors.name: Not able to interpret the inclinometer.
commonErrors.details: Point out that at the base of the triangle on the slip/skid indicator is a horizontal line that moves to indicate coordinated, or uncoordinated flight. Consider changing the expression, "step on the ball" to "toe the line." Also draw attention to the tick marks on top of the Heading Indicator which indicate a 3 degree per second standard rate turn.

commonErrors.name: Assuming the compass reading is always accurate.
commonErrors.details: Remember the compass is not reliable until it is in unaccelerated straight and level flight .

commonErrors.name: Placing objects near the magnetic compass.
commonErrors.details: Warn the pilot about the danger of putting any device such as an iPad, headset, kneeboard next to the magnetic compass. These can mess up a magnetic compass in a big way.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to correct the heading indicator on a timely basis.
commonErrors.details:
The HI has no north seeking capabilities. It must be checked and if necessary reset to the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes. Perform this check more requently if the HI wanders or drifts excessively while in straight and level flight. A precession rate of more than a 3° within 15 min should be reported to maintenance and corrected. 

Frequent turns, such as when training pilots to do steep turns or spins, will tend to make the HI precess more than is typical in straight and level flight.

commonErrors.name: Overemphasizing cockpit instruments instead of outside visual references.
commonErrors.details: Stress the importance of the pilot spending 90 percent of their time looking outside. Use the AOA indicator as a supplemental source of information.

commonErrors.name: Attempting to maintain altitude by reference to the VSI .
commonErrors.details: Because there is a "leak delay" it is not possible to maintain level flight with the VSI the aircraft will always be BEHIND the VSI.

commonErrors.name: Confusion when interpreting the airspeed indicator.
commonErrors.details: Emphasize the white arc, green arc and yellow. Use the POH to show V-speeds. WARNING this is the greatest area of negative transference if the person receiving instruction has flown other aircraft, for example, the white arc on a C150 has a different range on a C182 and so forth. Also be wary of the KNOTs to MPH conversion or vice versa. One mph = .87 knots. If the pilot is used to an aircraft calibrated in knots, he/she will fly the values, ergo "65 mph" not realizing that the airplane is slower than it would be in knots because 65 mph = 56.55 knots, which could lead to a stall and hard landing. Use the E6B to demonstrated True airspeed vs Calibrated airspeed on a hot day and discuss the impact misreading airspeed has on aircraft performance .

commonErrors.name: Anxiety or resistance to learning systems.
commonErrors.details: Some clients are resistent to learning the systems because of negative transference with their cars -- most people do not need to learn the systems of the car before they drive, so it is important to stress the concept of "know the systems so you know what is normal ops and what is not normal."

commonErrors.name: Difficulty making pitch and power adjustments during flight.
commonErrors.details: During the first flight the pilot may have a tendency to have trouble holding steady flight. A pilot used to using analog instruments (round dials) will not be used to the precise numbers displayed on an EFD. They may start to hyper focus on trying to get the exact altitude readout, RPM setting, airspeed, etc. that would have not been noticed when flying with analog instruments. Teach the pilot to return to flying with outside references and to be willing to accept that they will fly with the small deviations that went more unnoticed while using analog gauges. Sometimes the best thing to do is to cover the panel to reinforce how precisely the aircraft can be flown with solid outside visual references.

commonErrors.name: Confusing the turn coordinator with an instrument that provides pitch information.
commonErrors.details:
Stress the lack of pitch information on the TC. Many pilots mistake the TC for the AI (Attitude Indicator), and subsequently struggle when flying on instruments. 

You can verify the correct operation of the TC by monitoring it when taxiing. 

Remind all pilots that the TC is powered by the aircraft's electrical system, not the vacuum pump that powers the HI and AI.

activities.name: [04] PRE-SOLO: Human Factors: ADM (I.H: K4)
activities.what: Aeronautical decision-making (ADM) is decision-making in a unique environment—aviation. It is a systematic approach to the mental process used by pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances. It is what a pilot intends to do based on the latest information he or she has.
activities.why: The importance of learning and understanding effective ADM skills cannot be overemphasized. While progress is continually being made in the advancement of pilot training methods, aircraft equipment and systems, and services for pilots, accidents still occur. Despite all the changes in technology to improve flight safety, one factor remains the same: the human factor which leads to errors.
activities.groundPrep: There are many ground items for ADM, one of which is the Risk Management Handbook which is stored in the Resources repository.

checklistItems.name: Go/No-Decision
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
- Assess the big picture (e.g. FAA's PAVE or 5P checklists)
- I'M SAFE pilot checklist
- Have a Plan B
- Personal Minimums (ASI Personal Minimums contract)
- Legal currency vs. Proficiency
checklistItems.teachingTips: Consider having the pilot use a risk assessment tool to help them identify risks for a given flight. In addition to assessing the particular flight, it can help the pilot learn which factors should be considered. It is definitely a good idea to help the pilot develop their own set of personal minimums and to teach them the process of both assessing where they should be and when they should be changed. This can also lead into a discussion of legal currency versus  proficiency. Make sure the pilot understands that meeting the legal minimums does not necessarily mean that they will be ready or proficient to handle more challenging conditions that may occur on a flight.

checklistItems.name: In-Flight
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Passenger briefing: FAA's SAFETY brief - Single Pilot Resource Management (based on CRM) - Situational awareness - Cockpit stress management - Decision Making Loop Models - AOPA Air Safety Institute: Anticipate, Recognize, Act - FAA: DECIDE, - Manage your workload (Aviate, Navigate, Communicate) - How to exercise pilot in command (PIC) authority - Danger of inaction - Declaring an Emergency when necessary - Automation management
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Help the pilot understand and identify a decision making model that will work for them. Give them scenarios both on the ground and in the air or simulator so they can practice (and you can evaluate) their decision making skills. Use real world situations from your own experience or from accident/incident reports to help make it realistic. The Air Safety Insititute's "Do the Right Thing" online course has some decision making scenarios built into it.

An important concept is developing the ability and confidence to act as pilot in command. It is very common for new pilots to put all of the authority in the instructor to handle anything unforeseen. Give the pilot scenarios and ooportunities where they must make ciritical decisions in the flight. You can then help them evaluate the results of their decisions during postflight debrief. Part of the pilot in command training should be knowing when they might need to declare an emergency. It is important to help them get rid of any hesitation to ask for help.

Help the pilot become familiar with operating any avionics or other automation with ground/sim/flight training as appropriate. Be sure to help them understand the hazards of getting distracted by unfamiliar equipment while actively operating the aircraft. Teach them either become familiar before flight (or taxiing) or to have a backup system in the aircraft that they can use safely. Teach them to stop the aircraft on the ground before programming or otherwise operating any avionics or equipment.

checklistItems.name: Postflight (on the ground)
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
- Objectively evaluate flight
- Determine solutions
- Consider sharing lessons learned (e.g., NASA ASRS report or sharing at a pilot meeting)
checklistItems.teachingTips: An invaluable practice to develop is reflecting on the events of the flight in order to be able to learn from both successes and mistakes. Consider having the pilot complete a postflight analysis form. Also encourage them to honestly discuss any events with a trusted mentor or colleague. Be sure to model the desired behavior by being willing to share your own lessons learned.

checklistItems.name: Aeronautical Decision-Making
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Definition and research evidence that it works - Steps for good decision making (e.g., identifying personal attitudes hazardous to safe flight, learning behavior modification techniques, learning how to recognize and cope with stress, developing risk assessment skills)
checklistItems.teachingTips: During your introduction to the topic it might be helpful to include some of the results from the research studies on the use of ADM. For example, the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical knowledge quotes a range from a 10 to 50 percent reduction in judgement errors and a 54 percent reduction in the accident rate among several studies.

checklistItems.name: Hazard and Risk
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Risk Management (mitigating uncessary risk rather than eliminating all risk) - Accident Chain - Operational Pitfalls (peer pressure, mind set, get-there-itis, duck under syndrome, scud running, conitinuing VFR, getting behind the aircraft, loss of positional or situational awareness, operating without adequate fuel reserves, decent below the minimum en route altitude, flying outside the envelope, neglect of flight planning) - 5 Hazardous Attitudes (antiauthority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, resignation)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Consider having the pilot take a hazardous attitude inventory test and then review the results with them as a discussion starter. 

Remind the pilot that it is not realistic to eliminate all risk (otherwise we would just end up staying at home). Clarify that the goal is to 1.) identify and eliminate unacceptable or uncessary risk and 2.) take steps to minimize and mitigate the acceptable risks as long as the benefits outweigh the dangers.

commonErrors.name: Thinking the pitfalls or hazardous attitudes only happen to other people
commonErrors.details:
Thinking the pitfalls or hazardous attitudes only happen to other people. 
It might be helpful to use personal stories or accident/incident reports to illustrate how everyone is susceptible to these behaviors. Encourage the pilot to share their experiences when they happen and, be sure to share your own so they can see the value in learning from both our own and other's mistakes. We are human and these things will happen. The important point is to be aware so that we recognize when the behaviors arise and can hopefully take steps to mitigate them before anything bad happens.

Perception that the antidotes to hazardous attitudes are silly or ineffective.
Being able to recognize and take steps to mitigate the hazardous attitudes has been proven to be effective. Self talk with the antidotes can work to diffuse the attitude and help pilots make safer choices. The important step here is help the pilot understand the dangers of the hazardous attitudes (and the operational pitfalls). If they don't buy into their validity, the antidotes will have little effect. Illustrate the dangers with personal stories and accident/incident reports as needed.

commonErrors.name: Taking a look without a backup plan
commonErrors.details: Going to "take a look" without a backup plan. Advise students to be wary of the temptation to launch into marginal conditions to "take a look." Share accident stories to impress on them the potential consequences. Any attempt needs to have a clear out if weather along the route proves unacceptable. Consider taking them up on flight when visibility is poor, but safe to show them how limiting it can be for VFR flight.

commonErrors.name: Decision making is stupid
commonErrors.details: Impression that the decision making models are silly or stupid. The pilot may not realize how the potentially high workload of flying an airplane can affect the pilot's ability to make decisions. Explain that having formal steps (like checklist usage for other tasks) can help the pilot manage the high workload and avoid missing critical steps. Hesitancy to declare an emergency when flight is at risk. Pilots are often hesitant to ask for help or to declare an emergency because they might feel embarrased or fear getting in trouble with ATC/FAA. Assure them that ATC only wants to help and there is often not any paperwork. Even if there was, it is much better to be on the ground dealing with some paperwork than the alternative if they continue into poor conditions, can't find an airport, or the situation worsens. Share examples with them from NTSB and NASA reports about the results of continuing without help.

commonErrors.name: Fear of admitting to a mistake
commonErrors.details:
Fearing ridicule or getting in trouble for admitting to making a mistake while in flight.
Be willling to share your own stories and admit your own mistakes. Assure the pilot that everyone is human despite their certificates or levels of experience. They will likely appreciate or see the value in learning about other's mistakes. Enourage them to share their own experiences to not only help others, but to get an opportunity to learn how they can improve by sharing with a trusted mentor or colleague.

activities.name: [24] X/C: Night Preparation (XI.A and II.D.K6d)
activities.what: The procedures and factors affecting flight at night
activities.why: To enable the pilot to carry out safe operations at night

checklistItems.name: Physiological aspects of vision related to night flying
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Night Vision
- Night Blind Spot
- Dark Adaptation
- Scanning Techniques
- Night Vision Protection
- Self-Imposed Stress
- Distance Estimation and Depth Perception
- Binocular Cues
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Obtain a good picture of a cross-section of the human eye. Emphasize the location of the attachment of the optic nerve, as it is the attachment that results in the "blind spot" at night. Stress the difference between cones and rods, and that the rods are the more effective structure at night. Stress that of all the organs in the human body, the eyes use the most oyxgen. Stress that it can take 30 minutes OR MORE depending on the physical fitness of the person, for their eyes to adjust to the darkness. 

Explain that since the rods are more useful for night vision, side to side scanning and using off-center viewing works best at night. 

Stress the need for avoiding bright white lights at least 30 minutes before night flight. During the flight, use a green or red light in the cockpit to preserve night vision. You may find green provides better visual acuity that red light. Make sure the pilot knows where the cockpit light/panel light is before the flight begins. 

Night flight can be intimidating -- try to keep the student's anxiety level at bay by doing the first night flight in a familiar pattern. For the night cross country, fly to an airport that the pilot has flown into during the day. You may also want to do the night flights during a full moon. 

Depth perception can be a challenge at night, so be sure the client has a good grasp of the V-speeds for the airplane as well as the speeds for takeoff and landing. The airplane cannot tell if it is daylight or night, so it should be landed the same way as it is in the daylight. You may find it helpful to begin the first night flight at sunset and allow the client to watch the darkness build and the lights on the earth come up. 

For the night cross country, have the client plan and execute a flight to an airport where he/she has been before in the daylight. 

Stress that although it is not regulation, it is a good idea to use supplemental oxygen as low as 5,000 feet at night, because of all the organs in the human body, the eyes use the most oxygen and are tasked at night more so than in the daylight.

Stress that physical fitness, or a lack of it, can greatly impact the pilot's ability to fly at night. Colds, vitamin deficiencies, anemia -- all these things impact the bodies ability to process oxygen and therefore decrease the ability to see at night.

checklistItems.name:
Night Vision Illusions
- Autokinesis
- False Horizon
- Reversible Perspective Illusion
- Size-Distance Illusion
- Fascination (Fixation)
- Flicker Vertigo
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Autokinesis is caused by staring at a single light source for several seconds on a dark night, which gives the impression the light is moving. This can make the pilot mistake the light for another aircraft and take "evasive action" resulting in an unusual attitude. 

False horizon: Stress that on a clear night, distant stationary lights like houses on a hillside, can be mistaken for stars or other aircraft. 

Cloud layers can be mistaken for terrain and it is not uncommon for a pilot to mistake a cloud layer for a hillside and put the airplane into an abrupt climb resulting in an unusual attitude. 

Caution against losing situational awareness and controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) because the pilot mistook a house covered area for stars in the sky. Emphasize the need to use the flight instruments, especially the attittude indicator, to avoid spatial disorientation.

Caution to the pilot to study the airport diagram prior to night flight because it is not uncommon for pilots to mistake freeways or parking lots for runways. Teach them how to use the airport beacon to positively identify the airport location.

Stress extra caution on moonless or "dark" nights because the horizon is more obscured. Stress that without a visual reference otuside, situational awareness is challenging. Guard against over-reliance on the GPS as "the magenta line" will put the airplane through airspace and terrain. 

Flicker vertigo is caused by flickering lights -- this can be from the runway lights on either side of the aircraft during the takeoff roll, or even lights in the cockpit. Some people can have pronounced physical reactions to flicker vertigo such as seizures, nausea, headaches and confusion. Do your best to minimize flickering lights in the cockpit, and during the takeoff and landing keep the focus straight ahead.

checklistItems.name:
Night Landing Illusions
- Featureless terrain
- Black hole approach
- Use of visual apporach slope indicator (VASI)
- Visual obscuritiies
- Lights on ground: bright causing high approaches or dim causing low approaches
- Confusing runway lights with taxiway or approach lights
- Runway width
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
At night, with the exception of lights of cities and towns, all terrain is featureless. It is important to identify non-populated and therefore dark areas prior to the flight -- is that a lake or a open grass field below us? Perhaps a forest? This way the pilot can plan to fly around or be prepared for flying over the affected areas.

A black-hole approach: Caution the pilot to fly the approaches at night the same way they are flown in the daylight. To introduce the pilot to the 'black hole' approach plan a flight for dusk, and allow the client to fly until it gets dark so that he/she can she how confusing it can be to go from darkness to the runway lights.

Stress the importance of flying the approach glide slope, PAPI or VASI with the understanding that these are designed for business jets to land 1,000 feet down the the runway.

At night, fog and smoke sneak up on you. When flying, if you see rainbow rings forming around lights, this is a good indication that fog is about to form. When flying at altituide, be wary when the lights on the ground begin to 'wink out' as this often means fog or smoke.

Bright lights of the runway or the Walmart or other shopping area can give the illusion that the aircraft is closer to the runway than it really is. If you have access to GPS or DME, over fly the lighted areas and point out how close/far the object is to the runway.

Caution the pilot that a narrow runway gives the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it is. This is true in the daylight, but especially so at night when it is hard to judge runway width in the dark. Address this by verifying the aircraft's position above terrain by looking at the altimeter.

Illusions created by runway lights include the bright light close to the runway illusion --- the REILs and even shopping mall lights near the runway give the illusion of proximity. Use the GPS or DME to measure where the landmarks are in relation to the runway -- demonstrate this in daylight before bringing the pilot in at night. Bright lights or bold colors in advance of the runway make it appear closer. Night landings are further complicated by the difficulty of judging distance because at night most people do not have depth perception. Watch the altimeter and airspeeds and let the runway come to you.  

Review the color of the airport lights, such as white on the runway, blue for taxiway, prior to the flight so the pilot learns the cues. Also be prepped on how to turn on the runway lights and, if applicable, know how to increase and reduce illumination.

checklistItems.name:
Lighting systems identifying airports, runways, taxiways and obstructions, as well as pilot controlled lighting
- Airplane equipment and lighting requirements for night operations
- Personal equipment essential for night flight
- Night orientation, navigation, and chart reading techniques
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Incorporate a review of the airport lighting into the ground portion of the night lesson, including a review of airport beacons.

Make sure the pilot can identify runway lights, taxiway lights, and the airport beacon. ** If the pilot is red/green or blue/green color blind he/she will likely have a "night flying prohibited" restriction on his/her medical certificate. If this is the case, you will have to identify the colors of the airport beacons.

Make sure the pilot knows WHERE the interior light switch is in the airplane including the rheostat. 

The pilot should have at least two flashlights -- one with a white light to be used during preflight inspection, the other with a green or red or blue or yellow lens which shall be used in the cockpit. *Tip: green light promotes the best visual acuity. Remind the pilot that the colored lights will obscure some of the detail on the sectional/TAC chart so it is imperative that the client be familiar with the area before takeoff. 

The colored light in the cockpit will obscure the color coding on the airspeed indicator so saying "inside the white arc" may have no meaning -- this is why the pilot must have the flap operational speed memlorized OR at least recognize where the arc is on the indicator.

If flying a G1000 or similar glass panel turn down the intensity of the instrument display to protect the pilot's night vision.

Impress upon the pilot that the colored lights will obscure the color coding on the sectionals -- the dashed lines of Delta and Echo at the surface airspace will look the same.

commonErrors.name: Failure to understand the equipment limitations of night flight
commonErrors.details: For example,the position lights and rotating beacon need to be checked prior to flight, and if the aircraft is used for compensation or hire, it must have a working landing light. Review 91.205 for the night flight equipment requirements.

commonErrors.name: Failure to adequately prepare for night flight by not allowing enough time for eyes to adjust to the darkness.
commonErrors.details: Although the FAA approved materials indicate 30 minutes is enough time for eyes to fully adjust to darkness, it can take longer, especially for older individuals and smokers whose bodies do not process oxygen very well

commonErrors.name: Failure to bring an appropriate flashlight.
commonErrors.details: Attempting to use the light on their cellphone instead of a flashlight with a colored lens or using a white flashlight in the cockpit is a common mistake and must be avoided because it ruins night vision.

commonErrors.name: Failure to recognize and correctly interpret False Horizon, autokinesis, loss of situational awareness, the black hole approach and flicker vertigo leading to an unusual attitude.
commonErrors.details:
Address these by identifying each condition and when it might be encountered .

To counter act False Horizon: warn the pilot of how it can be caused and point out potential sources during the night flight training. Then train them to trust their instruments to avoid an unusual attitude if it occurs.

Autokinesis is caused by staring at a light. Don't fixate on a single light source, keep your scan going.

Loss of situational awareness: Use all available resources including the sectional, GPS if available, Flight Following. 

The Black Hole Approach: Practice approaches as the sun is going down to show the client that the approaches are made in exactly the same way, with the same powersettings at night as they are during the day. If you hold the proper power and landing attitude, the runway will come to you. 

Flicker vertigo: The lights along the runway can be very distracting so you must keep your focus ahead of the airplane. This is another time when practicing at Dusk can be beneficial, altough take care if the sun is setting through the propeller as it can be a source of flicker vertigo.

To avoid unusual attitude teach the pilot to rely on the aircraft instruments especially use of the altimeter, attitude indicator and airspeed more so than they would during the day -- to verify situational awareness. Even if the pilot does not wish to pursue an IFR certificate, he/she must have three hours of flight by reference to instruments. Consider incorporating instrument use into night flight. Teach the pilot to put the wings level and trim for level flight while referencing the flight instruments and to IGNORE bodily sensations that can lead to an unusual attitude.

commonErrors.name: Failing to identify 'night friendly' landmarks prior to night.
commonErrors.details: For example, expecting to see a large horse farm at night but at night it's nothing but a big dark area -- is it the horse farm or an empty field? To fix this, select landmarks that are illuminated such as a freeway cloverleaf. The night flight is an excellent time to show the client that the yellow outline of cities as seen on the sectionals is a VERY accurate depiction of the shape of the cities and towns when they are lit up at night.

prepItems.name: NIGHT FLYING TIPS FOR STUDENTS
prepItems.details: Learning night flying techniques brings up special challenges for students who are more familiar with daytime operations. To put anxiety at ease, Berkshire Aviation Enterprises certificated flight instructor and ground instructor Jason Archer shares a few tips that have worked for his students at Walter J. Koladza Airport in Great Barrington, Massachusetts.

prepItems.name: Sporty's: Night Preparation
prepItems.link: aopa.org/Training and Safety/Flight Schools/AOPA Flight Training Advantage/Sportys Night Preparation
prepItems.details: Sporty's subscription needed.

prepItems.name: ACS - Night Preparation (p. 62)
prepItems.details: Read Night Preparation (p. 61) to see the checkride requirements for this topic.

prepItems.name: AIM Illusions in Flight/Vision in Flight (8-1-5, 8-1-6)
prepItems.details: Many different illusions can be experienced in flight. Some can lead to spatial disorientation. Others can lead to landing errors. Illusions rank among the most common factors cited as contributing to fatal aircraft accidents.

prepItems.name: FAA Night Flying Tips
prepItems.details: Sometimes the simplest word can have a profound impact on the lives of pilots. NIGHT is one such word. The following nighttime safety tips provided by Adrian Eichhorn highlight the importance of the word N.I.G.H.T. The FAA Aviation News safety staff hopes you enjoy this interesting play on the word and heed its message.

prepItems.name: CHECKRIDE: NIGHT OPERATIONS THE CHALLENGES OF NIGHT FLIGHT
prepItems.details: The quiet, beautiful serenity of a night flight is not without its challenges and potential risks. But as with so much of aviation, risks should be mitigated through effective training, review, and practice.

prepItems.name: MASTER THE NIGHT
prepItems.details: The shorter days of autumn and winter create an opportunity for pilots to see the world from a new perspective, and night flying can be truly spectacular. Being well-prepared for the aeronautical challenges that night flying poses will make the experience more rewarding, enjoyable, and safe.

prepItems.name: NIGHT FLYING: Spectacular, safe with proper knowledge, training, and judgment
prepItems.details: You sit in the darkness at the end of the runway and carefully check the instruments and gauges in the soft glow of the cockpit lights. Ahead, two rows of runway lights lead into the star-studded sky. Pondering your departure, you wonder what's really waiting for you in the darkness.

activities.name: [23] X/C: Human Factors: Aeromedical, Alcohol, and Nitrogen in the bloodstream (I.H: K1, K2, K3)
activities.what: The subject matter of the physical and mental limitations that affect the operation an aircraft
activities.why: To maintain a safe flying environment by being aware of human medical limitations

checklistItems.name: Effects of alcohol, drugs, and over-the-counter medications
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Most citizens are aware of the danger presented by drinking and driving; or driving under the influence of a medication. Many new pilots may not, however, realize that some medications or OTCs that have no perceivable effect on the ground may have amplified effects at altitude. Refer them to the AOPA Medication Database to help them determine which medications are FAA approved for flight operations (see the link the resource section).

Instructors can introduce pilots to the I’M SAFE checklist as an outline for teaching aeromedical factors. Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and (either (Emotion or Eating).
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fatigue
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can ask pilots to describe the worst day they ever had after a poor night’s sleep, then say, “Do you think you would have been able to fly that day?” Invariably the answer will be, “No way!” Next drill down to days with milder fatigue to try and get pilots to realize that the bandwidth required for flying can be greatly affected by even small degrees of fatigue.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Instructors can share personal "war stories" to bring fatigue alive for pilots.

checklistItems.name: Stress
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: The “macho” self-image of pilots can lead to a denial of stressors. Instructors should inform pilots that stress is a normal part of both flight training and flying, but that excessive stress is dangerous, and that it’s OK to walk away from a flight if stress levels will impact on safe operation of the aircraft.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Instructors can use accident case studies as an alternative way to illustrate risks.

checklistItems.name: Dehydration and nutrition
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots may skimp on water consumption to avoid needing to go to the bathroom in flight. Instructors should urge proper hydration, and remind pilots of the “greenhouse” effect of many light training planes. (And inform pilots that drinks with caffeine are diuretics, which stimulate increased urination, adding to dehydration.)

checklistItems.name: Motion sickness
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Hints for instructors who have pilots that suffer from motion sickness in early training: Keep flights short, avoid “g-maneuvers” at first, re-assure pilot that some of the great names in aviation suffered motion sickness early in their careers (including Bob Hoover) and that it can be overcome. During attacks of motion sickness, open a window if possible, and advise the pilot to keep his or her eyes on the distant horizon to reduce the sensation of motion. Flying on a regular basis, rather than taking long breaks between flights also builds up resistance faster.

checklistItems.name: Optical illusions
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Various online optical illusion images can be used to dramatically demonstrate that what we see isn’t always “real.” One interesting free app, TheParallaxView, turns flat iPhones into 3D holes. Apps and illusion illustrations can serve as a springboard into discussing aviation-specific illusions. Case studies, where appropriate, can be used to further illustrate the dangers association of optical illusions.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Instructors can plan a cross country flight that lands and the narrowest runway in the vicinity and the widest, to illustrate runway height illusions.

checklistItems.name: Middle ear and sinus problems
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots can better visualize the effects of the differential pressure seen in middle ear and sinus blockages using science teaching aids like the Harbottle Differential Pressure Demonstrator (also useful in understand the operation of pressure-driven flight instruments).
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Interesting trivia: In the DC-3 days, flight attendants gave passengers chewing gum for descent.

checklistItems.name: Spatial disorientation
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ask pilots to recall as children how they spun in circles until they could hardly stand upright to illustrate vestibular illusions. 

You can demonstrate how important visual references are for human balance by having the pilot compare standing on one foot with eyes open to eyes closed. It demonstrates that our brain depends on visual references to adjust our balance. It is the same input we use for spatial orientation in the airplane. The pilot cannot trust kinesthetic clues while flying in poor visibility conditions.

checklistItems.name: Hyperventilation
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Hyperventilation is counter-intuitive for many pilots: How does breathing too much reduce oxygen? Instructors should explain that in hyperventilation, exhaling exceeds inhaling, throwing the CO2 balance of the body off, which in turn leads to a narrowing of the blood vessels to the brain, robbing it of proper oxygen supplies. The stereotypical breathing into a bag forces a recirculation of CO2 to restore the balance. This can be compared to using the “recirculation” control on a car’s heater on a cold morning. By recycling the warming air in the cabin, rather than brining cold air in from outside, the car can be heated up more quickly.

checklistItems.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning and other forms of hypemic hypoxia
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: A visit to a maintenance shop where pilots can easily see under the “hood” of an airplane is the quickest way to grasp the construction—and inherent CO risk—of cabin heat systems.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If you don't have access to a shop on your field, take pictures of one of your training planes during a 100-hour with your phone and used these as teaching aids with pilots.

checklistItems.name: Hypoxic hypoxia due to altitude increase or oxygen displacement
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Hint: “Hy-” rhymes with “high" as in high altitude. This is a way that pilots can remember this flavor of hypoxia. (Note, however, from the medical perspective, any factor that limits oxygen to the lungs is hypoxic hypoxia, the condition is not exclusive to high altitude.) To illustrate the effects a lack of oxygen on pilots, instructors can use internet videos of subjects in hypobaric chambers. Be on the lookout for the FAA’s traveling hypoxia simulator, PROTE, which can allow pilots to experience hypoxia safely—while earning WINGs credits!

checklistItems.name: Hypothermia
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots in training, especially in warm climates, might have a hard time understanding how hypothermia could ever be a concern to them. 
In airplanes that allow it, instructors can open a window at various times as the plane climbs to demonstrate the decrease in temperature with altitude, then ask pilots, “How cold do you think it could get at really high altitudes?” For pilots studying for advanced ratings, lapse rate can be discussed at this juncture.

checklistItems.name: Dissolved nitrogen in the bloodstream after scuba dives
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Instructors can use a “thinking” scenario with pilots to help teach this subject. For example, set up a case where the pilot is flying back from the Bahamas after a holiday weekend and mid-way between the islands and the mainland one of the passengers starts complaining of joint pain. What could be causing it? What actions should pilot take? (Kiss the waves and radio both the destination and the origin to determine the location of the nearest decompression chamber. Start oxygen, if equipped.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: A shaken soda bottle makes a nice visual for dissolved nitrogen coming out of solution in the blood.

checklistItems.name: Regulations regarding use of alcohol and drugs
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teaching regs is never an easy process, but if instructors lay a foundation of aeromedical factors first, the reasons for the regulations on pilot’s use of medications makes more sense.

commonErrors.name: Confusion about safety of flying on OTC medications.
commonErrors.details: Many people assume there are little-to-no side effects to worry about from OTC meds, while other problematic substances (like weight loss supplements) might not even be considered a medication by many pilots. Instructors should review a varied sample of “no fly” OTCs with pilots.
