activities.name: [10] PRE-SOLO: Airworthiness Requirements (I.B)
activities.what: The subject matter of legal requirements and documentation in aviation
activities.why: To enhance safety and legal conditions

checklistItems.name: General airworthiness requirements and compliance for airplanes
checklistItems.teachingTips: The airworthiness certificate can be thought of like a pilot’s license: It’s good forever, but it needs some extra papers to be able to exercise its privileges. Just like we have to have a medical to use our license, so to, does a plane need to have a registration cert. And just like we have required proficiency for carrying passengers or for exercising instrument privileges, the plane needs various inspections depending on its use.

checklistItems.name:
Certificate location and expiration dates
Airworthiness Certificate
Certificate of Aircraft Registration
Radio Station License (International)
checklistItems.teachingTips: Best taught at the plane (on a calm day). The instructor can show the pilot the location of the documents in the airplane, going through each one and explaining their purpose. Be sure to point out where the find the aircraft's N-number and serial number on the Airworthiness Certificate, Registration, and AFM/POH. Also be sure the pilot knows where to find the expiration date on the Registration Certificate.

checklistItems.name: Airplane Flight Manual (AFM)/ Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots can think of the POH as the user’s manual. Instructors can take the opportunity when introducing it to ask pilots questions like: “Suppose you had to make an emergency landing in a factory parking lot in bad weather. Once the weather cleared, how would you know if the lot is long enough for a safe takeoff?” Then show the pilot the performance section.

Make sure to point out the difference between the aircraft specific POH and the generic pilot infomation manual that is often used for study purposes. The pilot should be clear that the POH contains the aircraft specific N-number and serial number.

checklistItems.name: Aircraft Weight and Balance document
checklistItems.teachingTips: Make sure the pilot understands the difference between the weight and balance document in the aircraft and they weight and balance they calculate for a flight. Highlight the mechanic's signature or repair station's approval on the document so the pilot better understand how the document is unique to each aircraft.

checklistItems.name:
Required inspections and airplane logbook documentation
Maintenance Entries
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Airplane logbooks can be compared to pilot’s logbooks, with the oldest information in the beginning and the most recent information on the last page filled out.

New pilots may think that the owner or certified mechanic is responsible for ensuring the required maintenance has been accomplished. Make sure they understand the PIC's responsibility to ensure the aircraft is legally airworthy before operating it. Also show them how to check the logbook and how to interpret maintenance entries.

checklistItems.name:
Annual Inspection
100-Hour Inspection
Other Inspection Programs
Transponder Inspection
Emergency Locator Transmitter Inspection
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Help the pilot understand the purposes and requirements for the different types of inspections. For example, the annual can be thought of as an annual wellness exam. The 100 hour includes the same inspection items, but is for aircraft that are flown heavily like in a flight school or commerical operation (hence the regulatory requirement in 91.409). Make sure they understand when the transponder system inspection is requried for VFR flight and you might mention that IFR operations have additional requirements like the pitot-static and VOR checks.

It is useful to explain the purpose of the ELT (Nothing beats hearing one!) and add on the inspection requirement to the discussion. It ma be useful to point out that they ELT inspection has a 12 calendar month requirement just like the annul and therefore are often completed together. A good tip is to look for the ELT inspection in the maintenance entry for the annual when reviewing the aircraft maintenance logs.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If possible, arrange a “field trip” to a local maintenance shop when you know an annual is being performed. In addition to learning more about the nature of the inspection, it can be an excellent time for the pilot to learn more about the airplane’s systems.

checklistItems.name:
Airworthiness Directives and Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins
One Time
Recurring
Emergency
checklistItems.teachingTips: A good way to relate ADs and other service bulletins is compare them to recalls on cars or other products. They are typically for faulty parts or added maintenace when a safety issue is found. Be sure to review the differences between one-time, recurring, and emergency ADs. It might be useful to pull some examples from the FAA website so they see it in the "real" world. Be sure to teach them how to find and check ADs in the aircraft maintenance log as well.

checklistItems.name: Purpose and procedure for obtaining a special flight permit
checklistItems.teachingTips: This can be a good place to illustrate how airworthiness is a paper process, rather than a certification of flexibility. An airplane can be perfectly safe to fly, but not airworthy. (And for that matter, it can be airworthy but highly sketchy to fly.) Good potential scenarios are: The hurricane is coming and the plane is out of annual, but it needs to be rescued; or an airplane has had a minor breakdown on a field with no mechanics.

checklistItems.name:
Repairs and Alterations
Pilot-perform preventive maintenance.
- Examples of Preventive Maintenance
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ask the pilot if they think they could change a burned out light bulb. Then ask if they think they could change the oil. Service the strut. Swap out a defective instrument for a working one. (Having a copy of Part 43 Appendix A handy is helpful at the end of this discussion.) Be sure that the pilot understands the requirement to perform any maintenance, including preventive maintenance, to industry standards (e.g., as an A&P would do it according to the aircraft maintenance manual). They should seek guidance from somene who is experienced in performing the mainteance if they have never done it before. They will also need to be sure they properly enter the work they perform in the aircraft maintenance log.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
The list of preventive mainteance that pilots are allowed to perform can be found in 14 CFR Appendix A, Subpart C

For potential or existing pilots of experimental aircraft, they may believe that if they buy an experimental plane they get to be the mechanic for it (only true if they also build it, not true if purchasing an experimental someone else built).

checklistItems.name: Equipment requirements for day and night VFR flight
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Possible visual aid: Create a poster of a minimum cockpit showing the bare-bones requirements for day and night VFR flight.

Acronyms like TOMATOFLAAMES (for Day VFR) and FLAPS (for night VFR) may prove useful as well as making sure pilot knows how to find the appropriate regulation (91.205).

checklistItems.name:
Flying with inoperative equipment
Using an approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL)
Kinds of Operation Equipment List (KOEL)
Required discrepancy records or placards
checklistItems.teachingTips: The most common confusion here is making sure the pilot understands the 4 steps in complying with 91.213(d) when operating an aircraft without an MEL. When determining if a piece of inoperative equipment can be deferred, most will know about the Day and/or Night VFR requirements in 91.205, they will usually know about checking the equipment list in the POH, and possibly checking ADs. But the most commonly mistunderstood requirement is 91.213(d)(2)(i) - "The inoperative instruments and equipment are not— (i) Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment prescribed in the applicable airworthiness regulations under which the aircraft was type certificated." Be sure to show them how to periodically review the aircraft Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) which are available on the FAA's website. FAA Advisory Circular 20-106 explains the process in depth.

commonErrors.details:
Confusion on how an annual is correctly approved. 
First, the inspection must be done by an A&P mechanic with "IA" (inspection authorization) rather than a regular A&P. Secondly, simply having an annual performed does not necessarily guarantee a return to service. Teach the pilot how to properly vet the entries for an annual inspection.

Confusion on who is responsible for AD compliance before flight.
Unless the pilot is, or has been, an aircraft owner, they are unlikely to have any familiarity with ADs: but that does not change their responsiblity. Review 91.7 and remind them that ADs are part of required maintenance.

prepItems.name: Inoperative Anticollision Lights
prepItems.details: If your aircraft’s anticollision lights include both a red rotating beacon and white strobe lights, can you operate in VFR day conditions with only one of those working while the other is inoperative? The short answer is no unless authorized by a waiver. Placarding the equipment inoperative is not sufficient.

activities.name: [02a] BASICS: Straight and Level
activities.what: A flight maneuver that maintains constant heading and altitude.
activities.why: To develop the ability to stabilize the airplane in sustained straight and level flight at various airspeeds and configurations.
activities.groundPrep:
Before the first attempt in flight - focus on intro to straight and level (e.g. describe the procedures for maintaining heading and altitude)
Proper trimming procedures / technique (complete the Trim Control activity in conjunction with this activity)
Emphasize that primary pitch control is accomplished by comparing the pitch reference on the windshield (see expert tip below) to the outside horizon
Emphasize that primary bank control is accomplished by comparing the distance between each wingtip and the outside horizon
The ALT and HI let us know if we need to make a change to pitch and/or bank, but the actual changes are made when looking outside
Magnetic headings / 8-point compass
Traffic clearing procedures

After the seeing the process in flight follow up with more in depth aerodynamics.
Forces of flight (e.g. Why changes in engine power affect pitch; discuss tail-down force)

checklistItems.name: Pitch reference - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish and maintain altitude by keeping a point on airplane’s nose or spot on the windshield in a constant position in relation to a point on the horizon. Trim away any control pressures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Cover up the ASI, AI, and HI to require the pilot to look outside for pitch and bank references. Use the inclinometer for coordination control (step on the ball), TACH for power control, and the ALT/VSI for altitude information.
checklistItems.simulator:
An important concept is teaching the new pilot to fly using outside references. The simulator can be a powerful and effective tool for this, especially when explaining and demonstrating the concept initially. Use the pause button at key moments to let the pilot study the visual references you want them to see. While the sim does not allow the pilot to feel the coordination by the seat of their pants, the value of being able to isolate and freeze the visual references is a powerful teaching aid. Just emphasize and monitor the habit of applying rudder as appropriate to help build the habit.

For teaching straight and level, get the pilot flying at an easy to recall altitude (e.g., 3000') with a clear visual landmark to use as a heading reference. Coach the pilot in getting the aircraft trimmed for level flight by using an integrated scan of the outside pitch attitude, the VSI, and the altimeter. Teach them how to spend most of their time looking outside flying by pitch references with only quick glances inside at the appropriate instruments (e.g., VSI, altimeter, and heading indicator). Once they have identified and trimmed for the correct attitude and heading, cover up the flight instruments with a piece of paper (or something similar). Have them say when they are ready to scan a particular instrument and then raise the paper for a second or two so they can check it. Cover the panel again. Pilots will quickly discover that once they can identify the appropriate pitch attitude for maintaining straight and level, they will only need to look inside briefly to fine tune altitude and heading. Keeping the instruments covered except when they ask to check helps the pilot learn to trust the outside references and to be disciplined about only looking at the instruments briefly.

While helping the pilot learn the pitch and heading references, pause the sim often so you help them see which pitch references need adjustment and where they should be looking for those outside references. Emphasize the need to make all pitch corrections using outside references rather than while looking at the flight instruments.

checklistItems.name: Heading references - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish airplane on specific heading; adjust rudder to maintain coordinated flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. If a grid layout of roads and/or farm fields is available, that works best. The key is to teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right.

checklistItems.name: Bank reference - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain wings level by keeping wingtips a given distance above (high wing) or below (low wing) the horizon.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Focus the pilot on the sight picture outside and have reference the horizon to determine the aircraft's bank. You can have them reference the two sides of the cowling or the top of the instrument panel against the horizon as a guide to level flight - both sides should have the same amount of distance to the horizon. You could also have them check to verify that the wingtips are each equidistant from the horizon as well. Have the pilot focus primarily on the outside references with occasional checks of the attitude indicator to fine tune their bank and pitch. Help the pilot become disciplined to only reference the attitude indicator (or any other instruments) briefly and to make all corrections using outside references.

Teach the pilot that when properly trimmed, the airplane will fly steadily in smooth air with little to no control input.  Therefore, review proper trimming procedures and teach the pilot to fly in a hands off condition.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: In calm air, a properly trimmed airplane will maintain heading, altitude, and airspeed with little to no input from the pilot. While small corrections will need to be made, like when driving a car, the pilot should be able to remove their hand from the controls without the airplane deviating from its desired pitch or bank. Adjust the trim tab until little to no input is required.
checklistItems.teachingTips: [See Trim Control Activity Plan]

checklistItems.name: Power changes - Adjust pitch and trim
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The change in airspeed that accompanies power changes will cause the trim settings to be out of balance. When this occurs, use outside visual pitch references to adjust elevator to desired heading/altitude. Then trim to relieve control pressures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Read "Pitch for Altitude, Power for Airspeed - A Rule with Two Exceptions, by Jim Pitman" (in Resource section). Once the pilot has a feel for holding heading and altitude, practice holding the pitch reference on the horizon while changing power, trim, and flaps configurations. Note how these changes affect control pressures and altitude, even though the pitch is held level on the horizon.

checklistItems.name: Scan - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use an integrated scan of outside references and the flight instruments to monitor and correct any deviations in heading, altitude, or bank.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Demonstrate (or discuss) how up and down drafts will require abnormal pitch and power changes to maintain altitude and airspeed. Teach the pilot to start with a small correction, but then promptly increase the correction if the desired result/trend does not occur.

checklistItems.name: Level flight disturbed - Return to original heading and altitude
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Brief periods of inattention, power changes, turbulence, or wind gusts can cause airplane to drift away from desired course and altitude; Once change is detected in airplane’s position in relation to visual reference points, determine magnitude of deviation from desires heading/altitude by cross-checking flight instruments.

Adjust elevator and ailerons to return to original heading/altitude; simultaneously adjust power to maintain desired airspeed; Trim to relieve control pressures.

After return to desired heading/altitude, adjust controls to maintain proper wing and nose positions in relation to horizon; Adjust power to maintain airspeed and trim to relieve control pressures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Improper trim technique
commonErrors.details:
Improper trim technique including gripping the yoke or stick too tightly or over controlling.

Suggestion:
Have the pilot trim to the point of being able to fly "hands off" by literally making them take their hand off of the yoke. If the airplane pitches up or down from the desired attitude, help the pilot learn to properly trim the aircraft. You can use verbal reminders for them to relax their grip and breathe when you notice them holding the yoke tightly or if you anticipate that they will (e.g. on final approach). Help them develop the ability to fly with a very light touch with consistent encouragement and coaching to relax their hand and trim away undesired control pressure. [See Trim Control Activity Plan]

commonErrors.name: Using power/pitch/trim to control the wrong thing
commonErrors.details:
Misunderstanding of the relationship between power, pitch, and trim. Evidenced by trying to use power/pitch/trim to control the wrong thing.

Suggestion:
Help the pilot review the correct relationships by having them do some basic flight manuevering where they practice holding heading and altitude while making configuration changes (e.g. power, trim, and flaps).

commonErrors.name: Fixating on instruments
commonErrors.details:
Fixating on the instruments. Evidenced by staring at the instruments instead of using outside pitch and bank references.

Suggestion:
Have the pilot establish straight and level flight and to focus on the outside pitch and bank references while maintaining straight and level. Then cover up the instruments and have the pilot maintain the straight and level using only outside references. Periodically uncover the the insturments for just a few seconds to let them check their performance and cover them back up while make any necessary corrections using outside references. Typically within a short amount of time the pilot will discover how accurately they can fly the plane using only outside references. Reinforce this concept over the next few lessons while covering the instruments as needed until the pilot develops an consistent scan.

commonErrors.name: Improper use of heading references
commonErrors.details:
Improper use of heading references. Evidenced by losing track of which outside references he/she was using.

Suggestion:
You may need to help the pilot identify easy heading references at first while they develop their scan. Have them start with easily recognizable geographic references and gradually have them work on finding more subtle references that match any assigned heading.

commonErrors.name: Only using rudder for diretional control
commonErrors.details:
Flying with one wing low or maintaining directional control with only rudder control.

Suggestion:
Flying with one wing low is typically caused by the pilot using unintentional control inputs with an airplane that isn't properly trimmed. As they are applying pressure on the yoke to hold altitude, the are likely applying unintentional aileron input that causes the wing to be low. As the airplane turns from the slightly banked condition, the pilot may be applying rudder pressure to maintain directional control. The result of these unintentional inputs is a very slight slipping condition, uncomfortable flight, and pilot fatigue. The solution is to teach the pilot that when properly trimmed, the airplane will fly steadily in smooth air with little to no control input. Therefore, review proper trimming procedures and teach the pilot to fly in a hands off condition.

completionStandards.description: Can verbally explain, but not yet able to perform the manuever.
Performs maneuver with instructor coaching and guidance.
Correctly performs manuever without input from instructor to a level safe enough for solo flight.
Correctly performs maneuver without input from instructor to check ride standards (ACS/PTS)
Correctly performs manuever without input from instructor to an extremely high level of airmanship and safety.

prepItems.name: Four Fundamentals (part 2)

activities.name: [01] PRE-SOLO: Taxiing
activities.what: The controlled movement of an airplane under its own power while on the surface
activities.why: To safely move the airplane in the airport environment in calm and windy conditions.
activities.groundPrep:
- Intro to Taxiing (before first attempt)
- Describe the procedures for controlling the aircraft while taxiing on the ground
- What counts as flight time (14 CFR 1.1)
- Power settings and mixture leaning procedures for ground operations
- How to steer and use the brakes
- Throttle control and proper taxi speed
- How (and why) to position the flight controls when taxiing in windy conditions
- Using the airport diagram
- ATC requirements
- Local airport/flight school procedures
- Able to identify and explain safe taxiing procedures and airport markings/signs at other airports
- Able to identify and explain safe taxiing procedures and airport markings/signs at home airport

checklistItems.name: Airport diagram - Available
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Review the airport environment before starting taxi (use airport diagram, if available).
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot always has a current airport diagram out and ready to reference for every taxi operation, even when familiar with the airport.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Many EFB apps offer unofficial taxi diagrams and/or information that may be used when official FAA diagrams are not published for an airport.
checklistItems.simulator:
While simulator rudder controls can be a little sensitive when performing ground operations, it is still great practice to help the pilot experience airports they may not regularly visit. If you operate at an non-towered airport or a towered field with a relatively simple layout, consider placing the pilot at an airport with gradually more complicated taxiway systems. Some examples from simple to more complex are Frederick, MD (KFDK),  Atlantic City, NJ (KACY), and Los Angeles, CA (KLAX). Using a taxiway diagram, position the pilot at location on the ramp and assign them taxi instructions to a runway or other location on the airport. Repeat the exercise a few times with increasingly more complex taxi instructions. For example, at KACY start the pilot at the FAA hanger and clear them to taxi to runway 31 via Juliet and Bravo. A more complicated clearance from the FAA hangar could be to taxi runway 4 via Juliet, Bravo, Papa, Delta, Alpha. To help the pilot with any oversensitivity in the sim, help them realize that small inputs on the rudders often work better than trying to make large inputs. Encourage them by saying the getting proficient in operating the sim often makes the airplane relatively easy to operate in comparison.

If the simulator is able to support connecting to an EFB (electronic flight bag) it can be a great way to train the pilot both ground operations and EFB use simultaneously.

checklistItems.name: Stationary power - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When sitting still, most piston engines benefit from running a little more power than idle to prevent fouling the plugs (e.g., 1000 RPM). Check with your instructor and the airplane's AFM/POH to find out the recommended procedure.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Show the pilot how to set the proper power setting for idle when not moving.

checklistItems.name: Mixture - Set/Lean
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Leaving the mixture too rich at low power settings can foul the spark plugs and potentially lead to a dangerous situation.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Demonstrate how to set the mixture to maximum lean for taxi operations (to avoid fouling the spark plugs).
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: In most training planes, this is accomplished by setting the RPM to high idle and then leaning the mixture as far as possible without losing RPM. If the runup is able to be performed at this mixture setting, then the mixture was too rich for taxi. In other words, the mixture will need to be enriched after taxi to complete the runup.

checklistItems.name: Brake check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When ready to taxi, allow the plane to move forward a few inches and then apply brakes to get a feel for how they work. A brake check should be performed at the beginning of every taxi to ensure correct operation of the brakes.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Demonstrate how to perform a brake check.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Depending on how the brake system is designed, it may be advisable for both the pilot and the Instructor to perform a brake check before taxi.

checklistItems.name: Use of brakes - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Always reduce power before applying brakes. After stopping, set the RPM to the proper idle power setting for your plane.

Gently riding the brakes for an extended period of time can generate excessive heat and possibly start a wheel fire. When taxiing downhill and/or with a tailwind, avoid continuous brake application. The preferred method is to use heavy braking to significantly slow the plane and then completely release the brakes to allow them to cool. This may need to be repeated multiple times during the taxi, but it's important to have the cooling time between brake applications.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
It may be difficult to determine if the pilot is riding the brakes or not. To check, simply ask the pilot to momentarily lift their feet off the pedals to see if the plane accelerates. Teach pilots to use 3 different foot positions:
1) Full brakes position - Used when stopped or in the final stopping sequence after taxi/landing. Both heels are lifted off the floor and pressure is placed on both brakes.
2) Taxi position - Used when taxiing and immediately after landing. Both heels are on the floor with toes near the brakes.
3) Heels back position - Used when rudder is needed with no braking (i.e. takeoff, crosswind landing, touch-and-go). Both heels should be back far enough to ensure that only rudder is being applied with no braking.
Note: Actual foot position will need to be adjusted to accommodate different size feet and rudder pedals, but the general concept of teaching 3 positions is valuable in all planes that incorporate foot rudder controls and toe brakes.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If using a plane with a castering nose wheel, point out to the pilot that brakes are used for all turning and it may be necessary to ride the downwind brake slightly to maintain control when taxiing in a crosswind. A slightly faster taxi speed may be appropriate in this scenario to increase control effectiveness of the rudder and minimize time riding the brake.

checklistItems.name: Steering - Rudder pedals (or brakes) only
checklistItems.notesToPilot: After learning to drive a car, it is natural to try and steer the plane with the yoke on the ground. Taxiing a plane with your feet will feel very strange at first, but you will quickly get the hang of it.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot sit on his/her hands to prevent steering with the yoke. During this initial training, you can take control of the throttle and yoke to correct for any wind conditions. The proper habit should be solidly developed after just a few lessons with the pilot keeping his/her hands away from the yoke. Help the pilot taxi and make gentle turns. If your training plane is equipped with a steerable nose wheel, help the pilot learn the difference and the feel of turning with and without the use of brakes.

checklistItems.name: Flight controls - Set for wind
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Properly position the flight controls for wind conditions (real or simulated).
checklistItems.teachingTips: This element should be introduced after the pilot is comfortable taxiing with no wind. If the wind is calm, simulate a wind direction that favors the departure runway. This will create a scenario for demonstrating flight control positioning during taxi operations. When taxiing with a quartering tailwind, teach "Dive away from the wind" to remember which direction to move the controls.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Whether using "Dive away from the wind" or not, point out to the pilot that the aileron and elevator control inputs during taxi are to ensure the wind always hits the top of each control surface. Understanding that this helps keep the plane stable in case of a wind gust, the pilot should be able to simply look at the ailerons to logically determine which way to move the controls.

checklistItems.name: Taxi Power - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adjust power to help maintain proper taxi speed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Discuss proper taxi speeds for different portions of the taxi (ramp, long straight away, approaching intersection with possible traffic, etc.)

Teach the pilot to reference the tachometer for estimated RPM settings. Also, demonstrate several different power settings that may be used in taxi operations and help the pilot learn to recognize the sound of the engine at each power setting.

checklistItems.name: Centerline - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the pilot recognize visual cues for keeping the plane on the centerline. On a straight taxiway, take the controls so the pilot can focus on the sight picture and what you are demonstrating. While you are taxiing slowly on the centerline, have him/her shift back and forth to see the changing perspective depending on where his/her eyes are. When seated normally in the left seat of a typical trainer, it should look like the centerline of the taxiway is coming down the outside of his/her right leg.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Some common training planes have bungees that connect the rudder pedals to the nosewheel which results in delayed steering inputs while taxiing. This results in the pilot inducing control oscillations that look like s-turns across the centerline. Teach the pilot to anticipate the need to begin adding opposite and/or neutral control inputs before reaching the desired pathway to help him/her learn to lead the rollout onto the centerline. It may also help to have him/her watch the rudder pedals while you demonstrate taxiing to observe the numerous small or subtle inputs that experienced pilots make while holding a seemingly steady taxi path. It is very much like the small inputs and corrections a driver makes while driving down a straight road.

commonErrors.name: Off the centerline
commonErrors.details: Try to reset the pilot's visual reference by finding a mark on the cowling, windscreen, or even something in the cockpit (e.g., inside leg for a 172) that they can line up with the centerline. This could be accomplished before starting the airplane by lining the nosewheel up on an extended straight line and then having the pilot sit in the cockpit and determine a visual reference that can be used while taxiing.

commonErrors.name: Low idle setting
commonErrors.details: Build the habit in the pilot of increasing RPM to an acceptable level (e.g., 1000 RPM in a 172) when stopped to help prevent spark plug fouling. Explain how the low RPM setting can create too rich of a mixture and uneven burning of fuel that can lead to fouling. It will likely take a while of you reminding the pilot for them to eventually start remembering to do this on their own. You might try adding it as a item to an appropriate checklist as an added procedural reminder.

commonErrors.name: Mixture too rich
commonErrors.details: If not included as a step on the check list, it might help to add it. That way the pilot has a procedural reminder to lean the mixture prior to taxi. Be sure to explain to the pilot how too rich of a mixture can cause spark plug fouling - which would show during the mag check.

commonErrors.name: Using too much power/Riding the brakes
commonErrors.details: Explain to the pilot that taxiing too quickly can be a safety hazard. Additionally you can emphasize the point that you do not want to be using throttle and brakes at the same time. Any worries of fouling the spark plugs can be allayed with proper leaning.

commonErrors.name: Steering with yoke
commonErrors.details: One of the easiest ways to get the pilot to adjust to steering with the rudder pedals, is to have them put their hands under their legs while in the initial stages of taxi training. The instructor can handle throttle and any needed crosswind corrections at first. Within a few lessons the pilot will be able to also take on the yoke and throttle once they have built the habit of steering with their feet.

commonErrors.name: Improper wind yoke controls
commonErrors.details: This will take practice and reminding from the instructor. One potentially useful phrase that can help the pilot remember how to position the controls is to have them "turn into a headwind and dive away from a tailwind." The means that the yoke should be turned into a crosswind (full aileron and neutral elevator) that is at a 90 degree angle or forward of the wing. When the wind is beyond 90 degrees and coming from a rear quarter, the yoke is turned away from the wind and pushed down to deflect the elevator down as well. When turns are made during taxiing, remind the pilot to reassess where the wind is and adjust the controls accordingly. Of course, always refer to the AFM/POH for guidance on proper control placement while taxiing.

commonErrors.name: Overcorrecting to stay on centerline
commonErrors.details: This is normally most prevalent on airplanes with either bungee connected steering (e.g., 172s) or differential brake steering (e.g., RV-12). Explain how the steering system works and that the pilot will need to think a few moments ahead on steering corrections rather than expecting the controls to respond immediately. One way to think is that corrections will need to be made once you start to approach the centerline or your desired path. Oscillations usually occur when the pilot is waiting too long to make a correction rather than anticipating the lead time that is required for smooth control and inputs. It will normally take a few lessons for a new pilot to get the hang of smoothly taxiing.

activities.name: [09b] X/C: Straight & Level Flight (BIM)
activities.what: A flight maneuver consisting of constant heading and altitude with reference to only the flight instruments
activities.why: To fly solely by reference to instruments for the purpose of safely controlling the airplane during times of loss of visual horizon, night flight, and inadvertent flight into IMC
activities.groundPrep: Discuss the applicable Objective, Knowledge, Risk Management, and Skills listed in the Private Pilot ACS.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.simulator:
The simulator is incredibly valuable for teaching Basic Instrument Maneuvering. Start by teaching the basic scan for each flight fundamental (straight and level, turns, climbs, descents). Use the pause button and instrument covers to help the pilot develop their scan focused on the most applicable instruments. EXAMPLE: For straight and level you could initially cover up the turn coordinator, airspeed indicator, and vertical speed indicator to help the pilot learn which instruments are primary for maintaining straight and level.

Once the pilot is proficient in controlling the aircraft and has developed a basic scan, consider creating scenarios that simulate the most common ways that VFR pilots get trapped in instrument conditions. For example, while in cruise flight, gradually lower the ceiling and visibility to see if the pilot continues on their route (or even stays out of the clouds!). Hopefully the pilot avoids scud running and opts to land as soon as possible. Another good scenario is to set the pilot up in cruise on a night flight with a solid overcast ceiling. While they are distracted, bring the ceiling down below their cruising altitude. Once they realize they have lost visual reference, have them fly by reference to instruments and problem solve their way out of the situation (e.g., asking ATC for assistance, performing a 180 turn, etc). The major point is to show them how insidious the situations are and how pilots can unintentionally get trapped. Emphasize that caution is the better part of valor - so avoiding these conditions is critical.

checklistItems.name: Wings level pitch attitude - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Establish a straight and level flight attitude using visual references. 

Adjust the miniature airplane on the attitude indicator so the "dot" is sitting directly over the horizon line.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
In visual, wings level, flight check the attitude indicator and ensure it also shows wings level flight. If it shows a slight bank in wings level flight have the pilot use that slight bank as the "wings level" indication. 

Explain adjusting the attitude indicator on the ground will not be accurate for level flight. The attitude indicator must be adjusted in level cruise flight only.

checklistItems.name: View limiting device - On
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure it is properly adjusted to allow full view of the instruments, but nothing outside.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Create scenarios that involve loss of horizon due to smoke or haze, flying over featureless terrain like large bodies of water, flying at night, and "Emergency escape procedures" to return to visual flight conditions.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Teach the 4-step instrument scanned explained by Ralph Butcher in the article below.

checklistItems.name: Instrument scan - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
With the instructor maintaining level flight focus first on the attitude indicator. Observe the pitch and bank shown on the attitude indicator. This condition will be used to maintain straight and level flight. 

Practice moving eyes, without moving the head, from attitude indicator to altimeter and back to attitude indicator and attitude indicator to heading indicator and back. The altimeter and heading indicators should both show no change in this phase of flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: This step will eventually become unnecessary but it is very helpful to allow the pilot a 30 seconds to a minute to establish their scan and understand what level flight looks like before taking the flight controls.

checklistItems.name: Wings level pitch attitude - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use the attitude indicator to maintain the airplane in a wings level, zero pitch condition. Use the attitude indicator to make any pitch or bank changes or to re-establish straight and level if disturbed while in flight.

If the attitude indicator changes from the condition observed while the instructor was flying straight and level, return the attitude indicator to the previous condition. This will return the plane to straight and level flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure the plane is well trimmed for level flight before starting the exercise. Remind the pilot a light touch is all that's needed to maintain level flight by instruments the same as visual flight. 

If the pilot is using excessive aileron input to correct for roll produced by turbulence or gusts have them use a small amount of rudder pressure instead of aileron to correct.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: To help pilots determine each "Primary Instrument" for pitch, bank, and power, simply consider the goal and then ask the question, "Which instrument tells me if I need to make a change?" For example, if the goal is to hold altitude in cruise flight, the altimeter is the primary pitch instrument because it's the only instrument that tells you if you need to pitch up or down to achieve the goal. When climbing at Vy with full power, the airspeed indicator is the primary pitch instrument because it's the only instrument that tells you if you need to change pitch to achieve the goal. This is another reason it's important to understand the rule with two exceptions. As Ralph Butcher discusses in the article below, being primary does not mean that instrument should get most of the pilot's attention.

checklistItems.name: Power - Reduce
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
If necessary, reduce power for an airspeed below maneuvering speed (Va) to protect the airplane from potential turbulence.

If power reduction is necessary, an increase in pitch will be required to maintain level flight. Typically an adjustment to 1-2 degrees of pitch - or roughly 1/2 dot up on the horizon bar - will be sufficient to maintain level flight when transitioning from cruise to Va airspeeds.

Adjust the pitch using the attitude indicator, pause, verify level flight condition with the altimeter and VSI. If the plane is in a climb or descent, adjust the pitch attitude using the attitude indicator (dot down for a climb, dot up for a descent), pause, and reverify. Repeat as necessary.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Explain conditions in clouds can be quite turbulent. Reducing power to Va protects the aircraft from structural damage in severe turbulence. 

Remind pilot if airspeed changes angle of attack must also be changed in order to maintain level flight. 

Emphasize making small changes and evaluating those changes when slowing the plane down. For example, have the pilot make a small pitch change and monitor the performance. Make any necessary adjustments using small corrections to avoid creating oscillating movements or overcontrolling the plane.

A large power reduction will result in a slight right turning tendency in some planes if the nose is allowed to descend. Make sure the pilot is focused on maintaining a wings level condition using the attitude indicator as power is changed. 

Vary power, airspeed, and flap settings while flying straight and level to help the pilot get a feel for the airplane in different configurations. Correlate what the pilot has to do flying by instruments with the same control changes required in visual flight.

checklistItems.name: Carb heat and pitot heat - On (simulated)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: In an emergency situation where you could be inadvertently entering clouds, the potential for ice could exist. Applying carb heat and pitot heat could give you a little more time to successfully execute your escape maneuver.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Icing can occur on a metal airframe even if ambient temperature is above freezing. 

Instrument pilots often turn on pitot heat before entering any clouds, regardless of forecast temperature, to ensure no ice can form on the pitot tube and thereby preserve the operation of the airspeed indicator. If the pilot accidently encounters IMC turn on the pitot heat if the plane is equipped.

Remind the pilot to turn on carb heat any time they are operating out of the safe non-carb heat range for the engine (on a C172 this is the "green arc" on the tachometer). In case of any engine roughness in IMC carb heat should be applied immediately regardless of engine temperature.

Severe airframe icing can cause the air inlet to the engine to be restricted or blocked. If the aircraft is equiped with manual alternate air input turn on alternate air if engine roughness is encountered and carb heat does not resolve the issue.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Trim away any control pressures to help you maintain steady straight and level flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: To encourage proper trim technique, teach "Fly what you see, trim what you feel." This is a mantra that should be repeated to the pilot again and again. For basic instrument flying, this means positioning the flight controls as needed based on the information from the instruments, hold the controls there, and then trim any control pressures.

checklistItems.name: Instrument scan for constant heading and altitude - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Once established in steady straight and level flight, maintain the following scan: attitude indicator set for zero pitch and bank. If the correct zero pitch and bank settings are used the heading and altitude will not change.

Verify as follows: Altimeter for level flight, and Heading indicator for straight flight. Make any adjustments to correct altitude or heading deviations using the attitude indicator.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize zero pitch, wings level attitude WILL result in straight and level flight. The purpose of the scan is to verify that condition. 

To simplify the procedure, use a heading bug on the HI and/or start on a cardinal heading (N, S, E, or W)

Teach that the skill of switch-tasking involves looking at the right thing, at the right time, for the right amount of time.

Use your pen or other pointing device to point to each instrument and help the pilot understand "What to look at, when, and why" (as discussed in the preflight briefing)

Reference Ralph Butcher's article below for detailed information of what to look for and how to correct it.

If they continue to chase the other instruments cover the altimeter, vertical speed indicator and heading indicator until they can fly straight and level using attitude indicator only. Then reintroduce the other instruments one at a time.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: To aid in developing their scan, have the pilot maintain constant heading and altitude while changing power settings.

commonErrors.name: Chasing instruments
commonErrors.details:
Improper instrument scan

Chasing the altimeter, VSI, heading indicator, turn coordinator, airspeed indicator to maintain level flight. - Resulting in non-stop changes in pitch and bank.

commonErrors.name: Not aligning attitude indicator
commonErrors.details:
Incorrectly aligned attitude indicator. 

Adjusting miniature airplane on the ground.

commonErrors.name: Not scanning for traffic
commonErrors.details: Traffic - Exercise extreme caution to divide your attention to properly scan for traffic while you are teaching instrument procedures

commonErrors.name: Over-controlling
commonErrors.details: Over-controlling - Too aggressive and/or too much control input

commonErrors.name: Not using trim correctly
commonErrors.details: Improper trim technique

commonErrors.name: Not properly using power
commonErrors.details:
Failing to reduce power in turbulent conditions.

Allowing the nose to drop with a power reduction - resulting in a descent. 

Increasing pitch more than necessary - resulting in a climb. 

Allowing the plane to yaw if a significant power change is needed.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Established
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Using the attitude indicator, establish the airplane in a wings level, zero pitch condition. Use the attitude indicator to make any pitch or bank changes or to re-establish straight and level if disturbed while in flight.

The basic instrument scan for straight and level is: Attitude indicator for zero pitch and bank, Altimeter for level flight, and Heading indicator for straight flight. Make any adjustments to correct altitude or heading deviations using the attitude indicator.

Note this altitude because it will be re-established upon roll-out of the turn.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: To encourage proper trim technique, teach "Fly what you see, trim what you feel." This is a mantra that should be repeated to the pilot again and again. For basic instrument flying, this means positioning the flight controls as needed based on the information from the instruments, hold the controls there, and then trim any control pressures.

checklistItems.name: Roll into level standard rate turn - Initiate
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Focus on the attitude indicator, roll into a 15-degree bank or a standard-rate turn, and maintain the zero-pitch attitude. In a typical training airplane, standard-rate turns are between 15 degrees and 20 degrees of bank. Steeper bank angles result in rapid heading changes and can make altitude and airspeed control more difficult. 

While the standard rate turn is determined by using the marks on the turn coordinator (or rate of turn indicator on electronic displays), by flying basic instrument maneuvers consistently at the same airspeed you can determine the consistent bank angle that will result in a standard rate turn. This will help simplify the scan for this emergency maneuver.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Using 15 to 20 deg of bank, make several left and right turns to cardinal headings before introducing standard rate turns
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: To fly a standard rate turn, teach pilots to hold a specific bank angle, coordinated with rudder, and then occasionally reference the TC. The bank angle for standard rate turns = 15% of the true airspeed (TAS). If TAS is 100 knots, a coordinated turn with 15 deg of bank will result in a standard rate turn. To make the math easy, teach "10% + half of that." So if the TAS is 120 knots, 10% of that is 12 plus half of that (meaning 6) equals a bank angel of 18 deg. It's also important to teach that IAS does not equal TAS unless you are flying at a pressure altitude of 0 at standard temperature. Anything above that, TAS will be higher than IAS. Systems like the G1000 calculate and display TAS on the PFD. Otherwise, an E6B flight computer can be used to calculate TAS for the expected pressure altitude and temperature before flight (this is a useful exercise even for pilots flying systems like the G1000).

checklistItems.name: Level turn - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once the bank is established, scan the attitude indicator for quick heading and pitch information, the altimeter to verify level flight, and the turn coordinator to verify standard rate. Ocassionally glance at the heading indicator to make sure you are ready to roll out on the proper heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips: It is useful to have the pilot complete a Pitch, Power, Performance table for the aircraft used in training. By simplifying operations into a few standard settings, it is much easier for the pilot to anticipate the pitch and power settings for each of the basic instrument maneuvers. Use power settings that are already commonly used, for example do straight and level using the same power settings as the traffic pattern (see the example below for a C172).
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: To help pilots determine each "Primary Instrument" for pitch, bank, and power, simply consider the goal and then ask the question, "Which instrument tells me if I need to make a change?" For example, if the goal is to hold altitude in cruise flight, the altimeter is the primary pitch instrument because it's the only instrument that tells you if you need to pitch up or down to achieve the goal. When climbing at Vy with full power, the airspeed indicator is the primary pitch instrument because it's the only instrument that tells you if you need to change pitch to achieve the goal. This is another reason it's important to understand the rule with two exceptions. As Ralph Butcher discusses in the article below, being primary does not mean that instrument should get most of the pilot's attention.

checklistItems.name: Roll out to straight and level flight - Initiate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When you approach the desired heading, check the attitude indicator for overall sitautional awareness, the altimeter for level flight, and the heading indicator for bank. When the wings are level, scan the attitude indicator, altimeter, and heading indicator. Standard rate turns are benefical because they give a comfortable bank target, but also because they provide fixed turn times you can further reference. Regardless of the airsped a standard-rate turn will take two minutes to make a complete 360-degree turn, one minute to turn 180 degrees, and 30 seconds to turn 90 degrees. Knowing this should help to better make heading targets.
checklistItems.teachingTips: To simplify the procedure, perform the first several turns to cardinal headings (N, S, E, or W). Once the pilot is proficient with turns to cardinal headings, assign turns to other headings.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain basic straight and level instrument scan as described above.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Over/Under-shooting target heading
commonErrors.details:
Over-shooting or under-shooting target heading

Suggestion:
Have a heading in mind to begin rolling out of the turn prior to starting it. Typically this would be 10 degrees prior to the target heading. When reaching this heading, the eyes should go back to "window" (attitude indicator) and put the airplane in the known straight-and-level attitude. A quick check of the heading indicator and altimeter will verify straight and level.

commonErrors.name: Improper trim technique
commonErrors.details:
Improper trim technique
Student may try to "fly with trim" rather than fly with control wheel and trim out undesired control wheel pressure.

Suggestion:
Have student fly straight and level momentarily with aircraft out of trim. Allow student to touch trim wheel three times. Trim, let go of control wheel and check trim. Retrim as needed so that student can let go of control wheel with no resulting pitch change. (trim for hands-off flight)

commonErrors.name: Over-controlling
commonErrors.details:
Over-controlling - Too aggressive and/or too much control input

Suggestion:


Gaining or losing altitude during turn (student focusing on heading indicator or turn coordinator instead of attitude indicator) of major bank changes usually occur from the pilot either focusing on an instrument or too rapidly changing from one instrument to the next. Encourage the student to swap between the turn coordinator and attitude indicator during the turn, with a quick glance at the heading indicator to ensure the heading isn't missed. Alternatively, the attitude indicator can be used as primary, especially in a glass cockpit. 

Fly the airplane by looking out the "window" (attitude indicator). Tell the student: "Put the airplane where you know it should be to get what you want out of it" (attitude instrument flying). Suggest using the center of the airplane symbol for pitch indication--should be on the horizon. Teach the student about standard rate turns and that every 30-degrees of heading change takes approximately 10 seconds--so you can estimate approximately how long you have until you -need- to look at the heading indicator.

commonErrors.name: Altitude deviations
commonErrors.details:
Altitude deviations, usually a descent.

Suggestion:

Because back-pressure is required to maintain altitude and the pilot is task-saturated at this time, they often forget to pull back a little on the yoke to maintain altitude. Stress that the flight mechanics must remain the same with the view-limiting device on, and encourge the pilot to take a quick look at the altimeter as the bank is established to verify level flight.

commonErrors.name: Not maintaining standard rate
commonErrors.details: This often happens when the pilot is focusing on another instrument. Revert back to the basics. Some techinques include asking the pilot to call out each instrument as its considered, or covering up the six primary instruments with sticky notes and requiring the pilot to look under each instrument as needed.

commonErrors.name: Improper traffic scan
commonErrors.details: Traffic - Exercise extreme caution to divide your attention to properly scan for traffic while you are teaching instrument procedures

commonErrors.name: Improper instrument scan
commonErrors.details:
Improper instrument scan resulting in an inability to maintain straight and level.

Suggestion:
Developing an instrument scan takes time. It's time best spent in a simulator where the instructor can frequently pause the flight to explain what is hapening. First teach the theory of when to look at each instrument and why, and then put that in to practice in the simulator by first guiding the pilot through each instrument as part of the scan, then asking him or her to call out each instrument as its used. Finally, practice normally and note any deviations. Usually deviations happen when the pilot focuses on only one instrument.

activities.name: [02b] BASICS: Trim Control
activities.what: Properly use trim to relieve control pressures.
activities.why: To create proper trimming habits early in training.
activities.groundPrep:
Note: This activity focuses on procedures and techniques for elevator trim, but the principles may also be adapted to aileron and rudder trim if your training airplane is so equipped. 

Primary flight controls (elevator, ailerons, and rudder)
Secondary flight controls (trim and flaps)
Explain that "Fly what you see, trim what you feel" means the pilot is to use his/her left hand to control the yoke and physically move the pitch reference on the windshield (see expert tip below) to the correct position and then use his/her right hand to move the trim wheel to relieve any control pressures, all while holding the pitch reference in the desired location.
Discuss the effect of trim on the relationship between the Center of Lift and the Center of Gravity. Level flight results when the two are in opposition.
Note that trim establishes a stable airspeed to which the aircraft will return should the pitch be distrubed by a transient yoke movement or turbulence.
"Airspeed is the key performance reference to establish a climb with power set to a desired value (usually maximum).

Vertical descent rate (VSI) is typically the key performance reference for descent, although airspeed/power may also be used. Airspeed is the byproduct of the trim setting"

"Pre-Solo: Follow up lesson on more in depth aerodynamics and trim system operation
 (Value in learning this after seeing them in flight)"
"Intro to Trim Control (before first attempt in flight)
 Describe the procedures for maintaining Trim Control"

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: See details here
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to use the CAMELS check or other appropriate pre-maneuver procedure before each set of maneuvers.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If your school does not already provide a pre-maneuver procedure, AOPA recommends using the CAMELS check to ensure the ACS required clearing turns are completed as well as other important items.
checklistItems.simulator: Using the sim for teaching trim control is very similar to teaching the technique in the airplane. Take the time to explain the trim wheel orientation to the pilot (e.g., trim down = nose up and vice versa). Simulators can be a little more pitch sensitive than the airplane which can make finding the "sweet spot" for trimming more difficult, but it can give you the opportunity to focus on helping the pilot develop the initial technique without worry of looking for traffic, etc. Teach trimming in the simulator as part of a bigger lesson including straight and level, turns, climbs, and descents.

checklistItems.name: Pitch reference - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Although altitude is the reference datum to establish level flight, intial practice will concentrate on basic pitch/trim settings.

Set desired power setting for low cruise (e.g. 2300 rpm for the C172). 

Place the pitch reference point on the horizon.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the altimeter and airspeed are available to the pilot, there will be a tendancy to "chase" these values. Without proper instruction, the pilot can spend an inordinate amount of time achiving equilibrium.

Consider covering all flight instruments to help the pilot focus on pitch control and use of trim -- airspeed and altitude will be considered later.

Place a pitch reference marker on the windscreen directly in front of the pilot and approcimately on the horizon when in level flight. Teach the pilot to pitch to hold this reference at the needed position in relation to the horizon. Once the proper habit is formed for where to look (4 - 5 flight hours), the marker can be removed.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: To help the pilot get a feel for what the trim does, have them hold the pitch reference on the far forward horizon while moving the elevator trim several turns up and down. Repeat this exercise several times to help create muscle memory and the relative effectivness of the trim wheel.

checklistItems.name: "Rough" trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use pressure on the yoke to hold the nose on the desired horizon reference.

As pressure builds on the yoke in holding the point on the horizon, use the trim wheel to reduce/remove that pressure.

Moving the trim wheel down should reduce back pressure on the yoke.

Moving the trim wheel up should reduce forward pressure on the yoke.

Do a rough trim to reduce control pressures while airplane settles
checklistItems.teachingTips:
New pilots are often confused by the elevator trim wheel of a Cessna 172 because the relative movement may be counter-intuitive -- moving the wheel down provides pitch-up trim and vice versa. 

An effective way to help visualize the correct direction to move the trim wheel is to imagine a control stick coming out the top of the trim wheel. Pull the stick back pitches up, push the stick forward to pitch down.

Don't rush the pilot. Encourage the pilot to analyze the yoke pressure and determine the correct movement of the trim wheel.

Allow the pilot the opportunity to recognize and correct their own errors.

Remind the pilot to set the pitch using outside references and then trim away the control pressures so that the airplane will maintain the pitch attitude on its own.

checklistItems.name: Pitch attitude - Hold
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use pressure on the yoke to hold the nose on the desired horizon reference.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Periodically remind the pilot to "Fly what you see, trim what you feel." Don't use trim to change the pitch. Instead, set the pitch attitude to achieve the desired performance and trim away the control pressures.

checklistItems.name: Final trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This trim can be set once in unaccelerated flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the pilot continues to struggle with gripping the controls too tight, consider having him/her place a pen or pencil between their fingers so that it hurts when they squeeze tight. Emphasize a light, relaxed touch on the controls - often with just a few fingers. 

Have the pilot test their trim setting by taking their hands off of the controls. If properly trimmed in smooth air, the airplane should remain in steady flight at the desired airspeed and altitude.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Advise the pilot that you will periodically issue the command "hands off," at which time the pilot should release the yoke to demonstrate that they are not holding any control pressure.

checklistItems.name: EXERCISES FOR DEVELOPING TRIM SKILLS
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Transitioning to use of the flight instruments for straight & level following a climb or descent.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Upon reaching a desired altitude, cover the altimeter and transition to straight and level flight.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adjust pitch to an approximate level attitude and trim to "hands off." Remove the altitude cover and check to see how accurately the transition was made to the selected altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: The more quickiy the pilot can achieve "hands-off," the more consistant the end result. Pilots are often suprised at how consistantly they can make the transition within 100 feet or less.

checklistItems.name: Transitioning to use of the flight instruments for a climb.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: From straight and level cover the airspeed indicator and establish a Vy climb.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Pitch to the approximate Vy climb attitude, trim to "hands off," uncover the airspeed indicator.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Airspeeds within 5 knots are easily attainable IF the proper pitch attitude was established.

checklistItems.name: Transitioning to use of the flight instruments for a descent.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: From straight and level cover the airspeed indicator and establish a 500 fpm descent.
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Reduce the power (e.g. C172 rpm from 2300 to 1800).

Allow the nose to drop to the desired pitch attitude.

Use the yoke to avoid the nose pitching down excessively.

No trim should ultimately be needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the pilot initially "helps" the pitch stabilize, there should be no excessive airspeed or VSI excursions.

The power settings used will vary with the aircraft type and altitudes at which the maneuvers are performed. Initial maneuvers can establish the "best" numbers for the specific environment. 

The pilot will recognize from this maneuver that that trim determines airspeed, whether in straight and level or descent. Climbs are a bit more involved since the high power setting influences the airflow over the elevator/trim.

activities.name: [02c] BASICS: Level Turns
activities.what: A fundamental flight maneuver used to change or return to a desired heading.
activities.why: To efficiently follow and track a desired navigation course.
activities.groundPrep:
A turn is initiated by banking the wings in the desired direction of the turn through the pilot’s use of the aileron flight controls. Left aileron flight control pressure causes the left wing to lower in relation to the pilot. Right aileron flight control pressure causes the right wing to lower in relation to the pilot. In other words, to turn left, lower left wing with aileron by left stick (aileron). To turn right, lower right wing with right stick (aileron). Depending on bank angle and airplane engineering, at many bank angles, the airplane will continue to turn with ailerons neutralized. So the sequence should be like the following: 

(1) bank airplane, adding either enough power or pitching up to compensate for the loss of lift (change in vector angle of lift); 

(2) neutralize controls as necessary to stop bank from increasing and hold desired bank angle; 

(3) use the opposite stick (aileron) to return airplane to level;

(4) then take that control out to again neutralize the ailerons (along with either power or pitch reduction) for level flight.
Explain that "Level turn" simply means turning while holding a constant altitude and should not be confused with keeping the wings level
Forces of flight straight and level versus turning (horizontal component of lift is what makes an airplane turn)
Adverse yaw
Proper rudder control

Pre-Solo: Follow up lesson on more in depth aerodynamics for shallow, medium, and steep bank turns
 (Value in learning this after seeing them in flight)
"Intro to Level Turns (before first attempt in flight)
 Describe the procedures for maintaining Level Turns"

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: See details here
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to use the CAMELS check or other appropriate pre-maneuver procedure before each set of maneuvers.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If your school does not already provide a pre-maneuver procedure, AOPA recommends using the CAMELS check to ensure the ACS required clearing turns are completed as well as other important items.
checklistItems.simulator:
"Like teaching straight and level, the critical part is helping the pilot understand how to use outside visual references. What the simulator lacks in the feel for coordination while turning is made up by the ability to focus on teaching the visual references. Use the pause feature on the sim to freeze the visual so that you can emphasize the correct pitch attitude and bank angle for the pilot.

Get the pilot stabilized in straight and level at a reasonably high altitude (e.g., 3000' AGL) with a clear visual landmark to use for heading reference. Teach turns like you would in the airplane with a few modifications. Coordination will not be apparent in the simulator other than by looking at the inclinometer and the feel of yawing will be missing. However, you can build the habit of using rudder while rolling by teaching and emphaszing the skill. The sim will also display the visual cues of a coordinated roll by watching the movement of the nose against the horizon (see coordination exercises in the resource section).

Like when teaching straight and level in the simulator, once the pilot has identified the correct visual references for maintaing altitude and bank, cover the flight instruments to help the pilot develop the discipline and faith in flying by outside references. Allow them to check the instruments periodically by removing the cover for a second or two. Emphasize the need to make all attitude changes outside with visual references."

checklistItems.name: Pitch reference - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain altitude by keeping a point on airplane’s nose or spot on the windshield in a constant position in relation to a point on the horizon
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Cover up the airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, and heading indicator to require the pilot to look outside for pitch and bank references. 

Use the inclinometer for coordination control (step on the ball), TACH for power control, and the altimeter/vertical speed indicator for altitude information.

checklistItems.name: Heading references - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish airplane on specific heading; adjust rudder to maintain coordinated flight and trim to relieve control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Choose multiple heading references that are on the far horizon. A grid layout of roads and/or farm fields works best. 

Direct the pilot to use a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right. This encourages a scan for other aircraft.

Start with 90 deg and 180 deg turns in each direction by sole reference to outside heading references (using points on the wingtips).

checklistItems.name: Enter turn - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: From trimmed straight and level flight, smoothly apply aileron and rudder in the direction of the turn to maintain coordinated flight. Use about a 30 degree bank angle.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
[See Trim Control Activity Plan] Remind the pilot to "Fly what you see, trim what you feel" (watching the pitch reference, ALT, and VSI).

Coordination exercises can help the pilot develop the proper control inputs for using rudder in a turn. See the article "Training Tip: Let that be a Lesson" and the video "Coordinated Turns" in the resources for directions for how to perform them.

Coach the pilot to recognize a medium bank turn (30 degrees). Let the pilot experiment to find the bank angle (20-40 degrees) that allows that condition.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Demonstrate adverse yaw by having the pilot use aileron movement without any rudder input. 

Direct the pilot's attention to the heading reference on the horizon. 

Point out the initial movement of the nose in the opposite direction from the aileron input--adverse yaw.

checklistItems.name: Back pressure - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Smoothly apply back pressure to increase pitch slightly to maintain altiutude as bank increases. Compensate for anticipated reduced lift/airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The pilot likely misunderstands the relationship between power, pitch, and trim. Ensure the pilot understands that banking the aircraft results in less vertical lift component, thus the need for slight backpressure.

Read the article in the Resource section by Rich Stowell about Learning to Turn for an in depth explantion of how the elevator is used to the turn the airplane.

checklistItems.name: Aileron/Rudder - Neutralize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Neutralize aileron and rudder once desired bank is achieved, but be sure to use required back pressure to maintain altitude while turning steadily.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Once the pilot has a feel for medium bank turns based on looking outside, uncover the attitude indicator and teach the pilot to hold a specific bank angle. 20 and 30 deg work well to start with.

Demonstrate (or discuss) how up and down drafts will require abnormal pitch and power changes to maintain altitude and airspeed. 

Teach the pilot to start with a small correction, but quickly respond if additional small corrections are needed if the desired result/trend does not occur.

checklistItems.name: Roll out - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Return to straight and level flight by smoothly applying aileron and rudder opposite the turn.
checklistItems.teachingTips: The pilot has has not achieved full proficiency with the required control inputs. Using traditional coordination exercises can help the pilot develop the proper control inputs for using rudder in a turn. See the article and video in the resources for directions for how to perform them.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Consider demonstrating the "roll around a point" to provide an exercise in aileron/rudder coordination. Then have the pilot perform. It often takes a few iteraions before they can establish a good coordination of the controls.

It can be a worthwhile exercise but can induce air-sickness so use it carefully.

checklistItems.name:
Back pressure - Relax,
Exit turn - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Gradually relax backpressure as the bank is decreased. Lead roll out by approximately ½ of bank angle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Aileron/Rudder/Backpressure - Neutralize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once back to straight and level, neutralize ailerons and rudder. Backpressure should no longer be required to maintain altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
