activities.name: [09d] X/C: Constant Airspeed Climbs (BIM)
activities.what: A flight maneuver consisting of constant heading and turning climbs and level offs while holding constant airspeed with reference to only the flight instruments.
activities.why: To fly solely by reference to instruments for the purpose of safely controlling the airplane during times of loss of visual horizon, night flight, and inadvertent flight into IMC.
activities.groundPrep: Discuss the applicable Objective, Knowledge, Risk Management, and Skills listed in the Private Pilot ACS. Define control (AI) verse performance (Alt/ASI/HI) instruments and their relationship to Primary and Secondary reference for each maneuver. To help determine each "Primary Instrument" for pitch, bank, and power, consider the goal and ask the question, "Which instrument tells me if I need to make a change?" For example, if the goal is to hold altitude in cruise flight, the altimeter is the primary for pitch because it's the only instrument that tells if the goal is being met. It also reveals in which direction a control input is needed. When climbing at Vy with full power, airspeed is primary for pitch instrument because it's the only one that tells if a change in pitch is needed to achieve the goal. This is another reason it's important to understand the rule with two exceptions. As Ralph Butcher discusses in the article below, being primary does not mean that instrument should get most of the pilot's attention. Have the pilot complete a "Pitch, Power=Performance" table for the aircraft. Simplifying operations into a few standard settings, it is much easier for the pilot to anticipate the pitch and power settings for each of the basic instrument maneuvers. Use power settings already commonly used, for example do straight and level using the same power settings as the traffic pattern (see the example below for a C172). Show the pilot the basic scan based on the AI as the central focus, with meaningful excursions to each of the surrounding instruments. Discuss a "standard rate turn" and its implications in terms of bank angle.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator:
The simulator is incredibly valuable for teaching Basic Instrument Maneuvering. Start by teaching the basic scan for each flight fundamental (straight and level, turns, climbs, descents). Use the pause button and instrument covers to help the pilot develop their scan focused on the most applicable instruments. EXAMPLE: For constant airspeed climbs you could initially cover up the turn coordinator, vertical speed indicator, and intermittently the altimeter to help the pilot learn which instruments are primary for maintaining a constant airspeed climb.

Once the pilot is proficient in controlling the aircraft and has developed a basic scan, consider creating scenarios that simulate the most common ways that VFR pilots get trapped in instrument conditions. For example, while in cruise flight, gradually lower the ceiling and visibility to see if the pilot continues on their route (or even stays out of the clouds!). Hopefully the pilot avoids scud running and opts to land as soon as possible. Another good scenario is to set the pilot up in cruise on a night flight with a solid overcast ceiling. While they are distracted, bring the ceiling down below their cruising altitude. Once they realize they have lost visual reference, have them fly by reference to instruments and problem solve their way out of the situation (e.g., asking ATC for assistance, performing a 180 turn, etc). The major point is to show them how insidious the situations are and how pilots can unintentionally get trapped. Emphasize that caution is the better part of valor - so avoiding these conditions is critical.

checklistItems.name: View limiting device - On
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure it is properly adjusted to allow full view of the instruments, but nothing outside
checklistItems.teachingTips: Create scenarios that involve loss of horizon due to smoke or haze, flying over featureless terrain like large bodies of water, flying at night, and "Emergency escape procedures" to return to visual flight conditions.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Teach the 4-step instrument scanned explained by Ralph Butcher in the article below.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Established
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use the attitude indicator: 

To establish a wings level, zero pitch condition. 

To make any pitch or bank changes or to re-establish straight and level if disturbed while in flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Teach the skill of switch-tasking: looking at the right thing, at the right time, for the right amount of time.

Point to each instrument to emphasize "What to look at, when, and why" (as discussed in the preflight briefing)

Ensure the AI is set to zero pitch when S&L has been established.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: The basic instrument scan for straight and level is: Attitude indicator for zero-pitch and bank, Altimeter for level flight, and Heading indicator for straight flight.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure that no pressure is being exerted on the yoke. You should be able to remove your hand from the yoke or stick and the airplane should maintain its pitch attitude. If it doesn't, work to trim away the pressures.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize proper trim technique: "Fly what you see, trim what you feel." 

For basic instrument flying, position the flight controls based on the information from the instruments, trim-off any control pressures.

Periodically check the pilot's hands for a tight grip or exertion. You can also ask them to take their hand off of the yoke or stick to check the trim condition of the airplane. After a while, it is likely the pilot will do this check on their own.

checklistItems.name: Power - Full
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Direct attention to the attitude indicator; increase power to full (or recommended climb power setting). 
Allow the nose to rise in response.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Note that when the power is increased the airplane will tend to accelerate, but the added airspeed will cause the trim to pitch the nose up to maintain the previous trim speed condition.

checklistItems.name: Pitch for a straight, constant airspeed climb - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Assist the pitch-up tendancy to establish a two-bar, wings-level climb attitude; Focus on the AI only long enough to establish the attitude and trim to relieve the pressure
Apply right rudder as necessary to counteract P-factor left turning tendency. 
Check airspeed, return to the attitude indicator, and adjust pitch attitude as necessary to achieve desired climb speed. 
Never fixate at the airspeed indicator while changing pitch attitude.

Once climb is stabilized, trim to relieve control pressures; Continue instrument scan and make required corrections by referring to the attitude indicator.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Encourage the pilot to provide their thought process aurally to help the instructor validate the control changes the pilot is attempting to execute. 

Relate the Pitch+power=performance table (on their knee-board) to the various segments of the maneuver to correlate their input to the performance being obtained.

checklistItems.name: If performing a turn: Initiate a standard rate turn while climbing - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Roll into a 15-degree bank and maintain the climb attitude. Check airspeed, return to the attitude indicator, and adjust pitch attitude if necessary for the desired climb speed.

Note the different rudder input needed in right climbing turns versus left climbing turns
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The pilot may not be spending enough time monitoring the attitude indicator (see Ralph Butcher's articles on Elementary Instrument Flying and the 4 Step Scan). Help them with reminders either verbally or using a pointing device to get the proper tempo for the scan. If the problem persists trying doing isolated practice of specified bank turns. This will be especially effective both in cost and time if a simulator is available.

The pilot may is likely not scanning the inclinometer enough or may be overloaded with other inputs while scanning. Try doing isolated turn practice at various banks so they can practice proper rudder inputs in both directions. The simulator is a great tool for instrument practice and instruction on this.

checklistItems.name: If performing a turn: Roll out from the turn onto assigned heading - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
As the heading is within 10 tegrees of the desired target, roll out of the turn. 

When the wings are level, scan the attitude indicator, airspeed indicator, and heading indicator.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Consider alerting the pilot when the heading is about 20 degrees from the target as a reminder to scan the HI. On subsequent turns, allow the pilot to be responsible for including the HI in the scan.

If the pilot is having trouble rolling out smoothly, they may not be focusing enough on the attitude indicator during the transition. During any transitions, have them use the attitude indicator to establish straight and level. Trying to control the rollout with other instuments like the turn coordinator or heading indicator will make aircraft control much erratic and prone to overcontrolling.

checklistItems.name: Level off - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Smoothly initiating the level off about 50 feet (or 10% of climb rate) prior to assigned altitude. 

Begin by applying forward pressure on the yoke to position miniature airplane to the horizon of the AI. 

Use the altimeter and heading indicator to monitor performance and make required pitch and bank changes with the attitude indicator.

As the airplane accelerates, use less right rudder pressure to maintain coordination; 

Trim to relieve control pressures. As cruise speed is obtained, reduce power to recommended cruise setting and final trim for straight and level flight
checklistItems.teachingTips:
This is often a busy time for the pilot in the early stages.

Allow them to find their mistakes but don't hesitate to remind them when a reasonable time period has elapsed with no correction of an obvious problem or oversite.

Use key words like "pitch" "bank" and "yaw" to remind the student to check the primary instrument for a possible correction. Avoid any lengthly description as the pilot's mind is probably trying to evaluate lots of often conflicting information.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain basic straight and level instrument scan as described above at the new altitude and heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Following maneuvers that have required heavy concentration, pilots may lapse into a regressive mode in an effort to relax. Remind and encourage them to trim the airplane for level flight. If after a lot of reminders the pilot continues to not trim, you may need to allow them to make the mistake of not correcting trim and letting them get tired.

commonErrors.name: Under/overshoot target
commonErrors.details:
Under/Overshooting the target altitude by more than 100 feet. 

Failure to release rudder pressure causing a yaw to develop.

Failure to reduce power to the nominal cruise setting.

commonErrors.name: Improper instrument scan
commonErrors.details:
Improper instrument scan:
Fixating on an instrument.
Omitting an instrument. 
Incorrect interpretation of an instrument

Improperly set AI.

commonErrors.name: Not trimmed properly
commonErrors.details: The pilot fails to establish a "hands-off" trim condition.

commonErrors.name: Over control
commonErrors.details: Over-controlling - Too aggressive and/or too much control input

commonErrors.name: Erratic pitch changes
commonErrors.details:
Erratic pitch changes--often caused by fixating on the ASI and "chasing the needle." 

Failure to achieve a hands-off trim condition.

commonErrors.name: Over/under bank
commonErrors.details:
Over or under banking. 

The "ball" is out of the center.

commonErrors.name: Failure to rollout
commonErrors.details:
Failure to recognize the arrival of the target heading.

Failure to rollout smoothly.

commonErrors.name: Fail to properly scan
commonErrors.details: Traffic - Exercise extreme caution to divide your attention to properly scan for traffic while you are teaching instrument procedures

prepItems.details: Before the 1950's, most general aviation airplanes did not have equipment for instrument flight. After that period, weight and cost reductions made it possible to fully equip light airplanes for instrument flight.

prepItems.name: ACS - Instrument Constant Airspeed Climbs
prepItems.details: Read Basic Instrument Maneuvers: Constant Airspeed Climbs (p. 46) to see the checkride requirements for this maneuver.

prepItems.name: Technique: Constant Airspeed Climbs
prepItems.details: Check and cross-check for this fundamental instrument maneuver.

activities.name: [09a] X/C: Constant Airspeed Descents (BIM)
activities.what: A flight maneuver consisting of constant heading and turning descents and level offs while holding constant airspeed with reference to only the flight instruments.
activities.why: To fly solely by reference to instruments for the purpose of safely controlling the airplane during times of loss of visual horizon, night flight, and inadvertent flight into IMC.
activities.groundPrep:
Discuss the applicable Objective, Knowledge, Risk Management, and Skills listed in the Private Pilot ACS. Define control (AI) verse performance (Alt/ASI/HI) instruments and their relationship to Primary and Secondary reference for each maneuver. 
To help determine each "Primary Instrument" for pitch, bank, and power, consider the goal and ask the question, "Which instrument tells me if I need to make a change?" 
For example, if the goal is to hold altitude in cruise flight, the altimeter is the primary for pitch because it's the only instrument that tells if the goal is being met. 
It also reveals in which direction a control input is needed. 
When climbing at Vy with full power, airspeed is primary for pitch instrument because it's the only one that tells if a change in pitch is needed to achieve the goal. 
This is another reason it's important to understand the rule with two exceptions. 
As Ralph Butcher discusses in the article below, being primary does not mean that instrument should get most of the pilot's attention. 
Have the pilot complete a "Pitch, Power=Performance" table for the aircraft. 
Simplifying operations into a few standard settings, it is much easier for the pilot to anticipate the pitch and power settings for each of the basic instrument maneuvers 
Use power settings already commonly used, for example do straight and level using the same power settings as the traffic pattern. 
Show the pilot the basic scan based on the AI as the central focus, with meaningful excursions to each of the surrounding instruments. 
Discuss a "standard rate turn" and its implications in terms of bank angle.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator:
The simulator is incredibly valuable for teaching Basic Instrument Maneuvering. Start by teaching the basic scan for each flight fundamental (straight and level, turns, climbs, descents). Use the pause button and instrument covers to help the pilot develop their scan focused on the most applicable instruments. EXAMPLE: For constant airspeed descents you could initially cover up the turn coordinator, vertical speed indicator, and intermittently the altimeter to help the pilot learn which instruments are primary for maintaining a constant airspeed climb.

Once the pilot is proficient in controlling the aircraft and has developed a basic scan, consider creating scenarios that simulate the most common ways that VFR pilots get trapped in instrument conditions. For example, while in cruise flight, gradually lower the ceiling and visibility to see if the pilot continues on their route (or even stays out of the clouds!). Hopefully the pilot avoids scud running and opts to land as soon as possible. Another good scenario is to set the pilot up in cruise on a night flight with a solid overcast ceiling. While they are distracted, bring the ceiling down below their cruising altitude. Once they realize they have lost visual reference, have them fly by reference to instruments and problem solve their way out of the situation (e.g., asking ATC for assistance, performing a 180 turn, etc). The major point is to show them how insidious the situations are and how pilots can unintentionally get trapped. Emphasize that caution is the better part of valor - so avoiding these conditions is critical.

checklistItems.name: View limiting device - On
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure it is properly adjusted to allow full view of the instruments, but nothing outside
checklistItems.teachingTips: Create scenarios that involve loss of horizon due to smoke or haze, flying over featureless terrain like large bodies of water, flying at night, and "Emergency escape procedures" to return to visual flight conditions.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Teach the 4-step instrument scanned explained by Ralph Butcher in the article below.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Established
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use a low cruise power setting for initial 
introduction of the maneuver.

Use the attitude indicator: 
To establish a wings level, zero pitch condition. 
To make any pitch or bank changes or to 
re-establish straight and level if disturbed 
while in flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Teach the skill of switch-tasking: looking at the right thing, at the right time, for the right amount of time.

Point to each instrument to emphasize "What to look at, when, and why" (as discussed in the preflight briefing)

Ensure the AI is set to zero pitch when S&L has been established.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: The basic instrument scan for straight and level is: Attitude indicator for zero-pitch and bank, Altimeter for level flight, and Heading indicator for straight flight.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Ensure that no pressure is being exerted on the yoke. 

Note the cruise airspeed when the airplane is properly trimmed for S&L.This is the target speed for the descent.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize proper trim technique: "Fly what you see, trim what you feel." 

For basic instrument flying, position the flight controls based on the information from the instruments, trim-off any control pressures.

checklistItems.name: Power - Reduce
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Reduce power (about 300 rpm). 

Allow the nose to drop slightly using the yoke to stabilize at about one bar width (approx. -2 degrees).
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Pitch for a constant heading, constant airspeed descent - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Establish a wings-level, one-bar (-2 degree), nose-low attitude. 

Check airspeed, periodically revisit the AI; adjust pitch attitude for the desired descent speed. 

If descending at less than 500 feet per minute, reduce power slightly.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The pilot may set the pitch attitude too high or too low and cause the airspeed to exceed the +/-10 knot requirement from the target low-cruise setting. 

Remind the pilot to set and hold a pitch attitude using the attitude indicator and allow the airplane to settle into a new airspeed--adjusting trim as needed. 

Make small corrections on the attitude indicator and monitor the effect on airspeed. Otherwise constant pitch oscillations will result while trying to chase the airspeed indicator.

The pilot should be guiding the pitch to achieve that target airpeed so the aircraft does not oscillate in pitch while seeking its quescent pitch (trim) attitude.

Note to the pilot that the airplane will eventually assume the same speed in its descent as it had during S&L There should be little or no trim change necessary.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Allow the pilot to experiment with slightly different 
power settings to demonstrate that each 100 rpm 
will change the vertical speed by about 100 fpm.

checklistItems.name: If performing a turn: Initiate a standard rate turn while descending - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Attempting to start both the descent and the turn simultaneously will add undue difficulty to the combined manuever. Instead, start either the run or the descent and stabilize the manuever before adding the second part. 

Roll into a 15-degree bank while maintaining the descent-pitch attitude. 

Continue to scan the attitude indicator, altimeter, and heading indicator.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Too much bank angle may result if the aileron is not neutralized after starting the turn. 

As noted, each airplane has slightly different flight characteristics depending on the rigging (angle of incidence set into the wing when it was joined to the fuselage). Depending on the rigging of the wing, the airplane may roll out of the turn after the aileron is neutralized.

Help the pilot practice a proper scan. Be sure that they are using the attitude indicator to set the bank and pitch required for the descending turn. They should be using the turn coordinator and airspeed indicator to fine to the bank and pitch required for the constant airspeed descending turn. sSee Ralph Butcher's articles on Elementary Instrument Flying and the 4 Step Scan for a full explanation.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
After the pilot has demonstrated good technique, allow them to enter the turn when the descent is initiated. 

After the pilot has demonstrated good technique with shallow banks, require increased bank angles to 30 degrees. Note that this is to increase their skills and that a 20 degree bank should be the limit in an emergency turn in IMC.

checklistItems.name: If performing a turn: Roll out from the turn onto assigned heading - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
About 10 degrees before the desired heading, begin a slow roll out of the turn. 

When the wings are level, scan the attitude indicator, the airspeed indicator, and the heading indicator.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The pilot may have rushed the movement of the aileron or started the rollout too soon. 

Consider alerting the pilot when the heading is about 20 degrees from the target as a reminder to scan the HI. On subsequent turns, allow the pilot to be responsible for including the HI in the scan.

If the pilot is having trouble rolling out smoothly, they may not be focusing enough on the attitude indicator during the transition. During any transitions, have them use the attitude indicator to establish straight and level. Trying to control the rollout with other instuments like the turn coordinator or heading indicator will make aircraft control much erratic and prone to overcontrolling.

checklistItems.name: Level off - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Return to straight and level flight by smoothly initiating the level off about 50 feet (or 10% of descent rate) above assigned altitude. 

Use the altimeter and heading indicator to monitor performance and make any required pitch and bank changes with the attitude indicator.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Leveling out too soon is often caused by pitching up too rapidly. 

Leveling out too late can be attributed to: 
a) not including the altimeter in the scan in a timely manner pitching up to slowly, or 
b) not pitching enough to accomplish the transition to S&L.

Consider allowing the pilot to practice in a simulator so that you can isolate and give focused instruction on developing a proper scan.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain basic straight and level instrument scan as described above at the new altitude and heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
As noted, the maneuver should rarely require and change in trim.

Omitting the attitude indicator in the scan and not compensating for unstable or turbulent air can cause the airplane to deviate from straight and level flight. Remind the pilot to keep it as a central part of their scan and to make required corrections promptly.

commonErrors.details: The pilot fails to establish a "hands-off" trim condition.

activities.name: [02e] BASICS: Constant Airspeed Descents (Power On/Off)
activities.what: A fundamental flight maneuver in which the airplane loses altitude in a controlled descent with little or no engine power
activities.why: To get down in a safe and controlled manner
activities.groundPrep:
Intro to Constant Airspeed Descents (before first attempt in flight)
 -Describe the procedures for establishing and maintaining Constant Airspeed Descents
- When to pitch for airspeed (see Pitch for Altitude, Power for Airspeed - A Rule with Two Exceptions in Prep Section)

Pre-Solo: Follow up lesson on more in depth aerodynamics of Constant Airspeed Descents including L/Dmax. (Value in learning this after seeing them in flight)

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Your instructor will help you select the proper pitch reference spot on the windshield. Use this reference for all pitch changes.

Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. A grid layout of roads and/or farm fields work best to provide multiple references north, south, east, and west.

Note the starting heading and altitude with reference to the heading indicator and altimeter.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Using a small suction cup or corner of a sticky note, place a marker on the windshield that is directly in front of the pilot and on the horizon when in level flight. This is the pilot's pitch reference. Teach the pilot to pitch the airplane up or down to move or hold this reference at the needed position in relation to the horizon. Once the proper habit is formed for where to look (usually 4 to 5 flight hours), the marker can be removed.

For heading, teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right. Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. If a grid layout of roads and/or farm fields is available, that works best. The key is to teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right.
checklistItems.simulator:
You can start the session from either a focus on descents by starting the sim at altitude in straight and level or by incorporating it into a "normal" flight that combines straight and level, turns, climbs, and descents. Then give instruction like you would in the airplane. If the pilot would benefit from extended practice on descents, it is easy to reset the sim at a higher altitude each time you reach an altitude that is too low to allow further descents. Be sure to take advantage of the pause button to help the pilot focus on learning the correct pitch attitude to maintain the assigned airspeed, when to begin level off, and how to most effectively re-establish level flight. 

While teaching the fundamentals of flight in a simulator lacks the physical sensations found in the airplane, it is a valuable tool for teaching the visual cues and procedures for visual flight training. This skill will likely be integrated with the four fundamentals followed by combinations of simultaneous heading and altitude changes.

checklistItems.name: Power - Reduce (Carb heat as applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Reduce power to recommended setting. Your instructor may share a target power reduction (e.g., a 100 rpm decrease = 100 fpm descent).
If installed, remember to apply carburetor heat as recommended.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Follow the engine manufacturer's recommendations for use of carb heat.

checklistItems.name: Airspeed - Establish with pitch
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Using the outside pitch reference, lower the nose slightly to set the descent pitch attitude and maintain airspeed. Referencing the outside pitch reference, slightly decrease pitch to increase speed or increase pitch to decrease speed.

TIP: If descending at a slower speed than established in level flight, gradually apply back pressure to maintain altitude while airplane slows to descent airspeed, then lower the pitch to begin the descent.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Read "Pitch for Altitude, Power for Airspeed - A Rule with Two Exceptions" (see Prep section). Once the pilot has a feel for holding a coordinated descent with constant airspeed, practice holding the pitch reference constant while changing power, trim, and flaps configurations. Note how these changes affect control pressures and descent performance, even though the pitch is held constant below the horizon.

Help the pilot learn that smaller corrections sooner are better than larger corrections later.

checklistItems.name: Trim - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Always fly with a very light grip on the controls. Fly what you see, trim what you feel. When changes are needed, make small corrections, allow the airplane to stabilize, and then trim away control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pay attention to how the pilot is holding the yoke / control stick and remind him/her to keep a light grip on the controls. Remind the pilot to "Fly what you see, trim what you feel" (watching the pitch reference and ASI).

checklistItems.name: Heading and Airspeed - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Monitor both outside and inside pitch and heading references using an integrated scan. Make small corrections as needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Cover up the Attitude Indicator and Heading Indicator to require the pilot to look outside for pitch and bank references. Use the ASI to know if a pitch change is needed, the inclinometer for coordination control (step on the ball), TACH for power control, and the ALT/VSI for altitude information.

checklistItems.name: Altimeter - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Regularly scan the altimeter to check your descent progress. Once you are within about 500' of your target altitude, start preparing for the level off.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Level off - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Lead level-off by 10% of descent rate: If descending at 500 fpm, return to straight and level by gradually increasing pitch approximately 50 ft prior to desired level-off altitude. Referencing the outside pitch reference, adjust pitch to maintain the new desired altitude. Add power to maintain desired airspeed. If installed, turn off carburetor heat (as recommended by manufacturer).
checklistItems.teachingTips: Create different scenarios to practice power-off glides and powered descents at various airspeeds. For powered descents, have the pilot set the power at a fixed RPM and then pitch for the desired airspeed.

checklistItems.name: Mixture - Enrichen as needed.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If you have made a descent from an altitude where you leaned the mixture, be sure to gradually enrichen as you descend (using manufacturer recommendations).
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Trim - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Trim away controls pressures as described above.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

activities.name: [02d] BASICS: Constant Airspeed Climbs
activities.what: A fundamental flight maneuver used to gain altitude at a constant airspeed while holding a constant heading
activities.why: To gain altitude in a controlled and efficient manner
activities.groundPrep:
Turning tendencies
Proper rudder control
When to pitch for airspeed (see Expert Tips and Additional Resources below)
Pre-Solo: Follow up lesson on more in depth aerodynamics of Constant Airspeed Climbs
 (Value in learning this after seeing them in flight)
Intro to Constant Airspeed Climbs (before first attempt in flight)
Describe the procedures for establishing and maintaining Constant Airspeed Climbs

checklistItems.name: Climb pitch/power - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Simultaneously add power (Full) and apply back pressure on yoke; Add right rudder to compensate for left turning tendencies (from increase in power and pitch and decreasing airspeed); Trim away control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
To simplify this maneuver, set the power at a fixed value and then pitch for the desired airspeed in the climb (exception #1, see link below). Start with normal climb power (usually full power) and then practice lower power settings after that.

Once the pilot has a feel for holding a coordinated climb with constant airspeed at full power, practice holding the pitch reference constant while changing power, trim, and flaps configurations. Note how these changes affect control pressures and climb performance, even though the pitch is held constant above the horizon.

Read "Pitch for Altitude, Power for Airspeed - A Rule with Two Exceptions, by Jim Pitman" (Prep section).
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Using a small suction cup or corner of a sticky note, place a marker on the windshield that is directly in front of the pilot and on the horizon when in level flight. This is the pilot's pitch reference. Teach the pilot to pitch the airplane up or down to move or hold this reference at the needed position in relation to the horizon. Once the proper habit is formed for where to look (usually 4 to 5 flight hours), the marker can be removed.
checklistItems.simulator:
You can start the session from either takeoff into a sustained constant airspeed climb or just focus on the climb by starting the sim at altitude in straight and level. Then give instruction like you would in the airplane. If the pilot would benefit from extended practice on climbs it is easy to reset the sim at a lower altitude each time you reach an altitude where the airplane's performance starts to decrease below the normal training levels. Be sure to take advantage of the pause button to help the pilot focus on learning the correct pitch attitude to maintain the assigned airspeed, when to begin level off, and how to most effectively re-establish level flight.

While teaching the fundamentals of flight in a simulator lacks the physical sensations found in the airplane, it is a valuable tool for teaching the visual cues and procedures for visual flight training. This skill will likely be integrated with the four fundamentals followed by combinations of simultaneous heading and altitude changes.

checklistItems.name: Climb scan - Maintain and adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain climb airspeed and heading using outside references and instrument cross-check; Use changes in pitch attitude to maintain airspeed and bank angle adjustments to correct for heading deviations; make small adjustments as necessary – wait for airplane to stabilize and trim away control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Cover up the Attitude Indicator and Heading Indicator to require the pilot to look outside for pitch and bank references. Use the Airspeed Indicator to know if a pitch change is needed, the inclinometer for coordination control (step on the ball), TACH for power control, and the Altimeter/VSI for altitude information.

Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. If a grid layout of roads and/or farm fields is available, that works best. The key is to teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right.

Improper coordination is usually more of an issue during high power climbs and climbing turns when left turning tendencies are more pronounced. The inclinometer (ball) is the best way to determine coordination. Teach the pilot to ""step on the ball"" to achieve coordination. The amount of rudder movement and force will change depending on the phase of flight. With conscious effort and attention, the pilot should learn to anticipate the proper rudder inputs rather than just reacting to the position of the ball.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Demonstrate (or discuss) how up and down drafts will require abnormal pitch and power changes to maintain airspeed in the climb. Teach the pilot to start with a small correction, but then promptly increase the correction if the desired result/trend does not occur.

checklistItems.name: Level off - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If climbing at 500 fpm, return to straight and level flight by gradually lowering nose approximately 50’ prior to desired level-off altitude (10% of climb rate)
checklistItems.teachingTips: Initially as the pilot approaches the target altitude, you may want to provide verbal coaching so they can learn when to begin a smooth level off (e.g., 10% of climb rate). Then be sure to give them the opportunity to monitor it themselves as they being to gain proficiency.

checklistItems.name:
Return to level flight - Complete
Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain climb power to accelerate to cruise speed; as airplane accelerates, less right rudder pressure will be needed as left turning tendencies diminish; establish level flight and trim away control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Help the pilot remember what the typical indicated speed should for level flight so they know how long to maintain full power while letting the airplane accelerate. 

Be sure to watch for the pilot to trim the airplane back into a hands off state. Look for any struggling they may have with altitude control or an overly tight grip which could signify improper trim technique.

commonErrors.details: Misunderstanding of the relationship between power, pitch, and trim. Evidenced by trying to use power/pitch/trim to control the wrong thing.

activities.name: [03b] BASICS: Constant Airspeed Descending Turns (Power On/Off)
activities.what: A fundamental flight maneuver in which the airplane loses altitude in a controlled descent with little or no engine power while changing heading
activities.why: To get down in a safe and controlled manner
activities.groundPrep:
A glide is a basic maneuver in which the airplane loses altitude in a controlled descent with little or no engine power; forward motion is maintained by gravity pulling the airplane along an inclined path and the descent rate is controlled by the pilot balancing the forces of gravity and lift.
When an airplane enters a descent, it changes its flightpath from level flight to a descent attitude. In a descent, weight no longer acts solely perpendicular to the flightpath. Since induced drag is decreased as lift is reduced in order to descend, excess thrust will provide higher airspeeds. The weight/gravity force is about the same. This causes an increase in total thrust and a power reduction is required to balance the forces if airspeed is to be maintained. 
When to pitch for airspeed (see Additional Resources below)

checklistItems.name: Pitch reference - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Your instructor will help you select the proper pitch reference spot on the windshield. Use this reference for all pitch changes.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Using a small suction cup or corner of a sticky note, place a marker on the windshield that is directly in front of the pilot and on the horizon when in level flight. This is the pilot's pitch reference. Teach the pilot to pitch the airplane up or down to move or hold this reference at the needed position in relation to the horizon. Once the proper habit is formed for where to look (usually 4 to 5 flight hours), the marker can be removed.
checklistItems.simulator:
Like teaching constant airspeed descents, you can start the session either at altitude in straight and level flight or by incorporating it into a ""normal"" flight from takeoff to landing. Provide the pilot with instruction on how to enter descending turn and then how to either level off or rollout depending on which occurs first: assigned altitude or heading. Give instruction like you would in the airplane. If the pilot would benefit from extended practice on descending turns, it is easy to reset the sim at a higher altittude each time you reach an altitude that is too low to allow further descents. Be sure to take advantage of the pause button to help the pilot focus on learning the correct pitch attitude to maintain the assigned airspeed, when to begin level off and rollout, and how to most effectively re-establish straight and level flight. 

While teaching the fundamentals of flight in a simulator lacks the physical sensations found in the airplane, it is a valuable tool for teaching the visual cues and procedures for visual flight training. This skill will likely be integrated with the four fundamentals followed by combinations of simultaneous heading and altitude changes.

checklistItems.name: Heading references - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. A grid layout of roads and/or farm fields work best to provide multiple references north, south, east, and west.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right.

checklistItems.name: Altitude - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note the starting altitude with reference to the altimeter.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Heading - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note your starting heading with outside references.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. If a grid layout of roads and/or farm fields is available, that works best. The key is to teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right.

checklistItems.name: Yoke / Control stick - Hold lightly
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Always fly with a very light grip on the controls.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pay attention to how the pilot is holding the yoke / control stick and remind him/her to keep a light grip on the controls.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If the pilot continues to struggle with gripping the controls too tight, consider having him/her place a pen or pencil between their fingers so that it hurts when they squeeze tight. Emphasize a light, relaxed touch on the controls - often with just a few fingers.

checklistItems.name: Carb Heat - On (as applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This only applies to carbureted engines.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Follow the engine manufacturer's recommendations for use of carb heat.

checklistItems.name: Power - Reduce
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Desired airspeed - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Reduce power.

Gradually apply back pressure to maintain altitude while airplane slows to descent airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Read "Pitch for Altitude, Power for Airspeed - A Rule with Two Exceptions" (link below). Once the pilot has a feel for holding a coordinated descent with constant airspeed, practice holding the pitch reference constant while changing power, trim, and flaps configurations. Note how these changes affect control pressures and descent performance, even though the pitch is held constant below the horizon.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: To simplify this maneuver, set the power at a fixed value and then pitch for the desired airspeed in the descent (exception #1, see Additional Resources below). Start with normal descent power and then practice different power settings after that, including power-off glides.

checklistItems.name: Pitch - Reduce
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Referencing the outside pitch reference, lower the nose slightly to set the descent pitch attitude and maintain airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Cover up the AI and HI to require the pilot to look outside for pitch and bank references. Use the ASI to know if a pitch change is needed, the inclinometer for coordination control (step on the ball), TACH for power control, and the ALT/VSI for altitude information.

checklistItems.name: Trim - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Fly what you see, trim what you feel. When changes are needed, make small corrections, allow the airplane to stabilize, and then trim away control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips: Remind the pilot to "Fly what you see, trim what you feel" (watching the pitch reference and ASI).

checklistItems.name: Bank - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Begin a turn in the specified direction and at the specified bank angle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to establish the specificed bank angle using outside visual references, then reference the AI. Make small corrections while looking outside and cross-checking the AI.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Start with 90 deg and 180 deg turns in each direction by sole reference to outside heading references (using points on the wingtips).

checklistItems.name: Coordination - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Glance at the inclinometer to ensure the ball is centered.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Make small corrections - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Referencing the outside pitch reference, slightly decrease pitch to increase speed or increase pitch to decrease speed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the pilot learn that smaller corrections sooner are better than larger corrections later.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Demonstrate (or discuss) how up and down drafts will require abnormal pitch and power changes to maintain airspeed in the descent. Teach the pilot to start with a small correction, but then promptly increase the correction if the desired result/trend does not occur.

checklistItems.name: Bank - Wing level
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Roll wings level slightly before reaching the desired heading. Remember to match the aileron input with proper rudder input.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Altimeter - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Lead level-off by 10% of descent rate: If descending at 500 fpm, return to straight and level by gradually increasing pitch approximately 50 ft prior to desired level-off altitude. This may happen before or after the turn is complete.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.notesToPilot: This only applies to carbureted engines.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Follow the engine manufacturer's recommendations for use of carb heat.

checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

activities.name: [10] X/C: Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes (BIM)
activities.what: A flight maneuver consisting of recovery from either nose high or nose low unusual attitudes solely by reference to flight instruments
activities.why: To safely recover from unusual attitudes caused by pilot disorientation during times of loss of visual horizon, night flight, and inadvertent flight into IMC
activities.groundPrep:
Discuss the applicable Objective, Knowledge, Risk Management, and Skills listed in the Private Pilot ACS. 
"Point out that flying over large bodies of water in hazy conditions and night VFR away from lighted areas on a moonless or overcast night can be the same as flying under the hood." Review the basics of the scan (see Ralph Butcher's article "Elementary Instrument Flying")

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator: Teach the pilot the nose up/down recovery methods just like you would for a flight in the airplane. Taking advantage of the pause button can help you quickly focus the pilot on the correct technique. To simulate entry into an unusual attitude, try distracting the pilot (or let them distract themselves) by focusing on adjusting the radios, navigation, or other heads down task. Then bring their attention (if they don't catch it first) to the unusual attitude for recovery. Setting the pilot for a night takeoff in less populated area where there are few (simulated) lights and plenty of darkness can let the pilot get an introduction to VFR flight with few visual references. One good example is Casa Grande, AZ (KCGZ). Set the time for night, perhaps an overcast layer depending on the simulator visuals, and have the pilot takeoff and climb on runway 23. Consider giving them turns and various altitudes, but depending on the visuals in your simulator you may need to avoid turning them to the north where they city lights from Phoenix may be visible. You can always reduce the visibility to prevent that visual reference from appearing too easily. Challenge the pilot to run checklists and navigation tasks that can potentially cause distraction and have them recover as appropriate. Impress upon them the hazards and the need for good preparation and solid decision making.

checklistItems.name: View limiting device - On
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure it is properly adjusted to allow full view of the instruments, but nothing outside
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be vigiliant for traffic! Exercise extreme caution to divide your attention to properly scan for traffic while you are teaching instrument procedures

Create scenarios that involve loss of horizon due to smoke or haze, flying over featureless terrain like large bodies of water, flying at night, and "Emergency escape procedures" to return to visual flight conditions.

Teach that the skill of switch-tasking involves looking at the right thing, at the right time, for the right amount of time.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Teach the 4-step instrument scanned explained by Ralph Butcher in the article below.

checklistItems.name: Unusual attitude - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Eyes closed and head down with chin in the chest.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
With the pilot's eyes closed and chin down, perform climbing and descending turns to disorient the pilot's middle ear before establishing the unusual flight attitude. When ready, calmly say, "You have the controls, recover." 

While virtually all view limiting devices are not "peek-proof," impress on the pilot the need for them to experience the suprise effect of unusual attitudes. There will always be a few who, either because of fear or the challenge of cheating the system, will make an effort to peek. Confidence in your abilities as an instructor can address fear, and perhaps a serious discussion on the importance of the training--can make a difference with the latter.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: An alternate method of inducing an unusual attiude is to allow the pilot to fly the plane with the eyes closed while the instructor calls for various manuevers to be performed, such as rolling into and out of a turn. When they eventutally enter an unusual attitude, have them recover. You can also emphasize how easy it is to become disoriented when trying to fly be feel alone without outside references.

checklistItems.name: Airspeed and power - Identify and adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When told to recover, view the airspeed. If increasing, say and do, "airspeed increasing; reduce power." If decreasing, say and do, "airspeed decreasing, increase power."
checklistItems.teachingTips:
As with stalls, this series of manuevers can induce a high level of stress on the pilot. The instructor's demeanor is critical to establishing a calm and in-control thoght process in the student. 

If the pilot has a tendancy to respond before assessing the situation, consider having them delay their response until they announce to you the situation, such as "approach to stall" or "descending spiral."
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: As with most flight training, the instructor's demeanor sets the tone. Use a positive and calm presentation throughout. This is especailly true should the pilot react improperly. Corrective words should be few and meaningful and said with a positive and affirmative delivery.

checklistItems.name: Pitch attitude - Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Now view the attitude indicator. 

Identify if the aircraft is nose-high or nose-low pitch attitude by saying, ""nose high"" or ""nose low."" 

Make no response until the next step.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Using a simulator for inital training in Basic Instrument Manuevers will allow you to pause the action and give the pilot time to develop the correct thought process for responding to an unusual attitude.

checklistItems.name: NOSE-HIGH ATTITUDE
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Pitch and Bank - Level both simultaneously
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
If nose-high attitude, say and do, "decreasing pitch to zero (level) attitude." 

Lower the nose to place the airplane symbol on horizon bar of AI and add power (if available).

If in a bank, say and do, "leveling the wing."

Secondary indicators include increasing altitude, positive rate of climb, and decreasing airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Introduce each unusual attitude with small pitch and bank excursions, so the pilot does not feel an urgency to respond too quickly. After they have gained confidence in their ability to assess an unusual situation, increase the pitch and back gradually and allow their reponses to mature.

Emphasize to the pilot that it is more important to take a few seconds to properly assess the type of unusual attitude, than to rush a response that is incorrect.

Note any corrective suggestions and emphasize the need to positively identify the condition before attempting the remedy.

Help the pilot find the balance between jerking on the controls which could cause an inadvertant stall and reacting too slowly or too gently. Be sure to demonstrate the correct technique and then coach them through the procedured until they develop a solid response. The procedure can be drilled quite effectively in a sim to maximize instructional time while keeping the cost low.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
If a slow or incorrect response results in the airplane stalling or entering an incipient spin phase, say to the pilot in a normal but positive tone, "Incorrrect recovery, I have the airplane."

Note to the pilot what you are doing to recover. In subsequent maneuvers, allow the pilot to attempt the recovery with your short phrases to guide their actions.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level - Resume
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Return to straight and level flight and establish cruise setting and trim to relieve control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: NOSE-LOW ATTITUDE
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Bank and Pitch - Level wings, then pitch
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
If nose-low attitude, say and do, "nose low, reduce power."

If a bank exists, say and do, "unbank."

When bank is zero say, "increase pitch to zero-pitch attitude." 

(Raising the nose to a level flight attitude before leveling wings, increases the load factor can result in accelerated stall, spin, or overstressing airplane)

Secondary indicators include decreasing altitude, high rate of descent, increasing airspeed. 

Airspeed can quickly exceed maneuvering speed with potential for overstressing airplane.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
As with the nose-high situation, introduce the pitch and bank angles in small increments to avoid engendering any fear aspect.

Note the need to simultaneously reduce power and level the wings using coordinated aileron and rudder pressure and referencing the airplane symbol on the attitude indicator.

Emphasize to the pilot that it is more important to take a few seconds to properly assess the type of unusual attitude, than to rush a response that is incorrect.

Help the pilot find the balance between jerking on the controls which could cause an inadvertant stall and reacting too slowly or too gently. Be sure to demonstrate the correct technique and then coach them through the procedured until they develop a solid response. The procedure can be drilled quite effectively in a sim to maximize instructional time while keeping the cost low.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level - Resume
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Return to straight and level flight and establish cruise setting and trim to relieve control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Heading Indicator - Realign
checklistItems.notesToPilot: After the last recovery, align the heading indicator with the magnetic compass.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Following each maneuver, discuss briefly their perceptions and reactions to ensure their correct interpretations.

Compensation for the inherent stability of the airplane, overbanking tendencies, adverse yaw, propeller effects, reduction of the vertical component of lift, and increased drag must be managed by the pilot through the manipulation of the flight controls.

checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note your starting heading with outside references.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. If a grid layout of roads and/or farm fields is available, that works best. The key is to teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right.

checklistItems.name: Yoke / Control stick - Hold lightly
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Always fly with a very light grip on the controls.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pay attention to how the pilot is holding the yoke / control stick and remind him/her to keep a light grip on the controls.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If the pilot continues to struggle with gripping the controls too tight, consider having him/her place a pen or pencil between their fingers so that it hurts when they squeeze tight. Emphasize a light, relaxed touch on the controls - often with just a few fingers.

checklistItems.name: Power - Full
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Gradually increase to full power as you pitch up.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Pitch - Increase
checklistItems.notesToPilot: While looking at your outside pitch reference, gently increase pitch to the estimated climb pitch attitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Cover up the AI and HI to require the pilot to look outside for pitch and bank references. Use the ASI to know if a pitch change is needed, the inclinometer for coordination control (step on the ball), TACH for power control, and the ALT/VSI for altitude information.

checklistItems.name: Bank - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Begin a turn in the specified direction and at the specified bank angle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to establish the specified bank angle using outside visual references, then reference the AI. Make small corrections while looking outside and cross-checking the AI.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Start with 90 deg and 180 deg turns in each direction by sole reference to outside heading references (using points on the wingtips).

checklistItems.name: Desired airspeed - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Find the specific pitch angle that results in the desired airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Read "Pitch for Altitude, Power for Airspeed - A Rule with Two Exceptions" (link below). Once the pilot has a feel for holding a coordinated climb with constant airspeed, practice holding the pitch reference constant while changing power, trim, and flaps configurations. Note how these changes affect control pressures and climb performance, even though the pitch is held constant above the horizon.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: To simplify this maneuver, set the power at a fixed value and then pitch for the desired airspeed in the descent (exception #1, see Additional Resources below). Start with normal descent power and then practice different power settings after that, including power-off glides.

checklistItems.name: Trim - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Fly what you see, trim what you feel. When changes are needed, make small corrections, allow the airplane to stabilize, and then trim away control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips: Remind the pilot to "Fly what you see, trim what you feel" (watching the pitch reference and ASI).

checklistItems.name: Coordination - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Glance at the inclinometer to ensure the ball is centered.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Make small corrections - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Referencing the outside pitch reference, slightly decrease pitch to increase speed or increase pitch to decrease speed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the pilot learn that smaller corrections sooner are better than larger corrections later.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Demonstrate (or discuss) how up and down drafts will require abnormal pitch and power changes to maintain airspeed in the climb. Teach the pilot to start with a small correction, but then promptly increase the correction if the desired result/trend does not occur.

checklistItems.name: Bank - Wings level
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Roll wings level slightly before reaching the desired heading. Remember to match the aileron input with proper rudder input.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Altimeter - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Lead level-off by 10% of climb rate: If climbing at 500 FPM, return to straight and level by gradually decreasing pitch approximately 50 ft prior to desired level-off altitude. This may happen before or after the turn is complete.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Power - Decrease
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Reduce power to maintain desired airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Mixture - Lean (as needed)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Lean as needed for higher altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Altitude - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Referencing the outside pitch reference, adjust pitch to maintain the new desired altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Trim - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Fly what you see, trim what you feel. When changes are needed, make small corrections, allow the airplane to stabilize, and then trim away control pressures
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Climbs at different speeds - Explain/Demonstrate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Create different scenarios to practice climbs at various airspeeds ranging from Vx to cruise climb.

commonErrors.name: Not looking at pitch reference
commonErrors.details: Making pitch changes without looking at the pitch reference.

commonErrors.name: Improper use of heading references
commonErrors.details: Improper use of heading references. Evidenced by losing track of which outside references he/she was using.

commonErrors.name: Tight grip
commonErrors.details: Gripping the yoke / control stick too tightly

commonErrors.name: Fixating on instruments
commonErrors.details: Fixating on the instruments. Evidenced by staring at the instruments instead of using outside pitch and bank references.

commonErrors.name: Under/over banking
commonErrors.details: Under/over banking

commonErrors.name: Using pitch/power/trim for wrong thing
commonErrors.details: Misunderstanding of the relationship between power, pitch, and trim. Evidenced by trying to use power/pitch/trim to control the wrong thing.

prepItems.name: Four Fundamentals (part 2)
prepItems.details: Every maneuver you do with an airplane involves the four fundamentals of flight – turns, straight-and-level, climbs, and descents.

activities.name: [04] PRE-SOLO: Manuevering During Slow Flight
activities.what: A flight maneuver that demonstrates the flight characteristics and controllability when flying close to the critical angle of attack
activities.why: To develop an awareness of the airplane’s behavior in order to avoid stalls during maneuvers at low airspeed (i.e., takeoff, landing, and go-arounds); to develop mastery of the airplane in all phases of flight
activities.groundPrep:
Slow flight may be conducted in straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs, or descents. It can also be conducted in the clean configuration, landing configuration, or at any other combination of landing gear and flaps. While the FAA standard has one very distinct definition of slow flight for the pracitcal exam, flight training should cover a range of slow flight conditions in order for the pilot to gain an understanding and ability to control the aircraft in all phases of flight. In all cases, practicing slow flight should be conducted at an adequate height above the ground for recovery should the airplane inadvertently stall.
It’s important for the pilot to understand the total drag curve and how it relates to the area of reverse command. When performing slow flight, a small change in angle of attack causes a large change in induced drag. This is why we primarily pitch for airspeed and power for altitude during slow flight. This is known as the area of reverse command because unlike normal flight, more power is required to go slower.
Aerodynamics associated with slow flight in various airplane configurations, to include the relationship between angle of attack, airspeed, load factor, power setting, airplane weight and center of gravity, airplane attitude, and yaw effects.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver Check (CAMELS) - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the airplane - Verify that all switches and controls are in the proper position
Airspeed - Set power to obtain/maintain desired entry speed for the maneuver (just above stall warning)
Minimum safe altitude - Ensure minimum safe altitude requirements are met (so that maneuver can be completed no lower than 1500' AGL)
Engine gauges - Check engine gauges for proper readings
Landing site - Select an emergency landing site
Scan the area - Carefully scan for traffic and obstructions while turning at least two 90 deg turns or one 180 deg turn
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Help the pilot determine a speed just above the stall warning indicator (approximately Vs +5 kts) and a power setting that will reliably get them there for this maneuver.

A GPS ground speed readout is useful for pointing out the varying ground speed throughout the maneuver.
checklistItems.simulator:
The sim can be useful in introducing and reviewing maneuvering during slow flight. In particular, using the pause button can help the pilot learn how to see and control pitch attitude. While the sim will lack the kinesthetic sensation that is felt in the airplane, it is still a great tool for teaching the procedures and how to use the outside sight picture to control the airplane during the maneuver. Pilots will still likely to be able to notice the controls becoming less effective (or "sloppy") as the airspeed decreases, so be sure to point that out for them to notice as compared to normal cruise flight. Holding altitude, airspeed, and heading during slow flight tends to require more frequent monitoring of the flight instruments than other visual maneuvers. You will still want to encourage the pilot to make attitude changes with outside visual references, so consider covering up the flight instruments but allow more frequent checks to help them verify the airplane's performance.

Start the session at a typical altitude (e.g. 3000'AGL) in straight and level cruise flight. Then coach the pilot through configuring the airplane and how to perform slow flight while straight and level, climbing, descending, and turning (just like you would in the airplane). Be sure to have the pilot practice any pre-maneuver checklists and procedures to help reinforce what they will do in the airplane.

One of the main purposes of maneuvering during slow flight is to help the pilot develop a feel for the airplane during takeoff and especially landing. Consider having the pilot perform low approaches to the runway in the simulator that would otherwise be unsafe and impractical during actual flight.

checklistItems.name: Straight and level flight - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish a heading with a prominent visual landmark. One of the most difficult aspects of the maneuver is dividing attention between airplane configuration and outside references. Make it easier by selecting a prominent landmark and flying toward it. Doing so will eliminate the need to ever reference the heading indicator or compass.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Power - Reduce (Carb heat - As applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Simultaneously reduce power and pitch up in order to maintain altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once below Vfe, begin to add flaps incrementally (or as directed) while maintaining altitude, heading, and airspeed. You will feel the control pressures change as you extend flaps. Respond to configuration changes with appropriate pitch changes to maintain altitude. Anticipate the changes and trim away the pressures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Clearly point out the pitch changes that happen when extending or retracting flaps as a preparatory activity so that the pilot can learn to anticipate the control pressures and how to adjust/trim them away.

checklistItems.name: Altitude, airspeed, heading, coordination - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: As the aircraft slows more back pressure will be required to maintain altitude. As the airspeed drops to around Vx, slowly begin adding power to maintain altitude. Remember as you add power at low speeds you will need to use more right rudder to counteract the airplane's turning tendencies. The Airmen Certification Standards (ACS) call for a speed slow enough that any increase in angle of attack or decrease in power will result in the stall warning indicator activating. In order to prevent having to recover from the stall indicator sounding on your checkride, consider flying at a speed 5 knots above where the stall warning indicator normally activates.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Speed and altitude control is the most difficult aspect of this part of the maneuver. Although simultaneous pitch and power changes are the best practice to maintain airspeed and altitude, beginning pilots often find it easier to think in terms of pitching for airspeed and power control for altitude. After practicing once with the student, establish a target power setting for your load factor and use that as an initial reference point for established straight and level flight. That will keep the pilot from having to search for a proper setting. 

To help teach proper rudder control during power changes, have the pilot practice holding a constant heading while making large power changes. Then make smaller and smaller changes to help him/her fine tune the technique and learn how much rudder pressure is required.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: The ACS standard calls for an airspeed by which any further increase in AOA or decrease in speed will result in the stall warning device activating. Thus, some advocate for the entry to the maneuver to include slowing down to the point of hearing the horn or seeing a light, and then adding five knots as a target airspeed. The FAA isn't clear on this point, so it is best to confirm with your local examiner prior to teaching in this manner.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use trim to help relieve control pressures as you establish your airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: NOTE: The use of trim is debated while maneuvering during slow flight, with some instructors saying it works well to help establish an airspeed, and others saying it goes against the intent of the maneuver, which is for the pilot to be able to actively control the aircraft through all phases of flight.

checklistItems.name: Climb/Descend/Turn - As required
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use power to climb or descend as requested. Slow flight is an unstable flight condition so all configuration changes should be done slowly. For climbs, begin by adding 100 or 200 rpm and slightly adjusting pitch downward. Wait for a response. If necessary, add more, but only in small increments. For a descent, decrease power by only 100 or 200 rpm and increase pitch slightly. Wait for the descent to begin and adjust as necessary.

Add 100 or 200 rpm as you slowly roll in to a left or right turn. Turns should be very gentle, with bank at no more than about 15 to 20 degrees. Ensure proper rudder coordination by increasing right rudder for right turns and decreasing right rudder for left turns.
checklistItems.teachingTips: You may consider starting the pilot out with flying at speeds that are 10-15 kts above stall warning to help them get comfortable controlling the airplane at various speeds and configurations. This will help them transition to slow flight with a little less anxiety as well as getting a feel for how the airplane feels and responds at wider range of speeds.

checklistItems.name:
Recover to cruise - Perform
 Throttle - Full
 Pitch - Level
 Flaps - Retract incrementally
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Recover. Add power to come to cruise power while slowly lowering the nose. Flaps should be retracted in increments, with an initial retraction immediately, an additional retraction when the airplane accelerates, and another upon reaching Vy. Be sure to adjust rudder and elevator pressure to maintain coordination, heading, and altitude as the airplane returns to cruise flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Point out that recovery from slow flight is the same as full flap power off stall recovery and go arounds. By keeping the procedure consistent it will be easier for the pilot to remember the correct procedure and to develop a ingrained habit of correct control inputs when under pressure later.

commonErrors.name: Unstable climbs/descents
commonErrors.details:
Rapid or large power changes that result in unstable climbs and descents.

Suggestion: The pilot should focus on small changes while in slow flight, using the tachometer as a guide to make only minor adjustments. He or she can then reassess to fine-tune the adjustment, resulting in a gradual climb or descent.

commonErrors.name: Uncoordinated flight
commonErrors.details:
Uncoordinated flight.

Suggestion:
With coordination it should be emphasized that most training aircraft will require more right rudder on right turns, and less right rudder on left turns. This is contrary to level turns, where left rudder is necessary. With slow flight a lessening of pressure on the right rudder pedal is usually all that is necessary to stay coordinated for a left turn.

Unintentional stall.

Suggestion:
A stall can be avoided with a power increase and a limit to bank angle. Steep banks will result in an accelerated stall.

Altitude deviation.

Suggestion:
Adding power at the beginning of the turn will ensure altitude is maintained.

commonErrors.name: Unintentional stall
commonErrors.details:
Unintentional stall.

Suggestion: During intial practice, explore stalling from a slow flight configuration so the pilot knows what that attitude looks and feels like, and therefore knows better how to avoid it. Stress speed control as a primary consideration of the maneuver, and to think of the yoke as a stall device. Pull back farther and a stall will occur.


Failure to slow down enough to get in the region of reverse command.

Suggestion: Many pilots are timid going in to the region of reverse command. It can help to set the airplane up and then hand over the controls while already established. Exploring the stall in the configuration should also help to calm anxiety of what happens when the aircraft slows too much.


Failure to maintain heading.

Suggestion: Teach the importance on focusing on an outside landmark. The heading indicator is unnecessary during this manuever, and relying on it usually makes the maneuver more difficult. Cover up the indicator if the pilot is spending too much time focused on the flight instruments.


Stall warning horn activation.

Suggestion: Although not necessarily a safety condition, activating the stall warning horn could result in a practical test failure. Spend time with the pilot to understand where the stall warning horn activates in 1G unaccelerated flight, and then set an acceptable speed margain to avoid activating it.


Uncoordinated flight.

Suggestion:
Stress the importance of right rudder during the maneuver, even to the point of encouraging only the right foot on the rudder pedals until proper coordination can routinely be established.

commonErrors.name: Early flap extension
commonErrors.details:
Deploying flaps before slowing to flap extension speed.

Suggestion:
Explain to the pilot the importance of being below flap extension speed prior to adding flaps.

Gaining or losing altitude during configuration changes.

Suggestion:
Practice repeatedly making power changes first before configuration changes. When power is reduced, pitch must always been increased if the desire is to slow down. Have the pilot practice simultaneous pitch and power changes while staying on alttiude.

commonErrors.name: Improper selection of landmark
commonErrors.details:
Not selecting a visual landmark or selecting an improper landmark.

Suggestion:
Ensure the pilot selects a landmark prior to beginning the maneuver, and flies toward it. The landmark should be prominent, such as a mountain, water tower, road, town, or other large object.

commonErrors.name: No clearing turns
commonErrors.details:
Not completing clearing turns or having configuration errors. 

Suggestion:
By completing a pre-maneuver checklist you can ensure your student remembers to complete the required configuration and entry speeds. Especially important for ground reference maneuvers is selecting a suitable emergency landing site close to the course.

commonErrors.name: Unintended altitude deviation
commonErrors.details:
Altitude deviation caused by improper configuration change.

Suggestion:
Stress configuration changes be done in incremenets, and that will usually keep the airplane on altitude as well. Pilots who fully retract the flaps in one change tend to cause the airplane to sink on recovery.

Heading deviation.

Suggestion:
Heading deviations can be avoided by flying toward the visual landmark selected at the outset. No compass or heading indicator reference is necessary.
