activities.name: [11] X/C: Radio Communications, Navigation Systems/Facilities, and Radar Services (BIM)
activities.what: Maneuver the airplane solely by reference to flight instruments while using radio communications, tracking of navigation systems, and radar services (real or simulated).
activities.why: To fly solely by reference to instruments for the purpose of safely controlling the airplane while navigating and communicating during times of loss of visual horizon, night flight, and inadvertent flight into IMC
activities.groundPrep: Point out that flying over large bodies of water in hazy conditions and night VFR away from lighted areas on a moonless or overcast night can be the same as flying under the hood. Review available navigation / radar services and how they can be utilized in an emergency such as inadvertent entry of IMC. Operating communications equipment to include identifying and selecting radio frequencies, requesting and following ATC instructions. Operating navigation equipment to include functions and displays, and following bearings, radials, or courses. Air traffic control facilities and services. When and how to seek assistance or declare an emergency in a deteriorating situation. How access and utilize available resources (e.g., auromation, ATC, flight deck planning aids).

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator:
Once the pilot is proficient in aircraft control while flying by reference to the flight instruments, you can introduce them to tracking navaids and following simulated radar vectors from ATC. Help them develop the scan required to keep the VOR, GPS, or other relevant navaid in their scan while using the simulator's pause button to maximize the pilot's ability to pay attention to your instruction.

Like when teaching the basic fundamentals, setting up realistic cross country scenarios where pilots will inadvertently enter marginal VFR or instrument conditions are an effective way to help the pilot practice decision making and problem solving. Have them contact ATC (you) and request assistance. You can then give them a combination of vectors/headings and navaid tracking so they practice controlling the airplane while navigating out of trouble.

checklistItems.name: View limiting device - On
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure it is properly adjusted to allow full view of the instruments, but nothing outside
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Exercise extreme caution to divide your attention to properly scan for traffic while you are teaching instrument procedures

Create scenarios that involve loss of horizon due to smoke or haze, flying over featureless terrain like large bodies of water, flying at night, and "Emergency escape procedures" to return to visual flight conditions.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Teach the 4-step instrument scanned explained by Ralph Butcher in the article below.

checklistItems.name: AVIATE
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Aircraft control - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use the basic instrument scan and maneuvers learned in previous lessons to maintain safe aircraft control.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the pilot learn to safely fly the airplane on instruments while performing other tasks such as navigating, looking up information on a chart, flying through busy airspace while talking to ATC, dealing with simulated passenger issues, etc. Demonstrate what happens when fixating on an instrument, and what can happen on the transition when flying in and out of clouds. Finally, stress the importance of flying the airplane above all else.

checklistItems.name: Poor weather - Escape
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Keeping the airplane under control is the primary goal. Returning to visual conditions may require a turn, climb, or descent. A level 180 degree turn is the safest way to escape, but might not be the most efficient. Consider what put you in the clouds in the first place. If you entered a layer above you, a shallow straight descent might be the best option. Similarly a climb might be called for. The most difficult escape, and the one to avoid, is the need to turn and change altitude at the same time.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the Pilot simulate going into a cloud and making a 180 degree turn to exit the cloud, then have the Pilot climb 1000 feet on the new heading to simulate climbing above the cloud, have the Pilot turn 90 degrees and descend 1000 feet to simulate getting below the clouds. Focus on level turns and straight climbs and descents. Discuss the various scenarios that indavertent VFR into IMC occurs.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: See video in Prep: VFR into IMC- Tips For Teaching

checklistItems.name: NAVIGATE
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Navigation radios/avionics - Set up
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Hopefully things were set in advance and you are on a usable frequency and tuned to a usable navaid. Consider your current situation. If you know the clouds, fog, or haze are temporary and you'll soon exit, concentrate on flying.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to systematically set up navigation radios with consistent steps. For example, tune the desired frequency, switch it to active, verify (or ident) the navaid), check that the correct CDI indication is selected. This should be the same for each change of navaid to help avoid accidently choosing an incorrect navaid or CDI setting.

checklistItems.name: Navaid/Waypoint - Identify/Verify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If not already set, tune to a nearby navaid or program the GPS with a nearby airport, considering terrain and airspace. Always concentrate on flying first, and look down to find and tune a navaid for only a second or two at a time.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Minimum safe altitude - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure your escape course clears terrain.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Give the pilot scenarios where they in the clouds near high terrain and have "ATC" give them instructions that would direct them toward terrain that is too high. Help the pilot learn to check and plan for terrain clearance as part of their situational awareness.

checklistItems.name: Course - Select, intercept, and maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use whatever navigation system is easiest and most accessbile. If you're already tracking a VOR use that. If you're using the GPS and have easy access, use that. Head toward an area of known better weather with a standard-rate turn.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Have the Pilot do a series of navigational exercises while under the hood:

1) Have the pilot tune in a VOR, identify it, and fly to the VOR on the correct heading with the proper OBS orientation

2) Have the Pilot reverse course and track the radial outbound, with the proper OBS orientation

3) Have the Pilot intercept a cross radial from another VOR (if one is available) and track it inbound or outbound, with the proper OBS orientation (make sure they identify it when they tune it in); if only one VOR is available, tune the OBS to a new radial and have the Pilot incept the new radial and track it.

4) Have the Pilot climb or descend to a different altitude while tracking the VOR radial.

checklistItems.name: COMMUNICATE
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Communication radio - Set up
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If you know you'll need assistance and your frequencies are set to a CTAF or something else that can't help, tune to 121.5 or a local ATC frequency for assistance.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Use a similar methodical procedure as described in the Navaid step. Tune the frequency, move to active, verify that the correct facility has been selected. Also check that the correct radio has been selected and that volume is audible.

checklistItems.name: Air Traffic Control - Contact and confess
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If you need help, contact the ATC facility, say your registration number and location and ask for help escapting IMC.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Discuss the type of assistance offered and how to use it.

checklistItems.name: ATC Directions - Comply
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Follow only the instructions you feel you can safely accomplish. Say "unable" for everything that you think will exceed your ability to handle at that moment. Don't hesitate to declare an emergency if necessary.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Make sure the pilot understands he or she is in control of the situation and shouldn't go beyond their limitations because of an ATC instruction. Provide personal examples or relay stories of when a pilot has had to exercise PIC judgement and authority. Assure the help that ATC is there to help, and that the pilot needs to be assertive and clear with ATC as the situation dictates.

commonErrors.name: Improper instrument scan
commonErrors.details:
Improper instrument scan; fixation; not focusing on flying tasks.

Suggestion:
Teach that the skill of switch-tasking involves looking at the right thing, at the right time, for the right amount of time.
Reference Ralph Butcher's article below for detailed information of what to look for and how to correct it. Demonstrate fixation, and show what happens when aircraft control is ingored in favor of lesser tasks such as navigating and communicating.

commonErrors.name: Failure to set radios prior to IMC
commonErrors.details:
Failure to have radios/avionics set up in advance of entering simulated IMC

Suggestion:
Ensure that the Pilot sets up their radios / avionics so that the standby frequency is the next frequency they'll need after they depart. (i.e. Approach Control) Whenever the Pilot changes frequencies on the radio or navigation, have them tell you what the "next thing" needs to be loaded into standby frequency.

commonErrors.name: Failure to set GPS/CDI
commonErrors.details:
Failure to identify and verify Navaids. Failure to set up GPS navigator (if equipped) and select the proper setting on the CDI button (GPS or VLOC) for the selected navigation source.

Suggestion:
Be sure to establish and consistently have the pilot use a standard procedure for setting up the navigation equipment. If needed, an additional checklist section could help remind the pilot of what to check. activities.name: [05] PRE-SOLO: Steep Turns
activities.what: A flight maneuver consisting of 360˚ turns at a bank angle of 45˚
activities.why: To develop a high degree of pilot skill (smoothness, coordination, orientation, division of attention, and control techniques) while executing high performance turns
activities.groundPrep:
ACS definitions and standards for the maneuver
Four forces of flight
Vertical and horizontal components of lift and the relationship between pitch and bank at high bank angles
Overbanking tendency
Visual illusions caused by sitting on the side of the cockpit (the pilot in the left seat sees a lot of sky in left turns and a lot of ground in right turns)
The importance of using a pitch reference on the windshield right in front of the pilot
Trim technique

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the airplane - Verify that all switches and controls are in the proper position
Airspeed - Set power to obtain/maintain desired entry speed for the maneuver
Minimum safe altitude - Ensure minimum safe altitude requirements are met
Engine gauges - Check engine gauges for proper readings
Landing site - Select an emergency landing site
Scan the area - Carefully scan for traffic while turning at least two 90 deg turns or one 180 deg turn
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to use the CAMELS check or other appropriate pre-maneuver procedure before each set of maneuvers.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If your school does not already provide a pre-maneuver procedure, AOPA recommends using the CAMELS check to ensure the ACS required clearing turns are completed as well as other important items.
checklistItems.simulator:
The sim can be useful in introducing and reviewing steep turns. In particular, using the pause button can help the pilot learn how to see and control pitch attitude. While the sim will lack the kinesthetic sensation that is felt in the airplane, it is still a great tool for teaching the procedures and how to use the outside sight picture to control the airplane during the maneuver. Be sure to cover the flight instruments if you observe the pilot trying to fly primarily by instrument indications.

Start the session at a typical altitude (e.g. 3000'AGL) in straight and level cruise flight. Then coach the pilot through configuring the airplane and how to perform the steep turns to the left and right (just like you would in the airplane). Be sure to have the pilot practice any pre-maneuver checklists and procedures to help reinforce what they will do in the airplane.

checklistItems.name: Heading and Pitch references - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain altitude by keeping a point on airplane’s nose or spot on the windshield in a constant position in relation to a point on the horizon. Establish airplane on specific heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Cover up all of the flight instruments to force the pilot to look outside. This is a great technique when first teaching every visual maneuver. It emphasizes that the primary pitch and bank references are outside.

Choose multiple heading references that are far away on the horizon. If a grid layout of roads and/or farm fields is available, that works best. The key is to teach the pilot to look at a reference point straight ahead, while also referencing 90 deg points to the left and right.

checklistItems.name: Airspeed - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish the manufacturer’s recommended airspeed; or if one is not available, a safe airspeed not to exceed VA
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: 45 deg bank - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Smoothly roll into coordinated 45° bank turn; Increase elevator back pressure and throttle as you roll past 30° bank to maintain level flight and airspeed. Maintain angle of bank and altitude; confirm attitude with both natural horizon and AI; Use ALT and VSI to determine need for pitch changes.
checklistItems.teachingTips: It is common for pilots to apply too much or too little rudder when rolling into a turn. In the case of steep turns, coordination problems can be exaggerated. Practicing coordination exercises where the pilot rolls the airplane left and right while maintaining a stationary point on the horizon is a great way to let students develop a feel for how much rudder is needed while rolling. If the nose of the airplane slides one way or the other rather than pivoting around the spot, the pilot needs to adjust how much rudder they are using to correct.

checklistItems.name: Altitude and Airspeed - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Altitude deviations: adjust with elevator pressure, and throttle/bank (1-3°) as necessary: [high - reduce elevator and slightly steepen bank; low - slightly shallow bank and increase elevator]. Make power adjustments to maintain entry speed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Use a pitch reference that is on the windshield, directly in front of the pilot flying. Start with a small suction cup or corner of a sticky note. After experience is gained, the same technique can be performed by simply imagining something is on the windshield, but that same point must be used for pitch reference and adjustments. Also, demonstrate how going just a few degrees past 45 deg of bank reduces the vertical component of lift and causes the nose to fall. Proper altitude control during the steep turn is a combination of pitch and bank control. Use of elevator trim is discouraged (see Additional Resources below).

Airspeed is controlled with power. Teach the pilot to reference the TACH fo the power setting that provides the desired airpeed in straight and level flight (adjustments will be needed for different density altitudes). Ensure everything is stabilized before starting the steep turn and then teach the pilot to add a little power as they roll into the turn.

checklistItems.name: Bank and Coordination - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain angle of bank and altitude; confirm attitude with both natural horizon and AI; Use ALT and VSI to determine need for pitch changes. Monitor the inclinometer and use rudder to maintain coordination in the turn by applying rudder to the same side as any deviation (e.g., "step on the ball").
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Help the pilot learn what 45 deg of bank looks like out the windshield. For the pitch reference mentioned above, a square sticky note can be used with one corner pointing straight up. In addition to a pitch reference, the left and right sides of the sticky note will also provide a 45 deg bank reference. Note that the sight picture of the horizon in relation to the noise/glareshield is different to the left and right. Both sight pictures should be memorized. To fine-tune the exact bank angle, teach the pilot to quickly glance at the attitude indicator while dividing his/her attention inside and outside the cockpit.

With so much to focus on, new pilots often neglect proper rudder inputs. Help each pilot understand the aerodynamic effect of adverse yaw (drag from the down aileron). In most training planes, a healthy amount of rudder will be required during the entry and exit of the steep turn and a slight amount of rudder will need to be applied during the turn. In some planes, no rudder will need to be applied during the left turn (due to the left turning tendencies). Simply teach pilots to glance at the inclinometer and step on the ball as needed. Note that during a steep turn, a large rudder input will cause the nose to move above or below the horizon. Rudder corrections should be made gently and attention will be needed to simultaneously control pitch with the yoke.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: For coordination control, teach the pilot to relax his/her neck muscles and pay attention to whether his/her head feels like it wants to fall to the left or to the right. With a little practice, the pilot's head can be "the ball." Once the pilot is comfortable with this, uncover one instrument at a time and teach the pilot to quickly glance at the instrument(s) to fine-tune the control inputs.

checklistItems.name: Rollout (360 deg turn) - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: About 20° (½ bank angle) before entry heading, begin rollout to straight and level flight; reduce elevator pressure and throttle to maintain altitude and airspeed; Trim as needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Most new pilots become disoriented and lose track of their starting point when first learning steep turns. Adequate outside visual references are the key to rolling out on the proper heading. A movable heading bug on the HI is also helpful, but the primary references should always be outside. It's best to use fields and/or roads that form a grid pattern. Doing so will make it easy for the pilot to see when he/she is coming through the last 90 degrees of the turn.

activities.name: [06] PRE-SOLO: Power-Off Stalls
activities.what: A ground avoidance maneuver that simulates a stall during the turn from base to final, final approach, and/or landing
activities.why: To recognize an approaching stall and take prompt corrective action
activities.groundPrep:
- Stall recognition awareness.  Recognizing stalls by sound, sight, and the feel of the aircraft.
- Control responsiveness.  Note that the controls, particularly the ailerons lose their effectiveness at slow speeds and in a stall.
- Smooth use of the flight controls is critical for positive control of the the aircraft.
- Maintaining coordinated flight.  Coordinated use of rudder and ailerons is necessary to prevent spins.
- Performance (reaction) timing.  When the aircraft stalls, prompt reaction with the flight controls and power is needed.
- Control of assigned headings.  Headings should be maintained to demonstrate control of the aircraft.
Power management as recommended.
- Safe entry altitude, and clearing the practice area.
- Establish entry from straight and turning flight.
- Overview!Stall warning indications adherence.  Recognize the signs of an impending stall.
- Ground proximity awareness.  The maneuver should be completed to maintain a minimum altitude of 1500 feet AGL.
- Airpeed control and avoiding excessive airspeed gain.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the airplane - Verify that all switches and controls are in the proper position
Airspeed - Set power to obtain/maintain desired entry speed for the maneuver (typical final approach speed; e.g. 65 kts in a 172)
Minimum safe altitude - Ensure minimum safe altitude requirements are met (so that maneuver can be completed no lower than 1500' AGL)
Engine gauges - Check engine gauges for proper readings
Landing site - Select an emergency landing site
Scan the area - Carefully scan for traffic and obstructions while turning at least two 90 deg turns or one 180 deg turn
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator:
The simulator is a great place to introduce stalls and stall recovery procedures - especially for nervous flyers. They can practice the setup and recovery procedures without the stress of being in the airplane for initial training. Quite often introducing stalls in the sim leads to less stress during the first attempts at trying them during flight.

Start the session at cruise altitude (e.g. 3000'AGL) in straight and level flight. Then coach the pilot through configuring the airplane and how to perform a power-off stall just like you would in the airplane. Be sure to have the pilot practice any pre-maneuver checklists and procedures to help reinforce what they will do in the airplane. You can start with having the pilot recover at the first indication of a stall (likely the stall warning horn) and work into a full break recovery. Once the pilot is proficient in stall recovery, the simulator is an excellent place to demonstrate the how inadvertent stalls can occur during critical phases of flight like the base to final turn or during the flare. Set the up the common scenarios and allow the pilot to experience how these types of stalls could occur, the effects, and most importantly how to recognize and avoid a low altitude stall.

Note that some simulators exhibit unrealistic characteristics when operating at and beyond the edges of controlled flight, so be sure to test your sim before using it for stall introduction/instruction. However, the technology continues to improve and with many they only adverse stall characteristics you will notice are a more pronounced nose-down tendency or potentially dropping a wing. Just brief the pilot on differences between the sim and the airplane's performance.

checklistItems.name: Landing configuration - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Put the aircraft into landing configuation. Lower the landing gear and apply carb heat, if applicable. Note the heading and altitude. After reducing power, maintain altitude by applying back pressure on the yoke. The airspeed will decrease as the aircraft pitches up to maintain altitude. Add power back in to maintain altitude at approach airspeed. Add flaps in increments until in landing configuration (Generally full flaps). Retrim for approach airspeed with flaps added.
checklistItems.teachingTips: The Power Off Stall is simulating an approach to landing. It is good to set up a scenario in the pilot's mind that they are coming in for landing on a "runway in the sky" over a road and the runway is 3000 feet above that road.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Have the pilot establish a slow flight in a flaps up configuration. Maintain altitude and have the pilot make a series of 90- degree turns to simulate maneuvering in the traffic pattern. This will also help the pilot take the time to get the aircraft stabilized and trimmed.

checklistItems.name: Straight Power Off Glide - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Reduce power to idle and release the back pressure on the yoke. Set a pitch attitude that maintains approach air speed and retrim as needed to maintain that airspeed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The pilot needs to transition from cruise flight to a landing configuration. They can do this either in straight flight or by simulating a traffic pattern two thousand feet above a normal traffic pattern. The objective is to transition from powered cruise flight in a clean configuration to a landing configuration with power at idle and descending at approach speed.

As flaps are added, emphasize the need to retrim for the new configuration.  The pilot will want to retrim so that the aircraft maintains approach speed with each succesive addition of flaps.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Incremenetally add flaps, add power to maintain altitude, while continuing slow flight practice, including making 90 degree turns. Reduce power to idle and select a pitch attitude that maintains approach air speed which should result in a descent of approximately 500 feet per minute.

checklistItems.name: Level off altitude - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once stabilized in a power off glide, select a "runway" altitiude where the simulated round out and flare will take place.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Usually once the glide is established, you can have the pilot level off within 500' or so. Just pick an altitude that is easy to identify and will ensure the maneuver is completed no lower than 1500' AGL.

checklistItems.name: Round out and Flare - Simulate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: At or just prior to your selected altitude, simulate your round out and flare. Do not let the airplane descend below this altitude. You will be performing a gradual and continuous pull that will result in the airplane stalling in a relatively low pitch attitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Coach the pilot by reminding them that they are just above the (simulated) ground. Have the pilot continually increase backpressure so that the airplane doesn't descend below the simulated runway altitude.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: At a predetermined altitude, bring the yoke back to level off at that altitude. Don't let the pilot descend below that altitude. This simulates "landing" on a runway in the sky. The pilot should continue to bring back the yoke until the full stall.

checklistItems.name: Wings level and coordination - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use your rudders to keep the nose from drifting and the ball in the turn coordinator centered.  Ailerons should be neutral as you pull back on the yoke (increasing the angle of attack) to maintain altitude without power.

If a wing drops pick it up with opposite rudder and keep ailerons neutral.  Aileron use needs to be finessed with rudder to maintain coordination. Aggressive use of ailerons may cause as the adverse yaw of the stalled wing which could put the aircraft into a spin. Control nose drift with rudder to maintain coordination.

Continue to use your rudders to maintain the heading and correct for any drift using opposite rudder.  Watch outside the aircraft for signs that the nose is drifting. Look for a spot on the windshield or a rivet on the engine cowling to see if its drifting versus a cloud or use your peripheral vision to look out of the front window just to the left of the instrument panel to see if the nose is drifting across the ground. If you keep the nose still, the airplane will stay coordinated
checklistItems.teachingTips:
As the power off stall is simulating coming in for landing the pilot will want to keep the wings level and stay coordinated using the rudder just as if they were coming in for landing and doing a roundout. The pilot will need to use smooth control inputs and continuous small adjustments to stay coordinated. Appyling back pressure on the yoke should be smooth and not jerky.

Help the pilot develop the ability to keep the airplane coordinated while looking outside to help avoid a stall/spin condition. One way is to use a cloud as a reference to the airplane's nose. If the nose moves left or right in relation to the cloud, have the pilot use rudder to correct the motion. There may be some need for minimal aileron movement to assist the rudder input to keep the wings level (Note: this will take discipline to develop since many new pilots will tend to react with way too much aileron). With good coaching and instructor demonstrations, you help the pilot develop the proper habit.

Assist the pilot by calling out signs of lack of coordinated flight. The pilot will be uneasy and distracted with the aircraft at the edge of stall with mushy controls, a blaring stall horn, and airframe buffeting.  Point out if the nose is drifting or the ball is not centered. 

Demonstrate to the pilot that a lowered wing can be raised by applying opposite rudder.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: One technique for helping the pilot maintain coordination by using outside references. If there are clouds, have the pilot pick one as a reference for the nose of the airplane. As pitch is increased, use the rudders to prevent the nose from moving sideways in reference to the cloud. This will help the pilot keep their scan outside rather than looking at the inclinometer. If no clouds are present, the pilot can also use ground references by looking at an angle to the front side of their view. Again, use the rudder to prevent any sideways movement while performing the maneuver.

checklistItems.name: Stall onset - Recognize/Announce
checklistItems.notesToPilot: As you are approaching the stall, notice the controls are getting "mushy", the airflow noises change, the stall warning horn comes on, the nose is getting higher, and the airframe will start to buffet as you reach the onset of the stall. When you get the buffet and the nose drops, announce the stall and begin recovery.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Point out to the pilot the various indications of impending stall.  The pilot is likely to be fixated on the pitch attitude or on only one of the various indications.

The pilot may be reluctant to pull the final bit of yoke travel to achieve a full stall.  Assist the pilot with callouts to have them bring the yoke fully back and if necessary give the yoke a little pull to achieve full stall. It is common for pilots to have the yoke almost all the way back and mushing along in a descent with the nose in a high pitch attitude but not fully stalled.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Assuming the training airplane has stable stall characteristics and depending on the pilot's comfort, it can help some to become a little more comfortable by demonstrating a floating leaf stall to show that as long the airplane is coordinated - it will NOT spin.

Consider practicing "no power added" stalls with this "flying/not flying" exercise. It will show you how small changes in the angle of attack move the wing between unstalled and stalled flight.

Begin by climbing at least 1,000 feet above a minimum safe altitude and clearing the area. If you wish, your instructor can temporarily cover the flight instruments so you can focus your attention on the visual, audible, and kinesthetic cues associated with stall practice. If desired, remove your headset (and open the windows, if that's an option) to hear the airflow better. Set up a long glide with partial or idle power. (Use carburetor heat according to the POH and remember to clear the engine frequently.)

Next, slowly raise the pitch attitude until the wing is on the verge of a stall and then recover by lowering the pitch attitude just a few degrees. Keep the wings level using the rudder. You should be able to feel the mushy, sluggish ailerons when making roll inputs. You should also be able to feel the authority of the rudder by making small rudder inputs. After you've sampled the feel and effects of the controls, raise the pitch attitude quickly enough to induce a full stall and then release it. You should be able to definitely feel when the wing is "flying" versus "not flying." This is especially notable in the aileron response. When the wing is stalled, the ailerons are noticeably ineffective.

Now lower the flaps and repeat the exercise to see the difference in pitch attitudes with the flaps deployed. Recover from the exercise at or above the minimum safe altitude. This exercise clearly demonstrates that the elevator and rudder, along with power, are your primary controls when responding to a stall.

checklistItems.name:
Recovery - Perform
- Back pressure - Reduce
- Power - Full (Carb heat as applicable)
- Pitch level/climb - Establish
- Flaps - Retract in increments
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Reduce back pressure on the yoke to stop the stall and simultaneously add FULL power. Turn carb heat off (if applicable).  Right rudder pressure may be needed with the application of full power.  Nose attitude should be just below the horizon. Remember that your goal is recover from the stall with minimum loss of altitude, so take care not to push the nose forward forcefully, but rather stop the stall and get back to level flight.

As airspeed increases to Vy, and altimeter reverses direction, retract flaps in increments and increase pitch attitude to climb back to original altitude. Here is a suggested flow to flap retraction: a.) full power and retract first notch of flaps, b.) once you verify that the airplane is either holding altitude or climbing slightly, retract the next notch, and c.) at or just before reaching Vy, retact remaining flaps. This method will help you get the airplane to accelerate while minimizing loss of altitude.

Then resume climb in normal climb configuration to original altitude and on heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
When the nose drops, have the pilot control the pitch down so that the nose is just below the horizon to get below the critical angle of attack. Add FULL power to limit the amount of altitude loss, and be aware of torque effects with the sudden addition of power requiring right rudder. Be sure to help the pilot understand that they should not blindly shove the yoke forward. All that is needed to recover most airplanes is to reduce backpressure. The airplane is stalling because the pilot is pulling back on the yoke.

Don't let the pilot raise the nose too fast to prevent a secondary stall.  Allow the aircraft to regain flying airspeed before smoothly raising the nose.

Once flying airspeed has been achieved, have the pilot stop the descent and immediately establish a climb. While climbing and accelerating to Vy, retract the flaps in increments. 

Demonstrate and then challenge the pilot to be able to perform the maneuver with minimum loss of altitude. Many new pilots will have a tendency to push forward on the yoke instead of relaxing the necessary backpressure to end the stall. This results in a big loss of altitude. By explaining that the real world danger is having a stall occur close to the ground, learning to minimize the loss of altitude takes on a practical goal of being able to recover if they inadvertantly encounter a stall near the ground.

Have the pilot resume climb in normal climb configuration to original altitude and on heading.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Release back pressure and simultaneously add FULL power and carb heat to off (if applicable).  Retract flaps to 20 or 25 degrees depending on the aircraft.

Two common problems that new pilots experience with stall recoveries are that they are too aggressive with the ailerons and they don't use enough rudder.

At slow airspeeds and high angles of attack, the ailerons become mushy and ineffective, a result of the disrupted airflow over the top of the wing. In fact, aggressive aileron usage during stall recoveries can exacerbate roll control difficulties by stalling the outboard section of the wing and causing adverse yaw.

In contrast, the rudder is very effective throughout the stall regime. It can be used to ""lift"" a wing that is beginning to roll off. For example, if you feel the wing starting to bank left, quickly apply some right rudder pressure -- this will stop the yaw that caused the wing to drop, and bring the wing back to level.

By eliminating yaw and keeping the flight controls coordinated, this technique will prevent a spin from developing. You'll find this technique works especially well in airplanes with good rudder authority.

checklistItems.name: Practice stalls in straight flight and while turning
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Stalls should be performed in both Straight flight and Turning flight. Performing a turning power off stall is very similar to a straight ahead stall. Set up the power glide, select a target altitude, and start a gentle turn (less than 20 degrees). When reaching the target altitude, continue the turn while leveling off at your target altitude. The added challenge while performing a turning stall is to monitor your coordination. The outside visual clues are a little more subtle since the airplane is turning so you will likely need to monitor the ball (inclinometer) to verify correct rudder usage.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Practice stalls in turning flight to simulate the base to final turn in the traffic pattern and demonstrate to the pilot that as long as coordination is maintained, the stall proceeds normally like in straight flight. Make sure the pilot is confident in shallow turning stalls by giving them enough practice at it. You will likely need to coach them on how to develop an efficient scan of the outside reference with quick glances at the inclinometer to verify correct rudder input.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Have the pilot fly a normal traffic pattern using roads (or a rectangular course) several thousand feet above normal traffic pattern altitude. Have the pilot fly a downwind, base and final leg and during each segment use it as an opportunity to demonstrate when and how a power off stall can occur, both in straight flight and in turning flight.

activities.name: [07] PRE-SOLO: Power-On Stalls
activities.what: A ground avoidance maneuver that simulates exceeding the critical AoA in climb-out or departure with associated full throttle power setting.
activities.why: To be able to recognize and recover effectively from an inadvertant power on stall.
activities.groundPrep:
Stall recognition awareness.  Recognizing stalls by sound, sight, and the feel of the aircraft.
Control responsiveness.
Smooth control of the flight controls.
Maintaining coordinated flight.
Performance (reaction) timing.  When the aircraft stalls, prompt reaction with the flight controls to reduce angle of attack is needed.
Control of assigned headings.
Power management as recommended.
Safe entry altitude, and clearing the practice area.
Establishing entry from straight and turning flight.
Stall warning indications adherence.
Ground proximity awareness.
Airpeed control and avoiding excessive airspeed gain.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the airplane - Verify that all switches and controls are in the proper position
Airspeed - Set power to obtain/maintain desired entry speed for the maneuver (takeoff or climb)
Minimum safe altitude - Ensure minimum safe altitude requirements are met (so that maneuver can be completed no lower than 1500' AGL)
Engine gauges - Check engine gauges for proper readings
Landing site - Select an emergency landing site
Scan the area - Carefully scan for traffic and obstructions while turning at least two 90 deg turns or one 180 deg turn
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator:
The simulator is a great place to introduce stalls and stall recovery procedures - especially for nervous flyers. They can practice the setup and recovery procedures without the stress of being in the airplane for initial training. Quite often introducing stalls in the sim leads to less stress during the first attempts at trying them during flight.

Start the session at cruise altitude (e.g. 3000'AGL) in straight and level flight. Then coach the pilot through configuring the airplane and how to perform a power-on stall just like you would in the airplane. Be sure to have the pilot practice any pre-maneuver checklists and procedures to help reinforce what they will do in the airplane. You can start with having the pilot recover at the first indication of a stall (likely the stall warning horn) and work into a full break recovery. Once the pilot is proficient in stall recovery, the simulator is an excellent place to demonstrate the how inadvertent stalls can occur during critical phases of flight like takeoff or a go-around. Set the up the common scenarios and allow the pilot to experience how these types of stalls could occur, the effects, and most importantly how to recognize and avoid a low altitude stall.

Note that some simulators exhibit unrealistic characteristics when operating at and beyond the edges of controlled flight, so be sure to test your sim before using it for stall introduction/instruction. However, the technology continues to improve and with many they only adverse stall characteristics you will notice are a more pronounced nose-down tendency or potentially dropping a wing. Just brief the pilot on differences between the sim and the airplane's performance.

checklistItems.name: Takeoff configuration - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Configure the aircraft for takeoff per the POH (e.g., ear and flaps up). Establish a heading and slow the aircraft to rotation speed by pulling power to idle and maintaining altitude with back pressure on the yoke.
checklistItems.teachingTips: The Power On Stall is simulating a takeoff or go around.  It is good to set up a scenario in the pilot's mind that they are taking off from a "runway in the sky" over a road and the runway is 2000 feet above that road. Ensure that the pilot is configured for "takeoff" per the aircraft's POH. Remind they pilot that they are simulating a takeoff or go-around stall and the airplane's configuration should match the profile.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Pull power to idle and maintain altitude to allow the aircraft to slow to rotation speed.

checklistItems.name: Power - Full (or as recommended)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Apply takeoff power.  Apply right rudder as needed to overcome left turning tendencies.  Maintain coordination using the inclinometer or outside references to keep the nose from drifting and to help you maintain coordination (see below).  Ailerons should be neutral simulating taking off, or they may be used to establish a bank of approximately 20 degrees for a stall in turning flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the pilot develop a smooth transition to full power while applying right rudder to maintain coordination. If they have trouble with this, you may want to focus some practice just on applying power and rudder a few times. In preparation for performing a power on stall, it helps to get the airplane slowed down (e.g., 55 kias in a 172) before applying full power to minimize the time they will have to hold the airplane in a nose high pitch attitude.

checklistItems.name: Climb - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Transition smoothly from the takeoff or departure attitude to the pitch attitude that will induce a stall (typically about 15-20 degrees pitch up). Note that nose will be higher than in Power-Off Stall.
checklistItems.teachingTips: It's important to get the pilot to pitch the airplane to a climb attitude that cannot be sustained so that the power on stall will occur. Help the pilot identify the most effective power on stall attitude that will balance quickly getting to the stall with being as realistic as possible in demonstrating what might happen with an inadvertent stall on climbout.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If full power will result in excessive pitch to indue a stall, the FAA allows no less than 65% horsepower to be applied. For the initial attempt at the maneuver with a timid pilot, it may be wide to try 65% horsepower at first, and then increase to full power on later practice.

checklistItems.name: Wings level and coordination - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use your rudders to maintain the heading as the nose comes up. Keep the ailerons neutral to maintain wings level. It will take an increasing amount of right rudder to keep the nose from drifting. 

Continue to use your rudders to maintain the heading and correct for any drift using opposite rudder.  Be watching outside the aircraft for signs that the nose is drifting. Look for a spot on the windshield or a rivet on the engine cowling to see if its drifting versus a cloud or use your peripheral vision to look out the front window just to the left of the instrument panel to see if the nose is drifting across the ground.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Teach the pilot to maintain coordination throughout the maneuver in order to alleviate the possibility of a stall-spin. As the Power-On stall is simulating a takeoff or a go-around, help them learn to keep the wings level and stay coordinated using the rudder just as if they were taking off down a runway or going around from an aborted landing. Ensure the pilot learns to use smooth control inputs and continuous small adjustments. Applying back pressure on the yoke should be smooth and not jerky.

One technique for helping the pilot maintain coordination is the use of only outside references. If there are clouds, have the pilot pick one as a reference for the nose of the airplane. As pitch is increased, use the rudders to prevent the nose from moving sideways in reference to the cloud. This will help the pilot keep their scan outside rather than looking at the inclinometer. If no clouds are present, the pilot can also use ground references by looking at an angle to the front side of their view. Again, use the rudder to prevent any sideways movement while performing the maneuver.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Two common problems that students experience with stall recoveries are that they are too aggressive with the ailerons and they don't use enough rudder.

At slow airspeeds and high angles of attack, the ailerons become mushy and ineffective, a result of the disrupted airflow over the top of the wing. In fact, aggressive aileron usage during stall recoveries can exacerbate roll control difficulties by stalling the outboard section of the wing and causing adverse yaw.

In contrast, the rudder is very effective throughout the stall regime. It can be used to "lift" a wing that is beginning to roll off. For example, if you feel the wing starting to bank left, quickly apply some right rudder pressure -- this will stop the yaw that caused the wing to drop, and bring the wing back to level.

By eliminating yaw and keeping the flight controls coordinated, this technique will prevent a spin from developing. You'll find this technique works especially well in airplanes with good rudder authority.

checklistItems.name: Stall onset - Recognize/Announce
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
As you are approaching the stall, notice the controls are getting "mushy", the stall warning horn comes on, and the airframe will start to buffet as you reach the onset of the stall. In a Power On stall the nose attitude will seem quite high and it will take a LOT of right rudder to keep coordinated.  Announce the signs of the impending stall.

When you get the buffet and the nose drops, announce the stall and begin recovery.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Point out to the pilot the various indications of impending stall.  The pilot is likely to be fixated on the pitch attitude or on only one of the various indications. Have the pilot verbally call out each indication to help verify their recognition.

The pilot may be reluctant to pull the final bit of yoke travel to achieve a full stall.  Assist them with callouts to have them bring the yoke fully back and if necessary give the yoke a little pull to achieve full stall. It is common for pilots to have the yoke almost all the way back and climbing at a high pitch attitude and the stall horn blaring, and just on the verge of a full stall.

checklistItems.name: Recovery - Perform (Reduce backpressure; Level wings; Return to level pitch/Vy Climb)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: With full power already applied, the nose only needs to be lowered to reduce the angle of attack to break the stall. Remember that your goal is recover from the stall with minimum loss of altitude, so take care not to push the nose forward forcefully, but rather stop the stall and get back to level flight. You need to be active on the rudders and use opposite rudder to lift a wing if one wing drops. Resume the climb at a normal Vy attitude on the specified heading (nose on horizon).
checklistItems.teachingTips:
When the nose drops, have the pilot control the pitch down so that the nose is just above the horizon to get below the critical angle of attack. The pilot will need to be very active on the rudders to maintain coordination with the engine at full power.

Demonstrate and then challenge the pilot to be able to perform the maneuver with minimum loss of altitude. Many new pilots will have a tendency to push forward on the yoke instead of relaxing the necessary backpressure to end the stall. This results in a big loss of altitude. By explaining that the real world danger is having a stall occur close to the ground, learning to minimize the loss of altitude takes on a practical goal of being able to recover if they inadvertently encounter a stall near the ground.

checklistItems.name: Practice stall in straight flight and while in a turn
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Power On stalls should be practiced in both straight and turning flight.

Stalls should be performed in both Straight flight and Turning flight. Performing a turning power on stall is very similar to a straight ahead stall. Set up a climb or simulated takeoff, then start a gentle turn (less than 20 degrees) while increasing pitch to an angle that cannot be sustained (try about 15-20 degrees to start). The added challenge while performing a turning stall is to monitor your coordination. The outside visual clues are a little more subtle since the airplane is turning so you will likely need to monitor the ball (inclinometer) to verify correct rudder usage.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Practice power on stalls in turning flight and demonstrate to the pilot that as long as coordination is maintained, the stall proceeds normally like in straight flight. Make sure the pilot is confident in shallow turning stalls by giving them enough practice at it. You will likely need to coach them on how to develop an efficient scan of the outside reference with quick glances at the inclinometer to verify correct rudder input.

commonErrors.name: Not maintaining enough pitch to induce stall
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
If full power will result in excessive pitch to induce a stall, the FAA allows no less than 65% horsepower to be applied.  For the initial attempt at the maneuver with a timid pilot, it may be wide to try 65% horsepower at first, and then increase to full power on later practice.

commonErrors.name: Failure to recognize/achieve stall; delayed recovery
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Consider practicing "no power added" stalls with this "flying/not flying" exercise. It will show you how small changes in the angle of attack move the wing between unstalled and stalled flight.
- Begin by climbing at least 1,000 feet above a minimum safe altitude and clearing the area. If you wish, your instructor can temporarily cover the flight instruments so you can focus your attention on the visual, audible, and kinesthetic cues associated with stall practice. If desired, remove your headset (and open the windows, if that's an option) to hear the airflow better. Set up a long glide with partial or idle power. (Use carburetor heat according to the POH and remember to clear the engine frequently.)
- Next, slowly raise the pitch attitude until the wing is on the verge of a stall and then recover by lowering the pitch attitude just a few degrees. Keep the wings level using the rudder. You should be able to feel the mushy, sluggish ailerons when making roll inputs. You should also be able to feel the authority of the rudder by making small rudder inputs. After you've sampled the feel and effects of the controls, raise the pitch attitude quickly enough to induce a full stall and then release it. You should be able to definitely feel when the wing is "flying" versus "not flying." This is especially notable in the aileron response. When the wing is stalled, the ailerons are noticeably ineffective.
- Now lower the flaps and repeat the exercise to see the difference in pitch attitudes with the flaps deployed. Recover from the exercise at or above the minimum safe altitude. This exercise clearly demonstrates that the elevator and rudder, along with power, are your primary controls when responding to a stall.

commonErrors.name: Improper pitch, heading, bank, or coordination
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
One technique for helping the pilot maintain coordination by using outside references. If there are clouds, have the pilot pick one as a reference for the nose of the airplane. As pitch is increased, use the rudders to prevent the nose from moving sideways in reference to the cloud. This will help the pilot keep their scan outside rather than looking at the inclinometer. If no clouds are present, the pilot can also use ground references by looking at an angle to the front side of their view. Again, use the rudder to prevent any sideways movement while performing the maneuver.

commonErrors.name: Failure to establish specified configuration
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
By completing a pre-maneuver checklist you can ensure your student remembers to complete the required configuration and entry speeds. Remind the pilot to simulate setting up for landing just like operations in the pattern.

activities.name: [08a] PRE-SOLO: Turns Around A Point
activities.what: A ground reference maneuver consisting of 2 or more complete circles of a uniform radii or distance from a prominent ground reference point using a max bank angle of 45˚ while maintaining a constant altitude
activities.why: To develop the ability to subconsciously control the airplane while dividing attention between the flight path and ground references and watching for other air traffic
activities.groundPrep:
This maneuver has a practical side, this is a technique the pilot would use to circle over a point on the ground for purpose of photography or reconnaissance.
Bank angle required in the turn for varying ground speeds (wind speed)
Maintaining ground track
Flight control coordination
Entry and departure downwind
Constant airspeed
Constant altitude (600' - 1000' AGL)
Pilot able to view reference area
Equidistant from reference while maintaining circular path (selecting aim points)
Division of attention (integrated scan: outside/inside)
Collision Avoidance and traffic vigilance
Selection of emergency landing area

checklistItems.name: Determine wind direction
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Obtain a Winds Aloft  forecast as well as the nearest METAR to assess the wind.  Observe any other indications of the wind direction and speed such as smoke or power plant steam, the wind across a pond or lake, blowing trees or windmills.

Once the wind direction is determined, select an easily visible reference point that is clear of houses, obstacles, or other hazards.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Observe the wind on the ground by looking for smoke, flags, ponds or a local airport AWOS. Help the pilot pick out appropriate references in the air so that they can monitor their position and assess wind direction at altitude. Find a direction that a ground reference is not moving in the windshield as the pilot flies toward it to get a true indication of the wind speed and direction at the selected altitude.
checklistItems.simulator:
Teaching ground reference maneuvers in a simulator is possible if you can easily see the view to the side and up to 45 degrees from the rear so that they ground reference can be easily identified. This might be found in a simulator with a wraparound view, using a control to readily switch views on the screen, or with VR for example. The scenery in many modern simulators is detailed enough to provide adequate ground references if the view of it can be maintained from the cockpit.

If feasible, start the session by positioning the airplane near a visible ground reference at an appropriate altitude (e.g., 1000' AGL) in straight and level cruise. Coach the pilot in configuring and performing the maneuver. Be sure to take advantage of the pause button to help them learn aircraft control using outside references with only the required glances at the flight instruments to monitor the airplane's performance.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the airplane - Verify that all switches and controls are in the proper position
Airspeed - Set power to obtain/maintain desired entry speed for the maneuver (at or below Va)
Minimum safe altitude - Ensure minimum safe altitude requirements are met (600-1000' AGL)
Engine gauges - Check engine gauges for proper readings
Landing site - Select an emergency landing site
Scan the area - Carefully scan for traffic and obstructions while turning at least two 90 deg turns or one 180 deg turn
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot does clearing turns and especially looks for towers. When maneuvering so low to the ground ensure that the pilot has selected a suitable emergency landing spot in the vicinity of the ground reference.

checklistItems.name: Pitch and Heading references - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Take the time to get the aircraft stabilized and trimmed before beginning the maneuver.  Ensure that you have a visual reference on the windshield for level flight in order to maintain a constant altitude throughout the maneuver.

Also get the aircraft stabilized and establish with clear heading references that will help you assess the wind's effect on the aircraft. It can be helpful to also pick 4 reference points that are equidistant from your main point. These can be used to help you keep a uniform distance away from the main reference point during the maneuver.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure that the pilot has the aircraft trimmed for level flight before entering the maneuver. The pilot will need to learn division of attention between the reference point, outside for pitch/bank reference and flight instruments for reference to altitude and airspeed throughout the maneuver. Coach the pilot to scan through each input without fixating on one. Having the verbalize or you coach them verbally with "outside, (ground) reference, inside" can give the pilot an idea of the proper flow. The CFI should demonstrate that as well as talking the pilot through the maneuver the first few times.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Suggest a three point scan of: outside pitch/bank, ground reference, quick glances at the flight instruments to verify altitude and airspeed.

checklistItems.name: Abeam reference point on downwind heading - Enter
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abeam reference point on downwind heading, roll left (max. 45° bank) to begin maneuver; turn is steepest at this point due to ground speed (allow proper lateral distance to point to prevent wing blocking view (nose toward inside of turn to prevent drift); Check wingtip reference for correct crab angle
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot pick equidistant points around the circle every 90 degrees and inscribe an imaginary circle along the ground that connects those points. The pilot should then use varying bank angle and crab to follow that imaginary circle around the point. Picking out a road intersection that has a significant landmark (a house, a pond, a treeline, etc.) each 90 degrees around the point will help in judging a constant radius around the circle.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Have the pilot make a constant bank angle turn about the point and observe the effects of the wind on the radius and path around the point, or away from the point if the wind is very strong.

checklistItems.name: First crosswind segment - Reduce bank angle
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Turning crosswind, gradually reduce bank angle to compensate for decreasing tailwind
checklistItems.teachingTips: Emphasize that groundspeed is constantly changing and so the bank angle and crab angle should be constantly and smoothly changing as they progress around the circle. Smooth and continuous manipulation of the controls are required in such a way the pilot banks the aircraft at the maximum bank while entering the maneuver to the minimum back once the aircraft is directly into the wind 180 degrees around the circle. This is accomplished by slowly relaxing the bank as necessary to stay at a constant radius from the reference point, and then increasing the bank back to maximum as needed as the aircraft completes the circle.

checklistItems.name: Upwind - Shallow bank angle
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Heading upwind, bank angle will be shallowest to due slow ground speed (directly upwind may be at or nearly level flight - nose toward outside of turn to prevent drift. See attached graphic.)
checklistItems.teachingTips: Compare the wind correction angle in turns around a point to wind correction angle on the Rectangular Course. On the base leg and crosswind leg the aircraft must be crabbed into the wind to maintain ground track. A turn around a point requires that same wind correction angle however it is constantly and smoothly varying depending the aircraft's position relative to the wind.

checklistItems.name: Second crosswind segment - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Turning crosswind, gradually increase bank angle to maintain uniform ground track
checklistItems.teachingTips: Maintain coordination throughout the maneuver with quick glances at the turn coordinator to keep the ball centered.

checklistItems.name: Abeam reference point on downwind heading - Exit
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Either repeat maneuver (a number of complete 360° turns) or, when ready, exit the maneuver on the downwind while maintaining entry altitude and airspeed. It is not uncommon to perform at least 2 turns as the first turn is often used to assess the effects of the wind and any subsequent turns are used to practice the necessary wind corrections.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

activities.what: A ground reference maneuver in which the ground track of the airplane is equidistant from all sides of a selected rectangular area on the ground; maintain constant airspeed and altitude
activities.why: To develop skills used in the traffic pattern (division of attention/control; wind drift correction; maintaining a set rectangular ground track around the runway)

Planning turns

checklistItems.name: Wind direction and Ground reference - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Obtain a Winds Aloft  forecast as well as the nearest METAR to assess the wind.  Observe any other indications of the wind direction and speed such as smoke or power plant steam, the wind across a pond or lake, blowing trees or windmills.

Once the wind direction is determined, select a rectangular field ½ - 1 mile sides with the wind parallel to long side. Ensure that there are no houses, obstacles, or other hazards around your field.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Make sure the pilot has obtained the winds aloft forecast before departure. Draw the rectangular course on a whiteboard and demonstrate the desired track with wind correction versus the track with no wind correction.
checklistItems.simulator:
Teaching ground reference maneuvers in a simulator is possible if you can easily see the view to the side and up to 45 degrees from the rear so that they ground reference can be easily identified. This might be found in a simulator with a wraparound view, using a control to readily switch views on the screen, or with VR for example. The scenery in many modern simulators is detailed enough to provide adequate ground references if the view of it can be maintained from the cockpit.

If feasible, start the session by positioning the airplane near a visible ground reference at an appropriate altitude (e.g., 1000' AGL) in straight and level cruise. Coach the pilot in configuring and performing the maneuver. Be sure to take advantage of the pause button to help them learn aircraft control using outside references with only the required glances at the flight instruments to monitor the airplane's performance.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the airplane - Verify that all switches and controls are in the proper position
Airspeed - Set power to obtain/maintain desired entry speed for the maneuver (at or below Va)
Minimum safe altitude - Ensure minimum safe altitude requirements are met (1000' AGL [TPA])
Engine gauges - Check engine gauges for proper readings
Landing site - Select an emergency landing site
Scan the area - Carefully scan for traffic and obstructions while turning at least two 90 deg turns or one 180 deg turn
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot does clearing turns and especially looks for towers. When maneuvering so low to the ground ensure that the pilot has selected a suitable emergency landing spot in the vicinity of the rectangular course.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: The pilot may want to perform the maneuver lower than 1000' AGL in order to get used to maneuvering near the ground. The ACS standard is 600-1000 feet AGL. The CFI may also want to choose a square field initially to give the pilot more practice time on the crosswind legs.

checklistItems.name: Heading and Pitch references - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Take the time to get the aircraft stabilized and trimmed before beginning the maneuver. Ensure that you have a visual reference for level flight in order to maintain a constant altitude throughout the maneuver. Then get the aircraft stabilized on a heading and established in a crab to hold that ground track before beginning the maneuver. Ensure that you have visual references on the horizon to assess the wind and crab required throughout the maneuver.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure that the pilot has the aircraft trimmed for level flight before entering the maneuver. All the common errors listed can apply to each of the legs of the pattern but are only listed once for reference. Help the pilot pick out appropriate references so that they can monitor their position as they fly parallel to the rectangular course. If the reference is moving in the windshield, they need to adjust their crab to compensate for the wind drift.

checklistItems.name: Entry and downwind leg - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Enter on 45° angle to downwind leg; fly parallel to field boundary (about ¼ - ½ mile out). Once established on Downwind, note the position of the wing or strut with reference to the rectangular course boundaries (usually a road or fenceline). Establish a crab if required to maintain this distance from the boundary and use the reference you picked on the horizon to help detect wind drift. Crosscheck altitude and airspeed. Continue to divide your attention scanning for traffic, cross checking altitude, speed, any wind drift corrections required and the distance to the next turn.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the pilot monitor their progress on Downwind and point out small corrections needed to keep them on ground track and at the proper altitude. Suggest a three point scan of: outside pitch/bank, ground reference, quick glances at the flight instruments to verify altitude and airspeed. For the first time doing this maneuver, the CFI may want to demonstrate the maneuver and then let the pilot try it.

checklistItems.name: Base leg - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abeam crosswind segment, begin turn to base leg and remain parallel to the field boundary (will require a steep to medium bank turn of more than 90° to establish crab angle). With the wind behind you, your ground speed will be at its highest and so the bank will start out steepest of the four turns and reduce to a medium bank, and it will be greater than 90° to establish a crab on the base leg. Continue to divide your attention scanning for traffic, cross checking altitude, speed, any wind drift corrections required and the distance to the next turn.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Relate this turn from Downwind to Base as the Key position in the traffic pattern. Initially the pilot will just want to be concentrating on making a coordinated turn and establish a crab on Base leg. With more proficiency, the CFI can relate this turn to Base in the traffic pattern will give the pilot a chance to assess height and distance to the runway to establish a stabilized approach.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Help the pilot monitor their progress on Downwind and point out small corrections needed to keep them on ground track and at the proper altitude. Suggest a three point scan of: outside pitch/bank, ground reference, quick glances at the flight instruments to verify altitude and airspeed. For the first time doing this maneuver, the CFI may want to demonstrate the maneuver and then let the pilot try it.

checklistItems.name: Upwind leg - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abeam upwind segment, turn (<90° due to crab; medium to shallow bank) to upwind leg and remain parallel to upwind boundary. This turn will start out as a medium bank and shallow out as the turn is made into the wind as the ground speed will slow as you turn into the wind. You may need to establish some crab depending on the actual wind direction in relation to the field boundary.
checklistItems.teachingTips: The pilot may experience difficulty smoothly rolling into the Upwind leg at the appropriate distance from the field boundary. The turn will require a medium banked turn shallowing out as the turn into the wind is completed.

checklistItems.name: Crosswind leg - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abeam next crosswind segment, begin turn (<90° for crab; shallow to medium bank) to crosswind leg and remain parallel to boundary. This turn will start out shallow and increase as you get into a crosswind. Establish a crab to keep proper distance from the field boundary. Continue to divide your attention scanning for traffic, cross checking altitude, speed, any wind drift corrections required and the distance to the next turn.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure that the pilot recognizes this is primarily a visual maneuver and does not get fixated on instruments or the rectangular field. As the pilot gains proficiency, the CFI can cover up instruments to make sure the pilot is developing the visible and aural references to keeping the plane in level flight and maintaining altitude and airspeed.

checklistItems.name: Downwind leg - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abeam downwind segment, turn (>90° due to crab; medium to steep bank) to downwind leg and remain parallel to boundary. This turn will be the most surprising in a strong wind. This turn will start as a medium bank and steepen as the aircraft turns downwind. The turn will be greater than 90° and the aircraft may pick up ground speed dramatically if there is a strong wind.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the pilot understand the relationship to the wind speed and direction and the timing of their turns as well as the bank angle required. This is best described in the preflight briefing showing the effect of ground speed (air speed plus or minus wind speed) on the bank angle required to maintain the desired ground track in the turn. While flying the rectangular pattern, have the pilot fly all the turns at a medium bank and observe the aircraft's ground track. On the next circuit, have the pilot vary the bank angle as prescribed for the maneuver, steeper bank angle with higher ground speed and shallower bank angle with slower ground speeds.

checklistItems.name: Exit (from downwind) - Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Before exiting the rectangular pattern look for other traffic and exit on a 45° angle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: It's useful to give the pilot turns in the opposite direction (left turns in one rectangular pattern and then repeat one with right turns) or a perform a random pattern of left turns and right turns along country roads if available. This will provide practice adjusting the crab angle and timing the turns for the rectangular pattern maneuver and breaks the monotony of "going around in the pattern".

commonErrors.name: Bad timing on turns and bank
commonErrors.details: Failure to execute turns with accurate timing and bank angle.

commonErrors.name: No clearing turns
commonErrors.details: Failure to clear the area above, below, and on either side of the airplane for safety hazards, initially and throughout the maneuver.

commonErrors.name: Not establishing altitude
commonErrors.details: Failure to establish a constant, level altitude prior to entering the maneuver.

commonErrors.name: Improper wind assessment
commonErrors.details: Failure to properly assess wind direction.

commonErrors.name: Did not maintain altitude
commonErrors.details: Failure to maintain altitude during the maneuver.

commonErrors.name: Uncoordinated flight
commonErrors.details: Failure to apply coordinated aileron and rudder pressure, resulting in slips and skids.

commonErrors.name: Failure to divide attention between airplane and ground references
commonErrors.details: Failure to properly divide attention between controlling the airplane and maintaining proper orientation with the ground references. Becoming fixated on the field instead of dividing attention between controlling the aircraft

commonErrors.name: Rough flight control management
commonErrors.details: Failure to manipulate the flight controls in a smooth and continuous manner.

Can perform the basic procedure/maneuver with instructor coaching
