prepItems.name: ACS - Rectangular Course
prepItems.details: Read Ground Reference Maneuvers: Rectangular Course (p. 36) to see the checkride requirements for this maneuver.

prepItems.name: STAND YOUR GROUND:
prepItems.details: Ground reference maneuvers help you tame the wind.

prepItems.name: Rectangular Course: Understanding the most basic ground reference maneuver
Ground Reference Maneuvers
prepItems.details: The air mass in which you're flying may also be moving – many times not in the same direction that you want to go. The net effect is that the direction your airplane's nose is pointed may not necessarily be where you’ll end up, and your airspeed is not always the same as your groundspeed. So, how do we compensate for the effect of the wind?

prepItems.name: Rectangle Course (Maneuvers Guide)
prepItems.details: To develop the pilot’s ability to maneuver the airplane while compensating for drift during turns, and orient the flight path with ground references while dividing attention inside and outside the airplane.

prepItems.name: AFH-(Ch7.5-7) Rectangular Course
prepItems.details: Read (Ch 7.5-7) the section on Rectangular Course

activities.name: [08c] PRE-SOLO: S-Turns Across a Road
activities.what: A constant altitude ground reference maneuver in which the airplane describes equal radii semicircles on each side of a selected straight line on the ground.
activities.why: To develop wind awareness, develop the ability to compensate for drift during turns, orient the flight path with ground references, and divide the pilot’s attention.
activities.groundPrep:
Determining wind direction
Effect of wind/ground speed on turn radius        
Bank angle required in the turn for varying ground speeds (wind speed)
Maintaining ground track
Flight control coordination
Entry and departure downwind
Constant airspeed
Constant altitude (600' - 1000' AGL)
Pilot able to view reference area
Equidistant from reference while maintaining circular path (selecting aim points)
Division of attention (integrated scan: outside/inside)
Collision Avoidance and traffic vigilance
Selection of emergency landing area

checklistItems.name: Wind direction and Reference Line - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Look for surface clues, such as wind on a lake or smoke; check GPS ground speed readouts for various headings; or fly a drift circle and note drift on the ground. The reference line should be as straight as possible, and ideally at least a few miles long. Typical references are a road, fence line, or section line long enough for series of turns aligned perpendicular to the wind. Select at least 3 equidistant crossing points to help you keep your turns symmetrical. Sometimes it is necessary to pick two lines and connect them. For example, farm fields from two different farms can sometimes be pieced together if no better reference is available.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot has practice selecting different reference lines and understands the criteria and can choose one without assistance.
checklistItems.simulator:
Teaching ground reference maneuvers in a simulator is possible if you can easily see the view to the side and up to 45 degrees from the rear so that they ground reference can be easily identified. This might be found in a simulator with a wraparound view, using a control to readily switch views on the screen, or with VR for example. The scenery in many modern simulators is detailed enough to provide adequate ground references if the view of it can be maintained from the cockpit.

If feasible, start the session by positioning the airplane near a visible ground reference at an appropriate altitude (e.g., 1000' AGL) in straight and level cruise. Coach the pilot in configuring and performing the maneuver. Be sure to take advantage of the pause button to help them learn aircraft control using outside references with only the required glances at the flight instruments to monitor the airplane's performance.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the airplane - Verify that all switches and controls are in the proper position
Airspeed - Set power to obtain/maintain desired entry speed for the maneuver (at or below Va)
Minimum safe altitude - Ensure minimum safe altitude requirements are met (600-1000' AGL)
Engine gauges - Check engine gauges for proper readings
Landing site - Select an emergency landing site
Scan the area - Carefully scan for traffic and obstructions while turning at least two 90 deg turns or one 180 deg turn
checklistItems.teachingTips:
By completing a pre-maneuver checklist you can ensure your student remembers to complete the required configuration and entry speeds. Especially important for ground reference maneuvers is selecting a suitable emergency landing site close to the course.

Help the pilot determine Va and a power setting that will reliably get them there for this maneuver.

A GPS ground speed readout is useful for pointing out the varying ground speed throughout the maneuver.

checklistItems.name: Downwind entry - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The maneuver should be started at a level attitude, and downwind which will result in first turn having the steepest bank. Set up your entry so that your airplane crosses perpendicular to the reference line (i.e., the wings parallel to the road). It is also critical to be at the appropriate airspeed and altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Whether the pilot enters upwind, too close to the reference line, or turns the wrong way - it all comes down to planning. There's no need to rush into the maneuver. Make sure the pilot is settled for a few seconds in straight and level before beginning the maneuver. The turn should begin immediately after crossing the reference line. 

If pitching up while turning is a continuous problem, stop practicing the maneuver and review level turns and how to maintain the pitch attitude for level turns.

checklistItems.name: Left/right turn over reference line - Enter
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Upon crossing the reference line downwind, roll immediately into a left or right turn, as assigned by the instructor or examiner. This is the steepest part of the turn because it is the point of highest ground speed. It is better to overbank here and decrease bank than it is to underbank and have to catch up by increasing bank later.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Although bank angle must vary depending on conditions, an initial target of 30 degrees is a good rough estimate.

checklistItems.name: Symmetrical half circle - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Continue the turn, adjusting bank angle to compensate for effect of wind to track symmetrical half circle. With a wind, the required bank will change from medium to shallow because of decreasing groundspeed. Your instructor will help you learn to estimate how far away from the reference line you want to fly to ensure the initial semicircle isn't too large.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize decreasing bank throughout the turn. Pilots tend to want to rush through the maneuver and maintain 20 or 30 degrees of bank through the entire turn. Doing so may result in a circle that is somewhat flat and very close to the reference line. Ensure the pilot takes his or her time through the circle and doesn't overbank.

Emphasize that bank can change as much as needed, both adding and decreasing, in order to make the goal. Although in a no-wind situation a constant bank is possible on both sides of the reference line, any amount of wind will require changing bank. Because of task saturation, pilots tend to hold constant, or near-constant banks through the maneuver. In the demonstration take time to point out the ever-changing bank angle, and emphasize there is nothing wrong with continually increasing or decreasing bank, to make the goal.

Altitude loss is likely due to the pilot fixating on another aspect of the maneuver like the ground reference, bank, etc. To help the pilot avoid fixating, teach them to develop a constant 3 point scan between outside references, scanning for traffic, and checking inside references like airspeed and altitude. Coach them how long to look at each type of reference by verbally explaining which you are scanning so they develop their own scan. You can coach them while they fly by verbally stating "outside, traffic, inside" and any needed corrections you identify while in the process of the scan.

checklistItems.name: At 180 degree point - Roll level and opposite turn
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Cross reference line after 180° of turn with wings level and parallel to reference line; at the instant of crossing reference line begin turn in opposite direction starting with a shallow bank to track symmetrical half circle
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Stress that most attention should be outside the cockpit with periodic checks of coordination and altitude. If the reference line is reached too early, explain how overall less bank angle is needed on the next turn to compensate.

If the pilot is having trouble with coordination, consider having them do coordination exercises (see the video in the prep section). It often takes a few iterations before they can establish good coordination. While it can be a worthwhile exercise, use it judiciously because it can induce air-sickness if done for too long.

checklistItems.name: Opposite symmetrical half circle - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Continue the turn, adjusting bank angle to compensate for effect of wind to track symmetrical half circle. The bank changes from shallow to medium because of increasing groundspeed. Match the radius of the first semicircle with bank through the first 90 degrees.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize small bank angles through the first 90 degrees. 

Verify position at 90 degrees and compensate as necessary. 

Remember to demonstrate the maneuver to help the pilot see how it should be performed. If needed, later demonstrations  can be used by having them focus on the aspect you had identified as a potential solution. CFIs often hesitate to take the controls and demonstrate a maneuver, but it valuable in helping the pilot better identify how to perform it correctly.

checklistItems.name: Cross reference line after second 180° - Wings level
checklistItems.notesToPilot: After second 180 degree turn cross with wings level and parallel to the reference line.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Patience and dividing attention are keys to success. The earlier guidance on rolling out and altitude control applies here as well. Help the pilot develop a scan between outside references, looking for traffic, and monitoring instrument references.

checklistItems.name: Exit maneuver straight on downwind - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Exit the maneuver at the completion of the downwind turn (or set of turns if you were doing more than one set). It is important to pay attention and maintain your situational awareness so that you can correctly identify when you are coming up on a downwind turn. Maintain your altitude and airspeed for a moment and then begin a climb to a higher cruise altitude at the direction of your instructor.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Periodically ask the pilot or have them verbalize where they are in the overall maneuver (e.g. upwind turn - requiring a more shallow bank) and what is coming next can help them develop and maintain their situational awareness.

Encourage the pilot to maintain a three point scan between outside references, scanning for traffic, and instrument indications to maintain precise aircraft control. Emphasize that all pitch and bank changes should be made using outside references and using the appropriate flight instruments to monitor and fine tune the aircraft's performance.

commonErrors.name: Early roll out
commonErrors.details: Rolling out too early as a result of overly agressive banking.

commonErrors.name: Too aggressive of a turn
commonErrors.details: Turning in too agressively.

commonErrors.name: Starting the turn too early
commonErrors.details: Starting the turn before crossing the reference line.

commonErrors.name: Altitude deviation
commonErrors.details: Failure to monitor altitude during turn.

commonErrors.name: Increasing bank angle
commonErrors.details: Excessive bank in second half of turn resulting in reaching 180 point before reaching the road.

commonErrors.name: insufficient bank on turns
commonErrors.details: Insufficient bank on initial turn.

commonErrors.name: Pitching up when beginning turn
commonErrors.details: Immediately pitching up when beginning the turn.

commonErrors.name: Incorrect entry
commonErrors.details: Incorrect entry (e.g. upwind, too close, wrong way)

commonErrors.name: No clearing turns
commonErrors.details: Not completing clearing turns or configuration errors.

commonErrors.name: Selecting incorrect reference line
commonErrors.details: Selecting a reference line that is too short, crooked, or parallel to the wind

prepItems.name: S-Turns (Maneuvers Guide)
prepItems.details: To develop the ability to maneuver the airplane while compensating for drift during turns and orient the flight path in relation to ground references while dividing attention inside and outside the airplane.

prepItems.name: Pre-Solo Maneuvers
prepItems.details: In this section we will discuss S-turns Across A Road and Turns Around A Point, as well as the techniques to do them successfully. Their objective is to maintain a prescribed ground track while in turning flight.

prepItems.name: STAND YOUR GROUND: GROUND REFERENCE MANEUVERS HELP YOU TAME THE WIND
AFH-S-Turns (Ch 7.8-10)
prepItems.details: Read (Ch 7.8-10) the section on S-Turns.

prepItems.name: ACS - S-Turns Across a Road
prepItems.details: Read Ground Reference Maneuvers: S-Turns (p. 36) to see the checkride requirements for this maneuver.

activities.name: [01] PRE-SOLO: Normal Takeoff and Climb
activities.what: A flight maneuver in which the airplane is safely accelerated to flying speed and lifted from the ground into flight.
activities.why: To make the safe transition from taxi to flight.
activities.groundPrep:
Flight preparation, including:
- Weather
- Surface Winds
- Likely runway
- Expected taxi route
- Avoiding runway incursions
- Emergency procedures
- Example: "Any failures before 500' AGL, we are landing straight ahead. After 500', anyplace ahead of the wing is fair game. After 1,000' a return to the airport can be considered."
Review climb speeds, Vx / Vy
Review ground affect and it's role in takeoffs
Discuss importance of see-and-avoid in vicinity of airports

checklistItems.name: Before Takeoff Checklist – Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure engine instruments are in the normal range; Brief takeoff emergencies
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to always conduct a takeoff briefing based on the current conditions that includes the takeoff plan if everything goes well and the plan if there is a problem with runway remaining, shortly after takeoff with no runway remaining, and with enough altitude to return to the airport.
checklistItems.simulator:
For teaching and practicing normal takeoff and climb, set up the sim at your local airport (or anything similar) and instruct the pilot as you would in the airplane. One great feature to use on the sim is the ability to quickly reset the aircraft at the departure end of the runway so the pilot can get a lot of repetition in a short amount of time. Many simulators have overly sensitive rudder control on the ground, so you will likely have to help the pilot learn how to effectively control the sim during the takeoff run. But explain to them that developing a light touch in the sim will help develop a similar feel in the airplane. 

The sim will allow the pilot to quickly develop proficiency in takeoff procedures and you can help them understand concepts like turning tendencies by pointing out the behavior of the airplane as power is added (corrective inputs will still need to be applied even though the sim will lack the full sensory input of flying in the airplane). Be sure to use the pause button to take opportunities to help the pilot correct any errors that may occur."

checklistItems.name: Frequency - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Monitor frequency and visually check for traffic
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot how to break the squelch to check radio volume when no one is talking.

checklistItems.name: Traffic - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Position aircraft for clear view of base leg and final approach path, especially in high-wing aircraft
checklistItems.teachingTips: Remind the pilot to always visually check base and final before entering a runway. Controllers and other pilots are human too. Trust, but verify.

checklistItems.name: Takeoff Clearance/Announcement – Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Wing Flaps – As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Flap settings for takeoff vary for different airplanes
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Carb heat – Cold (as applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Does not apply to fuel-injected engines
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Mixture – Rich
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This means richer than max lean, not neccesarily full rich
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel Pump – On (as applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Some airplanes do not have an electric fuel pump or do not require it for takeoff
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Runway centerline - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Taxi onto runway, line up with centerline, center nose wheel, verify wind direction (sock), position ailerons into the wind
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Teach pilots to use 3 different foot positions:
1) Full brakes position - Used when stopped or in the final stopping sequence after taxi/landing. Both heels are lifted off the floor and pressure is placed on both brakes.
2) Taxi position - Used when taxiing and immediately after landing. Both heels are on the floor with toes near the brakes.
3) Heels back position - Used when rudder is needed with no braking (i.e. takeoff, crosswind landing, touch-and-go). Both heels should be back far enough to ensure that only rudder is being applied with no braking.
Note: Actual foot position will need to be adjusted to accommodate different size feet and rudder pedals, but the general concept of teaching 3 positions is valuable in all planes that incorporate foot rudder controls and toe brakes.

checklistItems.name: Power - Set for takeoff
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Advance power smoothly to takeoff power (usually full power); select reference points (outside and cowl) to maintain alignment with runway

Smooth application of power to avoid engine stumbles, advancing to full throttle in 1-2 seconds

Apply right rudder for torque correction
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach pilots that most training airplanes are designed to takeoff with full power, but many airplanes are not. Once they start flying higher performance airplanes, it will be normal to takeoff with reduced power at precise settings, so it's good to get in the habit of checking the power setting during every takeoff.

checklistItems.name: Alignment references - Select
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: See video from Jason Miller video in Prep section.

checklistItems.name: Engine instruments and performance - Monitor/Verify
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Check engine instruments and performance; anything unusual – abort takeoff

A good practice is to verbalize "Engine instruments in limits" to acknowledge proper indications
checklistItems.teachingTips: The ACS requires appliants to, "Confirm takeoff power and proper engine and flight instrument indications prior to rotation." Teach the pilot to divide their attention inside and outside the cockpit.

checklistItems.name: Airspeed - Confirm
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Confirm positive airspeed indication

A good practice is to verbalize "Airspeed alive" to acknowledge airspeed indicator is working
checklistItems.teachingTips: Once takeoff power is set, check the instruments and state, "Instruments in limits, airspeed alive, rotate."

checklistItems.name: Directional control - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Directional control with rudder; neutral ailerons when the wind is calm (controls become more effective with airspeed). As you transition to takeoff attitude, additional right rudder will be required. Maintain the centerliine.

checklistItems.name: Elevator – Apply back pressure
checklistItems.notesToPilot: As you approach flying speed, begin to add a little more back pressure, allowing the nose wheel to lift off at rotation speed __ KIAS; immediately after liftoff, relax some of the back pressure to allow the aircraft to accelerate in ground effect to Vy (as appropriate).
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the student learn how the aircraft "feels" when ready to fly by applying a little back pressure as they accelerate toward liftoff speed. By doing so the aircraft will lift off when it's ready to fly.

checklistItems.name: Pitch attitude – Vy (as appropriate)
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Note position of cowling in relation to horizon and hold pitch attitude. 

Pitch for the desired speed, increasing pitch slightly if faster than Vy, or reducing pitch slightly if slower than Vy.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Monitor that the pilot is not fixating on instruments, emphasizing importance of collision avoidance in the airport traffic area.
Limiting scan to areas directly ahead of the airplane (pitch attitude and direction), causing a wing (usually the left) to drop immediately after lift-off.

checklistItems.name: Extended runway centerline - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain extended runway centerline (or as appropriate)
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Coordination - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use right rudder to correct left turning tendencies; "Step on the ball" to stay coordinated.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Brakes – Apply momentarily
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If vibration is felt from the wheels spinning after lift off, apply the brakes momentarily when airborne to stop tire rotation. Be sure that you are safely away from the ground so that you don't accidently cause the airplane to swerve or flat spot the tire if it touches back down to the ground.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Climb - Vy (as appropriate)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: After reaching a safe altitude (at least 500'AGL), pitch for the attitude that will give provide your desired airspeed, then trim away the control pressure.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Make sure pilot keeps most of their attention outside the aircraft, with quick glances at the airspeed.

checklistItems.name: Power – Set for climb
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Trim - As needed
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Avoid "chasing" your desired attitude with the trim wheel.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach the pilot to, "Fly what you see, trim what you feel."

checklistItems.name: After Takeoff checklist – Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: After 1000' AGL consider pitching for a slightly faster cruise climb attitude to enhance forward visibility while departing the airport traffic area.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Power - Set for takeoff
commonErrors.details:
Applying brakes during the takeoff roll.
Suggestion:
Confirm pilot has heels on the floor and is off the brakes during takeoff roll. Remind them to use the "heels back" position. Both heels should be back far enough to ensure that only rudder is being applied with no braking. See Teaching Tips for more detail.

Abrupt use of the throttle.
Suggestion:
Explain how increasing throttle too rapidly will cause the left turning tendencies to be exagerated making it harder for the pilot to control the airplane during the intial takeoff roll. Smoothly applying power will allow the airplane to accelerate so that increased airflow can begin making the flight controls more effective and give the pilot more control. Additionally, it is hard on engine to make power changes very rapidly. Explain how it is the same when driving where we don't slam on the throttle (gas pedal). Demonstrate the proper rate at which to increase throttle and bring their attention to listening to the engine rev for a smooth increase in power.

commonErrors.name: Before Takeoff Checklist – Complete
commonErrors.details:
Failure to review AFM/POH performance and charts prior to takeoff.
Suggestion:
Establish a standard practice for the pilot to complete a preflight performance sheet before each flight (e.g. weight and balance, takeoff and landing performance). Additionally, demonstrating the hazards of taking off with detrimental conditions (e.g. high density altitude, tailwind, or partial power) in a sim could help drive home the need to be aware of takeoff conditions and expected performance.

commonErrors.name: Frequency - Monitor
commonErrors.details: N/A

commonErrors.name: Traffic - Check
commonErrors.details:
Failure to adequately clear the area prior to taxiing onto the active runway.
Suggestion:
This takes building a habit of checking the runway and final before entering. Additionally, building situational awareness by monitoring tower/CTAF once at the departure end of the runway can help give the pilot solid safety habits. If a pilot stills seems resistant to following good procedure, consider using NTSB reports of runway incursion accidents or incidents to help emphasize the need for safety procedures.

commonErrors.name: Runway centerline - Maintain
commonErrors.details:
Failure to anticipate and/or overcorrecting for the airplane’s left turning tendency on initial acceleration.
Suggestion:
New pilots often struggle with how much control pressure is appropriate especially in a dynamic situation like the takeoff roll where the controls become more effective as airspeed increases. Help the pilot learn to feel and anticipate the change in control sensivity with speed. Have them closely holding a heading while transitioning in an out of slow flight. Have them be especially attentive to how the required control pressures increase as the airplane slows and vice versa. You can also practice some high speed taxiing on the runway during quiet traffic period to help them develop an awareness and feel for how control pressures change with speed.

commonErrors.name: After Takeoff checklist – Complete
commonErrors.details: N/A

commonErrors.name: Engine instruments and performance - Monitor/Verify
commonErrors.details:
Failure to check engine instruments for signs of malfunction after applying takeoff power.
Suggestion:
Explain to the pilot the importance of verifying that the engine is producing full takeoff power. Teach them what power setting to expect and to make a verbal callout when they check it. Using a simulator to demonstrate partial power takeoffs can be an enlightening experience for the pilot due to the lack of accleration and climb performance. Emphasize to them how catching a partial power situation prior to takeoff could mean the difference between a routine departure and an accident.

commonErrors.name: Airspeed - Confirm
commonErrors.details:
Relying solely on the airspeed indicator rather than developing an understanding of visual references and tracking clues of airplane airspeed and controllability during acceleration and lift-off.
Suggestion:
Help the pilot develop their kinesthetic awareness while practicing slow flight or during some high speed taxi practice on the runway (during less busy periods). With some practice paying specific attention to how the airplane control pressures change with airspeed, the pilot should be able to develop the ability to feel when the airplane is ready for takeoff rather than mechanically look at the airspeed indicator.

commonErrors.name: Directional control - Maintain
commonErrors.details:
Inadequate compensation for torque/P-factor during initial climb resulting in a sideslip.
Suggestion:
Verbal cues and practicing slow flight will help the pilot develop the control skills necessary to compensate for the airplane's turning tendencies. Be sure to remind the pilot while practicing slow flight that the skills developed apply directly to takeoff and landing. Be sure they periodically reference the inclinometer (ball) to verify the effectiveness of their control inputs.

commonErrors.name: Trim - As needed
commonErrors.details:
Overcontrol of elevators during initial climb-out and lack of elevator trimming.
Suggestion:
A common cause of overcontrolling and not trimming in new pilots is caused by unconsciously using a tight grip on the controls. Help the pilot break this habit with verbal coaching. Be sure to spend time in the practice area helping the pilot learn to establish a climb pitch attitude and then trim away the control pressures to allow "hands off" flight. You can give the pilot different speeds to maintain so they become proficient in the procedure.

commonErrors.name: Elevator – Apply back pressure
commonErrors.details:
Failure to add sufficent elevator, keeping the aircraft on the ground longer than necessary.
Suggestion:
In a tricycle gear airplane, teach the pilot to apply some backpressure to the controls as the airplane accelerates. With practice and coaching the pilot will develop the proper feel for the amount of backpressure needed to let the airplane lift off when it is ready to fly. Most new pilots will tend to apply too little backpressure, while some may pull hard resulting in the airplane jumping off the ground into a high pitch attitude. Be prepared to correct inputs that are too far out of safe limits until the pilot develops the feel. Encourage the pilot to maintain relaxed and light grip on the controls to help prevent overcontrolling. Watching for white knuckles and strained arm muscles can help you determine the amount of pressure the pilot is apply to the yoke.

Failure to attain proper lift-off attitude.
Suggestion:
Be sure to explain to the pilot why it is important to relieve the weight that is on the nosewheel (e.g., least robust of the landing gear) and how applying inadvertant forward pressure on the nosewheel could cause damage or wheelbarrowing. Coach the pilot during the takeoff roll to help them develop the correct feel establishing a lift-off attitude. Some practice in high speed taxiing may help them have more concentrated time in establishing the correct control pressures.

commonErrors.name: Pitch attitude – Vy (as appropriate)

commonErrors.name: Climb - Vy (as appropriate)
commonErrors.details:
Failure to employ the principles of attitude flying during climb-out, resulting in “chasing” the airspeed indicator.
Suggestion:
A very common challenge for new pilots is learning to fly by setting the pitch attitude outside. It usually takes a few lessons and consistent reinforcement to instill this skill in them. Be sure to spend time while to teaching the fundamentals to ensure they are able to control their climb airspeed with pitch attitude and are trimming away the control pressures once they have detemined their desired pitch. Consider covering up the flight instruments to demonstrate and help them learn to fly by outside visual references. Then periodically uncover the instruments so they can see how the flight instruments allow you to fine turn performance as a supplement to outside references.

Failure to attain/maintain best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY) or desired climb airspeed.
Suggestion:
As part of training the pilot in flight fundamentals, help them learn how to visually set a Vy pitch attitude. Emphasize the need to use best rate of climb as appropriate and explain it maximizes climb performance. If the pilot struggles with maintaining airspeed, cover the flight instruments and review setting speed by outside references at altitude.

prepItems.details: Takeoff is not difficult because the airplane is designed to fly – it wants to get off the ground.

prepItems.name: TAKEOFF AND LANDINGS: NORMAL TAKEOFFS
prepItems.details: A "normal" takeoff is what pilots use for the majority of their departures. But it often doesn't get the attention it deserves.

prepItems.name: Normal Takeoff and Climb (Maneuvers Guide)
prepItems.details: To develop proficiency in conducting normal takeoff and climb profiles.

prepItems.details: COMPLETE THE HEADWORK BEFORE STARTING THE LEGWORK

Private Pilot Airman Certification Standards (ACS)

activities.name: [02a] BASICS: Low Approach to Runway
activities.what: A flight training maneuver that consists of making a normal gliding approach to land followed by a controlled low pass along the length of the runway.
activities.why: To help the pilot develop their ability to control the aircraft low to the ground and with learning the sight picture judging height while landing.
activities.groundPrep:
This exercise can be used to help a pilot develop several skills:
A) ability to judge height over the runway
B) ability to control sink rate over a runway using pitch and power
C) directional control over a runway in crosswind conditions
D) confidence controlling aircraft low over the ground
In this module we use the example of a power off glide from abeam the touch down point to the runway. Common training aircraft such as Cessna 172 and Cessna 152s are capable of flying a standard rectangular pattern from abeam their touch down to landing without power. If the aircraft used for this exercise is unable to fly a normal traffic pattern with the power off, refer to the Normal Approach and Landing module for details and techniques for the pattern itself.

Accurately identify, explain how to perform stabilized approaches and landings using the recommended aircraft settings, speeds, and procedures
As above
Intro to Low Approach to Runway (before first attempt in flight)
 Describe the procedures for establishing a stabilized approach, proper aircraft control settings, and the transition from flight to landing (round out, flare, and touchdown)

checklistItems.name: Downwind leg - establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Downwind - Power - middle of green arc
Trim for level flight, Altitude = Traffic Pattern Altitude (1000 or 800 AGL)
Have the airplane at the correct altitude and power setting to maintain level flight and make sure it is trimmed to reduce workload.  
Apply wind drift correction to maintain ground track. 
Scan for traffic and mentally prepare the steps you'll take to begin the descent in the traffic pattern.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may become task saturated preparing for landing and ignore the trim.

Ensure that the pilot has the aiplane properly trimmed to make it easier to maintain altitude and speed for downwind. If there is a GPS groundspeed readout note the groundspeed to estimate the wind at TPA. Help the Pilot develop a mental picture of where the wind is coming from by referencing its direction on the Directional Gyro.

checklistItems.name: Checklist - complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Complete the pre-landing checklist.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Train the pilot to complete the before landing checklist well before beginning the landing sequence. For newer pilots, this could mean having them complete it before entering the pattern. As pilots gain more proficiency, they might be able to handle it effectively early on downwind. In any case, it's important to teach pilots to "stay ahead" of the aircraft and to constantly be anticipating the next step in the flight.

It is also a good idea to have a before landing flow that pilots can use while practicing multiple landings in the traffic pattern. That way you can help develop a habit of perfoming the before landing checklist everytime they are on downwind or preparing to land. The typical procedure would be to have the pilot complete the before landing checklist in preparation for the initial landing, then complete a more abbreviated flow on the repeated landings.

Before landing checklist should include setting up the radios so that tower is in active and ground is in standby (if equipped). Airport diagram should be accesible and ready to use upon landing.  Have the Pilot verbally anounce "Before Landing Checklist complete"

checklistItems.name: Abeam position: Power off glide - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Abeam desired landing spot
Apply carb heat (as appropriate)
Reduce power to IDLE
Lower one notch of flaps once at or below flap extend speed 
Maintain level flight until 5 knots above best glide speed
Pitch for best glide speed
Trim for hands off flight
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Train the pilot to always turn on carb heat when operating outside of the "green arc" or published safe engine settings.

Remind the pilot extending flaps above flap extend speed can damage the flaps.

Unlike a powered approach, a power off approach requires preserving altitude while slowing the plane to best glide speed. Allowing the plane to descend with the initial power and flap reduction will result in difficulty acheiving best glide speed and a low approach which will require additional power in order to reach the runway. 

Remind the pilot that P-Factor affects the plane when the nose comes down. P-factor causes the plane to yaw to the left in the climb. In a descent the plane will yaw to the right if allowed. A small amount of left rudder will counteract this right turning tendency. 

Typically failure to acheive best glide is the result of allowing the nose down and plane to descend before slowing the plane. Do not allow the plane to descend until approx 5 knots above best glide, then pitch for best glide speed.

If the pilot does not trim they are very likely to be unable to maintain a stable airspeed. Remind the pilot to trim away the control pressures once best glide speed is acheived.

checklistItems.name: Turn base leg
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Based on winds decide when you will perform the base turn. 

In winds less than 10 knots turning at the 45 degree position relative to the touch down point works well. Turn earlier in stronger winds. 

When at the desired position (45 degrees or earlier), check for traffic and turn base.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Remind the pilot the most common place for mid air collissions is a nice VFR day in the traffic pattern. Constant vigilance must be maintained. 

Unlike a powered approach, the timing of the base turn will vary depending on winds. Turn too late and the pilot will have to add power to make the runway. Turning too early will typically result in deploying all of the flaps or having to perform a significant foward slip to get down to an approapriate glide path on final. Have the pilot try various turning positions in various winds to learn how far they can glide in various wind conditions.

checklistItems.name: Double check flow - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once established on base, complete double check flow to ensure the airplane is in landing configuration.
checklistItems.teachingTips: At this point the final landing check should be verification of what was already completed. It makes a lasting impression on a pilot when the instructor lets them get to this point, and then asks if they're ready for landing. Especially if they forgot one or more landing configuration requirements.

checklistItems.name: Power off glide to runway - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Maintain best glide speed. Using pitch to control airspeed. 

Fly straight ground track perpindicular to the runway.

Evaluate altitude - high or low relative to the runway. Adjust as needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize airspeed control is critical for a successful approach and landing. 

Refer to "A Rule with Two Exceptions". 

Remind the pilot to expect winds blowing the plane away from the runway on base and to correct for those winds by crabbing into the wind. 

How to evaluate and correct for appropriate altitude for power off glide on base:

On base visually extend the runway centerline head of you and across the cockpit. If the extended runway centerline goes through the center of the instrument panel. No change is necessary maintain best glide. 

If the extended runway centerline is below the instrument panel, the plane is high. Extend flaps to increase descent rate.

If the extended runway centerline is above the instrument panel the plane is low. Reduced descent rate is needed. If the plane has excess airspeed pitch for best glide (pitch up). This will convert airspeed to altitude. If flying the correct airspeed the remedy is to add power to reduce descent rate.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Alternate: use engine power throughout the approach and landing.

checklistItems.name: Traffic on final - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Before turning final raise (or lower) the wing to verify no traffic on final prior to turning.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Emphasize the importance of checking for traffic before all turns in the pattern. This is important at both towered and non towered airports.

checklistItems.name: Turn to Final
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Perform a gentle, turn towards final. 
Maintain best glide airspeed by maintaining pitch in the turn.
Rollout on final with appropriate crab for winds.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize airspeed control is critical for a successful approach and landing. Descending turns will typically result in higher airspeed if the pilot does not add back pressure to maintain best glide pitch in the turn. The nose will naturally come down if allowed to due to the reduced vertical component of lift in the turn.

Refer to "A Rule with Two Exceptions". 

Overshooting the base to final turn, especially at an airport with parallel runways, can be deadly. Have the pilot draw a line extended for the runway centerline and identify prominent landmarks along that line. They can use the landmarks as a turning reference while they focus their eyes on the cowling of the plane to maintain pitch (airspeed).

Remind the pilot in the case of crosswinds that they will need to rollout so the airplane's nose is pointed into the wind in order to maintain a straight ground track on final.

checklistItems.name: Power off glide to runway - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
On final, make the gliding approach best glide speed. 
Choose runway aim point and adjust glide path as needed.
Ensure power is IDLE on short final.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize that airspeed control is critical for a successful approach and landing.  

Refer to "A Rule with Two Exceptions".

NOTE: a power off glide is typically steeper than the glide path indicated by VASIs and PAPIs. A "white over white" indication is good when on a power off glide. Use the following technique to evaluate power off glide path.

As the plane glides towards the runway, if the aimpoint gets bigger without moving on the wind screen, the plane is on glide path and nothing needs to be done. If the aimpoint goes up on the wind screen the plane will undershoot. Verify correct airspeed and add power if needed. If the aimpoint moves down on the wind screen the plane will overshoot and additional drag should be added (and/or power reduced).
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If doing a powered approach use the visual glide slope indicators (VASI or PAPI typically) to remain on or above glideslope until needed for the low approach/landing.

checklistItems.name: Flare, roundout and low approach to runway - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Fly the airplane over the runway as low as the pilot is comfortable using enough power to maintain level flight at the approach speed (the instuctor can control the throttle so the pilot focus on flying).
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Depending on the pilot's comfort level the instructor may need to start this maneuver 50 feet over the runway. Do multiple passes as needed to allow the pilot to gain confidence. 

The pilot will focus on maintaining a sight picture for level but very slow flight over the runway (resulting in a relatively high pitch). 

If the pilot is over controlling remind them small corrections are typically all that is necessary. If they continue to overcontrol it is likely they are uncomfortable being low to the ground. Repeat the maneuver at a higher altitude until they gain confidence in their ability to control the airplane.

See Normal Approach and Landing for details on the desired sight picture and how to maintain altitude when unable to see over the cowling. 

The instructor will have to adjust power to maintain altitude as needed in response to pitch changes.

checklistItems.name: Runway alignment and desired altitude - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Work to maintain centerline, longitudinal alignment, and a consistent height over the runway. As the pilot gains confidence and proficiency, fly the low approach at progressively lower altitudes with the end goal of being able to safely fly the airplane within a few feet of the ground during the low approach.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Depending on the pilot's comfort level the instructor may need to start this maneuver 50 feet over the runway. Do multiple passes as needed to allow the pilot to gain confidence. 

The instructor will need to constantly manage power to prevent touchdown. 

See Crosswind Approach and Landing for common errors and resolutions for correcting for wind drift.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Once the pilot has shown competence managing the aircraft while the instructor controls power, do low passes with the pilot controlling power also.

checklistItems.name: Go-Around - Initiate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: At a safe distance from the end of the runway, perform a go-around and reenter the traffic pattern. Be sure to use full climb power (as appropriate).
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure the Go Around is performed per the aircraft POH. 

Pitch control is critical in a Go Around. Remind the pilot failure to control pitch can result in an elevator trim stall. 

Because the low pass over the runway is performed with some power pilots may forget they need to climb out aggressively at the end of the runway to return to a safe altitude.

checklistItems.name: Climb at Vy or Vx - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish a climb at Vy or Vx as approprate.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Because the low pass over the runway is performed with some power pilots may forget they need to climb out aggressively at the end of the runway to return to a safe altitude.

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Retract
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Retract flaps one step at a time once the airplane is established at Vy or Vx and is safely away from the ground.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure the Go Around is performed per the aircraft POH. 

Retracting all flaps at once can result in excessive sink. Retract one increment of flaps at a time.

checklistItems.name: Continue climb at Vy to Pattern Altitude
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain Vy climb to pattern altitude (or as specified by noise abatement procedures).
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pilots sometimes level off low when doing a go around. Remind them to proceed all the way to pattern altitude.

commonErrors.name: Poor pattern
commonErrors.details: Not in a position to land.

prepItems.name: How to learn: MASTERING THE TOUCHDOWNWHEN IT CLICKS, YOU CAN LAND THE AIRPLANE
Landing With Flair: For a Perfect Touchdown, Slow Down—Slowly
prepItems.details: You’ve probably heard that a good landing starts with a good approach. But even a perfect approach can go from on speed and on glidepath to a bounce or a go-around in those last few seconds. The flare—that gradual pitch-up just prior to touchdown—slows the descent and allows the airplane to settle gently on the runway.

prepItems.name: Takeoff & Landing Variations
prepItems.details: In this section we will discuss the various types of takeoffs and landings you will learn, as well as the techniques to do them successfully.

activities.name: [07a] X/C: Soft Field Takeoff and Climb
activities.what: A flight maneuver that gets the airplane airborne as quickly as possible to eliminate drag and/or possible landing gear damage; weight from wheels to wings as soon as possible
activities.why: To maximize safe departure from airfields with tall grass, soft sand, mud, snow, or rough terrain (damaging)
activities.groundPrep:
Runway surface drag tends to push the nose wheel into the runway soft medium if yoke is not held aft.
Appropriate airplane configuration: Flaps per POH (typically 10 degrees). Yoke held full aft.
Special taxi conditions: Prefer paved surface for the run-up if available (to avoid FOD and slippery surface). Taxi requires more power because of surface drag. Yoke held full aft to avoid nose wheel digging in. Plan to move from a hard surface to the runway without stopping.
Importance of weight transfer from wheels to the wings early in the take-off run by using high angle-of-attack and flaps to reduce wheel drag.
Ground effect: With a high angle-of-attack and some flap extended, aircraft will become airborne at below stall speed.
Vx and Vy: Vx represents best climb angle to clear obstructions within minimum distance, and Vy  is best climb rate to achieve maximum altitude over time.
Most POHs do not have specific procedures for soft-field operations.

checklistItems.name: Pitch angle - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
During the preflight the instructor may seat the pilot in the cockpit while they apply body weight to the tail to raise the nose to the approximate desired pitch angle. 

Note the position of the cowling relative to the airport runway horizon. A small (about 1/2 inch) adhesive-back dot positioned on the inside of the windscreen will be useful in several maneuvers.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
While the instructor applies weight to the tail have the pilot note the position of the cowling relative to the airport runway horizon. 

A small (about 1/2 inch) adhesive-back dot positioned on the inside of the windscreen will be useful in several maneuvers.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
The pitch angle will vary with the type aircraft and requires that the instructor has previously established that optimum angle for the specific aircraft. 

The dot need not be placed in the "perfect" position. It is simply a datum (reference mark) that the pilot will use with occasional suggested adjustments by the instructor during the training process.
checklistItems.simulator: The simulator can help the pilot drill soft field takeoff procedures when first learning them. Consider setting the session up at a small grass field like Kentmorr (3W3) which is located on the eastern shore of Maryland's Chesapeake Bay. Taking off from 28 will take the pilot out over the water. Resetting the airplane back at the takeoff position is a quick way to let the pilot get a lot of focused practice in a short amount of time on setting up and executing soft field takeoff procedures. While it is not a replacement for practicing soft field techniques in the airplane, the sim is much more efficient for helping a pilot quickly drill the procedures that will help make flying in the airplane much easier for the pilot.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify the trim is in the take-off position.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Run-up - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure proper flap setting per the POH.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
If the procedure is being used on snow
consider removing wheel pants (if 
installed) for winter operation. 

Many airports with grass/dirt runways have a hard-stand near the departure end of the runway for the run-up.

checklistItems.name: Yoke - Full aft
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Reduces drag on the nose wheel from dirt, snow, and grass.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
In keeping with the "few words" mantra, use simple corrective comments such as "yoke aft" or "stick back."

 Avoid any extensive interchange with the pilot during periods requiring their mental and physical concentration.

checklistItems.name: Taxi Route/Timing - Plan
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Soft field taxi typically requires more power than on a hard surface. Plan the taxi to the runway (from the runup area) to avoid conflicting traffic in the pattern, so there is no need to stop before entering the runway.
checklistItems.teachingTips: While most Soft Field TO training is simulated on a hard surface, the instructor must evaluate actual soft field conditions that may be encountered and help the pilot determine if the conditions are safe for operation.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If extreme conditions exist, special equipment (such as tundra tires) may be required to safely operate on some fields.

checklistItems.name:
Taxi - Complete
Throttle - Full
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Taxi onto the runway and proceed into the take-off run, without stopping, adding full power. The plane may balance on the main gear with the nose wheel off the ground, with little pressure required to adjust the nose attitude. 

From this point until the Vy speed is attained, there should be no need to look back into the cockpit except to quickly verify the engine power, which the pilot will call out to the instructor (e.g. "2400 rpm").
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Have the pilot add full power over a period of about 3 seconds so the yoke pressure changes can be more readily anticipated and accomodated. 

When full throttle is achieved allow the pilot to glance at the tach and confirm the desired setting (i.e. "Power 2400 rpm").
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Low-wing aircraft such as the Piper Warrior may 
not be as pitch responsive as high-wing aircraft 
such as the Cessna 172, so be alert when 
transitioning between the two.

checklistItems.name: Yoke - Neutral
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The yoke will feel heavy until power is applied and some forward speed is gained. Then the yoke becomes much lighter and the transition to this new feel requires some adjustment on the pressure the pilot is exerting. As the aircraft accelerates, and the elevator gains more authority, progressively relax the yoke slightly to avoid over-rotating and striking the tail.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Allow the pilot to under-rotate on the first few take-offs to get the feel of the pressure on the yoke and establish the sight picture. As more experience is gained, then encourage more effective positioning of the yoke. 

Uneven surface conditions that may cause a sudden turning moment, this will require rapid rudder movement to realign the aircraft with the runway.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
When training in larger aircraft such as the C182 and C206 a considerable amount of yoke effort may be required. 

The pilot should be cautioned that there are runway conditions that require experience and skill that may be beyond their ability. 

High risk conditions should not be considered in the intial training environment.

checklistItems.name: Lift off - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Relieve the back pressure and allow the pitch to decrease with gradual movement of the yoke forward, to reduce AOA  allowing the airplane to accelerate .
The plane will lift from the runway (at below stall speed)
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The tone of the instructor's voice and the expressions used can help the pilot correct their control movements without having to over-ride the pilot. Use few (but meaningful) words such as "ease the yoke forward" (or back). 

Caution the pilot not to allow the aircraft to fly itself out of ground effect until Vx is attained. This may require forward pressure with the help of trim.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Noise cancelling headsets are helpful in keeping the voice volume down.

checklistItems.name: Fly in ground effect - complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Fly the aircraft a few feet above the runway. Avoid flying out of ground-effect.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Reduce the pitch angle as the aircraft accelerates to avoid flying out of ground effect until Vx is obtained.

The position of the yoke should be steady and based on the nose relative to the horizon (end of the runway). 

Apply right rudder to maintain directional control.

checklistItems.name:
Vx - Achieve
Pitch - Initiate climb
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Announce Vx and pitch to Vx attitude when confirmed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
When the pilot announces "Vx" (a value previously determined from the POH) either "confirm" or call out the actual current airspeed value with the added word "continue" (i.e. "55 continue"). 

When the pilot declares a value within a few knots of the POH the instructor responds "confirmed, transition."

checklistItems.name:
Flaps - Retract
Airspeed - Vy
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When clear of obstacles, retract and adjust the pitch to Vy. Resume the normal scan of the instruments.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot declare "in trim" after completing a maneuver and hold their hands in the air momentarily to confirm.

checklistItems.name: Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A

activities.name: [07b] X/C: Soft Field Approach and Landing
activities.what: A flight maneuver in which the airplane is held 1-2 feet off the surface as long as possible to dissipate speed and touchdown gently at minimum speed
activities.why: To minimize drag and stresses imposed by rough landing surfaces on landing gear (snow, sand, mud, or tall grass)
activities.groundPrep:
Practical application of technique: landing on grass and dirt airstrips, snow covered paved runways, very wet runways, and off airport emergency/precautionary landings
Risks associated with landing on soft/rough surfaces - aircraft control, damage from hidden objects, nose gear dipping in hole resulting in prop strike or nose over, being unable to move at normal taxi power settings
Importance of maintaining the full aft elevator, minimum weight on nose gear, minimum braking and power required to exit the soft surface all of the way to the exit.
The higher than normal power setting and use of minimal braking on landing roll out will result in a faster than normal landing rollout/taxi when practicing on paved surfaces.
This is expected. When these techniques are used on a soft surface the drag created by the soft surface will result in much closer to normal rollout/taxi speeds.
As a matter of fact, depending on the surface, additional power may be required to keep the plane moving until it is on a harder surface.

checklistItems.name: Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Complete the Before Landing checklist.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator: The simulator can help the pilot drill soft field landing procedures when first learning them. Consider setting the session up at a small grass field like Kentmorr (3W3) which is located on the eastern shore of Maryland's Chesapeake Bay. Resetting the airplane on final is a quick way to let the pilot get a lot of focused practice in a short amount of time on setting up and executing soft field landing procedures. While it is not a replacement for practicing soft field techniques in the airplane, the sim is much more efficient for helping a pilot quickly drill the procedures that will help make attempting them in the airplane easier for the pilot.

checklistItems.name:
Frequency - Monitor
Traffic - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Raise or lower wing to visually scan for traffic before every turn. 

Develop a mental picture of the locations of other aircraft in the pattern based on position reports or ATC clearances/readbacks.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize looking for traffic before and after every turn. Remind the pilot how they look both ways before crossing the street, the same applies in the pattern. Aircraft may be where they "shouldn't be" even at towered airports.

If told by the tower to follow a particular plane, require the pilot to look for (and hopefully spot) the traffic they are to follow before every turn. If the pilot does not make the effort to look, intervene and tell them you need them to look so you can see and avoid that traffic.

To help a pilot develop situational awareness by listening, use a hand held radio and listen to ground and tower traffic at a busy airport. Using whiteboard or piece of paper, have the pilot indicate where each plane is located based on the radio calls and where they are likely to go next.

checklistItems.name: Landing Clearance/Announcement - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Downwind:
Power - bottom of green arc
Airspeed - As appropriate
Trim - Set
Altitude - As approrpiate
Checklist/Flow - “GUMPS”
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Parallel runway at correct distance, apply wind drift correction as needed.

Ensure you are at pattern altitude - your instructor will help you determine a visual reference for establishing the correct distance.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Drifting toward the runway shortens the base leg and, if the pilot is slow to respond, will result in an excessively steep bank on the base to final turn in order to avoid overshooting the runway. Once established on downwind have the pilot choose a visual reference in the distance to fly "at" to help ensure proper wind drift correction. Often keeping the runway along a specified reference point on the wing can help the pilot maintain the correct distance while flying downwind.

checklistItems.name:
Abeam landing spot:
Power - Set
Flaps - Set
Airspeed - As appropriate
Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Pilot should lose about 300’ altitude to key position
checklistItems.teachingTips: Teach pilots to anticipate the increase in lift caused by deploying the flaps and to use some forward pressure on the controls to prevent the airplane from gaining altitude. Usually a few moments of forward pressure will allow the airplane's airspeed to settle and it will no longer require control pressure to maintain its desired flight.

checklistItems.name:
Key Position (about 45° from landing spot):
Turn Base - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be ready to adjust turning position based on wind conditions, stronger winds can require turns before the 45° position. Calm winds may require turning slightly after the 45° position.
checklistItems.teachingTips: When pilot raises (or lowers) their wing to check for traffic, have them pick a landmark to use a turn aiming reference. Then have them perform the turn while looking straight ahead until their reference comes into view.

checklistItems.name:
Base:
Power - Set for descent
Flaps - Set
Airspeed - As appropriate
Trim - Set
Checklist/Flow - “GUMPS”
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Pilot should lose about 300 AGL altitude on BASE leg. Time the turn to final so that the plane is lined up with runway.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot pick a landmark to use a turn aiming reference. On the base to final turn it's helpful to choose an aim point that is along the extended runway centerline. Then have them perform the turn while looking straight ahead until their reference comes into view.

checklistItems.name:
Final:
Flaps - Set
Power - Set (adjust as necessary)
Airspeed - As appropriate
Trim - Set
Checklist/Flow - “GUMPS”
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Pilot should keep their aiming point (about 200’ prior to landing spot) from moving up or down in windshield. A useful technigue is to compare a set reference on the windshield or canopy to an aiming point on the runway. This aiming point will typically be located before the desired landing spot since most airplanes will glide in ground effect before settling to the runway.

Keeping the aiming point from moving up and down is a method of staying on glide slope that works for all landings. You will know you're on glide slope when the aiming point doesn't move up or down. It will just get bigger. 

If the aiming point starts to move up in the windshield you are too low and you will undershoot your spot. Adjust the airplane's pitch to maintain the spot in proper location on the windshield and make a coordinated power adjustment to maintain the desired airspeed. Be sure to trim away any control pressures. Anticipate that when you are back on glide slope that you will need to reduce about 1/2 of the power you added to remain on glide slope.

If the aim point starts to move down on the windshield you will overshoot. Adjust the airplane's pitch to maintain the spot in proper location on the windshield and make a coordinated power adjustment to maintain the desired airspeed. Be sure to trim away any control pressures. If you are not already at full degrees flaps you can increase flaps to increase drag.

If your power is idle and you are above glide slope you may do a GENTLE foward slip. - Check POH to verify.
If you cannot reestablish yourself with the aiming point stable in the windshield you may need to go around.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Review the article "Pitch for Airspeed, Power for Altitude - A Rule with Two Exceptions" (Link below)

In the case of operating on final the pilot will usually be operating under Exception #2. Emphasize use of coordinated use of pitch and power to maintain the desired airspeed and descent rate. 

Revisit the Constant Speed Descent lesson in the new context of flying an approach to landing at a specific airspeed and descent path. Have the pilot observe the affects of deploying flaps or changing power settings when descending at a constant airspeed so they can learn how to coordinate the use of pitch and power to maintain the desired glide slope.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
In case the pilot has difficulty acheiving the light touchdown at a nose high attitude using power to "cushion" the touch down, the following alternate approach can be used. This approach forces the pilot to use elevator to keep the airplane over the runway until touchdown at a nose high attitude is inevitable. 

Conduct the approach power on or power off with minimal (or no) flaps at a slightly higher than normal airspeed. 3-5kts additional airspeed is sufficient. On short final reduce power to idle and then attempt to fly the plane over the runway using elevator only to control the sink of the aircraft. As the pilot detects the airplane's sink towards the runway they use back elevator pressure in small increments to keep the plane above the runway. The use of back pressure must be carefully applied in order to prevent baloooning. As the aircraft slows elevator back pressure increases until the controls are in the full aft elevator position. The plane will touch down shortly thereafter lightly on the mains and with the nose gear off the runway.

checklistItems.name:
Roundout - As appropriate
Back pressure - Hold
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Hold the airplane just off of the runway, as you feel it sink, increase back Elevator to keep it just off of the runway. Smoothly and in small increments increase elevator back pressure as the plane sinks. 

The goal is to touch down lightly on the mains with nose gear off the ground. Ideally the elevator will be in full aft position at the moment of touchdown.

As the nose of the plane rises this will block your forward vision, as this happens shift your eyes to the window on the left side of wind screen and instrument panel. You will be able to see the runway and horizon through that window, use that view judge your height over the runway and maintain your position over the runway centerline.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize airspeed control on final and short final to prevent excessive float. 

In the case of ballooning have the pilot freeze their elevator control input, this will let the plane settle back towards the runway. Once back at the appropriate height over the runway the pilot will resume increasing elevator back pressure as the plane sinks normally.

Similar to a normal landing, a focus on flying the plane in a low approach over the runway and keeping it in the air as long as possible without adding power will help the pilot perform this maneuver. The CFI should take control of the throttle on short final so the pilot can focus on flying the airplane. Challenge them to fly as low as they are comfortable without letting the airplane land. Encourage them on progressive passes to go lower as they gain proficiency. Once they can fly a properly aligned, steady low appoach over the runway about a foot off of the ground, have them practice making passes while you reduce the power to idle. It should result in the pilot making well controlled landings.

The instructor can instruct the pilot to imagine the runway is covered with something distasteful (e.g. snakes, spiders, etc.) and use that as extra motivation to do what's required to keep the plane in the air. 

Pilots can also be uncomfortable with not being able to see straight ahead with full aft elevator. In those cases emphasize looking out the window to the left of the instrument panel where they can see the runway and horizon to judge their position over the runway.

checklistItems.name:
Touchdown:
Power - Adjust as necessary
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Add 100 RPM if needed just before touchdown to cushion touchdown on the mains.
 
Maintain full aft elevator on touchdown, do not relax backpressure.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Have the pilot smoothly remove the excess power while allowing the plane to settle back towards the runway. When the plane returns to the proper height over the runway the pilot can return to increasing elevator back pressure to control the plane's descent. 

Similar to a normal landing, a focus on flying the plane just over the runway and keeping it in the air as long as possible without adding power will help the pilot perform this maneuver.

The instructor can instruct the pilot to imagine the runway is covered with something distasteful (e.g. snakes, spiders, etc.) and use that as extra motivation to do what's required to keep the plane in the air. 

Pilots can also be uncomfortable with not being able to see straight ahead with full aft elevator. In those cases emphasize looking out the window to the left of the instrument panel where they can see the runway and horizon to judge their position over the runway.

It takes some time to develop a feel for the aircraft, how fast it will sink and how fast it will climb with the application of power in ground effect. One exercise to accelerate development of that "feel" is to go to an airport with a long runway, e.g. 6000, 9000 or 12000 feet and have the pilot fly the plane just over the ground with a nose high attitude for the length of the runway. Have them fly as low as possible without landing and use gentle power application to keep the plane off the runway. Once they are able to do that, they will be abe able to more easily judge the control inputs required to touchdown gently on the runway as required in this exercise.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If using the alternate method of slightly higher than normal airspeed and minimal flaps, addition of power on touchdown may not be required.

checklistItems.name:
Landing Roll:
Back pressure - Apply
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Maintain full aft elevator and power used for touchdown for landing roll. 

The gear will eventually touchdown on its own as speed decreases. Maintain full aft elevator until clear of the soft surface.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Remind the pilot the purpose of keeping the nose wheel up and power applied is to avoid digging the nose wheel into the soft surface, damage from objects hidden in the grass/mud/snow and avoid getting stuck and unable to move. 

Roleplay what happens if they don't do this. "OK, now your nose wheel is stuck." or "We'd better check for a prop strike, did you see that rock in the deep grass?"

Even if the pilot does a "hard" soft field landing, have them smoothly and carefully transition to full aft elevator for the remaining landing rollout and taxi until "clear of the soft surface". This will help them develop the muscle memory for the proper maneuver.

checklistItems.name: Braking - Minimum required
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use minimum braking, if any, until clear of the soft surface.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Before the start of the maneuver, remind the pilot that they cannot use normal braking until clear of the soft surface. If you are practicing on a hard/paved runway, tell the pilot you will let them know when they are clear of the surface. 

On some landings allow them to clear the soft surface soon, on other landings make it much later in the landing rollout. This will help them avoid rotely applying braking at a specific spot.

commonErrors.name: Poor taxi technqiue
commonErrors.details: Relaxing elevator back pressure before clearing soft surface. Reducing power before clearing soft surface. Using normal braking technique before clearing soft surface.

commonErrors.name: Improper touchdown technique
commonErrors.details: Adding too much power, preventing touchdown. Relaxing elevator back pressure, allowing the nose to touch immediately. Not controlling excessive sink with back pressure or power, resulting in firm touchdown.
