activities.name: [02b] BASICS: Power Off Approach and Landing
activities.what: A flight maneuver that consists of approaches and landings made by gliding with the engine idling, through a specific pattern to a touchdown beyond and within 500 feet of designated line or mark on the runway
activities.why: To instill in the pilot the judgement and procedures necessary for accurately flying the airplane, without power, to a safe landing; A simplified approach to teaching landings to new pilots in which power and configuration changes are removed from the workload during roundout and flare
activities.groundPrep:
Goals of power approach and landing: instill judgement and procedures to accurately fly airplane without power to a safe landing. While a great training aid because it simplifies the procedures for learning to land, it is also a great skill for training emergency approach and landing later. 
This activity differs from a Commercial Pilot Power Off Approach and Landing in its intent and procedure. The pilot is learning when to pull power on base once they determine that they can make a power off glide to the runway. Additionally, they are targeting the first 1/3 of the runway rather than a spot landing.
How to determine distance and altitude including target distances and altitudes - use of key position on base leg.
How to judge aiming point that shows where the airplane will land on runway.
Use of pitch to control airspeed and the effects on glide distance when deviating from recommended glide speed.
Importace of a stablized approach.
Effects of atmospheric conditions, including wind, on approach and landing.
Wind correction techniques on approach and landing.

checklistItems.name: Downwind - establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish normal downwind leg.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the Pilot fly a slightly closer downwind pattern than a normal powered approach. For a new Pilot it is good to suggest references on the aircraft where to help position the aircraft the proper distance from the runway. On a high wing aircraft, the runway is normally hald to two-thirds up the strut. For a low wing aircraft the runway should two-thirds to three-quarters of the way to the wingtip.

checklistItems.name: Checklist - complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Complete appropriate checklist.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Abeam postion:
Power - Reduce
Carb heat - ON (as appropriate)
Flaps - lower
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abeam desired landing spot, reduce power, apply carb heat (as appropriate), and lower flaps to one notch or no flaps as desired.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the Pilot estimate the strength of the tailwind at altitude. (It may not be, and usually is not, the same as the ASOS is reporting on the surface. If the aircraft is equipped with a GPS this will be easy, if not they will have to estimate visually. With a strong tailwind the turn to base will need to be much earlier than a normal powered descent.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Power may be pulled abeam the landing spot to execute a 180 degree power-off approach.This is an extension of the concept of the 90 degree power-off appraoch and requires more judgement of when to turn base.

checklistItems.name:
45 degrees from desired landing:
Turn base - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When 45 degrees from desired landing position on downwind, check for traffic and turn base. Ideally you will have decended 300 feet below pattern altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Depending on how strong the tailwind is, the pattern will have to remain closer to the runway. It may not be possible to go to the normal 45 degree point to turn base.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: With a strong tailwind, some pilots prefer to make a circular pattern and immediately start turning toward final from the downwind. The resultant pattern is more of a semi-circle instead of a rectangular pattern.

checklistItems.name: Double check flow - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once established on base, complete double check flow to ensure the airplane is in landing configuration.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Power off glide to runway - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
While on base, determine when you are close enough to the runway to make a power-off glide to the runway. At first, your instructor will help you determine this.

Pull the power to idle, and use the airplane's normal approach speed for the glide to the runway.

Ideally you will descend another 300 feet on base - or to about 400 above the runway elevation.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Help the Pilot to determine whether they are close enough to the runway to make a power-off glide to the runway. Depending on the aircraft's glide characteristics and the tailwind on downwind, the base leg may need to be modified to ensure making the runway. In a strong wind situation, the Pilot may need to make an immediate turn toward final to be able to make the runway. Ensure that the Pilot is compensating for wind drift while on base if they are flying a normal base leg.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If the aircraft is high, have the Pilot use a forward slip to lose altitude. If the aircraft is high, this is also a good time to demonstrate that an airspeed above or below best glide will result in a shorter glide distance.

checklistItems.name: Traffic on final - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When turning final, check for traffic that may be coming on a straight-in approach.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Turn final - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Make a gradual turn to align the airplane with the final approach path. Be careful not overshoot the runway centerline.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure that the Pilot is making a gradual coordinated turn on final and not trying to use rudder to force the nose around. Instruct the Pilot on the danger of cross-controlled stalls and potention for stall/spin accidents. It is better to have them add full power and go-around parallel to the runway (Upwind leg) than to force the plane in a dangerous turn.

checklistItems.name: Stabilized final approach - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: On final, make the gliding approach at normal approach speed using one notch or no flaps. Add flaps as necessary once making the runway is assured. Remember to control your speed using pitch changes. If you get too low you can add power, slip, or go-around for another try.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure that before landing checks are complete with a retractable gear aircraft.  In addition to GUMPS check, teach the Pilot to verbally say out loud and physically check,  Mixture (full rich), Prop (full forward), Gear - 3 Greens (if so equipped), on Downwind, Base, and Final.  They should say it three times while in the pattern to confirm the gear are down.

If the aircraft is not going to make the runway call for a go around and don't try to stretch the glide. 

Ensure the Pilot is making a stabilized descent on final and don't deploy additional flaps until you are sure the runway has been made. 

The throttle may be used to clear the engine momentarily but not to increase the glide.

checklistItems.name: Roundout - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: At about 10-20 feet from the runway, begin your roundout to transition the plane to level flight a few feet from the runway surface.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Touchdown - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
As the airplane slows just over the runway surface, gradually increase back pressure on the yoke to keep the airplane's nose from touching down. As airspeed is dissipated, the airplane will settle gently onto the runway with the main wheels touching first. Then gradually and gently lower the nose wheel.

Take care to keep your feet off of the wheel brakes to prevent accidently flat spotting or otherwise damaging the tires on touchdown.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Explain to the Pilot that it is better to execute a good landing than to try to force the aircraft down to hit the selected landing spot.

commonErrors.name: Overextension of downwind
commonErrors.details: Not turning to base leg soon enough, requiring power adjustment.

commonErrors.name: Premature flap extension
commonErrors.details: Extening flaps before runway is made, requiring added power.

commonErrors.name: Forcing aircraft on runway
commonErrors.details: Flaring with too much speed and not waiting for it to bleed off.

commonErrors.name: Downwind too far from runway
commonErrors.details: Flying too wide a pattern.

commonErrors.name: Diving to runway
commonErrors.details: Trying to correct for a high position by lowering the nose instead of slipping or going around.

Emergencies
prepItems.details: In this section we discuss emergencies. Pilots need to recognize the possibility that emergencies can occur and be prepared.

activities.name: [04] PRE-SOLO: Traffic Patterns (Towered/Non-Towered)
activities.what: A flight maneuver used by aircraft to flow into and out of an airport in an orderly manner using a rectangular pattern
activities.why: To provide a safe and orderly entry/exit to the airport environment
activities.groundPrep:
AC 90-66B should be read by the pilot and its content used as a basis for discussion
Traffic pattern terms and definitions
Standard traffic pattern operations
Importance of flying traffic pattern altitude (to better see traffic)
Non-standard traffic pattern operations (as applicable for local airport)
Expected power, pitch, and trim procedures
Radio procedures
Definition of two-way radio communication (Class D entry requirements)
Checklist procedures
The primary responsibilities when requesting to remain in the pattern.

checklistItems.name: DEPARTING THE AIRPORT
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator:
Teaching traffic patterns naturally in a simulator will typically require the ability for the pilot to easily change views from straight ahead to left and right up to 135 deg off the nose. Otherwise it will be difficult for the pilot to judge their downwind distance and the turns from downwind to base/base to final. This problem might be overcome by having the pilot use headings and estimated the time it takes to reach each key point, but as a result will definitely be different from how it is performed in the aircraft. There may be value in having the pilot practice their cockpit procedures (e.g.before landing checklist and flow) while flying the aircraft while you take advantage of the pause button to focus your instruction.

If your simulator provides appropriate visual cues, treat the sim session like you would any other landing practice session by starting either from takeoff and entering closed traffic or from cruise to practice pattern entries. The advantage of the sim is that you can select the wind direction and velocity to customize the training session for maintaining ground track and dealing with crosswinds. A major advantage with using the sim for traffic pattern instruction is that the pilot can work on becoming proficient with standard procedures without the distraction of other traffic while they are introduced to the concept.

As the pilot becomes more proficient consider incorporating radio communications (with you acting as ATC) and emergency procedures like engine failure on takeoff, climb, or on downwind to practice engine out procedures to power off landings.

checklistItems.name: Before Takeoff Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Configure the aircraft for the runway conditions--short, soft, obstructions, high density altitude--per the POH/AFM.

Ensure any NOTAMS are considered.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize to the pilot the critical nature of methodically verifying all of the steps in the POH/AFM checklist.

Error: Skipping procedures and checklists.

Suggestion:
Pilots may be tempted to skip checklists and procedures when external pressures like traffic or environmental conditions make them eager to get in the air. Emphasize to the pilot the critical nature of methodically verifying all of the steps in the POH/AFM checklist.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Council the pilot to constantly inquire of themselves as to what is the next "event trigger" that will occur. This can be the arrival of the aircraft at a specific location whether in the air or on the ground. The question that should be asked is what is the next heading/altitude/facility/frequency to be considered.

checklistItems.name: (Towered) Takeoff Clearance - Obtain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Change to the tower frequency when the aircraft is taxied to the hold bar or when joining a line-up of aircraft waiting for departure.

Call for take-off clearance when the aircraft is number one. Monitor the tower frequency when joining the lineup to be aware of any problems preceding aircraft may be experiencing.
Advise the tower of intended departure direction.

If remaining in the pattern for a series of landings, advise the tower "Remaining in the pattern."
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Demonstrate to the pilot a method to double-check the selected radio and frequency.

Have the pilot write the basic items to be communicated (facility being called, caller N-number, location, request).

Hesitancy with communications is a common problem early in the training process.

Making a departure briefing standard practice can help the pilot ensure that they have considered and are prepared for the events that can happen quickly during initial takeoff and climb. The briefing should include items like rotation and climb speeds, emergency plans for each phase of the takeoff and initial climb, initial headings and altitudes of turns during the transition to cruise.

Error: Failure to switch to the radio with the tower frequency and thus broadcasting on the previous radio frequency, or failure to dial-in the correct tower frequency. 

Suggestion:
Demonstrate to the pilot a method to double-check the selected radio and frequency. 

Error: Using inappropriate or wordy communications.

Suggestion:
Hesitancy with communications is a common problem early in the training process. Have the pilot write the basic items to be communicated (facility being called, caller N-number, location, request).

Error: Failure to plan ahead for the direction to depart the pattern or when remaining in the pattern.

Suggestion:
Making a departure briefing standard practice can help the pilot ensure that they have considered and are prepared for the events that can happen quickly during initial takeoff and climb. The briefing should include items like rotation and climb speeds, emergency plans for each phase of the takeoff and initial climb, initial headings and altitudes of turns during the transition to cruise.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
There are occasions where the pilot may advise the tower that they are "Number 2 for departure" so the tower may have more latitude in handling a delayed aircraft in the number one position..

Planning ahead with respect to the departure begins with the preflight. whether the pilot is simply going to the practice area or flying a cross-country, the direction of flight and the anticipated communications have to be considered. As noted, have the pilot "script" the expected communications.

checklistItems.name: (Non-Towered) Radio/CTAF - Announce takeoff
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Change to the common traffic Advisory frequency (CTAF) after engine start and before the aircraft is taxied to the run-up area.

Advise traffic of intended departure direction, or if remaining in the pattern advise "Remaining in the pattern."
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Demonstrate to the pilot a method to double-check the selected radio and frequency.

Have the pilot write the basic items to be communicated (facility being called, caller N-number, intentions).

Hesitancy with communications is a common problem early in the training process.

Making a departure briefing standard practice can help the pilot ensure that they have considered and are prepared for the events that can happen quickly during initial takeoff and climb. The briefing should include items like rotation and climb speeds, emergency plans for each phase of the takeoff and initial climb, initial headings and altitudes of turns during the transition to cruise.

Error: Failure to set the proper radio frequency. 

Suggestion:
This can result in transmitting on an incorrect frequency. Demonstrate to the pilot a method to double-check the selected radio and frequency to help minimize errors.

Error: Using inappropriate or wordy communications. 

Suggestion:
Have the pilot write the basic items to be communicated (facility being called, caller N-number, intentions).

Error: Failure to plan ahead for the direction to depart the pattern or when remaining in the pattern.

Suggestion:
Making a departure briefing standard practice can help the pilot ensure that they have considered and are prepared for the events that can happen quickly during initial takeoff and climb. The briefing should include items like rotation and climb speeds, emergency plans for each phase of the takeoff and initial climb, initial headings and altitudes of turns during the transition to cruise.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Planning ahead with respect to the departure begins with the preflight. Whether the pilot is simply going to the practice area or flying a cross-country, the direction of flight and the anticipated communications have to be considered.

As noted, have the pilot "script" the expected communications.

checklistItems.name: Traffic - Clear
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Scan the final approach and base segment for traffic.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Remind the pilot to be vigilant because controllers are human and they can make mistakes too.

To see traffic that is blocked by the wing, consider turning a high-wing aircraft nose to face about 45 degrees towards the final approach path.

Error: Failure to clear the final approach corridor.

Suggestion:
Remind the pilot to be vigilant because controllers are human and they can make mistakes too.
To be sure to see traffic that is blocked by the wing, consider turning a high-wing aircraft nose to face about 45 degrees towards the final approach path.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Advise the pilot that on rare occasions the tower may clear the pilot "for immediate take-off." When this expression is used the pilot must determine if they are ready to proceed into the take-off, otherwise simply advise the tower "unable."

checklistItems.name: Takeoff - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Always taxi to, and align the aircraft with, the centerline of the runway before applying take-off power.

If the take-off must be aborted, advise the tower only after the aircraft has been slowed to a taxi speed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Note the requirement to verify the expected RPM or Manifold pressure and to correct the cause or abort the take-off if there is any question.

Error: Failure to advance the throttle fully, or a mis-adjusted mixture, may cause the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge to indicate less than the value anticipated.

Suggestion:
Note the requirement to verify the expected RPM or Manifold pressure and to correct the cause or abort the take-off if there is any question.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: With a fixed pitch prop the RPM, early in the take-off roll, will be less than that shown in the POH/AFM.

checklistItems.name: Upwind climb
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Compensate for crosswind and P-factor to track the extended centerline.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Direct the pilot's attention to the Slip indicator (ball), which may be out of the center for lack of adequate right rudder to compensate for P-factor.

To help maintain the extended centerline, have the pilot line-up two points straight ahead (at different distances) to define the airplane's path.

Error: Failure to maintain an upwind track to accommodate crosswind/P-factor.

Suggestion:
Direct the pilot's attention to the Slip indicator (ball), which may be out of the center for lack of adequate right rudder to compensate for P-factor. 

Error: Failure to track the centerline can place the aircraft in the path of an adjacent parallel runway.

Suggestion:
To help maintain the extended centerline, have the pilot line-up two points straight ahead (at different distances) to define the airplane's path.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Unless the pilot is aware of the local environment they may be unaware that they are not tracking on the extended centerline.

checklistItems.name: (Towered) ATC - Communicate (as needed)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The tower may provide traffic location advisories.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
In the first few lessons it's not uncommon for the instructor to handle the radio calls. This can be helpful to the pilot in learning correct phraseology. Use the same aircraft when possible, to help tune the pilots ear to the N-number.

Emphasize the three basic elements of a radio call: who you are calling, your N-number, what you want.

Error: Failure to acknowledge the tower's traffic callout or other advisory or clearance information.

Suggestion:
In the first few lessons it's not uncommon for the instructor to handle the radio calls. This can be helpful to the pilot in learning correct phraseology. Use the same aircraft when possible, to help tune the pilots ear to the N-number. Emphasize the three basic elements of a radio call: who you are calling, your N-number, what you want.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
The instructor should avoid being a "radio hog." Direct the pilot to make those calls that are less than critical and be supportive when the inevitable mistakes are made.

On occasion the instructor may advise the pilot "I've got the radio" to correct a misstatement by the pilot to ATC or recognition of pilot overload.

checklistItems.name: (Non-Towered) Radio/CTAF - Announce altitude and departure heading
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Advise traffic of current position (upwind) and altitude.

If a "non-standard" pattern departure is to be made ensure the pilot's intentions are clearly stated.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Remind the pilot of their responsibilities to keep other traffic advised of their position and intentions.

Error: Failure to announce position and intentions.

Suggestion:
Remind the pilot of their responsibilities to keep other traffic advised of their position and intentions.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
The AIM notes only two "standard" departures from a non-towered field (straight out and the 45-degree left) climbing to 1500 feet agl.

Depending on traffic, the pilot may elect to use any other segments of the pattern to depart but must make intentions clear.

checklistItems.name: Initial Turn - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Avoid starting any turn from the upwind leg until the aircraft has reached a "safe altitude" typically is between 500-700 AGL, but to follow local procedures

Announce to the instructor "clearing crosswind/downwind... and turning" to affirm that there is no traffic conflict.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The tower may request "Start your crosswind, speed and altitude permitting." Emphasize that the altitude is the pilot's judgement call and that 500 feet is an accepted minimum.

Coach the pilot on observing traffic and establishing reasonable following or crossing distances.

Error: Starting the turn before a minimum safe altitude is attained.

Suggestion:
The tower may request "Start your crosswind, speed and altitude permitting." Emphasize that the altitude is the pilot's judgement call and within 300 feet of pattern altitude is an accepted minimum.

Error: Failure to clear the intended turn, or failure to allow reported traffic to pass abeam before starting the crosswind leg.

Suggestion:
Coach the pilot on observing traffic and establishing reasonable following or crossing distances.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Whether departing or remaining in the pattern, it is vital to clear the crosswind turn to avoid any conflict with aircraft in the downwind segment.

The tower should have advised the pilot if there is any possible conflicting traffic to be followed that might be joining the pattern or who have had an extended upwind.

checklistItems.name: Departure Leg - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Follow any departure procedures provided by the tower.

When remaining in the pattern, proceed as practiced to the Pattern Altitude on Downwind segment.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Coach in the early lessons to ensure procedures are followed. Allow the pilot time to work through the process. Remind them only when any further delay might be create problems with ATC or other aircraft.

Error: Failure to follow the procedure issued by the tower.

Suggestion:
Coach in the early lessons to ensure procedures are followed. Allow the pilot time to work through the process. Remind them only when any further delay might be create problems with ATC or other aircraft.

checklistItems.name: After Takeoff Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use either a mnemonic or printed checklist to ensure all pertinent items are covered.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Have the pilot place checklists on a kneeboard or tablet and remind/encourage their use at the appropriate times.

Error: Failure to address an obvious need such as retracting flaps, gear or establishing an appropriate climb power setting in high performance aircraft.

Suggestion:
Have the pilot place checklists on a kneeboard or tablet and remind/encourage their use at the appropriate times.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: A combination of a memory flow mnemonic backed-up with a written checklist tends to help the single pilot gain some of the benefits of a dual crew environment. Memory flow can be a weak link in the chain.

checklistItems.name: [If remaining in the pattern:] Crosswind - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Frequency Change - Obtain (as needed)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This is only required if the pilot needs/wants a frequency change while still in Class D airspace, or is transiting into adjacent Class/B/C/D airspace.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Positional/situational awareness is a primary concern. If a communication faux paux is imminent, consider gentle reminders, but avoid allowing it to happen.

Use the "event trigger" memory aid (noted earlier to help positional awareness.

Error: Failure to notify the tower when another frequency change is needed while within Class D airspace.

Suggestion:
Positional/situational awareness is a primary concern. If a communication faux paux is imminent, consider gentle reminders, but avoid allowing it to happen. 
Use the "event trigger" memory aid noted earlier to help positional awareness.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Note to the pilot that the tower may issue an advisory that they are cleared off frequency. Unless there is another facility to contact, it may be advisable to remain on the tower frequency to be aware of any incoming traffic from the direction being flown.

checklistItems.name: ARRIVING TO THE AIRPORT
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Weather/Radio/CTAF - Monitor (as appropriate)
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Before entering non-towered airspace monitor the AWOS/ASOS for current weather and preferred runway.

Then monitor the CTAF frequency to determine the amount of traffic and the runway being used.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Early in the training process advise the pilot that as soon as a decision is made to proceed to an airport, the basic requirements of communication should be determined and frequencies set into the radio.

Regardless of the airspace an airport is located, the pilot should have a plan at least 20 miles out. Help identify landmarks that can provide distance information. While using GPS and electronic flight bags can definitely make it easier to determine the distance and orientation to the airport pattern, be sure to build the pilot's fundamental skills of pilotage and situational awareness so they are not completely dependent on technology for navigating and setting up for the pattern entry.

Having the pilot practice drawing out the entries both in ground training and in the air can help them practice basic situational awareness and planning for the entry.

Error: Failure to execute required communications procedures before entering and operating in the pattern (e.g. monitoring weather and making calls).

Suggestion:
Early in the training process advise the pilot that as soon as a decision is made to proceed to an airport, the basic requirements of communication should be determined and frequencies set into the radio. Regardless of the airspace an airport is located, the pilot should have a plan at least 20 miles out. Help identify landmarks that can provide distance information. While using GPS and electronic flight bags can definitely make it easier to determine the distance and orientation to the airport pattern, be sure to build the pilot's fundamental skills of pilotage and situational awareness so they are not completely dependent on technology for navigating and setting up for the pattern entry.

Error: Failure to plan for the proper entry to the pattern.

Suggestion:
Having the pilot practice drawing out the entries both in ground training and in the air can help them practice basic situational awareness and planning for the entry.

checklistItems.name: (Towered) Two-way Radio Communication with Tower - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Before entering towered (Class D) airspace.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Typically this results from a failure to plan ahead or lack of familiarity with the local landmarks.

Early in the training process advise the pilot that as soon as a decision is made to proceed to an airport, the basic requirements of communication should be determined and frequencies set into the radio.

Help identify landmarks that can provide distance information.

Regardless of the airspace an airport is located, the pilot should have a plan at least 20 miles out.

Error: Failure to make the required communications call-up before entering Class/B/C/D airspace.

Suggestion:
Typically this results from a failure to plan ahead or lack of familiarity with the local landmarks. Early in the training process advise the pilot that as soon as a decision is made to proceed to an airport, the basic requirements of communication should be determined and frequencies set into the radio. Help identify landmarks that can provide distance information. Regardless of the airspace an airport is located, the pilot should have a plan at least 20 miles out.

checklistItems.name: (Non-Towered) Pattern Entry - Plan
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Determine the runway in use or preferred runway based on the information gained by checking the weather and monitoring the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency.

Visualize the segments of the pattern and determine how to enter based on the current position of the aircraft and the amount of traffic in the pattern.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Have the pilot diagram the traffic pattern on the sectional, identify the aircraft location and define the most appropriate entry.

Make sure the pilot understands that the runway that most closely matches the wind direction is the one they should use. It is common for new pilots to want to select the runway that would have a tailwind. This may be related to drawing the wind direction and thinking they will land in that direction. Drilling with some ground practice scenarios can help them develop this skill so they will be able to more easily complete it in the cockpit.

Error: Incorrectly identifying the pilot's position in relation to the airport and pattern.

Suggestion:
Have the pilot diagram the traffic pattern on the sectional, identify the aircraft location and define the most appropriate entry. 

Error: Incorrectly selecting the wrong runway because of confusion between reported wind direction and the runway numbers.

Suggestion:
Make sure the pilot understands that the runway that most closely matches the wind direction is the one they should use. It is common for new pilots to want to select the runway that would have a tailwind. This may be related to drawing the wind direction and thinking they will land in that direction. Drilling with some ground practice scenarios can help them develop this skill so they will be able to more easily complete it in the cockpit.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: This takes time and is best done as an exercise during the preflight briefing.

checklistItems.name: (Non-Towered) Radio/CTAF - Announce position/intentions
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Clearly state the aircraft position and intentions on CTAF. Be sure to follow through .
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The key to safety in the non-towered pattern is clear communication and predictability of the pilot's actions. Practicing the calls based on position can be practiced on the ground or in a simulator to help the pilot develop the correct terminology. Because non-towered communications have some very repetitive parts, it's something pilots can practice effectively on their own in between lessons.

Error: Misidentifying the aircraft position or using incorrect or confusing terminology.

Suggestion:
The key to safety in the non-towered pattern is clear communication and predictability of the pilot's actions. Practicing the calls based on position can be practiced on the ground or in a simulator to help the pilot develop the correct terminology. Because non-towered communications have some very repetitive parts, it's something pilots can practice effectively on their own in between lessons.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Occasionally it is better to not correct a poor communication if the clarification process may interfere with continued tasks.

checklistItems.name: Before Landing Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use a mnemonic with written checklist back-up for the necessary items of the POH/AFM being flown.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Advise the pilot that they may elect to circle outside Class D airspace to ensure sufficient time to communicate and assess the tower clearance given.

Error: Failure to address one or more items on the checklist.

Suggestion:
Advise the pilot that they may elect to circle outside Class D airspace to ensure sufficient time to communicate and assess the tower clearance given
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: WARNBIF is a useful mnemonic to help pilots plan and consider critical items as they approach an airport for landing.

checklistItems.name: (Towered) Pattern Entry - As Directed by Tower
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Visualize the segments of the pattern and determine how to enter based on the current position of the aircraft.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Have the pilot diagram the traffic pattern on the sectional, identify the aircraft location and define the most appropriate entry.

Once the pilot develops this basic situational awareness skill, it would be wise to show them how technology like EFBs can make this very easy to accomplish.

Error: Losing positional awareness and not proceeding as directed by the tower.

Suggestion:
Have the pilot diagram the traffic pattern on the sectional, identify the aircraft location and define the most appropriate entry. Once the pilot develops this basic situational awareness skill, it would be wise to show them how technology like EFBs can make this very easy to accomplish.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: This takes time and is best done as an exercise during the preflight briefing.

checklistItems.name: (Non-Towered) Appropriate Entry - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Execute the selected pattern entry as indicated in the pilot's CTAF announcement.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
As with many positional awareness problems, having the pilot audibly identify each leg and the next "event trigger" allows the instructor time to correct potential problems before they become real problems.

Error: Losing positional awareness and not proceeding in the most expeditious manner, and/or failure to proceed as the pilot indicated in their CTAF announcement.

Suggestion:
As with many situational awareness problems, having the pilot audibly identify each leg and the next "event trigger" allows the instructor time to correct potential problems before they become real problems. Work with the pilot on the ground to make sure they can visualize the traffic pattern to better help them keep track in the air.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: At airports without weather reporting and if no aircraft are in the pattern to establish a preferred runway, coach the pilot through overflight to identify the wind direction by locating the windsock.

checklistItems.name: [If remaining in the pattern: Proceed as below after performing Crosswind]
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Scan for Traffic - Continuously
checklistItems.notesToPilot: A busy time--the eyeballs are out the windscreen, all cockpit commitments completed.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize the importance of locating traffic identified by the tower, especially if the clearance is to follow a specific aircraft at a designated point in the pattern.

Refer to the Collision Avoidance activity plan for more details.

Error: Failure to locate/identify traffic.

Suggestion:
Emphasize the importance of locating traffic identified by the tower, especially if the clearance is to follow a specific aircraft at a designated point in the pattern.
Refer to the Collision Avoidance activity plan for more details.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: There should be no other tasks occupying the pilot.

checklistItems.name: Downwind - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Plan ahead to be at pattern altitude and at a low cruise airspeed/power setting when entering the downwind (or assigned) leg.

Space the downwind leg no less than one-quarter mile parallel to the intended runway.

Use a point on the strut of a high wing, or the point where the runway cuts through a low-wing to help the pilot establish the proper and consistent relative distance.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Getting behind in executing the pattern entry is the results from inadequately planning for the arrival or being too slow in executing due to distractions. Some pilots need more time to work through a plan. Avoid having the pilot engage in multiple tasks when their ability to multi-task is suspect. Help them build the habits of completing required checklists and procedures before entering the pattern to better manage their workload.

Determining the correct distance from the runway is often a matter of judgement gained through experience. Help the pilot learn references to assist with spacing. For example, noting where the runway cuts through the strut or wing when at the proper distance from the runway. Practicing Rectangular Course is a good way to help the pilot develop these skills and reference points.

Error: Maintaining an airspeed 20 knots greater than the target and/or more than 200 feet above the pattern altitude.

Suggestion:
Getting behind in executing the pattern entry is the results from inadequately planning for the arrival or being too slow in executing due to distractions. Some pilots need more time to work through a plan. Avoid having the pilot engage in multiple tasks when their ability to multi-task is suspect. Help them build the habits of completing required checklists and procedures before entering the pattern to better manage their workload.

Error: Positioning the downwind leg too close or too far from the runway.

Suggestion:
Determining the correct distance from the runway is often a matter of judgement gained through experience. Help the pilot learn references to assist with spacing. For example, noting where the runway cuts through the strut or wing when at the proper distance from the runway. Practicing Rectangular Course is a good way to help the pilot develop these skills and reference points.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Some pilots need more time to work through a plan. Avoid having the pilot engage in multiple tasks when their ability to multi-task is suspect.

Use non-towered airports that have little traffic whenever possible, but find an opportunity later in the training to acquaint the pilot with a "busy" non-towered airport..

checklistItems.name: (Towered) Landing Clearance - Obtain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Announce audibly to the instructor when the tower issues the landing clearance, then respond to the tower.

The the landing clearance may be issued by the tower at any point in the pattern dependant upon other traffic.

Consider the using a double check flow like the GUMPS check to assist in covering the required items.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize to the pilot the need to acknowledge virtually any communication addressed to their N-number and especially a landing or takeoff clearance.

For more detail, refer to Radio Communications plan.

Error: Failure to acknowledge the clearance.

Suggestion:
Emphasize to the pilot the need to acknowledge virtually any communication addressed to their N-number and especially a landing or takeoff clearance.
For more detail, refer to Radio Communications plan.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
When doing a series of landings the pilot may request (or the tower may dictate) a touch-and-go, a stop-and-go, or a full stop and taxi-back for an additional take-off.

A double check flow like the GUMPS mnemonic check (gas, undercarriage, mixture, prop, seatbelts) should be considered.

checklistItems.name: (Non-Towered) Radio/CTAF - Announce position/intentions (as appropriate on all legs)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Make positional calls while rolling into the turn. Aircraft are more visible when they drop a wing for a turn.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
It is easy for an instructor to lose patience or to become so redundant with their corrections that the student "tunes them out."

Just be consistent or maybe create a signal to remind the pilot to make the call. Eventually with repetition, the habit will become ingrained. Making routine traffic calls at the same point on each leg can help it become part of the procedure so that it triggers the thought in the pilot.

Error: Failure to announce on the CTAF.

Suggestion:
It is easy for an instructor to lose patience or to become so redundant with their corrections that the student "tunes them out." Just be consistent or maybe create a signal to remind the pilot to make the call. Eventually with repetition, the habit will become ingrained. Making routine traffic calls at the same point on each leg can help it become part of the procedure so that it triggers the thought in the pilot.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: There occasionally comes a time when the instructor should say calmly "I'll work the radio, you concentrate on piloting--it's more fun."

checklistItems.name: Base - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
The base leg turn may be initiated at the pilot's discretion based on the specific type of approach being flown, or delayed by the tower with "I'll call your base," for spacing purposes.

The tower may also simply indicate "Follow the Cessna on final" (or a similar call) and will expect the pilot to provide proper spacing.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
While the optimum point is typically based on the 45-degree perspective, there are many extenuating circumstances that the pilot must consider like wind and the type of landing (e.g. power off vs. power on landings).

As with other aspects of judgement that require accumulated experience, encourage the pilot to audibly provide their thinking process so the instructor can assess and provide immediate feedback. Work with them to learn the visual clues to judge height and glide slope to the runway. Giving them target airspeed and altitudes (AGL) on each segment can help them consistently stabilize the pattern and judge what corrections need to be made for varying conditions.

Error: Failure to properly initiate the base leg at the appropriate distance/time, based on the type of approach being flown.

Suggestion:
While the optimum point is typically based on the 45-degree perspective, there are many extenuating circumstances that the pilot must consider like wind and the type of landing (e.g. power off vs. power on landings).
As with other aspects of judgement that require accumulated experience, encourage the pilot to audibly provide their thinking process so the instructor can assess and provide immediate feedback. Work with them to learn the visual clues to judge height and glide slope to the runway. Giving them target airspeed and altitudes (AGL) on each segment can help them consistently stabilize the pattern and judge what corrections need to be made for varying conditions.

checklistItems.name: Final - Stabilized
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
The turn to final is at the discretion of the pilot to ensure the aircraft is properly aligned with the runway.

If the landing clearance has not been issued by the time the aircraft is on final, query the tower "N1234 is final awaiting landing clearance."
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Periodically query the pilot as to the status of the landing clearance to assure that all FARs are being followed.

Making a verbal confirmation of the landing clearance part of the double check flow can help remind the pilot. If in doubt, have them query ATC.

Assuming that your keeping performance notes on the pilot's performance, doing something like putting a check mark next to each landing can help remind you whether clearance has been received when doing pattern work.

Error: Failure to acknowledge the landing clearance.

Suggestion:
Periodically query the pilot as to the status of the landing clearance to assure that all FARs are being followed.
Making a verbal confirmation of the landing clearance part of the double check flow can help remind the pilot. If in doubt, have them query ATC.

Error: Failure to recognize that a landing clearance has not been issued.

Suggestion:
Assuming that your keeping performance notes on the pilot's performance, doing something like putting a check mark next to each landing can help remind you whether clearance has been received when doing pattern work.

checklistItems.name: Landing - Perform as per specified conditions.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Always be prepared for surprises like an unexpected go-around direction or conditions unfavorable for a safe landing.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Assure the pilot understands that a landing clearance can be cancelled and other instructions inserted, such as "Cessna N1234 execute a 270 on final for spacing." The pilot may declare a go-around at any time but must announce their intentions in a timely manner.

Error: Desire to answer radio calls while in the landing phase or rolling out.

Suggestion:
Advise the pilot not to respond to a radio call during any portion of the flare or landing. Wait until the aircraft is at taxi speed.

commonErrors.name: Poor traffic avoidance.
commonErrors.details: Trouble with identifying traffic or maintaining safe visual separation.

commonErrors.name: Improper or missed systems operations.
commonErrors.details: Had trouble with executing proper systems operations or missed performing an important procedure.

commonErrors.name: Improper pattern entry/legs.
commonErrors.details: Did not correctly fly the pattern entry or one or more legs.
See the Teaching Tips section for possible solutions.

commonErrors.name: Missed radio frequency change.
commonErrors.details: Missed or incorrectly entered a frequency in the radio.

commonErrors.name: Skipped or forgot checklist items.
commonErrors.details: Failed to use a checklist. Missed one or more key checklists or items.

commonErrors.name: Trouble with position reporting/awareness.
commonErrors.details: Did not maintain good situational awareness and/or had trouble making position reports.

commonErrors.name: Misunderstood or did not comply with clearance.
commonErrors.details: Trouble with understanding an ATC clearance. Missed complying with a clearance.

standards.name: §61.93 - Solo Cross Country Requirements for Student Pilots (e.5)

completionStandards.description: Is able to verbally describe the basic steps in the desired maneuver/procedure, although cannot perform the maneuver or procedure yet
Can perform the basic procedure/maneuver with instructor coaching
Can perform the procedure/maneuver independently and safely; can identify and describe the desired PTS/ACS performance level
Consistently meets PTS/ACS standards
Consistently exceeds PTS/ACS standards (e.g. holds tolerances within half of PTS/ACS; if tolerance was +/- 100 feet, is able to perform at +/- 50 feet)

activities.what: A flight maneuver that safely brings the airplane in a stabilized and gentle approach to contact with the ground
activities.why: To safely make the transition from flight to taxi
activities.groundPrep:
Flying a consistent traffic pattern

Understanding the proper sight picture
How to make small corrections to Power, Pitch, and Trim.
Getting configured early

checklistItems.name: Before Landing Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Train the pilot to complete the before landing checklist well before beginning the landing sequence. For newer pilots, this could mean having them complete it before entering the pattern. As pilots gain more proficiency, they might be able to handle it effectively early on downwind. In any case, it's important to teach pilots to "stay ahead" of the aircraft and to constantly be anticipating the next step in the flight.

It is also a good idea to have a before landing flow that pilots can use while practicing multiple landings in the traffic pattern. That way you can help develop a habit of perfoming the before landing checklist everytime they are on downwind or preparing to land. The typical procedure would be to have the pilot complete the before landing checklist in preparation for the initial landing, then complete a more abbreviated flow on the repeated landings.

Before landing checklist should include setting up the radios so that tower is in active and ground is in standby (if equipped). Airport diagram should be accesible and ready to use upon landing.  Have the Pilot verbally anounce "Before Landing Checklist complete"
checklistItems.simulator:
The simulator is useful for giving pilots repetition in setting up the airplane for landing and in being able to help them identify visual cues that aid landing. Specifically, you can teach pilots how to gauge the shape of the runway for alignment by monitoring the perceived lengths of the runway sides, how to judge where the airplane will flare by looking for the spot that doesn't move, and when to flare by watching for the quickly expanding runway view when you approach the runway. Use the pause button throughout these exercises to help the pilot learn how to identify some of the key visual cues during landing. 

For normal landing practice, your home airport or one that has some interesting scenery will make good choices. Since this is typically earlier in training, it's best to keep the wind calm to light when setting up the session. Most simulators will have a feature that allows you to place the airplane on final which makes repetition of landing approach quick and easy.

checklistItems.name: Frequency - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Traffic - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Landing Clearance/Announcement - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: The Priorities should always be "Aviate, Navigate, Communicate". Ensure that the Pilot is flying the plane first and foremost. Many new Pilots get distracted while talking on the radio, or listening for a break on a busy frequency trying to make their position announcement, and let their airspeed or altitude or ground track wander off when talking to the tower. Ensure that the Pilot is not fixated on the radio communications at the expense of flying the airplane.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: The CFI may want to make most of the radio calls for the first few sessions of landing practice. This will help the Pilot learn the proper phraseology and reduce their workload and stress until they are more adept with their traffic pattern procedures.

checklistItems.name:
Airspeed - Set
Altitude - As Appropriate
Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Downwind - Power - bottom of green arc, Airspeed 90 KIAS & Trim, Altitude 1000 AGL, GUMPS

Have the airplane at the correct altitude and power setting to maintain the airspeed and make sure it is trimmed to reduce workload.  Apply wind drift correction to maintain ground track. Scan for traffic and mentally prepare the steps you'll take to begin the descent in the traffic pattern.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may become task saturated preparing for landing and ignore the trim.

Ensure that the pilot has the aiplane properly trimmed to make it easier to maintain altitude and speed for downwind.  If there is a GPS groundspeed readout note the groundspeed to estimate the wind at TPA.  Help the Pilot develop a mental picture of where the wind is coming from by referencing its direction on the Directional Gyro.

checklistItems.name:
Abeam landing spot:
Power - Reduce for descent
Carb heat - ON
Flaps - Set
Airspeed - Set
Trim - As necessary
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adding 10° Flaps, will cause the nose to rise. Apply pressure of the yoke to maintain the desired airspeed and re-trim. This will set up an approximate 500 fpm descent.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Key Position (about 45° from landing spot):
Turn Downwind - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Base:
Power - Adjust as necessary
Flaps - Set
Airspeed - As Appropriate
Trim - As necessary
Check flow - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adding 20° Flaps, will cause the nose to rise once again. Apply pressure on the yoke to maintain proper airspeed and re-trim. This should maintain an approximate 500 fpm descent. Should lose about 300 AGL altitude on BASE leg, make turn to Final in order to line up with runway
checklistItems.teachingTips: Pick a point near the horizon to judge wind drift and apply a correcting crab angle. Start the base to final turn early enough so that the Pilot can shallow out the turn in they are going to undershoot the extended centerline. If the they undershoot the turn, have them parallel the runway and go around. Have the Pilot put the centerline "between their legs" when they turn Final.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: It may be easier for the new pilot to use round numbers. 90 KIAS on downwind, 80 KIAS on base, 70 KIAS on final, 65 KIAS over the numbers.

checklistItems.name:
Final:
Power - Adjust as necessary
Flaps - Set (once reaching runway is assured)
Airspeed - As appropriate
Trim - As necessary
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adding the last 30° of flaps will again cause the nose to change pitch attitude. Apply pressure to the yoke to maintain desired airspeed and re-trim. If the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL, the pilot should initiate an immediate go-around. Keep aiming point (about 200’ prior to landing spot) from moving up or down on windshield.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Just as the Pilot practiced in Slow Flight; use Pitch to maintain airspeed and Power to maintain altitude (or descent rate). To resist overcontrolling with ailerons make sure the Pilot has a three finger grip on the yoke with their left hand, right hand on the throttle. Have them take their hands off the yoke momentarily to ensure the airplane is in proper trim for the descent.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If the Pilot is overcontrolling on Final, try to have them just use the palm of their hand on the yoke. This will teach them to just use pressure on the yoke for control and to ensure the airplane is properly trimmed. Another technique to help a Pilot develop a three finger grip is to slip a pencil underneath the middle finger and over the index and fouth finger.

checklistItems.name:
Start Roundout (eyes down the runway):
Power - Idle
Pitch - Level
Back pressure - Apply
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When the runway gets wide (see Runway Expansion Effect), start to level off and smoothly reduce power to slow the airplane. As the plane begins to sink in your peripheral vision, slowly pitch up to arrest the descent. Pitch up slowly or the plane may balloon. Be patient and let the plane settle on the runway.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Before takeoff roll, have the pilot note the width and sight picture of the runway. Have them imagine how it will look when the plane is 2 feet off the runway. This is the sight picture they will have when about to touchdown for landing.  

Emphasize smooth power changes.  Eratic power changes will cause problems in attaining a smooth transition to the round-out. However, be ready to quickly add full power to go around if needed!

checklistItems.name:
Touchdown:
Main wheels - Complete
Lower nose - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The airplane should settle onto the runway in a slightly nose up attitude. Depending on the pilot's sitting position, the cowling will be just above the horizon. Have patience as speed bleeds off and aircraft settles in for touchdown. Continue to hold the nose up as the weight of the aircraft is transferred to the main wheels. Once the main wheels are rolling down the runway, the airplane will start slowing and and back pressure on the elevator can be slowly relaxed to lower the nosewheel.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot practice flying along the runway without touching down. Fly in a level flight attitude just a few feet above the runway (in ground effect) at landing airspeed but with just enought power so the plane doesn't settle on to the runway. Let the pilot gain experience flying just above the runway. At the completion of the exercise, the pilot can let the plane settle in for landing if enought runway remains or execute a go-around.

checklistItems.name:
Landing Roll:
Rudder - Use
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain some back pressure on the yoke to keep the aircraft weight predominantly on the main wheels. Maintain directional control with the rudder and attention outside the cockpit. Do not make any other configuration changes (flaps, carb heat, lights, etc.) until off the runway. Ailerons should be placed appropriately for crosswind.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Braking - Minimum required
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Brakes should be applied sparingly and steadily as needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ailerons should be placed in the proper direction for any crosswind. Apply brakes sparingly, use rudder to maintain directional control.

commonErrors.name: Poorly controlled rollout
commonErrors.details: Uneven braking and using ailerons to "steer" the airplane. Drifting from centerline.

commonErrors.name: Poor Pattern
commonErrors.details: Inadequate wind drift correction on base leg. Undershooting or overshooting the base to final turn. Flat or skidding turns from base to final.

commonErrors.name: Unsuccessful flare
commonErrors.details: Focusing too close to the airplane resulting in too high a round-out. Focusing too far from airplane resulting in too low a round-out.

commonErrors.name: Unstabilized approach
commonErrors.details: Poor trim technique. Attempting to maintain glideslope or reach the runway using elevator instead of small adjustments to power.

commonErrors.name: Centerline control
commonErrors.details: Failure to land on centerline.

activities.name: [09] X/C: Night Takeoffs & Landings
activities.what: A training flight for practicing aircraft control and airport operations at night
activities.why: To help the pilot learn to operate safely in nighttime visual conditions
activities.groundPrep:
The goal of this activity is to help the pilot learn basic aircraft control while flying at night and to complete at least 8 of the required ten night takeoffs and landings. You may also consider having the pilot practice their basic instrument maneuvers during lesson to give them a better idea of what it is like to fly without visual reference to the horizon.

NOTE: A Total of 3 hours of night training are required as per 14 CFR 61.109

NOTE: The notes in the lessons for Night Takeoffs and Landings and Night Cross Country are very similar due to the shared content.

Night takeoffs and landings differ from typical daytime operations in that outside visual references are often missing. The pilot must learn effectively integrate instrument indications to supplement the lack of visual references.

Benefits and hazards of night flying. 
Benefits - smoother air, better aircraft performance, easier to spot other aircraft, reduced air traffic and BEAUTIFUL. 
Hazards - being unable to see terrain and clouds, difficult to do off airport landings safely, high risk of spatial disorientation or controlled flight into terrain.

Night vision and adaptation. It takes approximately 30 minutes for our eyes to adapt to seeing at night and seconds to lose that adaptation. Try to spend 30 minutes outdoors or in a dimly lit or dark room before flying. Avoid looking directly at bright lights and shield your eyes when near planes with strobes or bright lights on to avoid losing night adaptation. Our night vision is poorest looking directly ahead. Need to use peripheral vision to see an object clearly. Our eyes are also especially sensitive to oxygen, which is why the FAA recommends using supplemental oxygen as low as 5000 feet MSL at night. 

Night illusions. Review the night illusions that commonly affect pilots. These illusions affect your ability to see and avoid other aircraft, avoid spatial disorientation and fly a safe approach path to the runway. Review the information in the AIM 8-1-5 Illusions in Flight and AIM 8-1-6 Vision in Flight. The lack of normal visual references at night, even in good visibility, makes a pilot susceptible to illusions often thought limited to IFR flight.                              

Airport, obstacle and aircraft lighting. Common runway, taxiway, approach lighting system and visual glide path lighting. How to interpret aircraft lighting. When aircraft lights must be used and how to avoid blinding other pilots. How to turn on pilot controlled lighting. How to review NOTAMs for airport lighting status.

checklistItems.name: Minimum required equipment - Verify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Additional equipment is required for night time operations by 14 CFR 91.205 (c). It is critical for safety that you verify that the equipment is properly operating prior to flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: IFR equipment - Consider
checklistItems.notesToPilot: During night flight, outside visual references are significantly reduced. The equipment required for instrument flight by 14 CFR 91.205(d) like the attitude indicator and heading indicator are invaluable during night flight. Strongly consider ensuring they are working correctly before a flight at night.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Similar to required night equipment, be ready to fly at night even if you are planning to complete your flight shortly before sunset. 

If the aircraft is not equipped with an attitude indicator the pilot must have adequate visual reference outside. Flight at night without a moon, over unlit terrain or over water is especially hazardous if the aircraft is not equipped with an attitude indicator. Flying with a full moon or over very well lit terrain can offset this risk.

checklistItems.name: White flashlight - Use
checklistItems.notesToPilot: While night vision is compromised by bright white light, it does provide the best illumination for catching any issues during the preflight inspection. If you choose to preflight using white light, remember to give your eyes at least 30 minutes to recover their night vision before flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Airport Lighting - Review
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use the Chart Supplement and Airport Diagrams to determine what lighting is available at the airport. It is important to determine the location of the airport beacon (if available) relative to the runways to help orient yourself with the runways. Learn what runway and approach lighting is available. Check NOTAMs for inop lighting systems.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flight Planning - Adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Clouds and terrain are not easily seen at night and, as a result, it is easy for a pilot to encounter one or both inadvertently. Carefully check forecasts for cloud bases and tops. Be sure to have plenty of cloud clearance to avoid inadvertant entry into the clouds. Watch for a close temperature/dewpoint spread in the forecast since that could signal the potential for fog to form.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Familiarity with instrument approach procedures can help the pilot select safe altitudes and routes to approach an airport to land at night. If the pilot plans on becoming instrument rated emphasize the benefits of filing and flying IFR at night even on VFR nights.

checklistItems.name: Cockpit materials - Organize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: A good idea in prepping for any flight, the added challenges of night flying make it even more important that you have your materials organized and ready for use prior to takoeff. Ask your instructor and other pilots about the system they use for organizing their materials and then gradually develop a system that will work for you.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Unintended forward movement - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: At night it can be more difficult to notice unintentional aircraft movement on the ground. This is even more critical during engine start and run up on a night flight. Maintain extra vigilance to ensure the brakes are set so you don't let the aircraft drift accidently.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flight instruments - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The reduced outside references during night flight can result in the pilot to experience spatial disorientation. Be sure to use the flight instruments to supplement aircraft control on all phases of night flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Do at least one lesson on basic instrument maneuvers before taking the pilot up at night. This will give the pilot some practice using the attitude indicator to determine the aircraft's actual attitude in reference to the natural horizon.

checklistItems.name: Heading bug - Reference
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If installed on your aircraft, the heading bug can be useful to maintain your situational awareness of runway headings on climbout, cruise, and during the approach for landing.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Interior lights - Dim
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be sure to dim the interior lights (panel, instrument, avionics, etc.) to improve your night vision. Keeping the interior lights too bright can decrease the effectiveness of your night vision and can cause a glare on the windscreen.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure students know how to control cockpit lights including the brightness level of installed avionics and GPS. 

Ensure the pilot knows how to turn down the brightness or switch to night mode when using tablets.

checklistItems.name: Exterior lights - Use as appropriate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When operating at night be sure to always use the beacon and position lights. Use of the landing, taxi, and strobe lights should done with consideration to other pilots' night vision and any environmental conditions that could affect your visibility.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Position/navigation lights and beacon must be on from sunset to sunrise before the aircraft is moved. It is simplest to turn on the beacon before starting the aircraft and then turn on the position lights immediately after starting the aircraft.

Landing light, while not required for private pilot flights, should be used for night landings as standard procedure.

checklistItems.name: Position/NAV lights - Interpret
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Knowing which combination of the green, white, and red nav lights signal another aircraft's orientation to you is not something to guess at during flight. Be sure to review this before flight so that you can immediately identify which way any traffic you see is flying in relative your path.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the opposing aircraft light is not moving and has a red light on your right, this means the plane is flying directly at your plane. Both aircraft should alter their course to the right. An easy way to remember this is "Red on Right, reTURN". 

A white light directly ahead of you with flashing red above or below indicates the plane is flying away from you.

A green light and white light indicates the plane is flying from your left to right. 

A red light and white light indicates the plane is flying from your right to left.

checklistItems.name: Runway lights - Activate/Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Many airports have pilot controlled runway lights that will automatically shut off after 15 minutes. Be sure to periodically activate the lights by clicking the radio on the CTAF (7 times for high, 5 for medium, and 3 for low low intensity). Be sure to review airport information during your flight planning to find out what type of lighting system is installed at your destination.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the runway lights don't activate, verify the appropriate frequency and try again with slower clicks.

Runway lights are on a 15 minute timer. Remind the pilot to turn on the runway lights when they arrive at the airport, even if they are already on. Otherwise the pilot risks the lights turning off automatically and unexpectedly. 

High intensity runway lights are VERY bright white lights and will blind the pilot easily if used in good visibility conditions. Even if the airport has high intensity lights, start at low or medium intensity and step up the lighting to high only if required due to low visibility.

checklistItems.name: Runway center - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If available, use the runway centerline lighting to maintain runway alignment during night takeoffs and landings. On runways without centerline lightning, the landing light will help you see the painted runway centerline. On runways without a centerline, use the runway edge lights to help you maintain an equal distance from either side during takeoff and landing. Once you start to climb, monitor the heading bug and flight instruments to help maintain the extended runway centerline since it may be hard to see any other clear visual references.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Red/blue/green flashlight - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Bright white light can ruin your night vision. Using a red light in the cockpit will allow you to see without compromising your vision, but if used on a chart the red light will wash out magenta colored markings. Using a flashlight with a blue light on charts can help you maintain your night vision and see all of the chart information. Another option is to use a green flashlight or very dim white light.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Some aircraft are equipped with appropriately dim white or red lighting in the interior. Even if the aircraft is equipped make sure to have a flashlight within easy arms reach in case of electrical failure or lighting failure.

Any colored lighting used will "wash out" that color on charts and instruments. A green light will make the green arc on the airspeed indicator very difficult to see. A red light washes out magenta on charts, blue will wash out blue markings.

checklistItems.name: Visual Glide Slope Indicators - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Choose runways and airports with visual glide slope indicators if at all possible. These lights help the pilot remain clear of terrain and on a safe approach path to the runways.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Non-VFR flight - Avoid
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Caution must be taken to avoid inadvertently flying into clouds or other low visibility conditions during night operations. Be sure to get a thorough weather briefing prior to flight. While in flight, look for signs that could signify poor visibility conditions. For example, if the ground lights begin to have halos around them or disappear altogether, you may be overflying fog or a cloud deck or even entering a layer of clouds. Immediately reference your flight instruments and exit the conditions.

Flying over water or large unlit areas at night can quickly lead to spatial disorientation. Use the of the flight instruments will be critical. Seriously consider not flying in these conditions without first achieving an instrument rating.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Instruct the pilot to carefully check forecasts for cloud bases and tops. If they are forecast within 2000' of the planned route/altitude, change the route/altitude or cancel the flight. The GFA tool provides cloud bases/tops forecasts. TAFs will provide cloud base forecasts. METARs and PIREPS provide current condition information.

The pilot needs to be especially aware of the temperature/dewpoint spread reported by ATIS/AWOS/ASOS/METARs. As night falls the air cools towards the dew point. Low clouds or fog can form very quickly when the temperature and dewpoint converge.

Emphasize the pilot should avoid flight at night over unlit terrain or water without a full moon to provide additional lighting. Flight in these conditions without a full moon will result in spatial disorientation for a pilot that is not using their flight instruments.

checklistItems.name: Basic maneuvers - Practice
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be sure to practice your fundamentals of flying at night to get more comfortable with the differing visual conditions. The fundamentals include straight and level, turns, climbs, descents, and steep turns. With the help of your instuctor make sure you practice recovery from unusual attitudes.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If the pilot struggles with performing basic maneuvers at night revisit the basic instrument flying lesson and exercises during the day. Then return to doing the same maneuvers at night (without the hood on) and emphasize using the instruments to supplement what the pilot ccan see outside.

checklistItems.name: Lights out - Practice
checklistItems.notesToPilot: With the help of a CFI, it is good to practice lights out maneuvers like straight and level, turns, climbs, descents, and steep turns to be prepared for flying during an electrical failure. You also might consider practicing landings without a landing light with a CFI as an emergency procedure.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Do this lights out practice only on nights with good illumination from the moon or ground lighting. Practice landing with the runway lights off but landing light on. Then practice with the runway lights on and landing light off.

commonErrors.name: Allowing the plane to  unintentionally move forward with the engine running.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Be especially vigilant about this and if the pilot allows this to happen call it to their attention.  If it does not happen naturally, find a safe location and have the pilot stare inside the cockpit as you (safely) allow the plane to move forward slowly and ask them to identify when the plane moves and stops. Then have them looking outside frequently and do the same exercise. This should demonstrate the benefits of frequent outside checks and the risks of failing to do so.

commonErrors.name: Not having flashlights and spare batteries available.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Have the pilot organize the cockpit as they would normally for a daytime flight and sit in the pilot's seat. Then walk them through various scenarios. How will they see the checklist before starting the engine? What would they do if their flashlight (headlamp) battery died? What would they do if the cabin lights failed? Then demonstrate how proper placement of back up lighting and backup light power makes these issues much easier to manage.

commonErrors.name: Not verifying night equipment is working prior to flight.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Emphasize to the pilot that while night equipment is not required for daytime flight. Flights can be unexpected delayed or diverted, requiring a later return to base than planned. If the pilot plans to fly within two hours of sunset it is a good idea to verify all required equipment for night flight is available and the lighting works in the aircraft.

commonErrors.name: Not setting the heading indicator to compass before take off, during flight or before landing.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Ensure the pilot has a strategy for setting the heading indicator to compass at night. Depending on the aircraft the magnetic compass may be unlit or poorly lit, requiring the pilot to illuminate the magnetic compass to get the current magnetic heading.

Emphasize the importance of setting heading indicator to compass in every phase of flight (doing so is on most checklists) and before doing turns to headings using the heading indicator. To demonstrate how important this is, do an hour long flight in the pattern without setting the heading indicator to compass and, at the end of the flight, have the pilot compare the actual compass heading with the heading indicator's reading. Most mechanical heading indicators will be reading significantly different from actual compass heading after one hour.

commonErrors.name: Failing to recognize night illusions (e.g. black hole approach) and flying a lower or higher than normal approach path._x000D_
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:

Emphasize the use of visual glide slope indicators to remain on a safe approach path to the runway that will ensure terrain and obstacle clearance and help combat the natural tendency to fly too high or low.
