activities.name: [08a] X/C: Short Field Takeoff and Maximum Performance Climb
activities.what: A flight procedure that results in the shortest ground roll and steepest angle of climb
activities.why: To permit safe takeoff from a short and/or obstacle obstructed field
activities.groundPrep:
Interpretation of POH Take-Off and climb gradient performance tables and graphs.
Significance and use of LIFT OFF and speed AT 50 FT verses Vx and Vy speeds.
Effect of density altitude on engine power, acceleration and climb performance.
Proper leaning procedure for high altitude airport operations.
Understanding the use of flaps for take-off operations.
Effect of headwinds, tailwinds and runway surface conditions on runway length requirements.
Effect of aircraft weight on take-off performance.
Limitation of full power for high performance aircraft.

checklistItems.name: Take-off performance - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use the POH to determine aircraft take-off performance.

Ensure the runway is long enough for the current conditions. 

Use a 50-percent safety factor, i.e. if the runway calculation is 1000 feet, ensure that at least 1500 feet are available.

Select an abort point down the runway calculated to be where the airplane should become airborne and mentally commit to aborting the take-off if not airborne by that spot.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Note to the pilot that the POH may refer to the "rotation" speed as "LIFT OFF" and a transition to Vx speed as "AT 50 FT." 

These speeds vary with altitude/temp and take-off weight.

Help the pilot select a visual reference for the halfway point and have them verbally announce as they check the airspeed at that point.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Teaching the 50/70 Rule may be useful in helping pilots safely monitor their takeoff performance--if they haven't reached 70% of takeoff speed by 50% of the runway length--abort.
checklistItems.simulator:
Take advantage of the simulator to give the pilot short-field takeoff practice at a much shorter runway than might normally be available. Consider trying Harris Hill Gliderport (4NY8) in Elmira, NY - a short paved runway (just over 1100') on the top of a mountain. Have the pilot practice short field technique from runway 34 to drive home the importance of mastering the technique. Teach the pilot the procedure just like you would in the airplane, but use the pause and reset location functions to coach them and give them plenty of repetitions to help prepare them for performing it in the airplane.

Once the pilot is proficient in the technique, if equipped, change variables like the weight loading of the airplane, the ambient temperature, or the amount of headwind/tailwind to demonstrate how those variables affect aircraft performance in a more dramatic way. In a slightly extended lesson, you could have the pilot determine the takeoff performance from the aircraft POH to see how it is reflected in the sim's performance.

checklistItems.name: Takeoff configuration and checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be sure to follow and verify the short-field takeoff procedures found in the AFM/POH. It will include how to configure the airplane and specify the procedures to get the best performance out of your airplane. This will include setting the flaps, carb heat (if installed), and mixture. Some considerations are to set and visually verify the flap setting and setting the carb heat and mixture to obtain maximum power.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
When departing a high altitude airport, run up the engine to full power with the mixure at full rich. Lean the mixture until the Tachometer shows maximum RPM. Reduce power and leave the mixture set for takeoff.

A double-check on the lean procedure is to use the carb heat as a final determination of the setting. 

If there is no drop in rpm when carb heat is applied, the mixture is too lean. 

Enrichen slightly and check again until the rpm shows a slight drop.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
One method of proper leaning is to set the power during the run-up to 2000 RPM (or as recommended by the manufacturer) and slowly lean the mixture while observing the RPM. 

The traditional use of the EGT can be misleading in static run-ups.

The use of slow increments is important to allow the engine to adjust RPM for the new mixture setting. 

When the RPM fails to show an increase, or drops slightly, the peak EGT has been found. Increase the mixture slightly (1/8) inch or a half-turn). 

Check with carb heat to ensure that a slight drop in RPM occurs.

Using full throttle may be required for mixture setting with some aircraft.

checklistItems.name: Takeoff position - Use all available runway
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Taxi to the very beginning of the departure runway in order to take advantage of all available runway.

Always use the full runway length to ensure that sufficient abort stopping distance is available.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Demonstrate positioning the aircraft at the very start of the runway to provide an example of ensuring the full length is available.

checklistItems.name: Brakes - Apply
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Apply the brakes to hold the airplane in position for takeoff while applying full power. Only release the brakes once engine power has been verified and you are ready to start the takeoff run.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Power - Apply full
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Ensure there is no roughness or hesitation in the engine.

Verify RPM is that expected for the conditions.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Yoke - Slightly aft
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Allow a slight elevation of the nose by the slipstream.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Brakes - Release
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Slide feet down to the lower part of the rudder to avoid inadvertant use of brakes when applying rudder
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Accelerate to Vr and lift off - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Accelerate to rotation speed (Vr) and then smoothly lift the airplane off of the runway.

If the abort point is reached before achieving the rotation speed, abort the take-off.
checklistItems.teachingTips: The LIFT OFF speed noted in the POH may be several knots below published Vx.

checklistItems.name: Climb to clear obstacles - Establish and maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Pitch to an angle that will produce the manufacturer recommended speed (Vx or Vy) at 50 feet. With the correct pitch angle, the aircraft will continue to accelerate to the recommeded speed during the transition to flight.

If the take-off is aborted, retract the flaps and use aft elevator to place maximum braking effectiveness on the wheels.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Some pilots may depend on the instructor's verbal cues rather than making their own decisions. Allow the pilot some leeway to make slight errors in judgment and then note them as a critique.

checklistItems.name: Cruise climb and configuration - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Once clear of any obstacles, pitch to an angle that will produce a Vy climb (or as recommended by the manufacturer). 

Retract flaps and gear, then visually verify desired configuration.

Adjust throttle for maximum continuous climb power.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Advise pilots to avoid flap and gear retraction during the climb over any obstacles to prevent them taking their attention away from flying the airplane. Once clear of the obstacles, they will be able to more safely operate the airplane during any configuration changes.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: High performance aircraft typically have a limitation on the time use of maximum power.

commonErrors.name: Failure to lean correctly for high altitude take-offs.
commonErrors.details: In addition to impressing the importance of a properly leaned engine to achieve maximum performance, be sure to teach the pilot the proper procedure explained in the teaching tips.

commonErrors.name: Uncoordinated during climbout at Vx.
commonErrors.details: Have the pilot anticipate the need for right rudder to counteract P-factor during the lower than normal airspeed climb.

commonErrors.name: Failing to consider density altitude, wind conditions, aircraft weight in calculating takeoff distance.
commonErrors.details: Emphasize the importance of calculating takeoff distance and performance when operating from a short runway. Consider using a simulator to demonstrate the effect of high altitudes and temperatures on performance. You could use a YouTube video of a density altitude accident to drive home the importance of calculating performance to clear obstacles.

commonErrors.name: Leaving unused runway behind the aircraft.
commonErrors.details: Impress on the pilot the need to avoid intersection take-offs when there is any question of runway length. Show the pilot examples of real world short runways compared with takeoff distances in the AFM/POH under various weather conditions. Emphasize the need to not give up any runway that will be critical if something were to go wrong during the takeoff.

activities.name: [03] PRE-SOLO: Go Around/Rejected Landing
activities.what: A flight maneuver that discontinues a landing approach for safety reasons through the use of power, climb pitch attitude, and a gradual reduction of drag (flaps/gear) on the airplane
activities.why: To allow the pilot to discontinue the approach to landing for safety reasons and set up for another approach under more favorable conditions
activities.groundPrep:
Reasons to execute the Go-around (unstable, poorly aligned, too high/low, obstructions or traffic, cross-winds or turbulance, or anything that doesn't feel right).
Basic procedure and rationale for each step of the power-up, clean-up, fly-up process; power, pitch, flaps, Vx, climb.
Awareness of out-of-trim yoke pressures.
Terminology to be used: abort, go-around, continue.
Blind-fold activity of locating/touching each control to be used.

checklistItems.name: If safe landing is in doubt, discontinue approach.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Make the decision early to reduce risk by allowing more time to make the transition steps.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Allow the pilot to make the decision and let them follow through. There may be a tendancy for the instructor to over-ride the pilot's decision and continue an approach that the instructor considers salvagable. 

As there may be occasions to encourage the pilot to continue an approach to challenge and develope their skills, it is a delicate judgement call.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
If the pilot fails to recognize a bad approach, use single word commands such as "Go-around" or ""Abort"" that have been discussed during the briefing. 

Find at least one occasion where the approach is going well and call for a Go-around to alert the student to situations where the tower might call for the abort due to reasons the pilot may be unware.

checklistItems.name: Power - Full
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be prepared to hold forward elevator pressure to oppose the adverse trim set during approach; and right rudder to correct torque.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot verbalize their actions while touching the various controls during the in-cockpit preflight briefing.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: This is another task that can be effectively practiced in the cockpit with the eyes closed.

checklistItems.name: Pitch for level - Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Aircraft may be in trim for a low power/full flap/low airspeed configuration.

Maintain level attitude to allow the airplane to accelerate.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Be prepared to assist the pilot with control inputs to avoid a nose wheel/prop-strike, or ballooning out of ground effect before sufficient airspeed is attained.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: One of the more difficult aspects to flight instruction is knowing when, and how much, control movement to provide when "assisting" the pilot.

checklistItems.name: Carburetor Heat - Cold (Off)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If applicable.
checklistItems.teachingTips: As previously noted, use the blind-fold exercise to help the student identify controls by memorized location and feel.

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Retract one increment
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Retract flaps to second increment to reduce drag and accelerate in a level pitch attitude. Building the airspeed required for climbing will make climbout safe and more effective when initiating a little later.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Monitor flap reduction to assure the pilot does not ""dump"" the flaps and cause the aircraft to settle onto the ground.

In extreme go-around situations the aircraft may not be over the runway so an inadvertant touchdown can have serious consequences.

Go-arounds from less than full-flap settings is normally introduced prior to solo as many instructors prefer to solo students prior to introducing flaps.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If this is a no-flap exercise consider having the pilot verbalize the flap reduction steps in-lieu of their actual use.

checklistItems.name: Begin acceleration to Vx or Vy (as appropriate) - Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Remove excess trim to reduce the need for high forward pressure on the yoke.

Resist the temptation to pitch the nose up too early. Allow the airplane to accelerate to avoid a climb while on the back side of the power curve.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Monitor the pilot's reactions carefuly.

Use one word descriptors when possible to direct the pilot's attention: Power, pitch, rudder, etc.

checklistItems.name: Holding level or positive rate of climb - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Shallow turn to non-pattern side of runway and then parallel to aid in seeing traffic.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Consider adding the maneuver after the pilot demonstrates competancy with the basics.

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Retract one increment
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Retract flaps to first increment.

This step will reduce drag and get the airplane configured to a typical short field takeoff conguration.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Pitch for Vx or Vy (as appropriate) - Climb
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Assume a Vx climb attitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Continue careful monitoring of pilots actions using short descriptors (more pitch/less pitch) to help provide corrective yoke movments.

Have the pilot proactive identifying the climb attitude sight picture for Vx, Vy, and cruise climb speeds. This can be done in the practice area. That way they can be more efficient and confident at setting the appropriate climb attitude during go-arounds and takeoffs.

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Retract fully
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Retract flaps fully once the airplane is safely climbing and cleared any obstacles.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: To remove all control pressure.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot audibly confirm the position of all controls and performance information.

checklistItems.name: Announce go-around on CTAF or notify ATC.
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Only after achieving a safe altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot understands that their first priority is achieving a positive climb rate, clean-up of the aircraft, and achieving a safe altitude before advising ATC or traffic of the go-around.

checklistItems.name: Re-enter pattern for next approach (if applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

activities.name: [08b] X/C: Short Field Approach and Landing
activities.what: A flight maneuver consisting of a low-speed power-on approach that clears any obstacles and results in little or no floating during flare, and stopping in the shortest distance possible.
activities.why: To safely make landings at airfields with a relatively short landing area or over obstacles that limit available landing area.
activities.groundPrep:
Interpreting landing distance charts and tables
The effect of gross weight and flap settings on stall speeds Vs0 and Vs1.
Establish five basic power settings for the aircraft being flown and the airspeed that results (full, low cruise, minimum cruise, approach descent, idle)Establish approach speed based on 1.3 x Vs0 and a second based on lower aircraft weight (max, min) if the POH/AFM provides that data or as recommended by the manufacturer.
Stabilized approach concept. Adjusting glide path with power, airspeed with pitch.
The concept of the region of reverse command--the backside of the power curve.
Note the difference between the terms "aiming point" and "touchdown point."

checklistItems.name: Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Select short-final 1.3 x Vs0 speed based on estimated landing weight and flap configuration or as recommended by the manufacturer.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If the POH/AFM has Vs0 speeds for different landing weights, calculate final approach speed using the one closest to the expected landing weight. When this occurs, select and calculate only one approach speed. Discuss this thoroughly with the pilot to ensure a sound understanding.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Example: the C172P POH/AFM notes a Vs0 of 44 KIAS (at gross weight) zero flaps and 33 KIAS with full flaps. 

This calculates to a 1.3 x Vs0 of 58 KIAS flaps up and 43 KIAS with full flaps. The POH/AFM only specifies 61 KIAS with full flaps, so the disparity is obvious without considering landing weight.
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Frequency - Monitor
Traffice - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use the minimum words to convey intentions.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Non-towered fields require extra vigilance. Teach pilots to look for traffic on each leg and on the runway. Have them anticipate traffic that may not enter using standard procedures and to use good traffic avoidance practices.

checklistItems.name: Landing Clearance/Announcement - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Downwind:
Power - Minimum cruise
Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Airspeed - top of the white arc
Altitude - no less than 800 feet AGL.
Maintain trim with each power or speed adjustment.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Abeam landing spot:
Power - Approach descent
Flaps - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Airspeed 1.3 x Vs0 +15 or as recommended by manufacturer. 
Establishing the initial descent and maintaining trim is important to a well-planned landing.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The touchdown point in actual short field conditions is the numbers on the runway. Landing short of the runway can have consequences if there is a lip to the pavement or rough terrain.

In simulated conditions during early training, the far side of the numbers assures that landing short will not be prior to the runway surface.

checklistItems.name:
Key Position (about 45° from landing spot):

Turn base - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Starting each approach from the same altitude, power setting and airspeed is important to achieving consistent and predictable performance.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Base: 
Flaps - Set
Turn final - Complete
Checklist/Flow - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
1.3 x Vs0 +10 or as recommended by the POH/AFM.
Start the turn a bit early so that shallow bank angles can be used.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Being too high, low, fast, or slow at this point almost certainly assures missing the intended touchdown spot or requiring a go-around. 

Encouraging an early turn to final will avoid the possibility of overshooting the extended centerline and the temptation to use undesirable steep bank angles to correct.

checklistItems.name:
Final: 
Flaps - Set
Power - Adjust as necessary
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
1.3 x Vs0 +5 or as recommended by the POH. 
Select an aim point 150’ in front of landing spot).
Aim point should not move up or down in the windscreen if the approach path is targeting it.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Emphasize that the final approach segment should be flown "stabilized" with respect to pitch and power. No significant changes should be needed. Have the pilot pilot trim away control pressures. Verify by having them briefly take their hand from the controls to see if any unwanted pitch changes occur.

checklistItems.name:
Clear of obstacles:
Power - As required
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
1.3 Vs0, +5 -0 or as recommended by the POH/AFM.
When the commitment is made to continue into the flare, adjust the focus to well down the runway, use peripheral vision to determine height above the ground.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the aiming spot cannot be maintained with modest power adjustments consider a go-around as the aircraft is being operated on the backside of the power curve where small changes have little or no effect.

There are two thought processes at this point: 
1) continue the approach with the current power setting to maintain a "stabilized approach" or: 
2) reduce the power to idle to achieve the steepest descent angle.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Many instructors prefer not to destabilize the approach by going to idle crossing over the obstacle. 

If the glide path was too shallow going over the obstacle because of the power needed to clear it, then execute a go-around and try again.

checklistItems.name: Flare - As appropriate
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Allow for a few feet to ensure the nose wheel does not strike before the mains.
Don't attempt a perfect rolling-on of the wheels with the runway. 
Maintain steady backpressure and avoid moving the yoke forward.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If the aircraft balloons noticeably, call for an immediate go-around.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Practicing low flight down the runway is a good learning activity for developing the sight picture.

checklistItems.name:
Touchdown:
Airspeed - Minimum controllable
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Hold a pitch attitude that assures the main gear will contact first and allow the plane to sink onto the runway.
Assuming a proper touchdown attitude, hold the yoke where it was and proceed to the next step.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Some POH/AFMs say "lower nose wheel gently." But, movement of the yoke forward may cause the airplane to wheelbarrow (ride-up on the nose wheel) if there is too much airspeed remaining.

If the pilot attempts to minimize touchdown speed using "float," it will lengthen the landing distance. Get on the ground early and use the brakes to reduce the landing roll. 

Bleeding-off speed by allowing the aircraft to float is not an acceptable technique in a short field landing.

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Retract (unless the POH/AFM recommends otherwise)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Retracting flaps helps to transfer the weight of the aircraft on the main gear to assist in maximum traction and effective braking.
checklistItems.teachingTips: A decision must be made as to whether any "handles" (flaps) will be moved until the aircraft clears the runway and is stopped, to avoid the possibility of an accidental gear retraction. At a minimum, require pilots to visually and verbally verify that they have the correct control. It might be more prudent to avoid touching the flap control until clear of the runway as a standard procedure. Retracting flaps during this critical phase of the landing can have adverse consequences if the aircraft has retractable gear and the pilot errounously selects the gear handle.

checklistItems.name:
Yoke - Move aft
Braking - Apply Heavily
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Apply heavy braking only after the aircraft is firmly on the ground.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Because initial training will probably be done on longer runways, there is no need to insist on heavy braking until the pilot has a good feel for the braking pressure and its effectiveness. 

Be sensitive to the possibility of the tires skidding and be ready to come off the brakes if that situation develops. 

Under no circumstances should tires be ""smoked"" in practice session.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: A possible practice is to have the pilot apply brakes moderately but call "max braking" so the instructor can recognize the pilot's simulated braking action.

commonErrors.name: Continuing with poor setup
commonErrors.details: Not going around when out of parameters.

commonErrors.name: Hard touchdown
commonErrors.details: Not flaring enough and hitting hard.

commonErrors.name: Too high on final
commonErrors.details: Landing too far down the runway.

commonErrors.name: Poor speed control
commonErrors.details: Too fast on final causing a float past the touchdown point.

commonErrors.name: Breaking too hard
commonErrors.details: Skidding the tires.

activities.name: [06] PRE-SOLO: Forward Slip to Landing
activities.what: A flight maneuver that increases the airplane’s descent angle without increasing airspeed by lowering one wing and simultaneously applying opposite rudder to keep the airplane from turning in the direction of the lowered wing
activities.why: To allow the pilot to safely make altitude corrections during an emergency landing or in an area with obstructions
activities.groundPrep:
Where a forward slip might be required (flap failure, aircraft with no flaps).
The concept of using uncoordinated flight to create drag to lose energy (airspeed and altitude).
The aerodynamics of offsetting the lift vector with aileron while directing the heading with yaw and the technique of reversing the heading control.
Accomodating inaccurate airspeed indications due to static port placement. Note the side of the aircraft on which the static port is located.
The difference between a forward slip and a side slip.
The definition and risks of the cross-controlled stall.

checklistItems.name: Proceed with appropriate landing, EXCEPT:
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Up
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Some aircraft POH/AFM caution that slips with full flaps can cause undesirable pitching moments and should be avoided.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Determine if the airplane being used can be safely slipped with flap extension.

checklistItems.name: Slip direction - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Generally slip to pilot’s side for best visibility or into wind. When a noticable crosswind component is present, lower the wing on the upwind side.
checklistItems.teachingTips: By lowering the wing on the upwind side, a wing-low crosswind correction can more easily be achieved when making the transiiton from a forward slip to a side-slip.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Practice repeated entry and recovery at altitude to allow the pilot to concentrate on these actions using a point on the horizon without the limiting factors of altitude and runway proximity.

checklistItems.name: Power - Idle
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Carrying any power will degrade the maximum performance capability of the forward slip.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Power reduction abeam the numbers is a good time to emphasize the double-check for carb heat and mixture setting.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: For training purposes have the pilot intentionally set-up for an approach that is too high.

checklistItems.name:
Wing - Lower
Rudder - Use opposite
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain alignment with runway. While un-coordinated flight can be uncomfortable and is to be avoided in most maneuvers, it is the key to this one.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Practicing entry, maintaining, and exiting forward slips at altitude is a great way to help the pilot learn how to successfully perform forward slips. Have them note the effect of the slip on the descent rate and how not fully utilizing the rudder takes away from the slip's performance. You can help them work toward maintaining heading while performing the slip by referencing a road or other ground reference.

To avoid stalls, help them focus on maintain the correct pitch attitude throughout the maneuver. Have them note how the airspeed indictator does not read correctly while in the slip, requiring them to control it through outside references. Developing their airspeed control will help them avoid increasing the pitch attitude to the point that a cross-control stall could occur.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Because rudder is the limiting control, and is typically the most effective, its use as the primary force ensures generating the greatest aerodynamic drag.

checklistItems.name: Pitch - Increase slightly
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Increasing the pitch angle slightly will help prevent an increase in airspeed. The airspeed indicator may be slightly inaccurate depending on placement of the static port. 

Use 1.3 x Vs0 +5 when slipping to the side with the static port and 1.3 x Vs0 -5 when slipping to the opposite side as the static port.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot to establishes the appropriate pitch attitude for the desired airspeed.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Note to the pilot how the airspeed varies during the entry and exit to the maneuver based on the relationship of the slip direction to the static port side location.

checklistItems.name:
At desired altitude:
Wing - Raise to normal position
Rudder - Relax
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Practice will help make this step a coordinated action.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Returning to a stabilized approach can be the most demanding aspect of the maneuver. Repeated practice is required.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Practice repeated entry and recovery at altitude to allow the pilot to concentrate on these actions using a point on the horizon without the limiting factors of altitude and runway proximity.

checklistItems.name:
Wings - Level
Pitch - Normal glide
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Re-establish a normal flight profile and confirm the aircraft is stable and in trim.
checklistItems.teachingTips: When working in the pattern, practice the recovery well before the flare to allow the pilot time to make the required adjustments.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: A proficient pilot can hold the forward slip to the flare and transition to a side-slip for crosswind in one deft move.

checklistItems.name: Land - as appropriate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abort the landing if the transition to a stable approach is not achived before the flare is required.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Make sure the pilot knows the recommended speed and glide path they should be using on final to ensure a stabilized approach. Then train and encourage them to monitor the actual airspeed and glidepath in relative to the recommended values. If necessary, train the pilot to recognize when the approach is not stabilized and that they should execute a go-around.

Emphasize that anytime the pilot feels uncomfortable with an approach it's a good opportunity to execute a go-around.

prepItems.name: Takeoff & Landing Variations
prepItems.details: In this section we will discuss the various types of takeoffs and landings you will learn, as well as the techniques to do them successfully.

activities.name: [05a] PRE-SOLO: Crosswind Takeoff and Climb
activities.what: A flight maneuver in which the airplane is safely accelerated to flying speed and lifted from the ground into flight while adjusting for the effects of a crosswind
activities.why: To make the safe transition from taxi to flight when the wind is not aligned with the runway
activities.groundPrep:
What is a crosswind? In the context of taking off and landing a crosswind is any wind that is not aligned "down" the runway. Crosswinds are a routine part of flying. It is very rare to not have some crosswind for a take off and or landing. Winds have no obligation to blow directly down the runway at all times.
How does a pilot determine what the winds are? By reviewing AWOS, ASOS, METAR, ATIS information if available, by looking at wind direction indicators like windsocks, observing the motion of trees, grasses, bushes, etc.  Noticing the drift of the plane when in the air. Does the ground track align with the direction the plane is pointed? if not the plane is in a crosswind.
All wind reports and observations have limitations. Windsocks and weather reports (ATIS, AWOS/ASOS, METARs) are accurate only for the location the reading was made at the time it was made. While all of these tools give the pilot an idea of what they may experience in the aircraft what will actually happen will likely not match these reports exactly. Buildings, trees, hills near the runway will influence crosswinds and can result in winds of varying strengths and directions in a single take off or landing.
How to determine crosswind component using EFB and Crosswind Charts (if available in POH)
How to estimate crosswind component using rules of thumb. Example: If wind direction is 30 degrees off runway heading the crosswind component is 1/2 of wind velocity; 60 degrees or more off runway heading results in the crosswind equaling the full wind velocity
What is the Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Velocity of the aircraft? (look up in POH) Can or should a pilot attempt flying in conditions that exceed the maximum demonstrated crosswind velocity for the plane?
Discuss proper control inputs for the start of the take off roll, changes to control inputs required during take off roll, and using a crab for wind drift correction after take off. Remind the pilot, the slower the plane is traveling the less effective the controls are. The amount of control input to correct for crosswinds will typically be greatest at the beginning of the take off roll. As a result of the variability of winds and limitations of weather reports and observations, a pilot should never "set it and forget it" when it comes to control inputs for winds, they need to be constantly detecting and reacting to changing winds every moment. This is easier to do that it may seem!
How to get a "wind check" from the tower when operating at a towered airport. This is very helpful when coming in to an airport with an older ATIS or when winds are rapidly changing.
NOTE: Runways are often aligned with the direction of the prevailing winds, depending on where the pilot is flying a strong crosswind may indicate approaching fronts or other weather that should be avoided.

checklistItems.name: Before Takeoff Checklist – Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Before Takeoff Checklist – Complete; engine instruments in normal limits

In a strong wind situation the pilot may notice a thrumming sound or unusual vibration resulting from the winds hitting the propeller blades from an unusual direction. This is normal.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be especially vigilant about checklist usage and missed steps if the pilot is showing nervousness or stress.

Reassure the pilot the strange wind noises are normal.

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Traffic - Clear
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Monitor frequency and visually check for traffic

Listening to the communications of other pilots can help the pilot develop a more complete picture of the wind situation at the time of take off.

Remember takeoffs are optional. If the winds have changed significantly and/or are causing other pilots difficulty this may be a good time to reschedule the flight for another day.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may ignore information that would advise them it is not wise to take off. Reports by other pilots of wind shear, multiple go-arounds, and the tower doing frequent wind updates with significantly different directions and speeds are all indications that this may not be a safe time to fly. 

Encourage the pilot to evaluate the communications of other pilots in their decision to fly or not. The only "wrong" time to make the decision not to fly is when past the safe abort point on a take off roll or in the air. 

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Takeoff Clearance/Announcement – Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Wing Flaps - 0°
Carb Heat – COLD (as applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Taxi into takeoff position - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Taxi onto runway, line up with centerline, center nose wheel, verify wind direction (sock)

Determine wind direction using the nearest wind sock, vegetation nearby, blowing leaves, etc. Get as much information as possible. If the wind sock is indicting winds in one direction while the grass nearby is indicating winds in another direction be ready to quickly adjust your control inputs.

Identify a prominent landmark aligned with the extended runway centerline (if available). The pilot will use this aim point as a reference to for the upwind leg to gauge the amount of wind drift correction (crab) they will need to use on climb out.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may assume the last weather report received (no matter how old) is what they will experience on this take off. In addition some will assume the wind sock is a 100% accurate represenation of winds throughout the airport. As winds change these assumptions may result in using incorrect control inputs for the start of the take off roll. 

Encourage the pilot to be a "detective" and get all available information about the winds from a variety of sources. Grasses and vegetation within 100 feet of their position will be more accurate than a wind sock 3000' away.

Ask "What direction is the wind coming from and how will you position the controls for these winds?"
 
Pilots may forget to identify a landmark to gauge wind drift correction. Without a reference the pilot will be guessing at the wind drift correction required and could drift into a parallel runway's departure path. 

Emphasize the importance of being able to do proper wind drift correction, for collision avoidance at airports with parallel runways and proper noise abatement at airports with noise sensitive environments. A good visual reference makes wind drift correction possible. 

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Ailerons - Into wind
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
FULL Ailerons into wind; up aileron on upwind side

Position the ailerons with the controls FULL into the winds. (Example: if the winds are coming from the left turn the control yoke all the way left.) This starting position provides the pilot with the maximum control effectiveness to prevent the plane from "skipping" sideways on take off roll due to cross winds at the low speed of the initial take off roll.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may resist using full aileron inputs thinking they may touch the wing tip to the runway. 

Reassure the pilot most GA trainers are designed to make it impossible for the wingtip to touch the runway when operating at or below the maximum demonstrated crosswind component. 

The pilot may not use any control input because they are unaware of the winds.

Do not allow the pilot to start the take off roll without the correct control inputs. If they do not put the control inputs in it's often helpful to ask them "What are the winds right now?" They will usually quickly look around and realize they need to put in the required control inputs.

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Takeoff - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Advance power smoothly to FULL; select reference points (outside and cowl) to maintain alignment with runway; Apply right rudder for torque correction

FULL ailerons into the wind at the beginning of the take off roll. While using right rudder as needed to counter left turning tendencies.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may relax their aileron inputs when they attention goes to applying power.

Remind the pilot to maintain appropriate control inputs. The instructor may need to provide the required control input for the pilot if they are unable. 

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Abnornalities during takeoff - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check engine instruments and performance; anything unusual = abort takeoff
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Directional control - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Directional control with rudder; Reduce aileron pressure so it is just sufficient to counteract rolling tendency as airspeed increases

Use aileron and rudder to maintain runway directional control in the winds. As airspeed increases both ailerons and rudder become more effective. As a result the pilot will usually slowly reduce aileron inputs while ensuring the aileron inputs are sufficient to prevent the plane from skipping sideways off the runway centerline. Rudder inputs will be adjusted as well to ensure the aircraft is aligned with the direction of travel.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilot may freeze the ailerons in the full position, as airspeed increases this will cause the downwind tire to lift off the runway. Or the pilot may prematurely relax the aileron controls, allowing the plane to skip sideways across the runway. 

The solution to address both freezing the controls and relaxing them prematurely is to emphasize constantly adjusting the control inputs to maintain directional control and no side drift. This is where the finesse of flying comes in. There will be no formula for perfect control input. The pilot needs to focus on identifying side drift or lifting of the tire and adjust as needed. 

If side drift to the downwind side of the runway is detected the pilot will need to increase aileron input until the drift stops. 

If the downwind tire lifts into the air, a slight reduction of aileron input is appropriate.

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Rotation - Higher speed than normal
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Elevator – rotate at a slightly higher speed than normal to ensure positive lift off in crosswind

Rotate with firm use of the elevator once above normal rotate speed. This slightly higher than normal airspeed prevent the upwind tire from touching the runway after take off.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Climb Speed – Vy or Vx (as appropriate)
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Climb at Vy or Vx as appropriate; note position of cowling in relation to horizon and hold pitch attitude; allow airplane to crab into the wind

Once in the air, immediately allow the plane to crab into the winds. This will allow the plane to gain the maximum altitude in the shortest amount of time.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The pilot may want to maintain a side slip on climb out to maintain runway heading. This will result in increased drag as the plane climbs "sideways" into the wind. 

Explain it is most efficient to climb in a crab for wind correction. This will allow the plane to reach a safe altitude more quickly than climbing in a side slip.

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Extended runway centerline - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Maintain extended runway centerline (or as appropriate)

Using the pre-selected visual reference crab into the crosswind to maintain a straight ground track on climb out. Adjust wind correction angle (crab) to maintain a straight ground track as the winds change on climbout. 

If the visual reference disappears below the cowling on climb out, the pilot should use the view to the left of the cowling to detect the plane drifting upwind or downwind of the desired ground track.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The pilot may assume the winds on upwind will be coming from the same direction as experienced on the runway. Wind direction can be dramatically different at altitude, even only 500 to 1000' above ground level. If the pilot does not adjust for these changing conditions they will not be able to maintain a straight ground track on departure. 

The pilot may use too much, too little, or no wind drift correction at all on climb out. This can result in drifting into parallel traffic when operating on parallel runways. If flying a downwind departure or in the traffic pattern, depending on the direction of drift this can result in the plane having a very short or extended crosswind leg and potentially flying downwind abnormally close or far from the runway.

Have the pilot focus on maintaining a straight ground path to the pre-selected visual reference point. If the plane starts to drift downwind of the desired ground track they will need to increase their wind correction angle (crab more into the wind). If the plane drifts upwind of the desired ground track they will need to reduce the wind correction angle. 

If the pilot makes no attempt to correct for wind drift on upwind remind them of the need to correct and the consequences of not correcting. 
 
Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
If there is no prominent landmark on the extended runway centerline available. The pilot will need to use the window/view from the top and eventually the left of the cowling to detect if the plane is drifting in the winds for the climb out.

Have the pilot look at the ground at about 45 degrees from the front view on their side. They can watch for drift by looking at landmarks or ground objects underneath and just to the side of them to help monitor their straight path. If new things keep appearing from under the plane or if things they can see disappear sideways under the plane, it's a good clue that they are drifting.

checklistItems.name: Rudder - Apply as appropriate
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use right rudder to correct left turning tendencies

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for tips not related to crosswind operations.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Brakes – Apply momentarily
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Apply brakes momentarily when airborne to stop any vibration caused by spinning wheels.

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for tips not related to crosswind operations.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
After safe altitude (at least 500’ AGL) – Climb Vy; Power – Full; Trim away control pressures.

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for tips not related to crosswind operations.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: After Takeoff checklist – Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Complete after takeoff checklist.

Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for tips not related to crosswind operations.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal takeoffs and Climbs for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

commonErrors.details: Not using full aileron into the wind at start of takeoff roll. Freezing the ailerons in the full position as airspeed increases causing the downwind tire to lift off the runway. Prematurely relaxing the aileron controls, allowing the plane to skip sideways across the runway.

commonErrors.details: Not using appropriate wind drift correction resulting in drifting away from standard traffic pattern paths.

prepItems.name:
CHECKRIDE: THE CROSSWIND CHALLENGE
WILL YOU BE READY?
prepItems.details: If you are like many pilots preparing for your private pilot checkride or even if you’ve already earned the certificate, your exposure to crosswind takeoffs and landings may have been minimal, especially if you’ve trained at an airport with multiple runways. Most pilots will naturally opt for runways more aligned with the winds, using the crosswind runway only when absolutely necessary.

prepItems.name: Takeoff & Landing Variations
prepItems.details: In this section we will discuss the various types of takeoffs and landings you will learn, as well as the techniques to do them successfully.

prepItems.name: Crosswind Takeoff and Climb (Maneuvers Guide)
prepItems.details: To develop proficiency in conducting crosswind takeoff and climb profiles.

activities.name: [05b] PRE-SOLO: Crosswind Approach and Landing
activities.what: A flight maneuver that safely brings the airplane in a stabilized and gentle approach to contact with the ground when the wind is not aligned with runway
activities.why: To safely make the transition from flight to taxi during crosswind conditions
activities.groundPrep:
Evaluating winds when approaching the airport. Tools: current crab angle vs ground track, airspeed vs ground speed, automated weather, ATIS, "wind check" with tower, reports from other pilots, wind sock. Estimate wind direction. Estimate crosswind component using rules of thumb. 30 degrees off runway heading crosswind will be half of wind velocity, 60 degrees crosswind will be close to full wind velocity. Compare with max demonstrated crosswind component / personal minimums / school minimums. Safe to attempt approach and landing? If not, is an alternate runway available? or choose an alternate airport?
Considerations: winds reported at surface may not be consistent with the winds aloft. Always use appropriate wind drift correction to maintain ground track. A significant difference between winds aloft and surface winds indicates wind shear and a change in control inputs will be required during approach and landing. Friction with the ground often results in lower wind velocities at lower altitude with the most significant reduction right over the runway.
Reminder: wind reports and wind socks are accurate for their location and the time issued only. Be prepared for any wind conditions and adjust control inputs as needed.
Review rectangular course ground reference maneuver. Discuss likely crab direction/angle in the pattern required to maintain ground track on upwind/departure leg, crosswind, downwind, base and final. Be aware of the wind direction, a tailwind on the base to final turn will result in overshooting final if the pilot does not adjust the timing or increase the bank angle on the base to final turn. 				
Introduce sideslip for wind drift correction on final and over runway. This is a deliberately uncoordinated flight condition, however, it is safe when the aircraft is not stalled. NOTE: The amount of aileron and rudder input required to maintain a straight ground track is a good indication of the strength of the crosswind the plane is in at the time. If full aileron and full rudder inputs are not sufficient to maintain a straight ground track the plane is in a wind that exceeds it's maximum crosswind component and controllability.
Timing of transition from crab to sideslip on final. Transition to sideslip on final allows the pilot to evaluate the winds and control effectiveness at a higher and safer altitude.
Control effectiveness decreases as airflow over the control surfaces decreases. Constantly increasing rudder and aileron inputs are typically required to maintain runway directional control from roundout through rollout. After touchdown use full aileron into the wind, and maintain appropriate control positions for taxi at all times.
Use of gust factor (1/2 of difference between steady wind and gust velocity) for turbulent air approaches.

checklistItems.name:
Checklist - Complete
Mixture - Set for best power
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Before Landing Checklist - Complete; mixture set to best power for possible go around.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be especially vigilant about checklist usage and missed steps if the pilot is showing nervousness or stress.

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Frequency - Monitor
Traffic - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Listen to other pilots communications to develop a picture of current wind conditions. 

Refer to Normal Approach and Landings for tips and collission avoidance techniques not related to crosswind operations.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may assume the last weather report received (no matter how old) is what they will experience on this landing. In addition some will assume the wind sock is a 100% accurate represenation of winds throughout the airport. As winds change these assumptions may result in using incorrect control inputs for the approach and landing.

Encourage the pilot to be a "detective" and get all available information about the winds from a variety of sources including the communications of other pilots and what the pilot is currently experiencing in the plane.

Ask "What direction is the wind coming from and how will you position the controls for these winds?"

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Landing Clearance/Announcement - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Downwind:
Power - Set for pattern
Airspeed - Set for pattern
Trim - Set
Altitude - As appropriate
Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain a ground track parallel to the runway by selecting prominent landmark in the distance and adjusting wind correction angle (crab) into the wind to stop any drift away from or towards the runway.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Call the pilots attention to the drift with the wind. Guide them through correcting and then maintaining ground track using distant references. Winds aloft often do not align with the winds reported on the ground. 

If needed return to ground reference maneuvers and flying a rectangular course in strong winds to develop the skills required to maintain a straight ground track in winds. 

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Abeam landing spot: 
Power - Reduce
Flaps - One notch 
Airspeed - Slow for Approach
Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Maintain a ground track parallel to the runway by selecting prominent landmark in the distance and adjusting wind correction angle (crab) into the wind to stop any drift away from or towards the runway. Should lose about 300’ altitude to key position.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Point out the plane's tendency to turn right when the nose is allowed to pitch down with the reduction of power. 

Emphasize using that distant landmark as a gauge for wind correction to maintain a straight ground track.

If needed return to ground reference maneuvers and flying a rectangular course in strong winds to develop the skills required to maintain a straight ground track in winds. 

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Key Position (about 45° from landing spot):
Turn base - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Plan on adjusting the timing of the key position if there are strong winds. Stronger winds may require doing the base turn sooner in order to have a stabilized descent on final. 

Plan on rolling out of the turn pointed slightly towards the runway (> 90 degree turn) to set up proper crab for wind drift correction on base.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Remind the pilot a tailwind on downwind, which is the typical case, may require adjustment in timing of the downwind to base turn. The same winds will also require the pilot to crab into the wind on base. The pilot should anticipate this and turn more than 90 degrees when turning from base to final.

If needed return to ground reference maneuvers and flying a rectangular course in strong winds to develop the skills required to maintain a straight ground track in winds. 

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Base: Power and Airspeed - Set for Approach, 
Flaps - Second notch (as appropriate)
Trim - Set
Double Check Flow - Complete
Turn to Final - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
The airplane should at about 300 feet on the base leg, make turn to Final in order to line up with runway

Using a distant landmark perpendicular to the runway, adjust crab to maintain a straight ground track perpendicular to the runway. 

Note wind direction on base leg. These winds will often not be from the same direction as reported on the ground or shown by the wind sock. A tailwind will require an earlier than normal turn to final to rollout aligned with the extended runway centerline. A headwind will require slightly later than normal turn or shallower bank angle will be required.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize using that distant landmark as a gauge for wind correction to maintain a straight ground track.

Overshooting and undershooting the turn from base to final is more common in crosswind conditions if the pilot does not adjust his/her turns for the faster than normal ground speed with a tailwind or slower than normal groundspeed with a headwind. Emphasize noting any tailwind or headwind and adjusting accordingly. Have the pilot constantly evaluate the potential ground track of the turn and adjust if needed to ensure rollout on final. 

If needed return to ground reference maneuvers and flying a rectangular course in strong winds to develop the skills required to maintain a straight ground track in winds. 

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Final: Power - Set (adjust as necessary), 
Airspeed - 1.3Vso or manufacturer recommendation (apply gust factor as necessary)
Trim - Set
Double-check flow - Complete 
Wing-low method - Maintain runway alignment
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Verify pre-landing checklist is complete.

If gusts are reported add 1/2 of the difference between the steady state and wind gust speeds to approach speed.

Align the plane with the extended runway centerline. Put upwind wing down with aileron pressure into the wind to stop side drift. Use opposite rudder to align the longitudinal axis of the plane with the runway centerline. Example: If the winds are coming from the left (the plane is drifing right) put ailerons to the left to stop drift and use right rudder to align the nose of the plane with the runway centerline. 

Make constant adjustments to maintain the extended runway centerline. Remember wind strength and direction are very likely to change, thus control inputs will have to change as well. Keep the aiming point (about 200’ in front of landing spot) from moving up or down in windshield.

The sideslip will increase descent rate on final. Additional power may be required to remain on glideslope if a significant sideslip is needed.

If unable to establish a stabilized approach and maintain alignment with the runway centerline using maximum control inputs, GO AROUND.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Emphasize using the runway centerline for alignment with the runway and flying a straight ground track. 

Use the visual aids identified on the ground to align the nose of the plane with the centerline. For instance, many C172s have a row of rivets on the cowling that aligns almost perfectly with the runway centerline from the air. 

Have the pilot use the rudder to swing the nose left and right while using aileron to stop the wind drift. This will help them see the response of the plane to the rudder inputs. After this they will find it easier to align the nose of the plane with the runway centerline. 

Go to a practice area with a long, straight, road/fence/canal/train tracks, etc. in an unpopulated area with a good crosswind across it. Practice using a sideslip to fly over the this straight path at 500-800 AGL. 

Pilots are very aware of the dangers of flying in an uncoordinated manner and this can make them uncomfortable with a sideslip. Assure them if they exercise proper airspeed control they will not be in danger of stall/spin. 

Help the pilot detect wind drift after they have established their sideslip or crab. Emphasize the winds are likely to change all the way down to the runway and over the runway. Constant adjustment of control inputs will be needed. 

If several go arounds are needed due to winds too strong for control inputs or too strong for pilot's skill the pilot needs to switch to a different runway or proceed to an alternate airport with runways better aligned with surface winds. 

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Use a crab to maintain extended runway centerline for a portion of final and then switch to the wing low sideslip to maintain directional control. 

Options include maintaining a crab into the wind on final until 200' AGL, maintaining a crab until shortly before roundout/flare and maintaining a crab until just before touchdown. In all cases touchdown with the runway must be in a sideslip, wing low condition.

checklistItems.name:
Roundout and Flare - Perform
Aileron/Rudder crosswind corrections - Adjust as necessary
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Start Flare about 10-20’ AGL, Hold the airplane just off of runway, as you feel it sink, increase back pressure on elevator to keep it just above the runway.

Maintain position over the runway centerline during and after the flare/roundout by increasing aileron pressure into the wind and opposite rudder as needed. 

Constant control adjustments will be necessary.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The following exercise will help develop runway directional control skills in crosswinds without the stress of landing:

Go to an airport with a long runway (6,000 ft or more is ideal) and fly a low approach over the runway. Empasize the use of aileron to stay over the centerline and rudder to keep the plane aligned with the direction of travel for the entire length of the runway. Repeat several times at varying heights over the runway, starting 50 feet over the runway and reduce altitude each time until approximately 2 feet over the runway. 

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Touchdown - Upwind main gear wheel first
Aileron - Smoothly increase pressure into wind
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Maintain position over the runway centerline and alignment of the plane with the direction of travel by increasing aileron pressure into the wind and opposite rudder as needed.

A proper crosswind touchdown will have the upwind main wheel touch first with the longitudinal axis of the plane aligned with the direction of the travel; aligned and over the runway centerline.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Pilots may resist using required aileron inputs close to the runway thinking they may touch the wing tip to the runway. 

Reassure the pilot most GA trainers are designed to make it impossible for the wingtip to touch the runway when operating at or below the maximum demonstrated crosswind component. 

Emphasize additional control inputs are needed to maintain directional control as the plane slows.

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name:
Landing Roll - Lower nose wheel gently, 
Ailerons - Full into wind, 
Rudder - Maintain directional control
checklistItems.notesToPilot: On the landing roll, put full ailerons into the wind and use rudder to maintain directional control on the centerline.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the plane is allowed to weathervane into the wind immediately before touchdown, the plane will roll out in the direction it is pointed at touchdown and proceed towards the edge of the ruwnay. 

The CFI needs to empasize the importance of touching down with no side loading and with the plane aligned with the direction of travel. This requires increased control inputs on touchdown. 

Relate the landing rollout with the take off roll. The crosswind take off roll starts with full ailerons into the wind. The crosswind landing roll ends with full ailerons into the winds.

Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

checklistItems.name: Braking - Minimum required
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: Refer to Normal Approach and Landing for errors and resolutions not related to crosswind operations.

commonErrors.name: Failure to go around
commonErrors.details: Failing to initiate a go around when unable to stabilize approach or establish runway centerline using full control input.

commonErrors.name: Poor control use
commonErrors.details: Using insufficient rudder and aileron in a sideslip to stop the wind drift. Freezing control inputs and not adjusting for changing winds.

commonErrors.name: Under or overshoot on final
commonErrors.details: Turning too early or late with too much or little bank, resulting in poor alignment on final.

commonErrors.name: Landing with crab or drift
commonErrors.details: Improper or no use of aileron and/or rudder inputs over the runway, allowing the plane to drift sideways or crab into the wind.

commonErrors.name: Poor directional control on runway
commonErrors.details: Lack of directional control on the runway with the plane going left or right of the runway centerline after touchdown.

activities.name: [05] X/C: Emergency Equipment and Survival Gear (IX.D)
activities.what: a procedure to familiarize and prepare for dealing with a forced landing or emergency in the conditions appropriate to operations
activities.why: to be prepared for the appropriate conditions that may be faced during emergency aircraft operations
activities.groundPrep:
Discuss common survival scenarios
Explore various off-airport landing outcomes and how to address each one
Show various commercial survival kits and discuss the merits of their contents. 
Examples: drinking water for over wilderness areas, flotation device over water, clothing for cold weather or terrain, etc.

checklistItems.name: Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check before flying to ensure the ELT has been inspected within the previous 12 calendar months. Both before takeoff and after landing you can tune the radio to 121.5 to verify the ELT hasn't accidentially activated. If you hear what sounds like a loud siren, verify that your ELT is off. You can also test your ELT in the first five minutes of every hour by manually turning it on.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fire extinguisher - Locate and check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If your aircraft has a fire extingusher make sure you are familiar with its location, how to operate it, and how to make sure it is properly secured. Also check that it is fully charged as part of your preflight inspection.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Appropriate equipment and personal gear - Identify and explain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Safety gear can be as minimal as a candy bar, a bottle of water, and a small first aid kit for local flights to as complext as a raft, life jackets, and an exposure suit for long overwater distances. What you carry will depend on your route, the time of year, and how populated--or not--the location is. As a minimum, make sure you have a basic first aid kit, you are wearing clothes appropriate to the season. Overwater flights, remote flights, and winter flying all have unique survival equipment challenges. All passengers should have life jackets for overwater flying, and a raft should be considered if flying beyond sight of shore. For winter flying, make sure to have a heavy jacket for all occupants, gloves, hats, and more. A good rule of thumb is to have enough clothing, food, and water to spend a night outside with the airplane in the event of a forced landing.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Passenger briefing - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The location and operation of the emergency equipment should be part of your preflight passenger briefing. Explain what duties the passenger should have in the event you are able to help, and if you're not able to help. Consider using the FAA's Passenger SAFETY Briefing (see Prep section).
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to check for a current inspection; not knowing how to test the ELT.
commonErrors.details: Guide the pilot through the aircraft logs and ensure he or she understands how to find current inspection endorsements. Make this a regular habit early. For ELT operation, quiz the pilot on what would happen in the event of an accident and discuss search and rescue operations, including what happens when an ELT is activated.

commonErrors.name: Inability to locate and operate fire extinguisher.
commonErrors.details: Spend time early in the training to take the fire extinguisher out of its bracets, and run through a mock exercise, demonstratng how to use the equipment. Discuss how to make sure it is charged.

commonErrors.name: Lack of survival gear preparation or inappropriate kit components.
commonErrors.details: Discuss with the pilot various survival scenarios and what may be required. Explore commercially available survival kits and encourage the pilot to consider making his or her own kit.

commonErrors.name: Failure to give a passenger briefing.
commonErrors.details: Make the pilot give a briefing before every flight so it becomes routine. This reinforces good habits later on.

activities.name: [01] PRE-SOLO: Emergency Approach and Landing (Simulated)
activities.what: A flight maneuver and procedure that provides practice for the successful resolution of a major aircraft malfunction
activities.why: To give practice in procedures and skills needed in dealing with a forced landing situation
activities.groundPrep:
Immediate action items and emergency procedures.
Airspeed, to include: importance of best glide speed and its relationship to distance, difference between best glide speed and minimum sink speed, effects of wind on glide distance
Effects of atmospheric conditions on emergency approach and landing.
How to configure the airplane in accordance with the POH/AFM and existing conditions.
A stabilized approach, to include energy management concepts.
ELTs and other emergency locating devices.
ATC services to aircraft in distress.
Selecting a suitable landing area considering altitude, wind, terrain, obstructions, and available glide distance.
How to plan and follow a flightpath to the selected landing area considering altitude, wind, terrain, and obstructions.
How to complete the appropriate checklist.

checklistItems.name: Operate aircraft in accordance with the aircraft's Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) or Airplane Flight Manual (AFM)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This information is meant as a supplement to the procedure found in the POH/AFM
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.notesToPilot: Mneumonic = ABCDE (Airspeed, Best landing spot, Checklist, Declare emergency, Emergency landing)
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Airspeed - Trim for best glide
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Maintain control of aircraft; pitch for best glide and once established, trim away control pressures (A = Airspeed)

Establish and maintain the recommended best glide airspeed, ±10 knots.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
It is possible to figure out quick trim references for best glide in many aircraft. For example, in a Cessna 172S, trimming all the way nose up, then 4-5 full trim motions down will result in the airplane being trimmed very closely to Vg. You might consider experimenting in your aircraft to see if there is a similar reference you could safely use.

Another trick is make the wing chord parallel with the horizon and trim for that pitch attitude will get you very close to best glide speed. Then trim to fine tune Vg.

checklistItems.name: Best landing spot - Select
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Scan terrain, traffic, and wind around the airplane and select best field within gliding distance (approx. 2 NM:1000’); look all around (B = Best landing spot)

Turn toward intended landing area; plan to approximate a landing pattern that looks much like what is done on every landing. Work to arrive abeam the touchdown point at a 1,000 feet above the ground. Dissipate excess altitude by circling over the while observing landing area for obstructions.

Select a suitable landing area considering altitude, wind, terrain, obstructions, and available glide distance.

Plan and follow a flightpath to the selected landing area considering altitude, wind, terrain, and obstructions.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Checklist - Perform restart checklist
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Complete emergency flow (Fuel selector - Both; Mixture - Full Rich; Carb heat - On; Ignition -Both; Aux Fuel Pump - On/Primer - In & locked); back up with checklist (C = Checklist)

Configure the airplane in accordance with the POH/AFM and existing conditions.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Declare emergency - Radio
Squawk - 7700
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If time, use radio to declare emergency (“Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, Cessna N_____ is going down [location], [#] souls aboard, aircraft is [color]”) on ATC or 121.5, Transponder 7700 (D = Declare). If already on a monitored ATC frequency, make the declaration on that frequency.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Emergency Landing - Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Set up landing approach to selected field; maneuver to be at 180° position on downwind at normal traffic pattern altitude (1000’ AGL) and then execute a normal power-off approach; if not possible adjust as necessary to intercept normal pattern.  (E = Emergency landing.)

Prepare for landing as specified by the evaluator or your instructor.

[Simulated emergency]: go around as specified by instructor; no lower than 500’ AGL unless over airfield

[Actual emergency]: Touchdown main wheels first, gently lower nose; apply brakes as required (heavily)
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: FIELD checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
If landing off-field, prepare the airplane for landing. Follow emergency landing without power checklist. 

Fuel- Off
Ignition- Off
Electronics- Off (After setting flaps if electric)
Lapstraps- Tight (Advise passenger to secure seatbelt and shoulder harness)
Doors- Open
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Land or Go-around - as appropriate
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
[Simulated emergency]: go around as specified by instructor; no lower than 500’ AGL unless over airfield

[Actual emergency]: Touchdown main wheels first, gently lower nose; apply brakes as required (heavily)
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Premature flap extension.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Without descending to an unsafe altitude, allow approach to progress to the point of demonstrating folly of premature extensions. Emphasize slips and extending ground tracks as the initial ways of losing altitude. Flaps and gear should remain retracted until the field is made.

commonErrors.name: Attempting to stretch the glide.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Teach the pilot the effect of not maintaining best glide speed. You use a sim or safely in flight to demonstrate how the airplane does not glide as far at too low/high of an airspeed. Make they undertand the effects of drag and maintain airspeed by pitch. At altitude you can demonstrate the danger of stalling while trying to stretch a glide. Teach them to trust the best glide speed.

commonErrors.name: Difficulty establishing/maintaining best glide speed.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Help the pilot learn the pitch attitude that will result in the best glide speed. As the airplane slows from cruise, it may require several trim adjustments until best glide is established. If the pilot can consistently identify the correct pitch attitude, it will be easier for them to maintain the proper speed until the airplane settles into the desired speed.

commonErrors.name: Difficulty or indecisiveness in selecting an appropriate landing field.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Help the pilot learn how to select a field based on key characteristics: size, color, obstructions, and slope.

Size- The more a field looks like a runway, the better. Remember that you can land in a much shorter distance than you might have at your airport. If you are used to a 3000' runway, you can easily land in half that distance.

Color- Cultivated fields are the best choice. They will be of an earth color. Second choice is the light green of a short crop, then the yellow-green of a recently harvested crop. The color of the field should be uniform. Light and dark spots indicate the field is not level. Any terrain gradient visible from the air is very steep.

Obstructions- Trees and utility lines along the edge of a field greatly decrease its usable size. Wires are not visible, poles are.

commonErrors.name: Picking a field too far away.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Picking a field within a 45 degree cone under the airplane (halfway between the horizon and directly under the aiplane) will more likely lead to success. Don't forget the wind. Gliding into a strong headwind will dramatically decrease glide distance.
