activities.name: [02] BASICS: Emergency 180 Turn Back to the Runway (Simulated)
activities.what: A flight maneuver and procedure that provides practice for the successful resolution of a major aircraft malfunction
activities.why: To give practice in procedures and skills needed in dealing with a power loss after takeoff
activities.groundPrep: The altitude available is, in many ways, the controlling factor in the successful accomplishment of an emergency landing. If an actual engine failure should occur immediately after takeoff and before a safe maneuvering altitude is attained, it is usually inadvisable to attempt to turn back to the field from where the takeoff was made. Instead, it is safer to immediately establish the proper glide attitude, and select a field directly ahead or slightly to either side of the takeoff path.

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: See details here
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If your school does not already provide a pre-maneuver procedure, AOPA recommends using the CAMELS check to ensure the ACS required clearing turns are completed as well as other important items.
checklistItems.simulator: Practice by having the pilot take off from a familiar runway and then fail the engine at the altitude determined in the exercise. It is a great way to give the pilot the opporunity to practice the procedure for real. You can then fail the engine at random points in the takeoff to drill the recommended procedures for each part of the takeoff.

checklistItems.name: Vy Climb - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish the aircraft in a stabilized climb at V y.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Throttle - Idle
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Retard the throttle
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Continue climb for 5 seconds - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Do nothing for 5 seconds and hold the nose in climb attitude to simulate delay in recognizing a real engine out.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Helping the student to achieve the mindset of being on guard during critical situations like an engine failure on takeoff. Train them to brief the emergency procedures before each takeoff including determining the current wind conditions and to turn into the wind to prevent drifting farther away from the airport. You might also add a standard gilder pilot procedure of calling out the altitude on takeoff where a turn back to the runway could be made that includes reminders to pitch for best glide. For example, "800 feet, nose down, turn left."

checklistItems.name: 45 degree bank turn at Vg - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Roll the aircraft into a 45-degree banked turn and maintain best glide speed. Be vigilant for any signs of a stall and be sure to reduce angle of attack as required.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Consider allowing the pilot to experiment with shallow, medium, and steep turns to compare the altitude loss with each type of turn. It is likely that the steeper turn will result in better performance than a shallow turn.

checklistItems.name: 270 deg turn - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: A turn back to the runway requires more than just a 180 degree turn. You will need to manuver to re-align the airplane with the runway using potentially two 45 degree turns. Simulate the additional maneuvering required by continuing the turn until the heading has changed by 270 degrees.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Roll out - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Roll out of the turn.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flare - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Simulate a moderately aggressive flare for a landing.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Level off altitude - Note
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note altitude when vertical speed becomes zero.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Total descent - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Subtract this altitude from the altitude at which you retarded the throttle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Safety factor - Add
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The minimum turn-back altitude should be increased by 50 percent.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Be sure to emphasize the importance of being proficient in flying and adding a healthy safety factor before using the number they determine from this exercise.

Also discuss with the student that just getting back to the airport environment may be a better choice than landing outside the fence. Perhaps even landing on a taxiway or the grass next to the runway might be a better option than a housing development. Pilots should consider outside of the box options. Even landing long on a runway, braking hard and running off into the grass might end up being a preferable option.

checklistItems.name: Reference distance - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Do not consider turning around unless two-thirds of the final turnaround altitude has been reached when passing over the departure end of the runway.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Hurrying to start the turn before 5 seconds have lapsed.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Impress upon the pilot that their reaction would be delayed in a real engine out situation. The 5 second delay is meant to simulate that delay and to help get a better idea of how much altitude will be lost when attempting a turn back to the runway.

commonErrors.name: Not taking wind into account.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
While it would benefit the pilot to practice this procedure in both directions, they should brief the wind direction and choose the appropriate upwind turn direction. Briefing the wind direction and which way to turn should become a standard part of the takeoff briefing.

commonErrors.name: Difficulty maintaining airspeed during turn.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Demonstrate the procedure and have them focus on the outside pitch references while you fly. Then have them fly the turn using the pitch references you demonstrated. They can quickly reference the airspeed indicator to monitor their performance, but should only make pitch corrections while looking outside.

commonErrors.name: Under- or over-banking during the turn.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Have the pilot use an integrated scan of outside references and quick check of the attitude indicator for the desired bank angle. Have the pilot practice gliding turns at several bank angles (shallow, medium, and steep) to help them develop the scan and desired bank angle control.

checklistItems.name: Operate aircraft in accordance with the aircraft's Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) or Airplane Flight Manual (AFM)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This information is meant as a supplement to the procedures found in the POH/AFM
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Mindset
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Anticipate: What could go wrong? - Actively monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: It’s a good idea to maintain an active mental “lookout” for potential problems before and during flight. But also recognize that different phases of flight call for different degrees of anticipation. For example, think about the takeoff and initial climb to cruise. Have you actively considered the possibility of an engine failure on takeoff and thought about the required response? In this case, you must recognize the problem immediately and be spring-loaded to take action. On the other hand, an engine failure over open countryside, at altitude, affords considerably more time to troubleshoot and decide on the best options for a successful outcome.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Recognize: Has something gone wrong? - Investigate
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Avoid problems in flight by paying attention! The sooner you recognize a problem and start thinking about how to handle it, the better.

Some problems are obvious. A broken crankshaft will make itself known immediately. But smaller, more insidious problems can be difficult to detect if you’re not paying close attention. For example, deviations from the weather forecast can be quite subtle, and trouble with the aircraft—such as a failing electrical system—can easily be overlooked.

The key is to stay alert and look for things that don’t seem normal, or don’t fit with expectations. Pay attention to anything that gives you “cause to pause.” These are signals that the situation is changing—possibly for the worse—and that you may need to take action.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Act: Evaluate your options - Choose and Evaluate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Here’s where many pilots fail. They recognize the problem, but don’t do anything to confront it. Why? It’s inconvenient. It means a major change in plans, and it may mean making a difficult or unpleasant choice. Regardless, once you’ve recognized a problem there is a choice to be made. That choice depends upon a number of factors—the type and seriousness of the problem, the rate at which the situation is deteriorating, and the available alternatives. Be prepared to act without delay, should the situation warrant it.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Framework
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fly the airplane! - Maintain as first priority
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Whatever the situation, one rule always applies: Fly the airplane! Troubleshoot, talk to ATC, calm the passengers—whatever it takes…but remember that it’s all for naught if you lose control of the airplane in the process.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Initial assessment - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
First, perform a very basic initial assessment:

What’s wrong?
How critical is it?
How much time do I have?
The most dangerous situation is one that’s both serious and requires immediate action. Engine failure shortly after takeoff, fire, oxygen system failure at 25,000 feet, or vacuum failure in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC) come to mind. These situations require you to be “spring-loaded” to deal with the issue and recall the immediate action steps so you can get the situation under control.

On the other hand, it’s equally important not to act rashly if the situation doesn’t call for it. Pilots have gotten themselves into deeper trouble overreacting to a problem that isn’t particularly time-sensitive or critical—for example, taking drastic measures to extend landing gear or close a door that popped open in flig
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Troubleshoot - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
If the problem is mechanical or electrical, it may not be immediately obvious what’s wrong. Given time, attempt to determine the cause—both because it might be fixable and on the chance that you can keep it from getting worse, or causing other problems.

Also, the situation may have been precipitated by something you did, or failed to do. Into the category of self-induced emergencies fall such blunders as switching to an empty fuel tank (or forgetting to switch tanks) and grabbing the wrong power lever—mixture instead of throttle. If a problem coincides with something you did, undo it!

Whatever the situation, one rule always applies: Fly the airplane! Troubleshoot, talk to ATC, calm the passengers—whatever it takes…but remember that it’s all for naught if you lose control of the airplane in the process.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Emergency checklist (as available) - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: See the POH/AFM for manufacturer recommended emergency procedures and checklist. Look for items that should be memorized and make a point of reviewing them regularly.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Declare Emergency - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Call for help! Declare an emergency: There’s no good reason not to. You only need to switch to the emergency frequency (121.5) if you aren’t already in contact with ATC.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Powerplant - Partial or complete power loss
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Engine roughness or overheat
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Engine roughness can be caused by many different things, including water in the fuel, bad cylinders, propeller imbalance, carburetor icing, and more. Overheating could be caused by oil system problems, blocked airflow over the engine, internal engine problems, or running too lean. Fixing the problems calls for first diagnosing them. For roughness, if all the gauges are within limits, try first to clear any carburetor ice, and consider switching fuel tanks. Otherwise, make a power reduction. Sometimes this will stop the roughness, but more often will ease strain on the aircraft. It can also make it easier to troubleshoot the problem. For issues with engine overheating, check oil pressure and temperature first. If oil pressure is low and temperature is high, a power loss could be imminent, so an emergency landing may be required. Slightly elevated temperatures are usually caused by running too lean or having the nose too high on climb. Enrichen the mixture, or if climbing, lower the nose. If neither of these fixes the issue, reduce power to see if that may help. If nothing changes it could be a sensor problem. Check if temperatures are within limits. If so, you may continue. If not, a precautionary landing is a good idea. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Carburetor or induction icing
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Carb or induction icing can occur on a day that is up to 90 degrees. It is more common on humid days with more moderate temperatures. Carb ice almost always shows itself with a slight roughness and/or an rpm drop. Fix the problem by applying full carb heat and waiting for the rpm to increase. Usually you'll experience an rpm decrease when applying carb heat and then an increase once the ice clears. Consider operating the remainder of the flight with partial carb heat to avoid more ice build up. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Loss of oil pressure
checklistItems.notesToPilot: A loss of oil pressure could be a sensor problem or something more serious. Regardless, a power reduction and precautionary landing is imperative. Keep in mind the engine could stop at any moment. If you feel any other engine symptoms, such as roughness, land immediately. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel starvation
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Fuel starvation occurs when the fuel supply is somehow interrupted. The first and most immediate response is to change fuel tanks. If there's an auxiliary fuel pump, turn it on. If neither of these fixes the problem, execute an emergency landing. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Airplane system and equipment malfunctions
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Electrical malfunction
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Electrical problems can be intermittent or permanent, and can impact one item, a set of items, or everything electrical on the airplane. The type of failure often indicates the cause of the problem. Intermittent problems can be caused by a poor connection, a screen problem, or other physical problem. Usually the remedy will call for deactivating the system and continuing the flight. More permanent problems can be due to battery, alternator, voltage regulator, bus problems, and more. If a set of electrical equipment fails that means a specific electrical bus has failed, whereas full failure will usually be caused by the battery, alternator, or other equipment. Refer to the voltmeter or ammeter to determine the load. If it shows a battery drain, shed as much electrical load as possible and prepare for a landing without electrical aids such as flaps, lights, and the radios. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Many instructors discretely pull circuit breakers to simulate electrical failures. If possible, turning off the alternator can cause an electrical problem as well.

checklistItems.name: Vacuum/pressure and associated flight instrument malfunctions
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Vacuum failure is a relatively common experience, and not an emergency in visual conditions. In most airplanes the vacuum system drives the attitude indicator and heading indicator. A failure will result in both instruments indicating incorrectly. The danger comes in relying on the instruments as the gyros slowly spin down. Because of their high rate of speed, gyros take a few minutes to fully stop, and in the meantime the instrument indications will slowly go from correct to obviously wrong. In the meantime it is easy to be lulled into believing their indications. Verify attitude with outside visual references and heading with landmarks and the compass. It's a good idea to keep instrument covers in your flight bag to cover up nonfunctioning instruments. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Pitot/static system malfunction
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Pitot/static failures have predictable behaviors. Refer to the ground lesson on system and equipment malfunctions for more information. In flight you have a few options. By practicing takeoffs and landings without reference to airspeed you can be prepared for any potential problems. An on board GPS or tablet giving groundspeed can also be helpful to aid in determining airspeed. Static failures will result in a nonfunctioning altimeter and vertical speed indicator. Ignore and cover both if they have failed. Altitude can be estimated from an on board GPS or tablet, or easily deduced in an area where you have flown often. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Electronic flight deck display malfunction
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Every EFD failure is unique and requires detailed knowledge of that unit's failure modes, which can be found in the aircraft handbook. Common problems include full screen failure, radio failure, and instrument failure. If a full screen failure occurs, treat it as the manufacturer recommends and transition to back up instruments. If it's a radio failure or a GPS failure, treat it as a typical radio failure scenario. If operating from a non-towered airport this means entering the traffic flow as prescribed in the AIM and landing in the normal traffic flow. The AIM also details no-radio procedures at controlled airports, which vary depending on the type of airspace.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If you are able to isolate certain circuit breakers on full-cockpit glass panels, these can be pulled to approximate various component failures.

checklistItems.name: Landing gear or flap malfunction
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Practice emergency landing gear extensions and no-flap or partial flap landings in order to be prepared for a possible failure. With a landing gear failure, climb to a safe altitude and troubleshoot the problem per the aircraft handbook. If the aircraft doesn't respond, deploy the gear via the emergency extension at a safe altitude and land as normal. With a gear retraction failure, climb to a safe altitude to diagnose the problem and then proceed as above. Flap malfunctions are only an emergency condition with asymmetric deployment. In this case, retract the flaps as quickly as possible. With no flap extension or only partial extension land as normal, expecting a longer landing. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Inoperative trim
checklistItems.notesToPilot: It's fine to continue a flight with inoperative trim if all the flight controls are otherwise operating normally. Simply expect harder control forces when making configuration and power changes. Runaway trim is an immediate emergency situation and must be addressed quickly. Memorize the applicable checklist in order to respond quickly. Typically this involves deactivating the autopilot, and pulling the trim circuit breaker. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Smoke/fire/engine compartment fire
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Reacting to fire or smoke in the cockpit depends on the source of the smoke or fire. The problem could be in the cockpit and caused by an electrical problem or in the engine compartment. Electrical fires have a distinct smell from oil or gasoline fires, and must be dealt with differently. Memorize the applicable checklists from the aircraft handbooks and execute them immediately. The presence of any smoke usually calls for an emergency descent, and depending on the severity, either a short flight to a nearby airport or a precautionary off-airport landing. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Any other system specific to the airplane (e.g., supplemental oxygen, deicing)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Deicing failures call for an immediate exit from icing conditions, which you hopefully won't be experiencing as a VFR-only pilot. Oxygen failures call for an emergency descent. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Inadvertent door or window opening
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Repeat after us: AN OPEN WINDOW OR DOOR IS NOT AN EMERGENCY. Although an open door or window can result in a distracting amount of wind and noise, these are benign problems that should be handled carefully and when the time is right. In many airplanes the window can be closed once a safe altitude has been reached. On the other hand most doors will not close with the pressure of the outside slip stream. In this case you must land and close the door. Fly the airplane as normal. Refer to the aircraft handbook for specific procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: At least once in training, pop open the instructor-side door right after the main wheels leave the ground to simulate an open door scenario.

activities.name: [04] PRE-SOLO: Emergency Descent
activities.what: A flight maneuver for descending as rapidly as possible to a lower altitude or to the ground for an emergency landing
activities.why: To safely recover from an uncontrollable fire, a sudden loss of cabin pressurization, or any other appropriate situation
activities.groundPrep: An emergency descent is a maneuver for descending as rapidly as possible to a lower altitude or to the ground for an emergency landing. [Figure 17-6] The need for this maneuver may result from an uncontrollable fire, a sudden loss of cabin pressurization, or any other situation demanding an immediate and rapid descent

checklistItems.name: Pre-Maneuver (CAMELS) Check - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Complete the pre-maneuver checklist. When performing clearning turns for this maneuver, also make sure to clear the area below.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Carb heat - ON (if applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Add full carb heat on, if applicable, prior to pulling back the throttle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Throttle - Idle
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The airplane descends the quickest when the throttle is fully to idle. Initiate the maneuver by fully closing the throttle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Bank - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Establish a 30 to 45 degree bank to maintain positive Gs on the airplane and to help clear traffic while looking for landing spot.
checklistItems.teachingTips: The manuever is easiest to perform when done as one smooth motion. Instead of thinking through throttle to idle, bank, and descent and discrete actions, teach the pilot to pull the throttle fully while rolling into a bank and letting the nose come down. This is the fastest way to begin the descent, and after a few tries usually leads to the best performance.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: The manuever is easiest to perform when done as one smooth motion. Instead of thinking through throttle to idle, bank, and descent and discrete actions, teach the pilot to pull the throttle fully while rolling into a bank and letting the nose come down. This is the fastest way to begin the descent, and after a few tries usually leads to the best performance.

checklistItems.name: Descent airspeed - Establish
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Airspeed should be a value where you can establish a rapid descent, but DO NOT EXCEED Vfe, Vle, or Vno as appropriate. If turbulent stay below Va.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Recover/Land (as applicable)

checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Descending straight ahead or establishing partial bank.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Demonstrate straight ahead descents and partially banked descents to reinforce the positive control that occurs during an emergency descent at 30 to 45 degrees. This will also demonstrate the greater descent rate that occurs with the additional drag of the bank.

commonErrors.name: Poor speed control.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: The pilot should think of Vfe, Vle, or Vno as hard limits that can't be broken. Once the throttle is fully closed, pitch becomes the primary speed control. After a few practice sessions, have the pilot set the same pitch as the starting point and make small adjustments from there to maintain speed control.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to apply carb heat.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Teach deliberate throttle changes. It's haphazard to change one parameter partially, then another. Instead, have the pilot focus on making a complete configuration change before moving on. In the case of the emergency descent, demonstrate the difference between a cruise power emergency descent and an idle emergency descent to reinforce the need to close the throttle.

prepItems.name: Nontowered Airport Communications
prepItems.details: This segment covers procedures for operating into and out of a non-tower airport. This type of airport will be found in Class G or Class E airspace.

prepItems.name: Operations at Towered Airports
prepItems.details: There are two kinds of airports—those with operating control towers and those without. When a part-time tower is closed, the airport is considered nontowered. Every year, there are more than 40 million arrivals and departures at FAA ATC towered airports. Nearly half of these are general aviation operations.

prepItems.name: Aviation Communications
prepItems.details: English is the international language of aviation, but the words and phrases used can be confusing to beginners. You are learning a new language. Be patient – it takes practice.

prepItems.name: Closer Look: Tower Controlled Field
prepItems.details: When ready to taxi to the takeoff runway at a tower controlled field, call ground control with your request. Remember the four Ws when making the call.

prepItems.name: Say Intentions...When you need ATC's help
prepItems.details: There are several reasons that pilots do not call air traffic control (ATC) for help: They feel in control of an out-of-control situation, fear of embarrassment or enforcement action, or simply a lack of knowledge. But avoiding that radio call can turn a small problem into a big one, or turn a big one into a disaster.

activities.name: [01] PRE-SOLO: After Landing, Parking and Securing
activities.what: The process of inspecting and determining the airplane’s readiness for flight/storage at the completion of a flight
activities.why: To increase safety and efficiency by noting damage as early as possible and having it repaired
activities.groundPrep:
In most phases of flight the only people who know if a pilot did a checklist are the pilot and anyone in the aircraft. This is not the case with afterlanding and securing checklists. Most renter pilots have flown a plane after someone that obviously didn't complete their after landing/securing checks. The plane had the lights left on, carb heat on, trimmed full nose up, etc. Describe what that makes the next pilot think about the pilot that left the airplane in that condition. Typically the next pilot is very much not impressed by the person that did that.
The after landing checklist can be considered the first step of the pre-take off checklist. This is the pilot's first opportunity to ensure the aircraft is configured for take off or parking. Pilots in training spend a lot of time in the pattern performing take offs right after landing. If they are in haste after landing or haste before take off, they are likely to miss a critical configuration step. Using the after landing checklist properly every time will reduce the likelihood of disaster on their next take off.
The shut down checklist provides the best order to shut down the avionics and engine to prevent damage to avoinics, potential engine damage and/or harm to people working around a propeller driven aircraft.
The securing checklist outlines the steps needed to best secure the aircraft to handle any weather conditions (winds, etc.) and inspect the aircraft for potential  issues to be fixed sooner than later.
Can explain allLanding, Parking & Securingprocedures and why they are performed.
Can explain Landing, Parking & Securing procedures as applicable to solo flight and why they are performed.
Introductory training on Landing, Parking & Securing procedures and why they are performed.

checklistItems.name: After Landing (Clear of runway and stopped)
Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be sure to clear any runway hold markings and come to a complete stop before addressing the checklist. Follow recommended procedures found in the AFM/POH. Some items to consider are listed below.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel selector - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Switch tanks or turn off fuel pumps as recommended by the manufacturer.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If flying a low wing plane and planning another take off this is the perfect time to switch tanks.

checklistItems.name: Cowl flaps - Set (as applicable)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Open or closed as appropriate to weather conditions.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Use the phrase "FLAPS/FLAPS" in the after landing flow. First flaps are for cowl flaps, the second flaps are the wing flaps.

checklistItems.name: Flaps - Retract
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Follow the manufacturer recommended procedures. Consider avoiding distraction during the rollout or potential confusion with the gear handle, by waiting until the airplane is stopped and clear of the runway to retract flaps.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Tell the pilot taxiing with the flaps down is like having a "KICK ME" sign taped to their back. A flaps down taxi announces to the world that the pilot didn't do their after landing checklists - other pilots WILL notice.

checklistItems.name: Power/Mixture - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: To avoid fouling the spark plugs during taxi many manufacturers recommend a minimum power setting (e.g., 1000 RPM) and to lean the mixture.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Discuss the impact of taxiing with the mixture too rich - this can cause spark plug fouling and a rough running engine. Also emphasize the pilot needs to ensure the mixture is set for best power prior to take off. The appropriate mixture for taxi is not the appropriate mixture for take off.

checklistItems.name: Carb Heat - Set (as appropriate)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Set carb heat to pre-take off position or as recommended by manufacturer.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Trim - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Reset for takeoff or neutral as recommened by manufacturer.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Lights - As required
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Switch off any lights that are not needed for current operation.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Avionics - Adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adjust radios for ground operations by switching to appropriate frequencies and setting transponder as required.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
It is good practice to have the ground frequency set up in the standby position on the radio as part of the descent checklist. 

Once the plane is fully clear the runway, switch to ground frequency (if instructed). Proceed with the complete after landing checklist and then contact ground for taxi clearance. Switching to ground frequency first - but not talking - lets ground communicate with the plane if needed. Do not ask for a taxi clearance until the after landing checklists are complete.

checklistItems.name: Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Follow manufacturer recommended procedures in AFM/POH. Some additional items to consider are listed below. These suggestions should be considered for propeller driven piston aircraft.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Throttle - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: For piston airplanes, the throttle will be set to 1000 RPM, but be sure to review the manufacturer recommendations for power during the shutdown sequence.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Magneto - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Consider checking the magnetos for broken ground wires by momentarily turning the ignition to OFF and then right back to ON while at idle power. If the engine does not stop running, the ground wires may be broken and will need to be addressed by a mechanic right away.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot understands the operations of the ignition system and combustion process. Remind them the battery / alternator is not needed to create a spark that could cause the engine to start if fuel is in the cylinder when the propeller is moved.

checklistItems.name: Avionics - Off
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Turn off avionics before shutting down the engine in order to prevent power spikes that may damage delicate electronic equipment.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Mixture - Lean
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Lean the mixture until the engine stops running completely.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Setting the mixture to full lean starves the engine of fuel. This shuts down the engine and it reduces the likelihood of accidental engine start in case a magneto is not grounded and the propeller is moved.

checklistItems.name: Magneto - Off
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Turn off magnetos only after the engine stops running completely. Take key out of ignition and place in visible location.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Taking the key out and putting it into a visible location lets people who may be around the aircraft know it is safe to approach the aircraft. This also ensures the magnetos are actually OFF.

checklistItems.name: Master - Off
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Turn off the master to prevent battery drain.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Some FBOs and flying clubs will charge a pilot $50 or more for recharging a battery. Teach leaving the beacon ON when shutting down the engine. If the master is left on after the engine shut down the pilot will usually notice the beacon is still flashing as they walk away from the plane.

checklistItems.name: Location - Select considering other aircraft and wind
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Preferably find a location that keeps the airplane clear of propeller or jet blast from other aircraft. If possible, secure the airplane in a direction that will face the current or forecast winds.
checklistItems.teachingTips: While it may be more convenient to taxi directly into a parking spot doing so can blast other planes with debris kicked up by prop wash. If there are planes or vehicles behind the parking spot. Shut down near the parking spot and then push or pull the plane into it's parking location once the engine is secured.

checklistItems.name: Nose(tail)wheel - Straighten
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Allow the airplane to roll straight forward so that the nose(tail)wheel is aligned with the longitudinal axis to minimum stress on the gear.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Aircraft - Secure
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Install both control locks and security measures to protect the controls and prevent theft.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Parking brakes - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use as recommended for parking.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If parking at an FBO do not set the parking break as the FBO may need to move your aircraft.

checklistItems.name: Wheel Chocks - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If available use wheel chocks to keep the aircraft from rolling freely.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Postflight Inspection - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Inspect the airplane for any damage or leaks that may have occurred during the flight. Streaks of oil or fuel under the cowling or wings may be clues that should be checked by maintenance personnel. Examine the gear for hydraulic leaks and brake/tire condition. Notify maintenance if any issues are identified.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Oil - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check the oil level for excessive consumption.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Allow several minutes before checking. This will let the oil drain out of the engine and back into the sump. The engine and oil cap will be very hot when the engine is shut down. Use a rag or glove to avoid being burned.

checklistItems.name: Fuel - Considered
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Taking into account the next flight operation, consider refueling the plane to prevent condensation in the tanks if it will be inactive for a while.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Tie down/Hangared - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Be sure to properly secure the airplane with tie down ropes or chains. Remember that unlike ropes, chains don't have any give so leave a little slack to allow the airplane to move slightly in the wind in order to help prevent structural damage to the airplane. If available, use any covers, sunscreens, and locks to keep the airplane secure and protected from the elements.

If hangaring, be sure to leave a little room around the airplane to prevent inadvertant damage from other aircraft or operations in the hangar.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Shutdown / Securing Checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Before leaving the aircraft take one more look at the shut down/securing checklist and verify each step was completed successfully.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Remind the pilot they don't want to leave their tablet, GPS devices, head set, phone, etc. in an aircraft. These items are often left in or on planes!

activities.name: [08] PRE-SOLO: Lost Communications and Light Gun Signals
activities.what: The procedure of communicating with ATC without an operating cockpit radio
activities.why: To efficiently communicate with ATC and enhance safety through clear exchange of information and clearances when radio communications are not possible
activities.groundPrep:
It is possible that a pilot might experience a malfunction of the radio. This might cause the transmitter, receiver, or both to become inoperative. If a receiver becomes inoperative and a pilot needs to land at a towered airport, it is advisable to remain outside or above Class D airspace until the direction and flow of traffic is determined. A pilot should then advise the tower of the aircraft type, position, altitude, and intention to land. The pilot should continue, enter the pattern, report a position as appropriate, and watch for light signals from the tower. Light signal colors and their meanings are contained in Figure 14-42.
Discuss the difference between non-standard, urgent, and emergency situations.
Discuss various loss of communication scenarios and how the pilot might react.

checklistItems.name: Appropriate use of transponders
checklistItems.notesToPilot: FARs require that if an aircraft is equipped with a functioning transponder that the transponder must be on. Transponders have different modes, including A (basic position), C (altitude reporting), S (enhanced surveillance information). Historically transponders were turned to standby mode on the ground and then either to On or Alt for mode A or C functions. Newer solid-state transponders can go straight to On or Alt. Only occasionally should the transponder be turned to Standby in flight. These situations may include formation flying, traffic-intensive events, or by request from ATC in the event of transponder malfunctions. If flying VFR, the transponder should be set to 1200. A discrete code is entered when ATC radar contact is requested and established.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Radio volume, frequency, and proper selection - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Most radio problems can be solved by checking the radio volume, frequency, and audio panel. Verify the proper frequency, check to ensure the volume is turned up, and that the audio panel is projecting the correct radio.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Headset plugs and batteries - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Headset and headset jack failures can also cause radio problems, both in transmitting and receiving. If you have a passenger ask if he or she can hear the radio. If you don't have passengers, switch your headset to another set of jacks. If that doesn't solve the problem, try the overhead speaker.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Aircraft microphone and speaker - Check/use
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The aircraft microphone and speaker are great back ups in the event of a headset or headset jack failure. Verify they are operational prior to departure.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Transponder 7600 - Squawk
checklistItems.notesToPilot: In the event of radio failure and if returning to a towered airport, squawk 7600 in the transponder. This lets radar facilities know your radio isn't functioning.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Remain clear of airspace, determine traffic pattern in use - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: First, consider returning to a less busy non-towered field. This will be easier and safer for all involved. Although you are allowed to land at most towered airports with an inoperative radio, it can cause a tense situation. At a non-towered airport it's practically a non-event. In either case, fly over the airport to determine the direction of traffic, ideally by spotting other airplanes in the traffic pattern. If the pattern is empty, check windsocks.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Enter downwind using standard 45 entry - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The air traffic controller will expect you to enter the pattern on a 45-degree midfield downwind.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: If receiver is inoperative:
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Advise tower of intentions - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If you have verified that you can make transmissions, but not receive anything from the tower, advise the tower of your intentions, including how you will enter the traffic pattern and which runway you plan to land on.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Light gun signals - Observe and comply
checklistItems.notesToPilot: In order to fly to a tower-controlled airport without a functioning radio you must know the ATC light gun signals. (Refer to the Prep section for articles that include the light gun signal chart.)
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: If transmitter is inoperative:
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Follow previously assigned procedures - Continue
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If the transponder is set to 7600 and you are overflying the airport, listen to the tower controller to give you instructions. He or she should be trying to contact you. Follow the instructions.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Rock wings or blink lights (at night) to acknowledge new ATC directions - Comply
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once you know the tower can see you, rock your wings or blink your landing light to acknowledge that you heard the instruction and will comply.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: If both receiver and transmitter are inoperative:
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Light gun signals - Observe and comply
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If you have no communication capability, following the appropriate light gun signals after entering the pattern. In most cases you will be given a steady green the first time, but be aware of other possibilities.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: No radio communication necessary, but follow standard procedures - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Aircraft without radios fly to non-towered airports all the time, so it's important to remember not to panic. Simply overfly the airport, observe the wind and direction of traffic flow, enter the traffic pattern on a 45-degree midfield downtown position, and complete a normal pattern to land.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Vigilance for traffic - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Many pilots don't expect to see aircraft without radios, so keep your eyes outside the cockpit even more than usual. It's not uncommon to see fast jet traffic making straight-in approaches, aircraft entering the traffic pattern at non-standard locations, and pilots flying unusual traffic patterns. Be aware of all these scenarios. If necessary, exit the traffic pattern and re-enter when things are less busy.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Failure to use all resources and listen for instructions; failure to follow ATC instructions.
commonErrors.details: Pilots can sometimes become overwhelmed when situations become tense or hurried. In the case of a lost comm, encourage the pilot to slow down, focus on flying the airplane, and think creatively about using all available resources. If the receiver is still working, the pilot should have no problem listening to ATC instructions and following them. ATC and others in the airspace will be depending on it. Encourage him or her to slow down and do what is necessary to make sure they remain ahead of the airplane and able to comply.

commonErrors.name: Entering the pattern in the wrong direction
commonErrors.details: Again, this can be practiced in a simulator, where you can determine the pilot's decision-making process. Encourage the pilot to keep this operation similar to a non-towered airport, entering the traffic pattern on a midfield 45-degree standard position.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to inform the tower of intentions.
commonErrors.details: The adage aviate, navigate, communicate applies here. The pilot has properly flown to the airport and figured out how to enter the pattern. Now encourage him or her to communicate those intentions to the control tower.

commonErrors.name: Failure to ID the light gun signals
commonErrors.details: Many pilots expect the light gun signals to be very bright. While they are reasonably visible, it is sometimes difficult to tell what the light is doing. Practice this by contacting the tower in advance and asking to practice with the pilot. Encourage the pilot to have a light gun signal chart in the cockpit in a place that is easy to access.

commonErrors.name: Failure to acknowledge tower instructions
commonErrors.details: It's important to keep as much communication as possible. To that end, tell the pilot to rock the wings or flash the landing light to acknowledge the instructions as much as possible.

commonErrors.name: Failure to follow standard procedures
commonErrors.details: Practice loss of comm procedures in the simulator at both towered and non-towered airports, and stress to the pilot to keep procedures as normal as possible. At a non-towered airport, proceed as normal, using standard traffic patterns. Stress that this is a common and accepted procedure for aircraft without radios, and not to panic.

commonErrors.name: Loss of situational awareness
commonErrors.details: Loss of communication in VFR conditions is not an emergency. In practice, stress the pilot to ensure he or she can maintain situational awareness throughout the session. Remind him or her of the importance of maintaining visual separation at all times, especially because many other pilots won't expect you to be there.

commonErrors.name: Failure to use the speaker and microphone as a back-up
commonErrors.details: Teach the pilot how to properly use the audio panel, including the speaker and microphone and make sure it is on the pre-flight checklist to verify their operation. Have the pilot actually use the speaker and microphone at least once during training. For example, making the call to get taxi clearance is a great way to make sure they have used the equipment.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to check headsets as the culprit to audio problems
commonErrors.details: By teaching a troubleshooting and diagnostic method to problems in the cockpit you better prepare the pilot for annoyances such as a bad headset or headset jack. Simulate an audio problem by turning down the volume or pulling a circuit breaker. Try to discreetly pull a headset cable to see if the pilot can fix the problem, and so on. Encourage the pilot to check all possible sources of the problem.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to set basic radio parameters
commonErrors.details: New pilots are often so task-saturated that they forget to perform basic radio functions, such as volume, proper frequency changes, and so on. This is an area that is best taught by letting the pilot make mistakes. If you know the volume is down or the frequency is wrong, let the pilot make a call or fumble with why he or she can't hear the ATIS or ATC. Learning occurs much faster when a pilot makes the mistake and personally fixes it than if the instructor intervenes before a radio call is made. Also, teach the pilot to complete one task correctly before moving on to the next. A good example is coming back to a towered airport after a practice session. New pilots will often quickly set a radio while grabbing a checklist and trying to navigate at the same time. Get him or her to focus on the task at hand (setting the radio and verifying the frequency is correct and can be heard) before moving on to the next step.

commonErrors.name: Inability to use transponder or understand its various modes
commonErrors.details: In terms of operation, ensure the transponder is on the checklist and the pilot follows it appropriately. If the pilot is weak on various special codes, such as 7700, 7600, and 7500 encourage him or her to write them on the checklist, or on a place that is easy to access in the cockpit.

commonErrors.name: Using the wrong traffic pattern
commonErrors.details: Explain to the pilot what happens at a towered airport when an airplane without a radio approaches, and explain the importance of safely fitting into the flow. Remind them that the traffic pattern operation will look like a non-towered airport, in that the pilot will have to overfly the airport to verify the traffic flow.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to squawk 7600 or showing the wrong code
commonErrors.details: Lost comm procedures can be practiced in the simulator, including the need to squawk 7600. Explain what happens when the pilot squawks 7600 and why it's important to do so, and verify that this step is on a lost comm checklist.

activities.name: [02] PRE-SOLO: Preflight Inspection
activities.what: The process of examining the aircraft for mechanical and operational irregularities that could affect safe and legal flight
activities.why: To ensure that the airplane meets regulatory standards and is in a mechanical condition for safe flight
activities.groundPrep:
Pilot in command responsibility - the PIC is responsible for the airworthiness of the aircraft before every flight. Renter or 
employee status does not relieve the PIC from this responsibility.
Inspect aircraft in accordance with the aircraft's Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) or Airplane Flight Manual (AFM). 
Commercially available checklists can be used if verified to cover all items listed in AFM or POH.Use of flashlight during inspection can be helpful, especially when looking in the engine cowling and is absolutely necessary when performing a preflight at night.
Address any issues with a mechanic before flight. Do not be afraid to ask questions about items found in preflight.
Avoid interruptions during preflight inspection. Have passengers/friends wait inside or complete preflight before their arrival. 
If interrupted return to either the beginning of the inspection or to a step known to be completed.
First flights occasionally present pIlots with a degree of anxiety that may interfere with the learning points of the Preflight Inspection. 
Consider NOT flying during the first instructional period but devoting full attention to the Preflight operation. You might also complete the preflight inspection before the new pilot arrives or inform the pilot not to worry about any of the details and just get the big picture of the process. Avoid too much (if any) explanation during preflight on the first flight.
Depending on the aircraft type and wing position, the procedure may be clockwise around the aircraft or counterclockwise, typically starting at the entry door.
This may be the passenger door on single entrance aircraft such as the Piper, or the pilot's door such as on the Cessna.

checklistItems.name: General appearance and condition - Note
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Carefully observe the plane's condition when approaching it. Verify the nose strut has appropriate extension, tires are properly inflated, no tools or equipment left on the plane, the plane sits properly (not listing to one side), etc. Look for puddles of fuel, oil, hydraulic fluid under the plane.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel Quantity - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify by looking into the tanks (or other visual verification - not the fuel gauges) the plane has the required fuel.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
Ensure either the pilot or the plane has a fuel sampler available.
Ensure the pilot knows the fuel available at reach "tab" level.
Have the pilot state the fuel quntity in both gallons anad duration.

checklistItems.name: Oil Quantity - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Verify the oil quantity is at or above operating minimum per POH. Add additional oil if necessary.
Secure the oil dip stick properly once verified.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Find an opportunity early in the training to show the pilot the proper method to add oil.

checklistItems.name: Cabin door ease of operation - Assess
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Door should open smoothly with minimum effort. Excessive force needed to open a door may indicate structural damage.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Interior Inspection
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Overall interior condition - Note
checklistItems.notesToPilot: It is not uncommon for the previous pilot to leave items in the aircraft.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Carpet, seat belts, and shoulder harness
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Wet carpet could be evidence of leaks. Unattached seatbelts could interfere with seat operation or rudder pedals. Frayed seat belts might be unsafe.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Seat tracks
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure seat tracks are clear of obstruction.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures:
An AD has been issued for certain Cessna Models for seat-track failure. 
Use this as an opportunity to review ADs and check the the AD has been complied with.

checklistItems.name: Fire Extinguisher - if equipped
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure fire extinguisher is charged, inspected and secured.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel Selector - SET
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Set Fuel Selector to proper tank or BOTH for high wing planes.
Move the fuel selector through all of its positions so the look and feel is familiar for each position.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Trim - SET
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Set trim to take-off position
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Alternate Static port- CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If equipped, when pulled the VSI and altimeter will "jump" briefly. Ensure alternate static is returned to off position.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Mixture - FULL
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This step prepares for start up.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Carb Heat - OFF (if equipped)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This step prepares for start up.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Beacon - ON
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
This step prepares for start up.
Alerts ramp personnel that the aircraft is ACTIVE.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Circuit Breakers - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If any circuit breakers are popped, the pilot may reset ONCE only. If the breaker pops again after the master is turned on, do not attempt to reset again.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Avionics - OFF
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Master - ON
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check fuel, oil temperature and oil pressure gauges. Turn coordinator gyro should spin up. Verify beacon is working. Verify no circuit breakers pop.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Don't be too quick to correct a mistake or omission if the consequences are not critical.

checklistItems.name: Flaps - EXTEND
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Listen to the sound of the flap motors. Flaps should extend smoothly and evenly..
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Lights - ON
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If flying at or near sunset ensure all position lights, strobes (if equipped) and landing/taxi lights are functional.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Master - OFF
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Hobbs/Tach Time - NOTE
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Write down hobbs and tach time as required.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Headset - ATTACH
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Plug in headset. Verify headset batteries (if so equipped) are sufficient for flight and spares are available.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Seat - ADJUST
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adjust the pilots seat as needed for proper visibility and smooth operation of the controls.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Exterior Inspection
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A

checklistItems.name: Windshield / Windscreen - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure clean and attached properly.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Outside of engine cowling - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Loose, worn, damaged or missing screws, fasteners, rivets, and latches. Inspect rivets for looseness: signs of black oxide film around head. Check chipped paint around rivets and fasteners - could signal a lack of security.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Propeller spinner - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Free from dents, cracks, corrosion, and in proper alignment. All screws attached and secure. Also check rear facing spinner plate. Check openings for internal ice build up.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Propeller - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check for blade erosion, nicks, cracks, pitting, corrosion, and security. Look for oil leaks on controllable pitch propellers. Check alternator/generator drive belts for appropriate tension.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Inside of cowling - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check for signs of fuel leaks, deteroration of oil/hydraulic lines, esnure oil cap/filter/cooler and drain plug are secure. Inspect for foreign objects. Visible wires and lines should be secure and in good condition.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Exhaust system - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Exhaust system should be free from white stains near the cylinder heads and no cracks on exhaust stack. Exhaust should be securely attached. Heater units should be in good condition and free from cracks or leaks.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Air filter - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Free from substantial dirt or restrictions, decomposition, and should be properly serviced.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Oil - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify quantity again. Look for large amounts of oil on the ground under the aircraft.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel Quality - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Sump the fuel from the engine sump. Look for signs of water or contamination.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If the fuel is uncontaminated it may be returned to the fuel tank. Otherwise it must be disposed of in an acceptable manner.

checklistItems.name: Shimmy damper (nosewheel airplanes) - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Free from leaks and in overall good condition; Links, collars, steering rods, and forks secure and minimal free play
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Nosewheel strut (nosewheel airplanes) - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Approximately 3" of strut showing minimum.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Nosewheel tire inflation, tread, normal wear pattern - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abnormal wear patterns, sidewall cracks, and damage like bulges, foreign objects, visible cords make the tire unairworthy.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuselage - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify there are no dents in metal sidings or tears or cuts in fabric.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Static Port - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Visually verify that the static port is unobstructed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Critical structural areas - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Spar lines, wing attach points, wing struts, landing gear attachment areas. Stress areas.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Left Wing - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check wing attach points, wing struts and strut attach points. Check leading edge of wing for dents/cracks. Verify fuel take vent is unobstructed. Check wingtip for cracks. Secure attachment of position lights.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Pitot Tube - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Remove pitot cover (if equipped). Verify ram air and drain holes are unobstructed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Ailerons - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Verify smooth movement of ailerons. As one moves the other aileron should move opposite. 
Verify control position changes with aileron position. Controls should turn towards the UP aileron. 
Verify all screws, bolts, hinge and safety wire are attached. Check for appropriate play in aileron rod. 
Verify that all counterbalances are firmly secured.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flaps - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Inspect flap top and bottom. A small amount of play in the flaps is normal. Inspect flap rails and rollers for obstruction or cracks.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Landing gear attachment points - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Inspect attachment points and airplane skin near them. Wrinkled or other damage, loose bolts, rivets, verify free from corrosion.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Main gear tire inflation, tread, normal wear pattern - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Abnormal wear patterns, sidewall cracks, and damage like bulges, foreign objects, visible cords make the tire unairworthy.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Wheel hubs - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Free from cracks, corrosion, rust; fasteners are secure; Air valve stem is straight, capped, and in good condition
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Brakes, brake lines, and brake pads - CHECK
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Free from cracks, corrosion, rust, leaks, and fastener/safety wire is secure; proper amount of brake pad material remaining. Check landing gear strut for fluid from broken brake lines.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Tie downs and wheel chocks - REMOVE
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Remove wing tie downs and wheel chocks to allow the airplane to move freely after start up. It's a good practice to stand back to review the "big picture" of the airplane before climbing in to verify that small details like removing the chocks and tie downs have been completed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Not taking the time to "survey" the overall appearance
commonErrors.details: Pause while approaching the plane and ask the pilot to give their overall impression.

commonErrors.name: Assumed plane was fueled
commonErrors.details: Fuel exhaustion / starvation is the most common cause of total engine power loss in flight. Emphasize a KNOWN quantity of fuel is required for safe flight. While this step is typically later in the preflight inspection checklists, it's helpful to determine if fuel is needed as early as possible so the fuel truck can be called (if used). Instill the pilot with a habit of completing one last "big picture" overview of the aircraft prior to flight that includes items like the fuel caps, chocks, tie downs, etc.

commonErrors.name: Over/underfilling oil
commonErrors.details: Overfilling or under filling oil reservoirs. Thinking there is no oil when the plane has a fresh oil change and oil is almost clear.  Verify oil levels meet required per POH.

commonErrors.name: Overtightening or leaving the oil dip stick too loose
commonErrors.details: Confirm the tightness of the oil dipstick the first few flights to verify that the pilot "knows" the degree of tightness desired.

commonErrors.name: Failure to return the dip stick or to close the oil inspection door
commonErrors.details: After the formal preflight, have the pilot stand back and assess the overall aircraft for common oversights such as dip stick, access doors, chocks and tie-downs.

commonErrors.name: Improperly closing the door
commonErrors.details: The door latch may be inadvertantly locked when the door is open. Explain that attempting to close the door with the latch in thte locked positon can damage the door. Show the pilot the proper method to verify the latching mechanism. Also explain that aircraft parts are designed to be light and that care must be taken not to damage the more delicate components when compared to a car.

commonErrors.name: Failing to check the seat tracks for both free movement and position locking.
commonErrors.details: Explain to the pilot how worn locking mechanisms could become a hazard in flight (especially during takeoff and climb). Emphasize the need to check the seat tracks for clear movement and proper locking operation for safety and ease of entry and exit to the cockpit.

commonErrors.name: Doesn't know how to release the extinguisher and activate
commonErrors.details: Verify the pilot knows how to release and activate. Spend time early in the training to take the fire extinguisher out of its bracets, and run through a mock exercise, demonstratng how to use the equipment. Discuss how to make sure it is charged.

commonErrors.name: Failure to visually verify the trim movement.
commonErrors.details: During the elevator inspection have the pilot change the setting from the cockpit and observe the result. This need not be done on every flight, but it helps the pilot to understand the function of the trim in dynamically positioning the CG as well as proper funcitoning of the control.

commonErrors.name: Failure to push the mixture to its full IN position.
commonErrors.details: The point/verify opportunity is emphasized here because there is a physical movement to press the mixture control. Be sure to explain that without the mixture pushed all the way in (as applicable) that the engine might not receive enough fuel to provide full power on takeoff and climb.

commonErrors.name: Failure to push the Carb Heat full IN position.
commonErrors.details: Another point/verify opportunity that should be physical action to assure the control is firmly up against its stop. Explain to the pilot that having the carb heat on is reducing the amount of power the engine can produce (you can explain the effect of heat on air density as appropriate). You can emphasize the effect of carb heat on engine RPM during runup to help the pilot correlate carb heat with less power available.

commonErrors.name: Failure to verify the beacon is ON.
commonErrors.details: A point/verify opportunity. The main idea is to help the pilot build the habit of checking the operation of all aircraft lights including the beacon prior to flight. Emphasize the safety factor of being visible to people and aircraft on the ground and in the air. And, of course, explain the regulatory requirement of operating an aircraft that are airworthy.

commonErrors.name: Failure to verify the flap extension and that they are at their limits.
commonErrors.details: Explain to the pilot the effect of assymetrical flap extension in flight as a way to emphasize the need to verify proper operation before flight. Checking that the flaps operate smoothly and evenly at each detent will help ensure safe operation for your flight.

commonErrors.name: Failure to check all positionlights/strobe are ALL operational.
commonErrors.details: Impress on the pilot the need to visually verify correct operation of the lights for both safety and legality. Make it standard practice to physically walk around the aircraft to check the lights after turning on the switches. Remind the pilot how the lights enable other people and aircraft to more easily see the aircraft both in flight and on the ground.

commonErrors.name: Failure to verify Master is OFF
commonErrors.details: A point/verify opportunity by pushing the OFF side of the switch. Emphasize that leaving the Master Switch on when not needed is only draining battery power that will be needed for starting the engine. Help them build of habit of double checking that it is off. Potentially adopting a policy of leaving the Beacon switch on will help them realize when they have accidently left the Master Switch on.

commonErrors.name: Failure to record hobbs/tach time.
commonErrors.details:
As renter pilots are charged for aircraft "time" this is an important step for the pilot to verify.
Its also a good reminder to go through the aircraft "log" to verify the various maintenence 
items that are required by the FARs (Annual/100-hour etc)

commonErrors.name: Having the seat too far back so some controls are not within reach.
commonErrors.details:
For pilots who have a smaller stature a seat cushion may be a mandatory requirement.
Verify that the pilot can fully extend the rudders and activate the brakes.

commonErrors.name: Not verifying the integrity of the cowling fasteners.
commonErrors.details:
Require the pilot to have a screwdriver (phillips and straight blade) in their flight bag. Show them the correct way to secure any loose fasteners (as appropriate). Explain the hazard that could come from a loose cowling.
Failure to attempt to verify the integrity by a firm push.

commonErrors.name: Failure to run the fingers the full length of the leading edge of the prop to detect surface irregularities.
commonErrors.details: Note to the pilot examples of surface irregularities and explain that some may be smoothed out by a qualified A&P.

commonErrors.name: Failure to make physical check of exhaust integrity
commonErrors.details:
As most aircraft do not have easy access to much of the engine compartment and the 
exhaust in particular, a firm tug on the exhaust stack can confirm its structual integrity. 
Be careful if the plane has been recently flown since the exhaust stack may be hot.

commonErrors.name: Failure to verify fuel quantity and sample ALL sumps.
commonErrors.details: On newer aircraft there are often numerous sumps. Ensure the pilot knows how many and the technique for each. Explain the risk of operating the aircraft with contaminated fuel.

commonErrors.name: Failure to elevate the nose and push down to allow the strut to return to its normal position.
commonErrors.details: Poorly inflated nose struts are another common occurance. Show the pilot how to test and evaluate.

commonErrors.name: Failed to inspect static ports
commonErrors.details: While unlikely that any impairment will be discovered, physically confirm that the port has been inspected. One more than one occasion, a plane has been either repainted or "power washed" and the port had tape placed over it to keep paint/water out. The tape had not been removed. Take care that the pilot does not run their fingers over the port as it could cause any debris on the surface to accidently get pushed into the static line.

commonErrors.name: Failure to verify the avionics switch is OFF.
commonErrors.details: A point/verify opportunity by pushing the OFF side of the switch. Explain that the avionics system contains equipment that is sensitive to power surges like when turning on the Master Switch. By ensuring the Avionics Master is off, the pilot is preventing potential damage to the radios, GPS, and other electronic equipment installed on the aircraft.

commonErrors.name: Failure to clean windshield
commonErrors.details: Not uncommon for pilots to ignore the bugs and dirt--until they start looking for traffic.

completionStandards.description: Is able to verbally describe the basic steps in the desired maneuver/procedure, although cannot perform the maneuver or procedure yet
Can perform the basic procedure/maneuver with instructor coaching
Can perform the procedure/maneuver independently and safely; can identify and describe the desired PTS/ACS performance level
Consistently meets PTS/ACS standard
Consistently exceeds PTS/ACS standards (e.g. holds tolerances within half of PTS/ACS; if tolerance was +/- 100 feet, is able to perform at +/- 50 feet)

prepItems.name: Air Facts: Purposeful Preflight
prepItems.details: In this section we discuss the importance of a good preflight inspection
