activities.name: [03] PRE-SOLO: Engine Starting
activities.what: The procedure for successfully initiating the operation of the airplane's powerplant.
activities.why: To safely and efficiently start the aircraft's engine.
activities.groundPrep:
Use of the Engine Start Checklist
Importance of ensuring any passengers are ready for flight.
Importance of ensuring that all required items are within easy reach in the cockpit.
Importance of observing the position and intentions of any ramp personel.

checklistItems.name: Operate aircraft in accordance with the aircraft's Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) or Airplane Flight Manual (AFM)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This information is meant as a supplement to the preflight procedure found in the POH/AFM
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: BEFORE START
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Visually check ramp area - Clear
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Move the visual scan through at least 270 degrees that is observable from the cockpit. Be sure to check behind the aircraft.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Caution the pilot that this is a mandatory check. Emphasize the critical responsibilty of ensuring a safe operating environment around the airplane.

checklistItems.name:
Anti-collision lights - ON
Position lights - ON (at night)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Lighting up the aircraft provides a visual cue to those on the ground that the aircraft is "active" and ready for engine start.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Note to the pilot the importance of these types of activities to help ensure the safety of eveyone involved. Using a checklist is both professional and smart to help minimize missed items. You may need to reinforce several times when each type of light is appropriate for use. Some pilots may think that they should only be used at night, but a good explanation and reinforcing the reasons why we use them when we do can help the pilot better understand and remember best practices.

checklistItems.name: Brakes - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Press evenly on the brake and verify the toes are up on the top of the rudder pedal to allow activation of the brake. 

Engage the hand-brake if available.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot press on the toe brakes (assuming the aircraft uses toe brakes). Emphasize "even" braking action on both feet.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Be aware of the few "odd-ball" brake locations (heel, and hand-brake only aircraft). Note too, that some aircraft only have toe brakes on the left side.

checklistItems.name:
Oil grade - Check (in cold weather)
Preheat engine - Complete (in cold weather)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: For weather conditions with temperatures below 10 degrees consider postponing the flight till later in the day if pre-heating is not available.

checklistItems.name:
Area - Clear
Starter - Engage
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure the window is open and use a loud voice.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Remind the pilot that the ramp area can be a busy and noisy place and they have a responsibility to communicate over these obstacles. Make sure they understand that they should actively listen for anyone in the area before continuing the engine start procedure.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: Check to the right and announce "Clear Right" following the pilot's announcement. Assuming the instructor is in the right seat.

checklistItems.name: DURING START
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Brakes - Hold
Throttle - Manage
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Do not engage starter for more than 30 seconds; allow cool down for 30 seconds to 1 minute
checklistItems.teachingTips: Note to the pilot the lack of adequate braking pressure to avoid any aircraft movement during the starting procedure. IF the engine fails to start after the 30 second period (and usually after 10 seconds of cranking) recheck the starting set-up of mixture/throttle/fuel selector.

checklistItems.name: AFTER START
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Engine RPM - Set (see AFM/POH)
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
This is typically 1000 RPM; allows oil pressure to rise and minimizes undue engine wear from insufficient lubrication. 

For high-density altitude operations, lean the mixture slowly until the engine shows a slight increase in RPM.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Double check the pilot by asking them to recite the desired RPM. 

On the first few flight demonstrate the proper method for leaning for taxi.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: It is not uncommon to lean slightly even at sea level airports to reduce the carbon content of the exhaust and avoid carbon build-up on spark plugs that can cause a rough runnning engine.

checklistItems.name: Oil pressure - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Recite the oil pressure. Ensure value is within specified range
checklistItems.teachingTips: Because the oil pressure is rarely out of spec. it is often neglected. Double check the pilot by asking them to recite the actual oil pressure reading if they failed to.

checklistItems.name: Starter disengaged - Verify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Look for a high current draw on ammeter or in some airplanes a "starter engaged" warning light. Shut down engine immediately if this occurs.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ask the pilot to tell how they verified the starter is disengaged.

checklistItems.name: EXTRA
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be aware of any sounds, vibrations, smells, or smoke that is out of the normal operating experience. It could be evidence of a current or pending malfunction. Check for any unusual sights or sounds.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Discuss briefly with the pilot what they perceive as "normal" regarding the sights and sounds in the cockpit.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: A slight "hint" of avgas is typically all that will be present unless jet aircraft are operating nearby.

commonErrors.name: Not aware of suroundings
commonErrors.details: Pilot not observant of ramp personel.

commonErrors.name: Not using the anti-collision light during daytime
commonErrors.details: Failure to understand that the anti-collision light should be used in daylight hours.

commonErrors.name: Not announcing engine start
commonErrors.details: Failure to open the window or not using a loud voice.

commonErrors.name: No brake check
commonErrors.details: Aircraft creeps forward when engine starts.

commonErrors.name: Not waiting for proper oil temp
commonErrors.details: Failing to verify correct oil pressure.

commonErrors.name: Incorrect idle RPM (high/low)
commonErrors.details: Failure to set the correct idle RPM (usually too high) or to compensate for an over-rich mixture.

Consistently meets PTS/ACS standard

prepItems.details: In this section we investigate the engine startup procedure for a Cessna 172. As a safety note, make sure no person, structure, or airplane is behind you.

prepItems.name: ACS - Engine Starting
prepItems.details: Read Engine Starting (p. 14) to see the checkride requirements for this procedure.

activities.name: [04] PRE-SOLO: Before Takeoff Check
activities.what: The systematic procedure for checking the engine, controls, systems, instruments, and avionics prior to flight.
activities.why: To help ensure safe flight by testing that engine is within its designed operational limits.
activities.groundPrep:
Purpose of pre-takeoff checklist items including: Reasons for checking each item, detecting malfunctions, and ensuring the airplane is in safe operating condition as recommended by the manufacturer.
How to calculate takeoff performance.
How to perform a takeoff briefing and how to act on it in the event of an emergency.

checklistItems.name: Operate aircraft in accordance with the aircraft's Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) or Airplane Flight Manual (AFM)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: This information is meant as a supplement to the preflight procedure found in the POH/AFM
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Taxi to suitable run-up area - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Area should be free of debris that may damge the propeller, airplane, or other people/aircraft.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot look all around the aircraft before begining the runup. In some cases it is best to conduct the runup in the ramp area and they need to ensure that any people, aircraft, or structures won't be affected by the prop blast.

checklistItems.name: Configure airplane for run-up - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Oil temperature should be within limits for high power. 

Ensure that the nose- or tail-wheel is aligned with the longitudinal axis of the aircraft before run-up to avoid undue stress on the nose gear.

On warm days, as much as possible, point airplane into the wind to aid engine cooling during run-up. Air cooled engines can overheat at high power settings with little to no forward movement. Set cowl flaps as recommended by the AFM/POH, if installed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Follow before takeoff procedure in AFM/POH - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: When working through the preflight checklist, have the pilot say everything out loud, even if they are soloing. Reciting the checklist out loud helps to ensure that no items are skipped.

checklistItems.name: During run up, divide attention between inside and outside - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure that you keep the brakes firmly engaged to prevent the airplane from unintentionally moving forward during run-up. To help prevent this, monitor the aircraft's position by regularly splitting your attention between inside tasks and outside references.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot continuously monitor outside the aircraft as they are doing the run-up. Be aware of any other aircraft or people that may be moving in the vicinity of the aircraft.

checklistItems.name: Check critical systems per AFM/POH:
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel system - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure is set per AFM/POH and verify that correct fuel tanks are selected.
checklistItems.teachingTips: On low wing aircraft, the fuel selector should be checked to ensure that fuel is being drawn from each tank, and then set to the fullest tank for takeoff. For high wing aircraft, the normal setting is "Both" for takeoff.

checklistItems.name: Trim - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: All installed trim systems (Elevator, Aileron, Rudder) set for takeoff as per AFM/POH.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure that the Trim system is set for the takeoff setting.

checklistItems.name: Flight controls - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Perform a complete control check on elevator, aileron, and rudder for correct movement and to the full limits of controls.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Engine operation - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check for all parameters to be within normal ranges and limits. Check ignition system, carburetor heat (if installed), constant speed/feathering propeller (if installed), and engine operation at minimum idle.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure that the pilot understands the process of checking each magneto and notes the drop in engine rpm or any engine roughness. Ensure the pilot understands the procedure for clearing fouled plugs if the mag check indicates plug fouling.

checklistItems.name: Electrical system - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure correct voltages and battery charging.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot turn on Pitot Heat as a way of checking the electrical system and verifying the alternator can accept the additional load.

checklistItems.name: Vacuum system - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure vacuum values are within limits and that gyroscopic instruments are properly functioning.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If the aircraft includes a Standby Vacuum system, ensure that it is checked as part of the Vacuum system check.

checklistItems.name: Flight instruments - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Check that directional gyro is aligned with magnetic compass.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot recheck the heading indicator after engine run-up. The gyro takes time to spin up to full rpm and well as precession that will allow the heading indicator to drift.

checklistItems.name: Avionics - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify correct frequencies, transponder codes, navigation sources, autopilot settings, and any other applicable settings are ready for planned flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot set up Avionics to be able to "Navigate" and "Communicate" after take off. Ensure that the VOR frequencies are set, that the GPS is set for the first waypoint or set for return to the airport, that the radios have the next frequency needed in standby position on the radio. (Reference: https://www.aopa.org/news-and-media/all-news/2008/august/flight-training-magazine/frequent-frequencies)

checklistItems.name: Takeoff Briefing - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
A takeoff briefing is a verbal review of your initial plan and emergency plan for the takeoff phase of flight. It should be said out loud - even when you are by yourself!

Here is a recommended list of briefing items:
Type of takeoff (normal, short field, etc)
Assigned runway number
Wind direction and velocity
Liftoff or Vr speed
Initial heading and altitude after takeoff
Emergency procedures (Develop a plan for the following stages)
"If anything abnormal occurs prior to rotation..."
"If engine failure occurs after rotation with runway remaining..."
"If engine failure occurs after rotation with no runway remaining..."
checklistItems.teachingTips: In addition to have the pilot verbally conduct the recommended Takeoff Brief, have them look for places to put the aircraft down after they take off. Its good practice for the CFI to say, " You are at 500 feet agl, if you lost an engine, where would you go?"

commonErrors.name: Failure to review takeoff performance.
commonErrors.details: The pilot should review the AFM/POH to ensure that aircraft takeoff performance is acceptable for the flight given the aircraft, runway and atmospheric conditions. Impress upon the pilot the safety implications for taking off under adverse conditions like a tailwind and/or high density altitude. A simulator is an effective teaching tool or you might possibly even simulate the effects in the airplane by demonstrating a partial power takeoff at an airport with a long runway. Of course, remember to add full power once the point is clear.

commonErrors.name: Failure to position the airplane considering other aircraft, vessels, and wind.
commonErrors.details: The pilot should ensure the run-up area selected is free of debris that may cause damage from prop blast to other aircraft, structures, or people. Instill a habit in the pilot of checking behind the aircraft before beginning runup to ensure no people or property will be affected by the prop blast.

commonErrors.name: Failure to complete the appropriate checklist.
commonErrors.details: Impress upon the pilot the potentially dangerous effects of forgetting a critical item during takeoff. The checklist is designed to help prevent missing those items. Perhaps using a few case studies from takeoff accident reports will help instill a healthy respect for following aircraft procedures.

commonErrors.name: Failure to not divide attention inside and outside the flight deck.
commonErrors.details: The Pilot should ensure that they are dividing their attention between checklist, the aircraft, and other aircraft or people that may be around the aircraft as they perform the preflight checks. Demonstrate how easy it is to miss gradual forward movement of the aircraft when you aren't monitoring it. For example, take the aircraft controls and assign the pilot a detailed heads down task. Then gradually release the brakes to see if they notice the forward movement. If not, point it out to them.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to perform the takeoff briefing.
commonErrors.details: Help the pilot understand the added safety of being in an alert mindset during busy and critical phases of flight like takeoff. Already having a plan can help them respond more quickly in the event of a problem during takeoff. You can help them practice these procedures to a high degree by drilling takeoff procedures in the simulator.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to set appropriate frequencies prior to takeoff.
commonErrors.details: Help the pilot remember setting these items by making a standard memory flow they can accomplish at each stage of flight. When done attentively, the pilot will typically complete all of the listed checklist items prior to looking at it. If the pilot consistenly forgets to set the appropriate radio frequencies, allow them to experience the increased workload of looking up and setting the radios during the initial part of flight. Impress upon them the need and significantly reduced workload of proper pretakeoff preparation.

commonErrors.name: Failure to verify that engine parameters are within safe limitations.
commonErrors.details: The pilot should ensure that the engine performance are within the specified range and settings as described in the AFM/POH. Emphasize how engine damage could occur or the effects of lowered performance could affect the safety of the takeoff and flight. Using a few case studies from takeoff accident reports could help to emphasize the point.

commonErrors.name: Failure to set trim for takeoff.
commonErrors.details: This can cause problems from a mere annoyance to major control difficulties depending on where the elevator trim was set prior to takeoff. While safely at altitude, demonstrate the effects of improper takeoff trim to the pilot by having them slow to takeoff speed, improperly setting the trim, and then applying full power. They should quickly get the point of how dangerous this could be on takeoff. Make checking the trim a critical part of the pretakeoff procedure by using a flow or other memory aid.

prepItems.name: Taxi, Run-up, Traffic Pattern
prepItems.details: Your instructor will probably have you taxi the airplane on your first lesson. Safe ground operations involve the coordinated use of the throttle, control yoke, and foot pedals. Steering with your feet is going to take some getting used to.

prepItems.details: Read (Ch 2.21-22) on Before Takeoff Check and Takeoff Checks

prepItems.details: Read Before Takeoff Check (p. 17) to see the checkride requirements for this procedure.

activities.name: [05] PRE-SOLO: Flight Deck Management
activities.what: The process of managing available resources to ensure the successful outcome of the flight
activities.why: To enhance safety of flight operations
activities.groundPrep:
The importance of cockpit organization, passenger care, and managing safety items
Passenger briefing requirements, to include operation and required use of safety restraint systems.
Use of appropriate checklists.
Requirements for current and appropriate navigation data.

checklistItems.name: Passenger briefing - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Conduct an appropriate pre-takeoff briefing, to include identifying the PIC, use of safety belts, shoulder harnesses, doors, sterile flight deck, and emergency procedures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Checklist(s) - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use of appropriate checklists. Know when it's appropriate to use checklists, and use them at those times consistently. Avoiding using checklists at inappropriate times.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Navigation data - Current
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Requirements for current and appropriate navigation data - both electronic and printed. Know how to check valid dates for electronic and printed data. Pilots are allowed to perform electronic navigation updates as part of preventative maintenance. Ask your instructor to follow as a database is updated.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flight deck - Organized and secure
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Secure all items in the flight deck and cabin. Develop a system to secure tablets, charts, pens/pencils, checklists, etc. and stick to it. Be sure to put things back in their place after use to prevent losing them and to help make sure you can find it again when you need it. If using printed charts, fold the chart to only the active area. Always be thinking about how to make the cockpit easier to navigate and have things ready for the next steps.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Cockpit organization makes flying easier and safer. Discuss how to pack for longer or overnight trips to keep the aircraft within weight and balance and the baggage secure.

checklistItems.name: Avionics/Automation - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If the aircraft has automation, know how to properly program and manage the systems. Know all the autopilot modes and their failure behaviors. Know how to disconnect the autopliot.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Doesn't understand tech failuers
commonErrors.details: No recognition of failure modes.

commonErrors.name: No passenger briefing
commonErrors.details: Lack of passenger briefing

commonErrors.name: Did not use checklist
commonErrors.details: Lack of checklist usage or using checklists at inappropriate times.

commonErrors.name: Using outdated data/charts
commonErrors.details: Operating with outdated data or charts and/or inability to determine expiration date.

commonErrors.name: Not familiar with tech
commonErrors.details: Inability to operate the automation.

commonErrors.name: Messy cockpit
commonErrors.details: Messy or unsafe cockpit

Closer Look: Tablets in the Cockpit
prepItems.details: Today, pilots are using tablets to assist with just about every aspect of flying. These devices can help you plan cross-country flights, provide preflight weather briefings, display electronic sectional charts, show G-P-S moving maps and much, much more.

activities.name: [06] PRE-SOLO: Operation of Systems
activities.what: The subject matter concerning the mechanical operation of the aircraft
activities.why: To enhance understanding and therefore safety in operating the aircraft
activities.groundPrep:
Knowledge and practice in using aircraft systems will increase safety, especially in avoiding or responding to emergencies.
Every aircraft is different, and each must be relearned from a system perspective.
Rely first on the aircraft manual to understand systems and begin to deal with failures.

checklistItems.name: Use appropriate checklists properly
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Checklist usage is critical to dealing with aircraft systems. Some must be committed to memory, such as fires, while others can be verified after a flow is conducted. Just using or dealing with a system error isn't enough. It must be backed up with proper checklist usage.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Proper operation of the following systems:
checklistItems.notesToPilot: N/A
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Primary flight controls
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Typically the primary flight controls are considered the rudder pedals and stick or yoke and their associated control surfaces of rudder, ailerons, and elevator. Know how moving each control impacts the operation of each control, and common failure modes. Check all controls in the preflight run-up to ensure proper operation.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Demonstrate a full "boxing" of the controls with full forward elevator, full left aileron, full aft elevator, full right aileron, and back to full forward elevator. This ensures full travel and makes for clear assessment of proper operation.

checklistItems.name: Secondary flight controls
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Secondary flight controls help to augment or relieve workload on the pilot, and on training airplanes are devices like trim and flaps. Know which type of trim system your aircraft has (servo or antiservo) and how it operates. If the aircraft has electric trim, know how to disable it in case of a runaway trim malfunction. Also understand trim's function on aircraft control, and its ability to keep the airplae at a consistent airspeed. Know and understand your aircraft's flap system, including failure modes. In the case of a flap imbalance where one flap goes down more than another, the first action is usually to retract the flaps to the previous position.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Powerplant and propeller
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Know and understand the operation of your engine and propeller. Be able to understand the impact of temperature and pressure on the engine's operation. Commit to memory the engine emergency flows, including power loss and fire. Properly preflight the engine and propeller, and be able to spot discrepencies and address them appropriately.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Landing gear
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Know and understand your aircraft's landing gear system. Be able to properly preflight the system and identify airworthiness items.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Fuel, oil, and hydraulic
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Know and understand the quantity of fuel, number of tanks, and how the tanks feed the engine. Know how much fuel the engine burns and how to impact that rate.Know how much oil the engine holds, the type, and how to check and add oil. If the aircraft has any hydraulic systems, be able to identify them and explain their operation.
checklistItems.teachingTips: From the first lesson ensure the pilot understands how much fuel is on board and knows how much is needed for the flight. Shortly after the start of training require the student to make fuel decisions under the instructor's observation. Regularly quiz the pilot on how much fuel is left on the aircaft and how much more will be needed to complete the flight. Make a game out of trying to guess exactly how much fuel is left after a flight and refuel to check results.

checklistItems.name: Electrical
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Know and be able to explain the operation of the aircraft electrical system. Know which voltage the system operates with, and the failure mode of the various electrical componenets and devices.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Avionics
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Understand how each piece of avionics work in the aircraft and be able to explain their operation. Know how each interacts and how to identify and deal with their failures. Know the limitations of each item.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Pitot-static, vacuum/pressure, and associated flight instruments
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Pitot-static, vacuum, and electrical systems are required for the primary instruments to operate in a traditional aircraft panel. Airspeed uses the pitot and static system, the altimeter and vertical speed indicator use the static system, and the vacuum runs the attitude indicator and directional gyro. Know how all these systems operate and when and why they may fail, and how to deal with those failures.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Environmental
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Explain and use the heat and cooling system; explain the carbon monoxide hazard of using heat. Also make sure that you know how to adjust the cockpit heating and cooling systems. Have your instructor demonstrate them to you.
checklistItems.teachingTips: On a simple, but often overlooked note, be sure that the pilot knows how to operate the environmental controls in the aircraft. Since they are on the CFI’s side of the cockpit, we don’t realize that the pilot cannot easily see how they are adjusted or the fine skill that is required to get them air temperature just right ;-).

checklistItems.name: Deicing and anti-icing
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If the aircraft is equipped with deice or anti-ice systems, know how they operate, how to refill any fluid tanks, how long the fluid will last, and when it's apprporiate to use the systems.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Oxygen system
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If equipped, understand when and how to use the oxygen system, including its hazards.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Explain the hazards of in-flight oxygen use, including the risks of smoking and hypoxia in the event of system failure. Stress the use of an oximeter.

commonErrors.name: Improper response to electrical system failures.
commonErrors.details: Point out normal and abnormal indications of volts and amps; simulate electrical failures and the appropriate response.

commonErrors.name: Failure to properly preflight the landing gear.
commonErrors.details: With steel spring landing gear, ensure the pilot understands how to check for cracks at the fuselage and other damage. For oleo landing gear, help the pilot determine the airworthiness of a strut that is too low or has unequal height when on the ground.

commonErrors.name: Inability to normally operate or to perform emergency gear operation on a retractable gear aircraft.
commonErrors.details: For retractable gear aircraft teach a method of operating the gear at the same time on every flight, and the proper use of checklist to ensure the gear is up and down, as appropriate. Teach and perform emergency gear extensions.

commonErrors.name: Improper use of fuel selectors.
commonErrors.details: Start by spending time with the airplane schematic, and then go to the airplane to help reinforce the system's operation. Using the checklist as a guide discuss the reasons for setting the selector in a particular way and work with the pilot to determine a method that ensures he or she will remember to use the selector at the proper time in cruise flight.

commonErrors.name: Inappropriate fueling or inability to self fuel or check/add oil.
commonErrors.details: Teach the pilot how to fuel the aircraft (including self fueling), as well as how to add oil during the training process. Discuss any balance or tank limitations and explore those during refueling. Emphasize the adverse effects of improper fuel loading on the aircraft's weight and balance and potentially redcued performance.

commonErrors.name: Inability to explain the aircraft electrical system.
commonErrors.details: Take the pilot to a maintenance operation to point out and explain the operation of the electrical system; start the aircraft with ground power at least once during training.

commonErrors.name: Inability to use all avionics systems or identify their various failure modes.
commonErrors.details: Explain in detail how to transmit and recieve on specified radios, how to tune and flip frequencies, and how to adjust volumes. Demonstrate how to enter transponder codes. Demonstrate how to program the GPS and ensure the student has practice doing the same.

commonErrors.name: Inability to identify or explain instrument operations.
commonErrors.details: If you have access, show the inside of instruments, which greatly reinforces how they operate. If not, there are numerous YouTube videos that explain in detail how they operate while showing the inside of the case. Assign these as homework.

commonErrors.name: Inability to recognize and deal with instrument failures.
commonErrors.details: Practice simulated instrument failures by flying with primary instruments covered; show instrument failures in simulators, which accurately represent the slow spinning down of gryos; have the student explain what happens in an instrument failure, and what constitutes an emergency and what is only an urgent situation; stress use of checklists and pulling out the manual in flight to verify how to handle instrument failures.

commonErrors.name: Inability to explain the hazards of using the aircaft heat.
commonErrors.details: Show the pilot the heating system forward of the firewall to stress the importance of carbon monoxide detection and avoidance.

commonErrors.name: Inability to use the anti-ice or deicing system.
commonErrors.details: Demonstrate and have the pilot operate the deicing or anti-icing system in flight; have the pilot refill the system under the instructor's supervision.

commonErrors.name: Inability to use or refill the system.
commonErrors.details: If equipped, have the pilot use the oxygen system and know how to refill it. Give several scenarios that might require oxgen use and have the pilot explain, simulate, or actually use the oxygen system correctly.

commonErrors.name: Lack of flap use or improper use of flaps.
commonErrors.details: Practice partial flap and no-flap landings, and simulate emergency procedures with a flap imbalance.

commonErrors.name: Lack of trim use or improper trim use.
commonErrors.details: Explain and demonstrate how trim can both relieve control pressure and maintain an airspeed. Determine a protocol for using trim in maneuvers and maintain consistency by ensuring the pilot uses the trim in the same way each time.

commonErrors.name: Lack of knowledge of what each control does, especially the relationship of ailerons and rudders.
commonErrors.details: Perform stability or dutch roll exercises to enhance coordination and show the relationship to roll and yaw. Spend time on the ground teaching the pilot the relationship to yoke and aileron and elevator movement. Manipulate the controls from both inside and outside the aircraft to see the relationship from both aspects.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to check flight controls during run-up
commonErrors.details: CIGAR is an effective acroynm to employ either during the pre-takeoff flow or as a checklist. C-Controls free and correct; I - Instruments operating correctly and set G - Gas quantity and on the correct tank A - Attitude or trim set and operational R - Run-up for magnetos, carb heat, and temperatures.

commonErrors.name: Not using checklists; incorrect checklist; using checklist at inappropriate moments
commonErrors.details: Emphasize proper checklist usage on all maneuvers and appropriate phases of flight to improve consistency. Ensure checklists are properly organized and easily accessible. Recommend completing a standard memory flow backed up by a checklist for redundancy and safety. Although checklists are important, the focus should always be on flying the airplane first, and verifying with a checklist when time and workload allows.

commonErrors.name: Inappropriate power changes or, in the case of constant speed propellers, inappropriate propeller changes.
commonErrors.details: Teach power and propeller changes be done in a deliberate and thoughtful manner, and are not to be used as a primary flight control.

commonErrors.name: Failure to properly preflight engine and propeller.
commonErrors.details: The engine and propeller are two of the most important systems to preflight. Make sure the pilot can identify discrepencies on the preflight, possibly by deliberately creating an airworthiness condition for the pilot to find. Show the pilot photos or an actual propeller that is damaged, and discuss ways in which propellers become damaged.

prepItems.name: AFM/POH - Operation of Systems
prepItems.link: www.aopa.org/Training and Safety/Flight Schools/AOPA Flight Training Advantage/AOPA Pre-Solo Operation of Systems
prepItems.details: Refer to the manufacturer's aircraft manual to learn about operating the systems. Section 4 (Normal Procedures) and section 7 (Airplane and Systems Description) will have procedures and in-depth information about operating your aircraft.

prepItems.name: Introduction to the Airplane
prepItems.details: In this section you will investigate the various aspects of the airplane – its controls, and the aerodynamics that make it fly.

prepItems.name: How it works
prepItems.details: Learn about aircraft systems by browsing this section that contains a wealth of articles on systems from the How It Works series.

prepItems.name: ACS - Operation of Systems
prepItems.details: Read Operation of Systems (p. 9) to see the checkride requirements for this procedure.

prepItems.name: Engines
prepItems.details: The use of internal combustion engines in aircraft presents a unique problem because fuel will only burn well when it is mixed with air in the proper proportion.

prepItems.name: Propeller, Fuel and Electrical System
prepItems.details: In this section we continue a discussion of airplane systems – most specifically, propeller, fuel, and electrical.

prepItems.name: Introduction to Airplane Engines
prepItems.details: In this section we investigate the typical training airplane engine. Most training airplanes use four-stroke, internal combustion, reciprocating engines which operate on the same principle as automobile engines. A reciprocating engine converts the back and forth motion of the pistons to the rotary motion of the crankshaft.

prepItems.name: Introduction to the Flight Deck
prepItems.details: In this section we will move inside the cockpit and take a look at the flight instruments and the rest of the airplane panel. Most training airplanes have fully functioning dual controls and can be flown from either side. Traditionally, the pilot flies the airplane from the left.

activities.name: [03] X/C: Pilotage and Dead Reckoning
activities.what: Cockpit procedures for pilotage and dead reckoning
activities.why: Backup to electronic navigation
activities.groundPrep:
This is why we fly! Go go places! Discuss any questions or concerns the pilot may have about what will happen on the flight.  Discuss how the pilot will be using a combination of dead reckoning (flying with a compass and timer) and pilotage (looking out the window and comparing what they see with what is on the sectional and what they planned to see) for a safe and precise cross country flight. Both skills together will be needed in this task.

Review pilot's cross country flight plan. Spot check distance/ground speed/heading/time and fuel required on a couple legs. 

Verify the weather used for the cross country flight plan was gathered no more than 3 hours before the flight to ensure most accurate flight planning. If the pilot used the weather from the day before or several days before describe a time that you saw the weather chance considerably from what was forecast 24 hours before. 

Review climb, cruise, communications, descent and pattern entry plan. Does the pilot have a plan for each phase of flight? Do they have an idea of how they will enter the pattern? Will they need to overfly the field? 

Review checkpoints. Does the pilot have multiple ways to identify each checkpoint in order to find the checkpoint in case the pre-planned headings are off due to unforecast winds?

Review NOTAMs and TFRs for the route of flight. Make sure to involve the pilot in this very important step. Even if there were no NOTAMS or TFRs the day before they can spring up unexpectedly. Especially in fire season in the west when TFRs will pop up without warning to protect fire fighting activities. 

Insist on a complete flight plan. If the pilot did not complete every aspect of their plan, has incorrect calcuations, is using weather data that is too old, etc. Turn this flight lesson into a ground lesson about cross country flight planning. 

Remind the pilot how important it will be to fly straight and level (no turning) on the cruise legs in order to ensure the flight plan works. Remind them flying the "correct" heading will often require crabbing into the wind in order to fly a straight ground track to their next destination. 

Discuss the weather expected on the route. Will it be windy, turbulent, cloudy, etc. Discuss the risk management the crew (pilot and CFI) will use to manage any risks - e.g. having a plan B to divert if needed, cruising more than 2000 feet below the cloud deck and 2000 feet above the ground, etc.

Discuss how incredibly accurate flight planning can be if flown as planned. Offer the opportunity to measure the fuel used on the flight by refueling or using a fuel stick. This is a great way to build the pilot's confidence in their cross country flight planning skills, or learn how mistakes or unforecast weather can have a large impact in the result of the flight.

checklistItems.name: Chart and navlog - Organize
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
If using paper - fold nav log on knee board with list of checkpoints, headings, distances and Estimated Time Enroute (ETE) and Actual Time Enroute (ATE) clearly visible. Fold sectional so the course is clearly visible without folding or unfolding if at all possible. Keep sectional on lap or in kneeboard, preferrably clearly visible with no movement required.
If using a tablet - keep printed navlog from tablet within reach, position tablet out of direct sunlight and for minimal glare. Place sectional, chart supplement and/or backup tablet, battery, phone, etc. in easy reach from the pilot seat.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot sit on a chair in the middle of the room with his or her kneeboard only. Have them practice organizing their paper charts/logs or tablet, including making room to write down taxi instructions, weather information, frequency changes, etc. Once they've developed a method for their cockpit organization, validate it in a parked plane.
checklistItems.simulator: If a simulator is available, set up the simulator based on forecast weather and have the pilot fly the complete flight from departure to destination in the simulator before attempting in a plane.

checklistItems.name:
First heading - Review
Altitude - Review
Time to checkpoint - Review
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Ensure heading indicator is set to compass on the runway before starting take off roll. On climb out it will be relatively difficult to see waypoints directly ahead of the plane. As a result flying an accurate initial heading using the heading indicator is needed. 
Note desired initial heading. Set the heading bug on the plane (if available). 
Review the planned top of climb altitude and time to checkpoint.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Takeoff time - Record
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When cleared for take off note the take off time. Start a timer (panel mounted clock, transponder "count up function", wrist watch, tablet timer, etc.).
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Track course - Use landmarks
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Adjust heading as necessary to maintain desired groundtrack. Note it may be hard to see landmarks directly in front of the plane. Fly the calculated heading and use the view out the side of the front wind screen and side windows to note if the plane is turning left or right off course. Lower the nose to check for traffic every thousand feet of climb and confirm the plane is flying a straight ground track.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
TOC - Record time
Cruise checklist - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Level off at Top of Climb and note time/leg time. Reset timer for the next leg.
Complete the cruise checklist - note any difference between compass heading and heading indicator. 
Adjust heading if needed after resetting heading to compass to remain on course towards first checkpoint.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Before checkpoint:
Next heading - Review
Altitude - Review
Time at checkpoint -Review
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Approaching the first checkpoint note if the current heading will place the plane directly over or to the side of the planned position. If the plane is to the side of the planned position be prepared to adjust the heading of the next leg to compensate for potential wind drift. 
Review the next checkpoint, the heading to fly to the checkpoint, any planned altitude changes and the estimated time to the next checkpoint.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
At checkpoint:
Time - Record
Course - Adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Crossing the checkpoint, note the time enroute and the time between checkpoints on the nav log. 
Reset the timer for the next leg. 
Set heading to compass. 
Set heading bug (if available) to new heading.
Turn to the next calculated heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If the pilot is struggling with rolling out on the desired heading, have them start their rollout at 1/2 of the bank angle they are using in the turn. For example, if the pilot is turning right to a heading of 270 with a 20 degree bank angle they will need to start their rollout at a heading of 260.

checklistItems.name:
At checkpoint:
Next heading - Review
Altitude - Review
Time at checkpoint - Review
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Once established on the new heading look ahead and identify far away land marks to fly towards on this heading. 
The checkpoints should also be close enough together that, if the actual checkpoint is not already visible, prominent landmarks around the checkpoint are visible to confirm the plane is going the right direction. 
Compare the time on the last leg to the precalculated time. Significant difference in time may indicate winds are different from forecast. Review planned fuel and recalculate fuel usage based on new data.  Identify alternate airports for refueling if needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
20 Miles from Destination:
Weather/ATIS - Listen
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Get weather information to help decide which runway to land on (or determine runway in use). 
Adjust approach and landing plan if needed. 
Decide if the airport is within personal weather minimums or diversion may be necessary. 
If the intended landing airport is a class C airport establish contact with the controlling ATC facility (Center or TRACON, not the tower) no later than 20 NM out from the destination airport.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name:
10 Miles from Destination: 
CTAF/Tower - Monitor
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
No later than 10 NM from an untowered airport or Class D airport listen on CTAF/Tower frequency to determine traffic flow, type and number of aircraft in the area and develop a mental picture of the airport environment. 
Compare traffic flow to weather data and determine if the general flow of aircraft will put the plane on a runway with favorable winds. If not, consider coordinating with traffic or requesting an alternate runway at the airport if available.
If arriving at a Class D airport, make the initial radio call at 10NM out or before entering airspace. If a non-towered airport make the initial radio call on CTAF no later than 5NM out.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Use a hand held radio on a busy airport day. Prepare a room with a whiteboard and a drawing of the airport runways and taxiways. Have the pilot listen to the radio calls on ground and tower frequency (or CTAF). As they listen to the calls have them mark on the white board where the planes are entering the pattern, in the pattern, exiting the runway, etc. 

After this practice go up in a plane and circle in a safe location near an airport. With the pilot listening to the radio and flying the plane, have them verbally describe what types of planes are operating at the airport, where they are and where they are going.

checklistItems.name:
TOD:
Descent - Start
Checklist - Review
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
At TOD, lower the nose and adjust power and pitch to acheive the pre-planned descent airspeed and descent rate.
Review the descent checklist - ensuring altimeter is set to the local airport, mixture is enrichened during descent and heading indicator is set to compass.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: High performance aircraft typically have a limitation on the time use of maximum power.

commonErrors.name: Failing to organize cockpit so essential items are in reach without additional clutter.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Remind the pilot they will be flying solo and not able to ask their CFI for assistance. They want to make sure they can reach, easily, everything required for them to navigate, enter unfamiliar airport environments and/or verify their location at any time.  Describe how you (the CFI) organize the cockpit for your own cross country flights.

commonErrors.name: Failing to descend at the preplanned rate and speed. _x000D_
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Pilots will typically descend much more slowly than planned or starting descent later than planned. 

Discuss why the goal is to be at pattern altitude for the destination airport 3-5 miles before arriving at the airport if not overflying the field. If overflying the field the goal is to be 500-1000 feet over pattern altitude 3-5 miles away from the airport. Both situations allow the pilot to get down and observe the traffic pattern, identify potential traffic conflicts, and prepare for a normal approach to landing. 

If possible let the pilot do this in a safe situation (e.g. non towered airport) where they realize they arrived 2000 feet too high at the destination because they didn't do as they had planned.

commonErrors.name: Not looking at the next planned heading or altitude until at the checkpoint.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Discuss the old saying ""Don't let the plane get to a place you brain wasn't 5 minutes earlier."" Waiting to decide what to do after passing a checkpoint will contribute to errors in course and, potentially significant delays turning to the next heading while looking that information up."

commonErrors.name: Getting "behind the plane" and not getting required information before arriving at the airport.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
At first you can cue the pilot to think about getting the approach items comlete as soon as possible. If they consistenly forget consider letting the pilot see consequences in a safe environment (not in a Class C airspace) until they realize they suddenly have too much to do and not enough time to do it. It will usually impress on them the need to stay ahead of the airplane.

commonErrors.name: Failing to record time at new waypoint.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Pilots record this information to compare against the pre-planned flight plan. If there is a significant difference in time from what was planned a fuel stop may be necessary before reaching the destination or before the planned fuel stop.

commonErrors.name: Not adjusting heading based on what is seen in flight.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Hopefully this will happen first on a flight with the instructor. Flight plans are extremely accurate when the winds are as forecast, however this rarely happens. If the pilot consistently finds the plane left or right of course at the next checkpoint they will need to adjust their heading (where the plane is pointed) to address the changed winds. If they do not do this and the winds are strong enough they may end up getting lost.

commonErrors.name: Forgetting to record take off time.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Most commercially available checklists include ""Time-NOTE"" in the pre-takeoff checks. Teach the pilot to note take off time on all flights as a way to determine how long they've been flying, estimate how much fuel is on board after flying for ""a while"". 
Remind the pilot the only way they will know if the flight is going as planned and they really do have enough fuel is to know how long they've been flying. This is not something they want to guess at.
As a backup to recording the take off time: 
If flying with a plane that has a hobbs meter the pilot can estimate how long they've been in flight on the basis of hobbs time minus the ""typical"" hobbs time to take off after start up. 
If flying with a Garmin transponder the transponder as a ""Flight Time"" function that starts a timer on the take off roll. This can also be used to estimate total time flying.

commonErrors.name: Failing to use cruise checklist.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
In every phase of flight, if the pilot feels like they have nothing to do, they are probably wrong. Train the pilot to always question, what phase of flight am I in (climb, cruise, descent, etc.) and what do I need to do - the checklist will help them answer that question. After going through the appropriate checklist the next question is, ""What do I have to do next? What is coming up that I need to prepare for?"" and prepare fo the next task, phase of flight, etc. coming. Lastly, teach them to ask themselves, ""OK, what is after that?"" and take the time to prepare for the next, next task. Continue this process until there really is nothing else they can do, and then start back at the beginning. ""What phase of flight?"" Even in a long cross country with a very long cruise leg, the altimeter should be reset multiple times and the heading indicator should be set to compass multiple times.  

Discuss the consequences of not using the cruise checklist. What happens if the plane is not properly leaned on a long flight? This means the plane will be burning more fuel than planned and could run out of fuel before arriving at the destination. Also, pilotage and dead reckoning requires use of the heading indicator. Discuss how the heading indicator precesses, sometimes significantly, if the heading indicator is not reset to match the compass the pilot may be flying a ground track 20 or more degrees off what is planned. This can result in the pilot becoming lost very quickly.

activities.name: [04] X/C: Navigation Systems and Radar Services
activities.what: The subject matter of using ATC radar facilities or radio navigation aids while flying enroute
activities.why: To enable the pilot to navigate more efficiently and safely while enroute
activities.groundPrep:
Ground-based navigation (orientation, course determination, equipment, tests, and regulations).
Satellite-based navigation (e.g., equipment, regulations, database considerations, and limitations of satellite navigation).
Radar assistance to VFR aircraft (e.g., operations, equipment, available services, traffic advisories).

checklistItems.name: VOR - Tune and Identify
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: CDI - Center on TO/FROM (as appropriate)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Find the station you would like to track TO or FROM. You can quickly identify VORs on sectional charts by looking for a compass rose. The VOR identification box will be inside or somewhere near that compass rose. Find the frequency in that identification box, tune it in to your navigation receiver, and listen to the station's morse code. You don't need to know morse code, but you should be able to follow dashes and dots and confirm that what you hear matches what's on the sectional. That's how you know you have selected the correct VOR and that it is working properly.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Turn - To heading on OBS
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Tracking TO or FROM a VOR is the easiest exercise. To track TO the station simply rotate the selector (OBS) until the TO flag shows and the needle centers. To track away FROM the station on the current course, move the OBS until the FROM flag is showing and the needle centers.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Station Passage - Mark (as appropriate)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Regardless of whether you are tracking TO or FROM the station, once the needle is centered turn the aircraft to the heading marked on the OBS. With no wind the needle will stay centered. With wind, the aircraft will drift off course and a wind correction angle will be required to maintain the current course.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Signal Loss/Interference - Identify and Address
checklistItems.notesToPilot: You will know you are getting close to a station when the needle starts to deflect quickly. Don't chase the needle to keep it centered. Simply hold a steady heading. Within a few miles the needle will fully deflect to one side, and the flag will switch to indicate that you are now flying to or from the station, as applicable. Again, don't chase the needle for the first few miles; simply hold a heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: VOR 1 - Tune and Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Find the two VOR stations you think are closest to you. You can quickly identify VORs on sectional charts by looking for a compass rose. The VOR identification box will be inside or somewhere near that compass rose. Find the frequency for the first VOR in that identification box, tune it in to your navigation receiver, and listen to the station's morse code. You don't need to know morse code, but you should be able to follow dashes and dots and confirm that what you hear matches what's on the sectional. That's how you know you have selected the correct VOR and that it is working properly.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: CDI - Center on FROM
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Center the needle with the OBS and a FROM flag. Note the heading under the OBS.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Line of Position - Draw
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Draw an extended course line on your sectional using the VOR location (center of the compass rose) and the current OBS heading as the two points.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: VOR 2 - Tune and Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Find the second VOR station you think is closest to you. You can quickly identify VORs on sectional charts by looking for a compass rose. The VOR identification box will be inside or somewhere near that compass rose. Find the frequency for the VOR in that identification box, tune it in to your navigation receiver, and listen to the station's morse code. You don't need to know morse code, but you should be able to follow dashes and dots and confirm that what you hear matches what's on the sectional. That's how you know you have selected the correct VOR and that it is working properly.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: CDI - Center on FROM
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Using VOR 2, repeat the procedure from the first VOR.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Line of Position - Draw
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Using VOR 2, draw another line, repeating the procedure from the first VOR.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Position - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Your current position (but not necessarily heading) is the intersection of the two lines drawn from the VORs.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: VOR - Tune and Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Find the station you would like to track TO or FROM. You can quickly identify VORs on sectional charts by looking for a compass rose. The VOR identification box will be inside or somewhere near that compass rose. Find the frequency in that identification box, tune it in to your navigation receiver, and listen to the station's morse code. You don't need to know morse code, but you should be able to follow dashes and dots and confirm that what you hear matches what's on the sectional. That's how you know you have selected the correct VOR and that it is working properly.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Radial - Enter OBS
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Find the radial on the sectional you would like to track. Because radials emanate out from the station, when flying away from the VOR you will be tracking and flying on the same radial. When flying to the station you will be tracking a radial opposite the station, but not actually flying on that radial. When flying away from the station you always want to have a FROM flag, and when flying to the station you always want to have a TO flag. For example, if you are east of the station and want to fly away FROM the VOR, your OBS will say 90, your heading will be 090, and there will be a FROM flag. When flying TO the station from that position, the OBS will say 270, your heading will be 270, and there will be a TO flag. Your heading and the OBS should be reasonably close. Find the course you'd like to track and select it in the OBS, making sure that if you are flying away there is a FROM flag, and if flying to the station there is a TO flag.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Intercept Heading - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: There is no rule to determine the intercept heading, so common sense prevails. If you are far from the VOR, a 45 degree intercept angle will work fine, but closer to the station you may only want 30 degrees or less of intercept. To determine the angle take your desired course and subtract the intercept angle if the course is to your left, and add the intercept angle if it is to your right. For example, if you are flying south, but want to intercept the 100 degree radial away from the station, and you are at least 10 miles from the station, turn to a heading of 055. If you are flying north and want to intercept that same 100 degree radial, turn to a heading of 145.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Heading - Turn
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once you have determined the intercept heading, turn to it and hold the course.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: CDI Centers - Turn to track radial
checklistItems.notesToPilot: As the needle begins to center turn so your heading matches the OBS course. After you have centered the needle, add or subtract any wind correction angle to keep the needle centered.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Destination - Enter Direct To
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Every GPS, whether VFR or certified for IFR approaches, has a way to navigate direct to a waypoint. Usually it involves pressing the "direct to" button (D with the vector line symbol) and entering the waypoint ID. US mainland airports with lettered identifiers will require that you put a K before the letters. Airports with numbers don't have a K in advance. You can also navigate to VORs, intersections, NDBs, and more, by inputting their particular identifiers.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Course - Track
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once you've entered the waypoint to fly "direct to," the GPS will show a course line and a heading. There are a few types of headings usually displayed. Look for DTK, or desired track, for a compass heading to follow. TRK is your current track. If the DTK and TRK are different you will fly off course. Turn to line up the DTK and TRK to ensure you stay on course.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flight plan - Entered
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Every GPS system has a different method for entering flight plans. Regardless of how the plan is entered, you should be able to navigate between any types of waypoints you like, including airports, VORs, VFR waypoints, and even user-defined waypoints. Enter waypoints into the flight plan while on the ground and stationary. With many systems you can even enter the flight plan before starting the airplane. Save the plan and bring it up when you're ready to taxi. Verify the waypoints you've entered are correct and that they make sense based on your expected course on the map.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Waypoints - Track
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Once you've entered the waypoint to fly "direct to," the GPS will show a course line and a heading. There are a few types of headings usually displayed. Look for DTK, or desired track, for a compass heading to follow. TRK is your current track. If the DTK and TRK are different you will fly off course. Turn to line up the DTK and TRK to ensure you stay on course. Most modern GPS units will count down waypoint passage and alert you to any turns in advance of reaching the next waypoint.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flight plan - Edit (as required)
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Read the manual in advance so you know how to edit the flight plan. Like entering original flight plans, ensure that you verify the waypoints are correct on the map before you begin following the plan. It's easy to make a mistake on a flight plan edit, and blindly following the waypoints without verifying their locations and correct input into the GPS can result in getting well off course.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Signal Loss/Interference - Identify and Address
checklistItems.notesToPilot: In order to be certified, a GPS must have a method to alert the pilot to a loss of signal. Most signal losses are short and the unit will quickly regain the signal. In this case, simply continue on your heading and wait a few minutes to see if signal is restored. If not, follow the manual's procedure to regain signal. As with all navigation, you must maintain situational awareness at all times. If the GPS signal is totally lost and you have been following your navigation on a sectional chart or with VOR navigation, simply switch to one of these new methods of navigation.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: ATC Facility/Frequency - Identify/Tune
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Find the closest radar equipped air traffic control facility so that you can request VFR Traffic Advisories - commonly known as Flight Following. Workload permitting, these facilites will give you a transponder squawk code and assist you with identifying air traffic in your vicinity. Typically these services are provided by approach control at Class B/C airports and by Center controllers. Use the Chart Supplement or an EFB (Electronic Flight Bag) to find their frequencies.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Traffic Advisories - Request
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use the Sample Radio Script in the Prep section to practice the typical commincations you'll use to request flight following.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Undershooting or overshooting the radial.
commonErrors.details: When the turn to intercept begins, ask how long it should take to intercept. Ask how they will know they have intercepted. In other words, get the pilot thinking early about capturing the course. If overshooting happens regularly, discuss smaller intercept angles. Teach the pilot not to wait until the needle is centered to begin the course heading change.

commonErrors.name: Chasing the needle.
commonErrors.details: Stress that the pilot must be patient with station passage, and to fly a constant heading for the few miles leading up to, while over the station, and a few miles beyond it.

commonErrors.name: Not centering the CDI
commonErrors.details: This is an exercise best practiced on the ground at the student's pace until he or she can do it well. Reinforce the fact that radials emanate out from the station, and that the OBS must be centered with a FROM flag.

commonErrors.name: Failure to ID a second VOR.
commonErrors.details: In the ground lesson ensure the pilot understands the need to triangulate a position with two sources, and explain why. Watch for other normal errors associated with selecting, tuning, and verifying a VOR.

commonErrors.name: Failure to find position.
commonErrors.details: If the pilot executes the procedure and can't find his or her position, determine if the problem is in the procedure or inability to spot the current position based on pilotage. Often pilots will correctly triangulate their position and then be unable to determine their exact position with pilotage. Regular practice can help, as can climbing to better spot landmarks. Finally, it can be beneficial to pick a heading toward a landmark and verify its position. If unable to verify, the pilot can retriangulate the position, or select a third station to help.

commonErrors.name: Doesn't know hot to use the GPS
commonErrors.details: Have the pilot use a digital simulator before using the GPS in the airplane. Teach proper waypoint programming, including rules for K prefixes. Stress the need to verify that the waypoints are correct on the map page.

commonErrors.name: Not following the course.
commonErrors.details: Teach the pilot the various course readouts on the GPS and what they mean, including DTK and TRK.

commonErrors.name: Speaking too quickly
commonErrors.details: It is likely nerves that are causing these kinds of errors in flight. Be sure to practice the typical exchange on the ground or in a sim while performing flying duties. Then offer to fly the airplane the first couple of times while the pilot handles the radio interchange. Once the pilot gains a little confidence, requesting flight following will become as routine as normal communication in the pattern. Also, encourage them to become proficient with flight following communications by letting them know that it not only aids with identifying traffic, but is also training on the same radio communications they will experience in Class B and C airspace.

commonErrors.name: Failure to identify station
commonErrors.details: Often pilots will tune a station and then starting spinning the OBS without first ensuring it is the correct station and that it is being received properly. Ensure the pilot follows a standard flow of identifying and verifying every time a VOR is tuned.

commonErrors.name: Failure to turn for intercept
commonErrors.details: Make sure the pilot understands that radials are electronic courses, and that the airplane can be on a course, but on the wrong heading. The airplane needs to turn to the course in order to stay on that continued course.

commonErrors.name: Wrong TO/FROM flag
commonErrors.details: Pilots will sometimes spin an OBS without giving the needle a chance to catch up. Teach the pilot to aim for a heading close to what they think is correct and then slowly turn the OBS to center the needle. Remind the pilot that when flying to the station, the flag should read TO and when flying from the station it should read FROM, and that the heading should be close to the OBS.

prepItems.name: VOR Navigation
prepItems.details: There are several types of air navigation systems in use today. Navigation systems include any method a pilot uses to follow a predetermined flight path over the earth's surface. One common radio navigation receiver is the VOR.

prepItems.name: Global Positioning System (GPS)
prepItems.details: GPS stands for global positioning system. It uses a constellation of 24 satellites or more to provide very accurate navigation anywhere in the world.
