activities.name: [01] BASICS: Navigating To/From Practice Area
activities.what: Procedures and techniques to get to and from local practice area.
activities.why: To safely navigate to the practice area and back in preparation for solo flight. Plus, you don't have unlimited fuel.
activities.groundPrep:
Use of the Sectional chart and locating key landmarks to be used. Ensure they understand the location and use of the legend.
Demonstrate the use of the pilot's EFB (if one is being used).
Identify and define selected airspace and associated frequencies and procedures.
Demonstrate the use of the avionics to include the audio panel.

checklistItems.name: Frequencies - Identify and Tune
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use the point/select method (hand gestures) to emphasize tasks that are often not obvious.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If the practice area is within the bounds of an Approach control consider remaining in communication for traffic advisories.

checklistItems.name: Orientation - Determine and Navigate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Identify the compass headings relative to prominent features (highways, mountains and waterways).
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have student navigate back from practice area with and without help of electronics.

checklistItems.name: Landmarks - Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Note landmarks on the Sectional that you anticipate being able to locate. 
Note those landmarks that were apparent while aloft that the Sectional didn't necessarily highlight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: When dealing with similar landmarks, note differences in details that will set one apart from the other.

checklistItems.name: Airspace - Identify and Navigate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure an awarness of all of the intervening airspace and that pilot reponsibilites are understood.
checklistItems.teachingTips: When training takes place near congested airspace ensure the use of TAC charts when available.

checklistItems.name: Distances - Estimate/Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note the distance between prominent landmarks identified earlier and observe that distance while airborne to develope pilot estimating skill.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
The GPS can be used as an effective distance training tool. 
Put in a visibile waypoint like an airport and dim or cover the GPS display. 
Have the pilot estimate the distance visually, then check the GPS for the actual distance. 
With practice they can learn to identify distances within 10-percent.

checklistItems.name: Descent profile - Detemine and Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Compare distances with altitudes required at a certain landmark and estimate start of descent points.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Consider using a "rule-of-thumb" such as 500 feet for every two miles. 
Ensure the pilot as a basic understanding of time to cover a certain distance (i.e. 3 miles in 2 minutes).

checklistItems.name: Obstacles - Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Note obstacles (such as towers) and their elevation.
This is especially true around the practice area itself to ensure low altitude manuevers are not attempted.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Note when there are multiple towers.

commonErrors.name: Mistaken highways or towns
commonErrors.details:
Point out landmarks, such as major roads, cities, rivers, factories and other prominent features that would help get to and from the practice area and avoid obstacles and airspace. 
Compare their location with what the pilot sees on the Sectional to gain perspective.

commonErrors.name: Failure to make a freq change or call
commonErrors.details:
Discuss frequencies to monitor going to, while in, and coming back from the practice area. 
If there is no standard local frequency, consider CTAF or Guard.

commonErrors.name: Failure to recognize obstacles
commonErrors.details: Point out towers and other obstructions around the airport and in the practice area. Compare their location with what the pilot sees on the Sectional to gain perspective.

commonErrors.name: Doesn’t know specific airspace regs
commonErrors.details: Use a chart to identify and explain the airspace to be avoided, or communicated with, before entering.

completionStandards.description: Is able to verbally describe the basic steps in the desired maneuver/procedure, although cannot perform the maneuver or procedure yet
Can perform the basic procedure/maneuver with instructor coaching
Can perform the procedure/maneuver independently and safely; can identify and describe the desired PTS/ACS performance level
Consistently meets PTS/ACS standard
Consistently exceeds PTS/ACS standards (e.g. holds tolerances within half of PTS/ACS; if tolerance was +/- 100 feet, is able to perform at +/- 50 feet)

prepItems.name: Taxi, Run-up, Traffic Pattern
prepItems.details: Your instructor will probably have you taxi the airplane on your first lesson. Safe ground operations involve the coordinated use of the throttle, control yoke, and foot pedals. Steering with your feet is going to take some getting used to.

activities.name: [02] BASICS: Navigating To/From Local Airports
activities.what: Procedures and techniques to get to and from local airports.
activities.why: To safely navigate from and back to the local airport in preparation for solo flight.
activities.groundPrep:
Use of the Chart Supplement; Identify each runway, the associated primary taxiways, any hot spots or non-movement areas.
Use of the Sectional chart and locating key landmarks to be used. Ensure they understand the location and use of the legend.
Demonstrate the use of the pilot's EFB (if one is being used).
Identify and define selected airspace and associated frequencies and procedures.
Demonstrate the use of the avionics to include the audio panel.
Listen to and Identify the ATIS information.
Identify the departure and entry landmarks and associated altitudes for each airport.
Define the use of progressive taxi instructions.

checklistItems.name: Communications - Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure proper use of phraseology to achieve concise and accurate communications.
checklistItems.teachingTips: When working complex airspace (such as Class C) consider an extended Preflight Briefing in which the proposed flight is plotted on a Sectional and the various communication points are identified.

checklistItems.name: Obstacles - Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Verify that a safe clearance altitude is maintained relative to any obstacles around the airport.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Locate nearby airports that have obstacles listed in the Chart Supplement for selected runways (e.g. RWY 33: P-line) and discuss procedures to identify and avoid.

checklistItems.name: Orientation - Determine and Navigate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Identify compass headings relative to the airport from various prominent landmarks.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Note to the pilot the importance of always maintaining positional awareness. Outline the practice area on the Sectional using such landmarks as prominent highways, lakes, and powerlines, along with tracking the current radial of a nearby VOR. Using pilotage is an essential skill that can be taught early in flight training including being able to navigate the area around the home airport and nearby airports without electronic navigations aids.

checklistItems.name: Determine Altitude - Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Using chart and considering airspace and obstacles, determine and climb/descend to appropriate altitude.
checklistItems.teachingTips: During the Preflight Planning, discuss with the pilot the minimum safe altitudes for the selected maneuvers.

checklistItems.name: Determine Course - Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Using GPS or other electronic navaid, enter destination (Direct To or Nearest), interpret course, and steer to airport.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Ensure the pilot updates the Heading Indicator every 15 minutes and verifys the current position with the surrounding landmarks.

checklistItems.name: Frequencies - Identify and Tune
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure a complete understanding of the airport data block (on your aeronautical chart) and the frequencies noted as well as the content of the Chart Supplement.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Because of the wide variety of avionics in today's aircraft, it may be a appropriate to have the pilot identify and tune selected frequencies before 'engine start'. In some cases, PC based simulators (such as with the G1000) can be very effective in orienting the pilot to the various locations of displays and their controls.

checklistItems.name: Landmarks - Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note landmarks that provide the lead-in to the airport from each of the cardinal headings.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Have the pilot cut the segment of the Sectional covering the "local" practice area and mount it on a piece of 6x8 carboard that fits the knee pad. This avoids much of the clutter in the cockpit. Highlight key landmarks.

checklistItems.name: Runways- Determine and Orient
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Listen to automated weather or ATIS to determine appropriate runway. Using compass, GPS, charts, or other available information determine heading to enter or leave the landing pattern.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Work with the pilot in an extended pre-flight briefing to assure they can retrieve key points of information from the Chart Supplement. This would include such aspects as the runway surface, availability of fuel, locations of obstacles close to the runway threshold.
checklistItems.alternateProcedures: If the pilot intends using an EFB, ensure they are well versed in accessing Sectionals, Chart Suppliments and weather data.

checklistItems.name: Airspace - Identify and Navigate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Ensure a complete understanding of all adjacent airspace that may impinge on the home airport and any communications that may be needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: If a simulator is available, establish a flight in an area in which Class B or C airspace is prevalent and note how to identify the proximity of the aircraft and methods to avoid incursion through positional and /or altitude adjustment. Using a GPS or EFB coupled to the sim (or in the airplane) is a great tool for clearly showing the airspace boundaries, but be sure to also explain how to use visual landmarks to navigate airspace.

checklistItems.name: Distances - Estimate/Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note the distance between prominent landmarks identified earlier and observe that distance while airborne to develop estimating skills.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
When a GPS moving map display is available, relate the aircraft position to airports or other significant features and note the distances related by the display to the estimates seen with the eye. When returning the airport or heading to another easily visible checkpoint, cover or dim the GPS display and have the pilot estimate the distance before verifying with the GPS. Routine practice will quickly develop the pilot's (and your) distance estimating skills.
You can also use a sectional chart to estimate and check distances when you are over clearly identifiable landmarks.

checklistItems.name: Descent profile - Detemine and Execute
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Compare distances with altitudes required at specific landmarks to ensure starting the descent at the appropriate point to arrive at pattern altitude using a comfortable descent rate.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Mark on the Sectional the required altitudes and distances from landmarks. Note to the pilot that a typical (and comfortable) descent is 500 fpm. At a typical descent speed of 90 knots, that allows for 750 feet per mile.

commonErrors.name: Failed to identify hostile airspace
commonErrors.details: Use the Sectional or TAC chart to identify and explain the airspace which must be avoided (or communicated with) before entering. (See Teaching Tips)

commonErrors.name: Not using the Chart Supplement
commonErrors.details: Have the pilot find selected airport attributes in the Chart Supplement to improve their familiarity. (See Teaching Tips)

commonErrors.name: Didn't use landmarks
commonErrors.details: Point out landmarks, such as major roads, cities, rivers, factories and other prominent features that would help get to and from the airport and avoid obstacles and undesirable airspace.

commonErrors.name: Not using right frequencies
commonErrors.details: Discuss frequencies to monitor while leaving or returning to local airport. (See Teaching Tips)

commonErrors.name: Excessive descent rates to pattern
commonErrors.details: Using either eye, GPS distance or landmarks, point out where descent must be started to reach pattern altitude. 2000' above the field at 5 miles is a good starting point. (See Teaching Tips)

commonErrors.name: Pilot positional disorientation.
commonErrors.details: Have student navigate away from (and back to) the airport with and without help of electronic nav aids. (See Teaching Tips)

commonErrors.name: Didn't recognize minimum safe altitudes
commonErrors.details: Point out towers and other obstructions around the airport.

commonErrors.name: Failed to communicate at key points
commonErrors.details: Discuss and simulate communications sequence for leaving and returning to local airport. (See Teaching Tips)

commonErrors.name: Poor choice of altitudes for the selected route.
commonErrors.details: Ensure the pilot understands the reason for altitude selection either for airspace or obstacle separation. Using scenario format, have the pilot practice determining the correct altitude during ground training. Be sure to vary the direction from which they approach the airport.

commonErrors.name: Inappropriate departure/incoming corridor.
commonErrors.details: Review the area on the Sectional to ensure the pilot's positional awareness with respect to local landmarks. Use scenarios on the ground with approaching local airports from different directions and with different wind conditions so they can practice determining how to approach an airport. Make sure they are proficient in these basic skills before having them attempt in the airplane.

completionStandards.description: Is able to verbally describe the basic steps in the desired maneuver/procedure, although cannot perform the maneuver or procedure yet
Can perform the basic procedure/maneuver with instructor coaching
Can perform the procedure/maneuver independently and safely; can identify and describe the desired PTS/ACS performance level
Consistently meets PTS/ACS standard
Consistently exceeds PTS/ACS standards (e.g. holds tolerances within half of PTS/ACS; if tolerance was +/- 100 feet, is able to perform at +/- 50 feet)

prepItems.name: Technique: Charting Your Course - Sectionals Contain a Wealth of Information
Cross-Country Departure Procedures (Maneuvers Guide)
prepItems.details: To develop the ability to properly establish the aircraft on a cross-country route after leaving the departure airport.

activities.name: [05] X/C: Lost Procedures
activities.what: The systematic procedure for reorienting when if you get lost.
activities.why: To help ensure a safe and successful conclusion to the flight.
activities.groundPrep:
Methods to determine position.
Use of prominent landmarks.
Importance of recording times over waypoints.
Assistance available if lost (e.g., radar services, communication procedures).
How to use navigation systems/facilities and/or contact an ATC facility for assistance.
Possible scenarios where a pilot could become lost (e.g. An EMP took out all your avionics and backups)

checklistItems.name: Time - Note
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Write down current time. Determine how much fuel is remaining (in terms of time) and write that time down minus 10 minutes. If you are not within gliding distance of an airport when the fuel duration deadline arrives, you will need to set up for an off-airport landing.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Advise the pilot that if an airport is not within gliding distance when the time listed as "fuel duration" expires, they must set-up for an off-airport landing.

checklistItems.name: Climb - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Increased altitude will provide better radio reception and visibility--5,000 feet AGL should be sufficient.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
At a point early in the flight training have the pilot fly to a location they haven't been exposed to at 1,000 feet AGL. Ask them to identify one or more prominent landmarks. Have them climb in successive 1,000 foot increments and repeat the exercise. They will gain a valuable awareness of the important perspective that altitude provides.

A further exericse would be to have the pilot brainstorm what they would do if a low cloud ceiling prevented them from being able to climb.

checklistItems.name: GPS or VOR fixes - Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Use the NEAREST function on your GPS to locate airports or waypoints.
Get lines of position from area VORs to get a fix on your position, or simply fly TO what may be the nearest VOR.
If the last checkpoint was a prominent one, consider reversing course and reestablishing its location.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Confidence in their ability needs constant reinforcement by repetition. At some point during several early flight lesson, have the pilot tune and identify a navaid using the Sectional chart. Then have them locate their position relative to that navaide and track to it.

checklistItems.name: Landmarks on chart - Identify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Look for distinctive landmarks on the ground, such as roads, rivers, and towns, and attempt to find them on your chart. Find the nearest airport as this may be the pilots best option. Don't spend any more than a few minutes trying to orient yourself before seeking help.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Make sure the pilot has the Sectional oriented for proper relationship with the direction of flight and is cognizant of the relative compass headings. Having check points that are no more than 10-15 minutes apart is an important aspect to the preflight planning to help prevent getting lost.

checklistItems.name: Power - Max endurance
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Conserve fuel--55% power setting is good.
checklistItems.teachingTips: This is a power setting that the pilot should have either memorized or that can be found quickly from the POH. It's a good item to write down on the flight log form.

checklistItems.name: Communicate - Nearest ATC facility
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
The nearest FSS frequency is available on the Sectional. They can provide the ATC frequency. If unable to reach FSS or ATC, use 121.5. 
ATC can provide radar services and can assist with more resources as needed.
The first questions ATC will ask is how much fuel is available in terms of flight duration--have this number ready. Verify the transponder is ON.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Typically FSS is the primary point of contact as its frequencies are listed on the Sectional. 
The FSS can provide the local ATC frequency for possible radar identification.  
Don't hesitate to declare an emergency, especially when less than 30 minutes of fuel remain. Ensure the pilot understands the use of transponder code 7700. 
At some point in the training (probably during the the dual cross-country), have the pilot locate the nearest FSS frequency and request the local ATC frequency as an exercise. Have the pilot monitor that frequency to hear the kinds of information being exchanged.

checklistItems.name: Confess - Admit you are lost
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Tell the controller you’re lost and you need assistance. They will give you a unique transponder code in order to locate you on her radar screen.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Emphasize to the pilot that being lost is not a major problem--because they will have techniques and procedures to locate themselves,. But not admitting to themself that they are uncertain of their current position is a problem.

checklistItems.name: Comply - Do what you're told
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Follow ATC's directions if they provide radar vectors. They are there to help and can see where you are.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure the pilot understands that, while they are getting assistance, they are still the PIC and must make responsible decisions. 
Pilots under stress may not recall critical tasks, procedures or numbers. Discuss this with the pilot so they are aware of that possibility.

commonErrors.name: Failure to seek assistance
commonErrors.details: Note to the pilot that the FSS and ATC controllers use standard procedures and that it is imperative that the pilot respond to the instructions they are given. Explain how the controllers can see the aircraft on radar and have a much "larger" persepective. Trust them to be able to get you to the closest available airport even though your instincts might be telling you otherwise. Disorientation is insidious and can lead the pilot in the wrong direction. Use NTSB report examples to illustrate this point.

commonErrors.name: Staying low
commonErrors.details: Have the pilot troubleshoot the reasons why communications might not be available. Be sure they understand the line of sight operation of VHF radios and how terrain, the curvature of the earth, or other obstacles can limit communications over long distances. Have the pilot fly a gradual 360-degree turn in the climb to assess the entire area.

commonErrors.name: Failure to use navaids
commonErrors.details: Often the inability to use the avionics is a result of apprehension on the part of the pilot and the mind gets fuzzy. Repetition is a key to building basic skills and confidence. If available, provide the pilot lots of practice in a simulator. There are also internet and tablet based apps that make learning VOR orientation much easier for new pilots.

commonErrors.name: Failure to use landmarks
commonErrors.details: This could the result of the heading indicator not set to the compass. Becoming disoriented due to low visibility. Have the pilot orient the Sectional to the direction of flight based on a cardinal compass heading (NESW). Locate a nearby landmark outside the cockpit and see if it can be found on the Section in the same relative position. Help the pilot develop the habit of setting the Heading Indicator to the magnetic compass regularly. This can be accomplished by having the pilot perform a regular flow of the aircraft's configuration and operating status.

commonErrors.name: Not conserving fuel
commonErrors.details: Use about 55% power to conserve fuel. Advise to the pilot that as soon as they are unsure of their position they should throttle back to not only conserve fuel, but to make the landscape go by more slowly so they have time to evaluate what they are seeing.

commonErrors.name: Unfamiliar with charts
commonErrors.details: Ensure the pilot has studied the Legend on the Sectional where this kind of information is portrayed. Give them practice during ground and simulator training to identify FSS frequencies and simulated radio communications with them.

commonErrors.name: Failure to follow instructions
commonErrors.details: Pilots are often hesitant to ask for help or to declare an emergency because they might feel embarrased or fear getting in trouble with ATC/FAA. Assure them that ATC only wants to help and there is often not any paperwork. Even if there was, it is much better to be on the ground dealing with some paperwork than the alternative if they continue into poor conditions or can't find an airport. Share examples with them from NTSB and NASA reports about the results of continuing without help.

commonErrors.name: Not confessing
commonErrors.details:
On a cross-country flight they should not allow more than the time to the next checkpoint before making the confession to themselves and taking action. 
Use the Four "C's" as a reminder of the tasks involved (Climb/Communicate/Confess/Comply).

Consistently meets PTS/ACS standard
Consistently exceeds PTS/ACS standards (e.g. holds tolerances within half of PTS/ACS; if tolerance was +/- 100 feet, is able to perform at +/- 50 feet)

prepItems.details: To develop the ability to explain and execute lost procedures, selecting the best course of action when given a lost situation.

prepItems.name: PHAK - Lost Procedures (Ch 16.34)
prepItems.details: Read (Ch 16.34) on Lost Procedures

prepItems.name: ACS - Lost Procedures
prepItems.details: Read Lost Procedures (p. 40) to see the checkride requirements for this procedure.

prepItems.name: VFR Flight Following
prepItems.details: While flying VFR, it can be useful to have an extra set of eyes on your flight. Radar flight following can be a valuable resource.

prepItems.name: Lost and Found
prepItems.details: In this section we will discuss the best way to handle getting off course, becoming lost, and asking for help.

prerequisites.name: [04] X/C: Navigation Systems and Radar Services

activities.name: [07] X/C: Night Cross Country Flight
activities.what: a training flight for practicing cross country navigation at night
activities.why: to enable the pilot to carry out the safest cross country operations at night
activities.groundPrep:
The goal of this lesson is to complete a night cross country training flight of over 100 nautical miles distance. NOTE: A Total of 3 hours of night training are required as per 14 CFR 61.109

NOTE: The notes in the lessons for Night Takeoffs and Landings and Night Cross Country are very similar due to the shared content.

Night flight planning. When planning a flight at night, local or cross country, the pilot has to use caution to avoid flying into unseen weather or terrain. When planning a cross country chose a route with easily identifiable and lit way points and plan on flying near airports in case of a emergency or precautionary landing is necessary. It will be very difficult to identify safe off airport landing spots at night.

Benefits and hazards of night flying. 
Benefits - smoother air, better aircraft performance, easier to spot other aircraft, reduced air traffic and BEAUTIFUL. 
Hazards - being unable to see terrain and clouds, difficult to do off airport landings safely, high risk of spatial disorientation or controlled flight into terrain.

Night vision and adaptation. It takes approximately 30 minutes for our eyes to adapt to seeing at night and seconds to lose that adaptation. Try to spend 30 minutes outdoors or in a dimly lit or dark room before flying. Avoid looking directly at bright lights and shield your eyes when near planes with strobes or bright lights on to avoid losing night adaptation. Our night vision is poorest looking directly ahead. Need to use peripheral vision to see an object clearly. Our eyes are also especially sensitive to oxygen, which is why the FAA recommends using supplemental oxygen as low as 5000 feet MSL at night. 

Night illusions. Review the night illusions that commonly affect pilots. These illusions affect your ability to see and avoid other aircraft, avoid spatial disorientation and fly a safe approach path to the runway. Review the information in the AIM 8-1-5 Illusions in Flight and AIM 8-1-6 Vision in Flight. The lack of normal visual references at night, even in good visibility, makes a pilot susceptible to illusions often thought limited to IFR flight.                            

Airport, obstacle and aircraft lighting. Common runway, taxiway, approach lighting system and visual glide path lighting. How to determine what lighting will be available at their destination airport and obstacle lighting. How to interpret aircraft lighting. When aircraft lights must be used and how to avoid blinding other pilots. How to turn on pilot controlled lighting. How to review NOTAMs for airport lighting status.

checklistItems.name: Minimum required equipment - Verify
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Additional equipment is required for night time operations by 14 CFR 91.205 (c). It is critical for safety that you verify that the equipment is properly operating prior to flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: IFR equipment - Consider
checklistItems.notesToPilot: During night flight, outside visual references are significantly reduced. The equipment required for instrument flight by 14 CFR 91.205(d) like the attitude indicator and heading indicator are invaluable during night flight. Strongly consider ensuring they are working correctly before a flight at night.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Similar to required night equipment, be ready to fly at night even if you are planning to complete your flight shortly before sunset. 

If the aircraft is not equipped with an attitude indicator the pilot must have adequate visual reference outside. Flight at night without a moon, over unlit terrain or over water is especially hazardous if the aircraft is not equipped with an attitude indicator. Flying with a full moon or over very well lit terrain can offset this risk.

checklistItems.name: White flashlight - Use
checklistItems.notesToPilot: While night vision is compromised by bright white light, it does provide the best illumination for catching any issues during the preflight inspection. If you choose to preflight using white light, remember to give your eyes at least 30 minutes to recover their night vision before flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Airport Lighting - Review
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use the Chart Supplement and Airport Diagrams to determine what lighting is available at the airport. It is important to determine the location of the airport beacon (if available) relative to the runways to help orient yourself with the runways. Learn what runway and approach lighting is available. Check NOTAMs for inop lighting systems.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flight Planning - Adjust
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Clouds and terrain are not easily seen at night and, as a result, it is easy for a pilot to encounter one or both inadvertently. Carefully check forecasts for cloud bases and tops. If they are forecast within 2000' of your planned route/altitude, change your route/altitude or cancel the flight. Watch for a close temperature/dewpoint spread in the forecast since that could signal the potential for fog to form. Use the MEF value in each quadrant on the VFR sectional as a quick reference to remain above terrain. Consider planning the flight near busy roads and over airports with beacons even if that is not the most direct route to your destination.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Familiarity with instrument approach procedures can help the pilot select safe altitudes and routes to approach an airport to land at night. If the pilot plans on becoming instrument rated emphasize the benefits of filing and flying IFR at night even on VFR nights.

checklistItems.name: Navigation systems - Set
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Just like with any cross country flight, be sure to program and set/program all navigation equipment prior to flight so you can minimize distractions while flying. Even on paper aeronauitical charts, make adjustments for night conditions by using a dark easily visible course line.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Flight instruments - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: The reduced outside references during night flight can result in the pilot to experience spatial disorientation. Be sure to use the flight instruments to supplement aircraft control on all phases of night flight.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Do at least one lesson on basic instrument maneuvers before taking the pilot up at night. This will give the pilot some practice using the attitude indicator to determine the aircraft's actual attitude in reference to the natural horizon.

checklistItems.name: Heading bug - Reference
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If installed on your aircraft, the heading bug can be useful to maintain your situational awareness of runway headings on climbout, cruise, and during the approach for landing.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Interior lights - Dim
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Be sure to dim the interior lights (panel, instrument, avionics, etc.) to improve your night vision. Keeping the interior lights too bright can decrease the effectiveness of your night vision and can cause a glare on the windscreen.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Ensure students know how to control cockpit lights including the brightness level of installed avionics and GPS. 

Ensure the pilot knows how to turn down the brightness or switch to night mode when using tablets.

checklistItems.name: Exterior lights - Use as appropriate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: When operating at night be sure to always use the beacon and position lights. Use of the landing, taxi, and strobe lights should done with consideration to other pilots' night vision and any environmental conditions that could affect your visibility.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Position/navigation lights and beacon must be on from sunset to sunrise before the aircraft is moved. It is simplest to turn on the beacon before starting the aircraft and then turn on the position lights immediately after starting the aircraft.

Landing light, while not required for private pilot flights, should be used for night landings as standard procedure.

checklistItems.name: Position/NAV lights - Interpret
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Knowing which combination of the green, white, and red nav lights signal another aircraft's orientation to you is not something to guess at during flight. Be sure to review this before flight so that you can immediately identify which way any traffic you see is flying in relative your path.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the opposing aircraft light is not moving and has a red light on your right, this means the plane is flying directly at your plane. Both aircraft should alter their course to the right. An easy way to remember this is "Red on Right, reTURN". 

A white light directly ahead of you with flashing red above or below indicates the plane is flying away from you.

A green light and white light indicates the plane is flying from your left to right. 

A red light and white light indicates the plane is flying from your right to left.

checklistItems.name: Airport beacon - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Nighttime conditions can make lighted landmarks appear closer than they actually are. Use airport beacons to help prevent descending too low when arriving at an airport (especially unfamiliar ones). By staying at safe altitude until you can identify the runway lights and set up for a normal pattern. Be way of descending to soon and utilize the the visual glideslope if available.
checklistItems.teachingTips: On the night cross country have the pilot practice finding airports using airport beacons. Ask them, based on beacon color and sequence, if the airport's they see are military or civilian, helipads or sea plane bases. Ask them which airports would be appropriate for a precautionary landing based on beacon color.

checklistItems.name: Runway lights - Activate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Many airports have pilot controlled runway lights that will automatically shut off after 15 minutes. Be sure to periodically activate the lights by clicking the radio on the CTAF (7 times for high, 5 for medium, and 3 for low low intensity). Be sure to review airport information during your flight planning to find out what type of lighting system is installed at your destination.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
If the runway lights don't activate, verify the appropriate frequency and try again with slower clicks.

Runway lights are on a 15 minute timer. Remind the pilot to turn on the runway lights when they arrive at the airport, even if they are already on. Otherwise the pilot risks the lights turning off automatically and unexpectedly. 

High intensity runway lights are VERY bright white lights and will blind the pilot easily if used in good visibility conditions. Even if the airport has high intensity lights, start at low or medium intensity and step up the lighting to high only if required due to low visibility.

checklistItems.name: Red/blue/green flashlight - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Bright white light can ruin your night vision. Using a red light in the cockpit will allow you to see without compromising your vision, but if used on a chart the red light will wash out magenta colored markings. Using a flashlight with a blue light on charts can help you maintain your night vision and see all of the chart information. Another option is to use a green flashlight or very dim white light.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Some aircraft are equipped with appropriately dim white or red lighting in the interior. Even if the aircraft is equipped make sure to have a flashlight within easy arms reach in case of electrical failure or lighting failure.

Any colored lighting used will ""wash out"" that color on charts and instruments. A green light will make the green arc on the airspeed indicator very difficult to see. A red light washes out magenta on charts, blue will wash out blue markings.

checklistItems.name: Visual Glide Slope Indicators - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Choose runways and airports with visual glide slope indicators if at all possible. These lights help the pilot remain clear of terrain and on a safe approach path to the runways.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Empasize the use of glide slope indicators to maintain obstacle clearance at night and at unfamiliar airports.

checklistItems.name: Non-VFR flight - Avoid
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Caution must be taken to avoid inadvertently flying into clouds or other low visibility conditions during night operations. Be sure to get a thorough weather briefing prior to flight. While in flight, look for signs that could signify poor visibility conditions. For example, if the ground lights begin to have halos around them or disappear altogether, you may be overflying fog or a cloud deck or even entering a layer of clouds. Immediately reference your flight instruments and exit the conditions.

Flying over water or large unlit areas at night can quickly lead to spatial disorientation. Use the of the flight instruments will be critical. Seriously consider not flying in these conditions without first achieving an instrument rating.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Instruct the pilot to carefully check forecasts for cloud bases and tops. If they are forecast within 2000' of the planned route/altitude, change the route/altitude or cancel the flight. The GFA tool provides cloud bases/tops forecasts. TAFs will provide cloud base forecasts. METARs and PIREPS provide current condition information.

The pilot needs to be especially aware of the temperature/dewpoint spread reported by ATIS/AWOS/ASOS/METARs. As night falls the air cools towards the dew point. Low clouds or fog can form very quickly when the temperature and dewpoint converge.

Emphasize the pilot should avoid flight at night over unlit terrain or water without a full moon to provide additional lighting. Flight in these conditions without a full moon will result in spatial disorientation for a pilot that is not using their flight instruments.

commonErrors.name: Failing to consider and plan for the reduced ability to see and avoid terrain and clouds at night.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Emphasize how difficult it is to see and avoid terrain and clouds at night. Careful planning with plenty of safety margin is required to ensure safe VFR flying at night. Take the pilot to an airport they are somewhat familiar with on a moonless night and ask them to locate unlit power lines and buildings near the airport. If in an area with hills, ask them how close the nearest hill is using visual references alone. They will quickly find out it is practically impossible to identify these obstacles visually at night. If this is a good weather night emphasize how much harder it would be to see the same objects in marginal VFR conditions. Do a search in the NTSB database for night time accidents. Review the accidents with the pilot. Two such accidents are in the resources links below.

commonErrors.name: Not determining the airport lighting available for the flight.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Ask the pilot how they will maintain proper glide path on final? Will a VASI or PAPI be available? Is it operating? Are these lights available on the left or right side of the landing runway? If the destination airport has all lighting available, search NOTAMS and find an airport with the runway lighting or airport beacon NOTAM'd out of service. Then ask the pilot to describe the lighting available to them when they arrive at the airport. How they will determine where the runway is relative to the beacon and how will they differentiate the runway from surrounding roadway or other lighting.

commonErrors.name: Flying on a moonless night without attitude indicator.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: If the aircraft is not equipped with an attitude indicator the pilot must have adequate visual reference outside. Flight at night without a moon, over unlit terrain or over water is especially hazardous if the aircraft is not equipped with an attitude indicator. Flying with a full moon or over very well lit terrain can offset this risk.

commonErrors.name: Ignoring instruments and, as a result, becoming disoriented.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Emphasize the concept of cross checking what the pilot sees outside with the flight instruments. There are several illusions that can cause the pilot to inadvertently get into an unusual attitude. Any time the pilot does not have clear view of the natural horizon they are at risk of spatial disorientation without reference to the instruments.

commonErrors.name: Not setting the heading indicator to compass before take off, during flight or before landing.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Ensure the pilot has a strategy for setting the heading indicator to compass at night. Depending on the aircraft the magnetic compass may be unlit or poorly lit, requiring the pilot to illuminate the magnetic compass to get the current magnetic heading.

Emphasize the importance of setting heading indicator to compass in every phase of flight (doing so is on most checklists) and before doing turns to headings using the heading indicator. To demonstrate how important this is, do an hour long flight in the pattern without setting the heading indicator to compass and, at the end of the flight, have the pilot compare the acutal compass heading with the heading indicator's reading. Most mechanical heading indicators will be reading significantly different from actual compass heading after one hour.

commonErrors.name: Starting with interior lights on at the brightest setting.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
If the aircraft has very bright interior lights, show the pilot what happens to their adapted night vision when the bright lights are turned on. Then demonstrate starting with the interior lights at their lowest possible setting and slowly turning them up to a useful level that does not blind the pilot.

commonErrors.name: Pilot confusion about when position/navigation lights and beacon must be working and on.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Beacon and position/navigation lights must be on sunset to sunrise. Remind the pilot if they can't see the sun, they need lights on to see and be seen.  "If you can't see the sun, turn lights on"

commonErrors.name: Not paying attention to the location of the airport beacon relative to the runway and airport.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion: 
In preflight planning have the pilot describe the location of the airport beacon relative to the airport itself and the runways. Where is the beacon located? On the field? in the center? on a hill near the field? From the direction of travel will the aiport beacon be before or after (or left or right) of the runway? Determining this information ahead of time will make finding the airport and runway much easier.

commonErrors.name: Clicking too fast, resulting in runway lights not turning on.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Find a video or audio recording of a metronome operating at 90 bpm (beats per minute) and play it for the pilot. This timing will activate pilot controlled lighting.

commonErrors.name: Failing to turn on the runway lights on arrival.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Train the pilot to turn on the runway lights to help find the airport. Then turn the runway lights on again on downwind. To help them see what can happen, consider staying at altitude and letting the lights turn off so the pilot can see what it would look like if they forget to restart the lights on downwind.

commonErrors.name: Turning the runway lights up so high that they blind the pilot.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Go to an airport with high, medium and low intensity runway lights. Approach and land with the runway lights on low or medium setting. Verify there are no aircraft on base or final. Once you've landed, stop on the runway and turn the lights up to the high intensity setting. Typically a pilot only has to be blinded once to know using high intensity lighting unnecessarily is not desireable. Turn the runway lights back to medium or low intensity and exit the runway.

commonErrors.name: Using a very bright light or looking directly into a light - resulting in loss of night vision.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Many pilots use a red LED headlamp for night flight, especially in aircraft with dim or no interior lighting. Some pilots may be disoriented by the motion of the light in the cockpit and may need another option. 

Lightweight/portable clip on reading lights with either very dim white lights or red lights are a great option to illuminate the cockpit without requiring the pilot to use their hands on the flashlight.

commonErrors.name: Assuming the same weather conditions that are good for VFR flight during the day are adequate for night flight.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
If a simulator is available set up a short similated cross country flight that starts with good visibility and then add a low undercast layer for the pilot to attempt descending through. Set up another simulation with a VFR legal ceiling of 1,200 feet and have the pilot attempt to fly to another nearby airport without entering the clouds. 

Review the NTSB report link below about the recent Cirrus crash in Colorado. While the airport had VFR conditions the plane's reported altitude was above the reported ceiling.  Review the NTSB's report on JFK Jr.'s Fatal Crash.

commonErrors.name: Not verifying attitude indicator and heading indicator are working when planning to fly near sunset/dark.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Check squawks before flight. During taxi the heading indicator should indicate turns to the left and right as the plane turns. In the runup the attitude indicator should be fully erect and accurately match the outside world (e.g. wings level with the nose "dot" on or very close to the horizon bar).

commonErrors.name: Not verifying night equipment is working when planning to fly near sunset/dark.
commonErrors.details: Suggestion: Emphasize to the pilot that while night equipment is not required for daytime flight. Flights can be unexpected delayed or diverted, requiring a later return to base than planned. If the pilot plans to fly within two hours of sunset it is a good idea to verify all required equipment for night flight is available and the lighting works in the aircraft.

commonErrors.name: Blinding other pilots with strobes, landing and/or taxi lights.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Remind the pilot how their lights affect other pilots. Use strobes only when entering/on the runway and in flight. Turn off the taxi and landing light while in the runup if other aircraft are taxiing towards you. If holding short of the runway at night turn off your landing and taxi lights when another plane is on short final. Turn the lights back on before taking the runway. If the plane is equipped with both a taxi and landing light turn off the landing light once clear of the runway and taxi using the taxi light.

commonErrors.name: Misinterpreting position and direction of other aircraft based on poor understanding of lighting.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
The following procedure can help quickly interpret the position and direction of other aircraft.
1. Does the plane appear to be moving? If not it is either flying directly away or towards you. CAUTION!
2. If the unmoving plane has a red light on the right it is on a collision course with you. Remember "Red on Right, reTURN". Adjust your course to the right. The other pilot should do the same thing.
3. If the unmoving plane has a white light and a beacon, it's flying away from you. Take care pass on the right if you will overtake the plane. "White light, you're all right."
4. If the plane is moving take a couple seconds to observe it's direction. The position lights become a secondary indicator at this point.

commonErrors.name: Failing to recognize night illusions (e.g. black hole approach) and flying a lower or higher than normal approach path.
commonErrors.details:
Suggestion:
Review common night illusions like black hole approaches and the resulting tendency to fly a lower than normal approach. Emphasize the use of visual glide slope indicators to remain on a safe approach path to the runway that will ensure terrain and obstacle clearance and help combat the natural tendency to fly too high or low.

activities.name: [06] X/C: Diversion
activities.what: Procedure to head to an unplanned airport
activities.why: Sometimes you can't get there from here
activities.groundPrep:
Situations that require deviations from flight plan and/or ATC instructions.
How to select an appropriate diversion airport.
The information required to make a safe diversion.
Balancing cockpit tasks and appropriately prioritizing.
Knowing when to abondon an original flight plan and divert.

checklistItems.name: Appropriate divert field - Determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Assess the situation and make a determination based on service needs, urgency, safety, and anything else that may apply. Choosing the nearest airport may be helpful in an emergency, but it may be unhelpful if there is a strong crosswind. Once you've settled on an airport, consider whether it can accommodate your aircraft- length, width, elevation, facilities, approaches. There are many tools to help, including the nearest function on the GPS. If you have time, a chart is often the best way to find a diversion airport and quickly determine whether it is suitable. An EFB with a current weather feed can help determine the winds and favored runways quickly.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Heading and altitude to airport - Estimate/determine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use whatever resources are available in order to determine the heading to the airport. You can program it into a GPS, tune in a VOR, or estimate a heading on a chart. If using a chart, take a straight edge and draw a line from your current position to the airport. Then, by holding the same angle, take the straight edge and line it up over a VOR and across the compass rose to get an estimated heading. Be sure to select an appropriate altitude for the direction and route of flight. Many EFBs have a feature that will allow you to quickly determine the distance and heading right on the chart.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Turn - To estimated heading
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Turn to the estimated heading.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Time - Note
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Note the time you diverted. This will be critical to your dead reckoning calculations.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Heading - Refine
checklistItems.notesToPilot: If using GPS, following the DTK heading to the airport. Otherwise, use a plotter and E6B to get an exact heading. Adjust your heading as necessary to fly the course to the airport.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Track - Confirm
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Using pilotage (chart and landmarks), confirm that you are heading in the right direction.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Airspace - Review
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Extend track on chart to confirm no airspace, terrain, or obstacle problems.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Speed, time, and fuel - Calculate
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Use an E6B, EFB, or other calculation method to determine the groundspeed, arrival time, and fuel consumption to your divert airport. Estimate first, refine as needed.
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

checklistItems.name: Approach and landing - Plan
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Review information on chart or in the Chart Supplement for frequencies, runway length, pattern, orientation, and elevation
checklistItems.teachingTips: N/A

commonErrors.name: Inability to calculate time, fuel, or distance.
commonErrors.details: Once established on the new heading, make sure the pilot can determine the time, fuel, and distance remaining and what's required to arrive at the new airport. They should be able to tell you how many minutes the flight will take, how much fuel will be required, and how much will remain upon landing. Practice using all available resources, including traditional E6B calculations, EFB applications, and GPS. Make sure the pilot knows how to easily and efficiently use all these resources in a classroom setting, in a simulator, and then in the airplane.

commonErrors.name: Selecting unsuitable airport
commonErrors.details: Practice this skill on the ground though a variety of discussion-based scenarios. Quiz the pilot to select a diversion airport based on different scenario questions, such as unforecast weather, low fuel, stronger-than-forecast winds, a closed runway at the destination, a sick passenger, mechanical problems, and more. Have the pilot go through selecting the airport, determining its suitability, and then determining heading, time, and fuel enroute. Transition the same practice to the simulator, which offers realistic weather scenarios, and can bring the pracitce up to real-time decision making. When the pilot is comfortable and making good choices in the simulator, transition the skill to the airplane.

commonErrors.name: Inability to determine a heading.
commonErrors.details: Encourage the pilot to use all available resources. Maybe there's a VOR near the new airport where he or she can track a radial, or if using a tablet or panel-mounted GPS, a quick direct-to will work. Many EFB applications enable the user to touch an airport and get time, fuel, and distance from the current position, which would save multiple steps in the diversion task. Finally, an initial estimate of the heading based on a guess from the chart will at least get the airplane headed in the correct direction.

commonErrors.name: Failure to turn
commonErrors.details: Many pilots will continue along the original route while they determine heading, time en route, fuel, and other parameters. Teach the pilot to turn immediately after determining the airport and an initial heading. To do otherwise wastes fuel and time.

commonErrors.name: Failure to note the time.
commonErrors.details: Explain to the student the reasons for noting the time, including fuel burn calculations and being able to determine when you should arriving or likely have passed your destination.

commonErrors.name: Being behind the airplane; not planning for approach and landing.
commonErrors.details: Especially if the diversion airport is close, this busy time can overwhelm new pilots. Provide skills to help them slow down the pace of the flight to what they need, including staying high and overflying the airport or circling outside the airspace until the arrival plan is complete. Work with the pilot to develop tasks that must be accomplished by a certain point. For example, by 20 miles from the airport the pilot should have received the weather, input the necessary frequencies, and repared a basic pattern entry plan. By 10 miles out the initial call to ATC or the CTAF should be made and a plan finalized to enter the pattern. By at least a mile and a half away the target altitude should be reached, and so on.

commonErrors.name: Not checking airspace
commonErrors.details: Remind the student that a diversion is like a new flight plan, and it requires a review of all classes of airspace and special use airspace along the route.

commonErrors.name: Failure to fly a correct heading.
commonErrors.details: By practicing the ability to flight plan and divert on the ground, the pilot should be able to easily transfer the skill first to a simulator, and then to the airplane. If possible, use GPS. Otherwise, a plotter on a chart works well.

commonErrors.name: Failure to confirm the new course.
commonErrors.details: Make sure the pilot draws a new course line and confirms that course through pilotage once the diversion has been made.

activities.name: [02] Postflight Analysis
activities.what: A methodical approach to assessing a pilot's performance during a flight and developing a plan for growth in future flights.
activities.why: To enhance efficiency and safety by improving pilot performance.
activities.groundPrep:
Benefits of post-flight debrief
How to make honest flight assessments
Importance of debriefs beyond trianing and into post-training flying"

checklistItems.name: Flight - Complete
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name: Postflight Analysis Form - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Following your flight, review the major maneuvers and grade your performance on each one. For any areas that were less than perfect, brainstorm ideas about how to improve your performance for the next flight. From the ideas, create a plan that you can use to practice prior to your next flight.

The Postflight Analysis Form is a useful guide to accomplish this procedure.
checklistItems.teachingTips: Post-flight debriefs are an oft-neglected part of flight training, even though they are arguably the most important part of the process. Imagine a student in school taking a test and never receiving a grade for her work. Learning would never take place becuase the student would have no broader knowledge of her progress. The same is true in flight training. Start by taking notes on each maneuver or decision. Then guide the pilot through a post-flight briefing by first asking for her feedback, and then adding constructive suggestions on how to move forward and improve.

checklistItems.name: Review and practice before next flight - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Although writing down a postflight analysis will help, reviewing the analysis prior to your next flight will help to make strong connections between what you previously accomplished, and what you are going to do next. Those connections are critical for learning to take place and skill to improve.

commonErrors.name: Not completing the analysis; not being honest with progress.
commonErrors.details: Make a habit of ensuring the student completes the postflight analysis every time, and spend time going over it then, and again prior to the next flight. Many pilots find honest assessment challenging, but it is important to be clear about progress. Doing so helps to mitigate numerous hazard attitudes and keeps the pilot safe on future flights.

commonErrors.name: Not reviewing the plan prior to the next flight.
commonErrors.details: Ask the pilot to recap the previous flight in the brieing of the next flight. These connections are important for learning to occur.

activities.name: [01] Preflight Assessment
activities.what: A preflight procedure in which the pilot, airplane, and environment are evaluated for potential risks.
activities.why: To ensure that the pilot and airplane are in a condition for safe flight.
activities.groundPrep:
"Methods and tools for pilot self assessment (e.g. I'M SAFE, proficiency and currency checks, etc).
How to ensure the airplane is legally airworthy including during the dispatch process (e.g. required inspections, etc)
Use of a checklist or other method to consider how environmental factors like weather, terrain, route selection, and obstructions will affect safety and success of flight.
Assessing external pressures and how they affect pilot decision making.
Development and use of personal minimums."

checklistItems.name: Pilot condition - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Evaluate whether the pilot's qualifications, currency, and proficiency are commensurate with the planned flight.
The IMSAFE memory aide can be useful to check the pilot's physical and mental well being (e.g. Illness, Medication,Stress/Alcohol/Fatigue/Environment).
Assure they have on their person the required documentation--pilot/student license, medical (if required), photo ID.
Must "make available for inspection" required logbook endorsements and entries (current for specific flight operation, Flight Review).
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Questions to be evaluated include:
Pilot experience with this type risk. How long ago? Any training for these conditions?
Risk more complex or different than previous exposure? Is there a backup plan should problems develop?
Stress and fatigue already encountered?
checklistItems.simulator: N/A

checklistItems.name:
Aircraft condition
(Not including preflight inspection) - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Check both required inspections and the physical condition to ensure the aircraft is airworthy. This includes the annual, 100-hour, ELT, transponder, and altimeter inspections as appropriate.
The acronym ARROWPC is helpful in this respect.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Questions to be evaluated include:
All aircraft equipment fully functional?

checklistItems.name: EnVironmental factors - Check
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
The pilot address FAR 91.103... "become familiar with all available information concerning that flight."
Check the airspace you're planning to fly through (or avoid, like TFRs) and be sure that you understand them including the dimensions and operating requriements.
Evlaute the overall conditions including: weather, NOTAMs, winds, runway information, density altitude, fuel planning, aircraft performance including takeoff and landing distances, weight and balance calculations, and anything else that will inform your decision.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Discuss Time-critical Risk Management—a review of an unplanned event during the flight to choose the appropriate course of action.

Some primary risks include—weather, nighttime, different airport environment, mountainous terrain, over-water, desolate, cold/heat.

checklistItems.name: External Factors
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
The pilot must be honest with themselves with respect to their motivation to undertake a flight that presents high risk factors.
Embrace flexibility in your planning and expecations - for both you and your passengers. Rather than taking on a "must get there" mission midset, expect that there will likely be delays or unplanned stops. Consider it part of the adventure. Help everyone involved to understand that flying GA should be thought of as a 90 percent solution. Having this conversation prior to the flight will help remove pressures and allow the pilot to better focus on sound decision making.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
External influences create a sense of pressure to complete a flight—often at the expense of safety.
Factors include: • Someone waiting for the flight’s arrival • The pilot does not want to disappoint • The desire to demonstrate pilot qualifications • The desire to impress • Desire to satisfy a specific personal goal • Emotional pressure associated with Pride.

checklistItems.name: Risk Management Tools - Utilize
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Consider the use of a worksheet to evaluate various risk factors. See the examples of the Preflight Brief, FAA and Civil Air Patrol risk management tools and resources in the Prep section.
checklistItems.teachingTips: One guide in the form of a checklist that helps the pilot examine areas of interest in his or her preflight planning is a framework called PAVE. Elements of PAVE are: Pilot-in-command (PIC), Aircraft EnVironment, and External pressures.

checklistItems.name: CRM - Brief
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Crew Resource Management
- Knock It Off: Anyone can end the flight if they're uncomfortable for any reason
- Positive Control Change: Three-way exchange of the flight controls
- Visual Lookout: All maintain, inform rest of crew of traffic
- Sterile Cockpit: Only operational or instructional conversation in the vicinity of airport
- Crew Responsibilities: Assign

checklistItems.name: Safety - Brief
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
SAFETY
- Hazards to Flight/TFR’s: Check and review
- MOA’s/MTR’s: Review military operations areas and training routes near flight path
- Towers: Review ground based towers that could affect flight
- Airports: Review airports near flight path
- Seatbelts: On while in motion
- No Smoking

checklistItems.name: Emergencies - Brief
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
EMERGENCIES
- T/O Abort: Review causes and procedures
- Engine Failure on T/O: Discuss plan
- Divert: What to do if destination airport is unavailable
- Egress: Procedure for exiting aircraft
- Non-Critical Malfunctions: Plan for how to assess and respond

commonErrors.name: Pilots may fail to consider that the level of acceptable risk varies with their experience factor.
commonErrors.details: Discuss with the pilot Deliberate Risk Management—identify hazards and develop controls for a planned flight in advance—when there's time to methodically make informed risk decisions—to integrate risk control into the flight plan. Hazards should be eliminated or mitigated if possible.

commonErrors.name: Failure to locate and understand the required entries in the aircraft logbook.
commonErrors.details: Show the pilot how to locate and validate the required aircraft inspections and documents. The aircraft provider must have the appropriate aircraft records for the pilot to review. Airworthiness Directives are often a difficult aspect to ferret out. Note to the pilot that ADs may be Recurring/One Time/Not Applicable. Be sure to show the pilot that the POH of AFM is specific to the aircraft serial number.

commonErrors.name: Failure to locate and understand the required entries in the pilot's logbook.
commonErrors.details: Review the pilot's logbook to confirm the required entries. Review the Pilot's personal documentation to confirm its validity.

commonErrors.name: Incorrect assessment of the higher physical and mental demands of flying safely.
commonErrors.details: Inexperienced pilots may treat piloting as similar to driving a car and fail to understand that it is more stressful and therefore requires a healthy body and alert mind. Emphasize to the pilot that the aviating requires them to be more proactive in evaluating their physical and mental state prior to each flight.

commonErrors.name: Allowing external pressures to affect decision making/performance.
commonErrors.details: The pilot may be tempted to allow external pressures such as the inernal compelling force to complete a flight to prove to themselves or others their competence.
