activities.name: [03] Collision Avoidance
activities.what: All pilots must be alert to the potential for midair collision and impending loss of separation.
activities.why: Most midair collision accidents and reported near midair collision incidents occur in good VFR weather conditions and during the hours of daylight.
activities.groundPrep:
Introductory training on Collision Avoidance procedures and why they are performed.
Can explain Collision Avoidance procedures as applicable to solo flight (e.g. pattern and local area) and why they are performed.
Can explain all Collision Avoidance procedures and why they are performed.

checklistItems.name: Windscreen - Clean
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Before flight remove bugs and dirt from the wind screen. Bugs and dirt make it harder to see aircraft, especially when flying near sunset/sunrise into the sun.
checklistItems.simulator: Some simulators have the ability to generate air traffic (either computer controlled or from an online network like Vatsim or Pilot Edge). If equipped, you could use this feature to teach or reinforce collision avoidance procedures like you would in the airplane. If your simulator does not support air traffic, then any training on collision avoidance (if you were to decide to incorporate it in the sim would be limited to procedures like looking before turning or checking final before takeoff and landing. Even with this limitation it's worth having the pilot practice calling out where they would be looking for traffic as a reinforcement of the collision avoidance mindset and procedures.

checklistItems.name: Cockpit - Organize/Secure
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
When done secure the checklist in the kneeboard or side pocket in the cabin. 

Attach GPS devices or other devices that need visibility to the sky in an area that will not block your view.

checklistItems.name: Proper scanning technique - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Air traffic tends to be far away from us and therefore hard to see. Imagine trying to see another car on the highway that is 2 miles away. Look for relative motion to find another aircraft against the background. Set up a pattern to systematically scan your viewing area. Let you eyes pause on a spot for at least 1 second and look for movement. Then move your focus 10 degrees along in your pattern and repeat. Note that traffic at similar altitudes to you will appear just above and below the horizon. 

Use the three fingers rule to help spot relevant traffic. This tip comes from AOPA Premier Partner PilotWorkshops. Most of us tend to look too high or too low for traffic at a distance. In reality, any traffic that is a potential conflict will be within a finger width above to two fingers below the horizon. The next time you get a traffic call (ATC or ADS-B), stretch your arms out in front of you, and put a finger on the horizon, and two fingers below. Your traffic is somewhere behind your fingers. Remove your hand and search the spot.

Caution! If you see an aircraft that has no apparent vertical or horizontal motion to you, it may be on a collision course. Prepare to take evasive action to avoid them.

checklistItems.name:
Before takeoff:
Scan area for landing traffic - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Perform appropriate maneuvers to get a clear view of the approach area. Before taking the runway verify no planes are landing in the opposite direction. 

At airports with multiple runways. If at all possible scan the entire length of any crossing runways and runways sharing approach or departure ends. At airports with parallel runways, ensure any landing plane you see is lined up with the correct runway before taking the runway.

If instructed to line up and wait on a runway. Listen carefully for landing traffic. Query ATC if waiting for longer than a minute.

checklistItems.name: Flight Following - Obtain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Contact ATC for VFR Flight Following. This service is provided on a workload permitting basis and provides an extra set of eyes to help avoid mid-air collisions. 

On initial contact to ATC provide the following information:
Facility Name - Approach, Departure or Center, e.g. Norcal Approach
Tail Number - e.g. Cessna 12345
Position - location relative to an airport, navaid or visual waypoint
Altitude - current altitude
Type - aircraft type (e.g. 172, PA28)
Equipment - /G for GPS equipped, etc.
Request - example: VFR flight following to XYZ airport

Once given a transponder code and inputting the transponder code, continue the flight as planned at appropriate VFR altitudes and desired heading unless directed otherwise by ATC.
checklistItems.teachingTips:
Some ATC facilities prefer a shorter version of initial contact. For these facilities the following is sufficient: 

Name of the approach facility.
Aircraft type/tail number - e.g. Cessna 12345
VFR Request

ATC will then assign a transponder code. Once input ATC will report radar contact and ask for the remaining request. 

Ask pilots who fly in the area which is the preferred method.

checklistItems.name:
Climb out from airport:
Lower nose to clear area - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: After every 1000' of climb lower the nose of the plane briefly and scan for traffic directly ahead and below the aircraft.

checklistItems.name:
Climbs and descents:
Gentle banks to clear area - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Gentle left and right banks during climbs or descents help improve visibility under the nose of the aircraft while changing altitude

checklistItems.name:
Straight and level:
Scan and altitude - Maintain
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Proper altitude—Adhere to the VFR and IFR cruising altitudes that correspond with your magnetic course. For VFR flights above 3,000 feet agl between zero and 179 degrees, fly altitudes of odd thousands plus 500 (e.g., 5,500 feet msl); between 180 and 359 degrees, fly even thousands plus 500 feet (e.g., 4,500 feet msl). For IFR flights between zero and 179 degrees, fly altitudes of odd thousands (e.g., 5,000 feet msl); between 180 and 359 degrees, fly even thousands (e.g., 4,000 feet msl).

VFR flight following—Request ATC radar advisories and flight following service. While only offered on a workload-permitting basis, ATC may provide another set of watchful eyes.

Avoid congested airspace—If VFR, avoid overflying approach fixes and navaids as that airspace can get congested. Also, find out which special use airspace along your route is active such as military operations areas and routes, warning areas, and alert areas.

When flying straight and level for long periods, performing a regular clearing turn can help you see traffic and by changing your profile can help other aircraft see you.

checklistItems.name:
Turns:
Clear before initiating turn - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot: Airplanes have blind spots. Verify that no traffic is in the direction of your turn. In a high wing airplane, briefly raise the wing on the side of your intended turn and check for traffic. In a low wing airplane, briefly lower the wing and clear the area before initiating your turn. Make sure to look around wing struts or other aircraft components that may block your view.

checklistItems.name:
Traffic pattern:
Do not descend into the pattern - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Descend to traffic pattern when well clear of the airport (3-5 miles) to avoid descending onto another aircraft. Enter the pattern when you are safely established at the appropriate pattern altitude. 

Scan for traffic at your altitude, slightly above and below, when approaching the pattern.

Switch to CTAF frequency at least 10 miles out and monitor. Make sure to make accurate radio reports of position in the pattern and intentions. Include altitude in reports if any other aircraft report being near you and also approaching the pattern.

checklistItems.name:
Intersections, VOR sites, GPS Waypoints, Visual Waypoints:
Exercise sustained vigilance and caution - Complete
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
Air traffic converges on navigation fixes like VORs, intersections, GPS waypoints and charted visual waypoints. Pilots need to be extra vigilant in these high traffic areas.

If below 3000' AGL flying a couple hundred feet off the normal VFR cruise altitude for the direction of flight is legal and will put the aircraft where other aircraft most likely are not.

Make sure to do radio calls (on CTAF or contact Tower) when approaching airports over or near popular waypoints.

checklistItems.name: Training Operations: Clearing turns prior to maneuvers - Perform
checklistItems.notesToPilot:
A common technique is to perform two 90 degree turns in opposite directions while clearing the area to the left, right, above, and below. Be sure to concentrate on scanning for traffic and avoid multitasking on other pre-maneuver setup while doing your clearing turns.

Some practice areas have published frequencies. Use those published frequencies to make position and altitude reports.

Even if not using flight following monitor the ATC frequency for the practice area. ATC may call your plane out to other pilots and, thereby, alert you to potential traffic conflicts. This also applies to maneuvers done in areas outside of a towered airport's airspace. The tower controllers will call out traffic to incoming and departing planes (workload permitting) which will create a more complete mental picture of other planes in the area.

commonErrors.name: Failing to perform clearing turns
commonErrors.details:
Failing to perform clearing turns.

Suggestion:
Most training maneuvers require the pilot to turn the plane and climb and descend in what can appear to be random directions. If there are aircraft in the immediate area they will not be able to predict what the pilot will do next. It is also quite common for multiple aircraft to be practicing maneuvers in the same area. As a result it is CRITICAL to clear the area prior to performing any training maneuvers. 

Failing to clear above and below the aircraft in addition to left and right.

Suggestion:
Remind the pilot that your own maneuvers and the maneuvers of other aircraft in the practice area are often not in level flight. Planes can climb or descend into each other easily. Clearing above and below the aircraft is a necessity in addition to left and right.

commonErrors.name: Placing items on top of panel blocking view
commonErrors.details:
Blocking a portion of the view out of the aircraft by putting the checklist or attaching a GPS device in the window.

Suggestion:
Remind the pilot to take no action that will result in reduced visibility outside of the aircraft. While it may be more convenient to put the checklist in the window or suction cup the stratus in front of the pilot to be turned on easily both of these can block the view of an aircraft approaching yours.

commonErrors.name: Failure to verify other traffic
commonErrors.details:
Failing to verify no planes on short final/final before taking the runway.

Suggestion:
Multiple accidents have occurred where a plane landed on a departing plane. The landing plane may have little or NO visibility of the runway on short final. So it is in the pilots best interest to ensure there is no one on final before taking the runway.

Assuming all aircraft are using the same departure runway.

Suggestion:
Remind the pilot that even if the winds are relatively strong and favoring the runway the pilot is about to take, there's a possibility of planes landing with a crosswind or tailwind deliberately (for convenience or crosswind practice) or accidentally. 

Failing to clear crossing runways.

Suggestion:
Emphasize the real possibility of aircraft taking off on a crossing runway without announcement at towered and non towered airports. Before starting a take off roll on a runway with a crossing runway, make sure to verbally announce "crossing runway clear".

Abdicating PIC responsibility to ATC and taking an action that would put the plane at risk.

Suggestion:
Recall controllers can make mistakes too. The pilot is ultimately responsible for the safety of the flight. Do not take a runway if not 100% sure there will be no conflict.

commonErrors.name: Turning blindly w/o checking for traffic
commonErrors.details:
Turning blindly without checking for traffic.

Suggestion:
Just like looking both ways before crossing the street the pilot should always look before turning. Because of aircraft blind spots this "look" must be more than just a turn of the head. The plane needs to be maneuvered to remove physical obstructions to the pilots view before starting the turn. Be sure to incorporate this into training right from the first flight so that the pilot learns this as a standard procedure before every turn.

commonErrors.name: Not cleaning the windshield
commonErrors.details:
Failing to remove bugs / dirt from the windscreen as part of the preflight procedure.

Suggestion:
Remind the pilot, a plane on a collision course with yours at a distance is often no bigger visually than a large bug smear on the window. The pilot needs to see aircraft as soon as possible to be able to avoid that aircraft. Even two 172s have a closing speed of 200 kts when on a head on collision course.
